News.title: Met Office issues yellow ice warning as freezing rain set to fall near major cities – & more cold expected over weekend
News.content:
BRRRRITAIN Met Office issues yellow ice warning as freezing rain set to fall near major cities – & more cold expected over weekend







Next

A YELLOW weather warning has been issued for parts of England over icy conditions as the country is hit by freezing rain overnight.

Brits can expect plummeting temperatures into the weekend as major cities reach 1C following -10.6C conditions in Scotland last week.



The Met Office has issued the yellow weather warning between 4am and 2pm today.

It has warned that freezing rain could leave roads and pavements icy, particularly on higher routes across the Pennines.



Up to 3cm of snow is also possible in these parts, the warning states.

Forecasters warn of a small chance of road closures, public transport disruption and injuries from slips and falls.



FIVE-DAY FORECAST Today:

– The rain and winds ease, with a legacy of cloud through much of Great Britain. To the west, sunny spells. Temperatures recovering in the south, but overnight frost further north. Outlook for Saturday to Monday:

– Saturday is expected to be wet and breezy for most, with a brighter showery interlude on Sunday before more rain bands sweep through on Monday. Starting to feel milder later.

Heavy rain will then sweep eastwards later today and could turn to snow over higher ground in northern England and Scotland, forecasters say.

A number of major UK cities are also forecast to see snow in the early hours of this morning according to the Met Office.

Conditions in parts of the country will begin to get snowy at around 6am before easing by 10am – no snow is forecast after 2pm.



Nottingham, Leicester, Loughborough and Sheffield will begin to see snowy conditions at 6:15am, according to maps, before snow moves more north.

By 7am, parts of Yorkshire including Leeds, Bradford and Harrogate are amongst locations anticipating snow, narrowly missing out Manchester.

Moving into the morning, parts of Durham, the Lake District, Ripon and Leyburn in Yorkshire will see snow, including central Scotland.



Cumbria should expect to see snow up until around lunchtime today, before conditions disperse and the weather gets drier.

And, chilly conditions are expected to continue long into the weekend as light showers make their way across the country.

Saturday is expected to be wet and breezy for most across the UK, with a brighter showery interlude expected on Sunday.

More rain will then sweep through on Monday before temperatures start to feel milder.

Met Office meteorologist Honor Criswick said: “The cold is here to stay over the coming days.



“Not only this, but it’s set to be rather unsettled at times, with heavy outbreaks of rain, possibly even some hill snow.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

She added: “Also, a chance we could see some freezing rain toward high ground in northern England.

“This can lead to some slippery surfaces, so do take care if you’re out and about early first thing on Friday.”

News.title: Burnham is deceiving the public with EU reset – here’s 8 reasons we can’t trust Andy on Brexit
News.content:
Next

NUMBER Ten would have us believe there is nothing out of the ordinary here, just a simple deal to make ­relations with the EU easier.

In truth, the PM’s EU reset bill is the road map to rejoin, and it leaves taxpayers with a whopping great bill they never voted for, which starts now and will only rise in the future — to £750million a week once we are back in.



Andy Burnham is deceiving the public.

At the Makerfield by-election in June he asked the people there for their votes on a promise not to undo Brexit, and he keeps telling us that his deal passes his own Makerfield test — yet the legislation he has now published fails it outright.



As documents published yesterday show, it authorises “any expenditure” arising from any partnership treaty with Brussels, with no limit on the amount or on what the money can be spent on.

That is an open cheque, signed by the Prime Minister and drawn on the account of every UK taxpayer.

The cheque covers treaties that have not yet been written. Ministers can bring further EU agreements within its scope by Order in Council, without another Act of Parliament, and the money follows automatically.

MPs are being asked to sign off deals they have never seen, at a price nobody in the Government will name, and the same legislation lets ministers put EU rules on our statute book without a vote.

This is how the Prime Minister means to take us back in, by moving us closer and closer to Brussels, step by step, with each step making the next one easier and going back harder — until the day he tells us we are following so many of their rules and paying so much into their budgets that we might as well rejoin.

Burnham has said he wants Britain back in the EU in his lifetime despite his empty promises to Makerfield.



He is now ready to do exactly that, by giving them our money, which should be going on the cost of living and the NHS. We must stop him.

Here are eight reasons why you can’t trust Burnham on Brexit . . .

1. HE told Makerfield voters he was not proposing to rejoin the EU.



Makerfield, May 18: He said he respected the decision made at the referendum.

Then on September 30 he said Britain “could go all the way”, and when asked about an in-out referendum in Labour’s next manifesto, he replied: “Yes, things are possible.”

2. HE was adamant that Britain should not re-open the Brexit wars.

Andy Burnham, Makerfield, May 18: “The last thing we should do right now is re-run those arguments.”

This week he said that six former Prime Ministers who warned him against reopening the Brexit debate were “stuck in the past”.



3. IN October he told MPs that his position is “entirely consistent” with the Makerfield by-election.

Since then he has listed full membership as an option, said a referendum is possible and reopened the question of EU migration.

4. HE said in Dec 2016, when he was last an MP, that open borders with the EU had been defeated at the ballot box. Now he is up for a debate.



The Sunday Times, October 2026: “I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”

5. ON November 18 he said the EU reset deal passed his “Makerfield test” two days before there was a deal.

It was not agreed until November 20, and on the eve of the summit the EU’s demand on tuition fees for its students was still open.

He set the test, marked it and passed it himself before the result even existed.

6. HE said Brexit is “the reason” for the small boats shambles.



On Good Morning Britain in October he said: “The reason the small boats crisis has arisen is because we can’t return people.”

Arrivals rose from 299 in 2018 to 8,466 in 2020 while the EU returns rules still applied to Britain. In 2019 Britain sent 263 people back under those rules and took in 714.

7. HE said Britain has lost the control of immigration it once had.

Inside the EU, Britain could not limit migration from the EU at all. Since 2021 it has set every visa route itself.

Yesterday, figures showed net migration down to its lowest level since 1997 — somethng only possible because of Brexit allowing us to limit visa numbers.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

8. HE called his EU reset deal a “£17billion boost”.

Stay Out puts the cost at up to £3billion a year. The Treasury figure is up to 0.5 per cent of GDP by 2040, and the main measures do not start until 2028.

News.title: Iranian woman, 21, sentenced to death after being forced to ‘confess’ or watch her sister be raped by barbaric regime
News.content:
VILE TORTURE Iranian woman, 21, sentenced to death after being forced to ‘confess’ or watch her sister be raped by barbaric regime







Next

AN Iranian woman has been sentenced to death after making a forced confession as IRGC guards threatened to rape her twin in front of her.

Taraneh Rahimi, 21, has been left unable to walk properly after enduring weeks of brutal beatings on death row in Iran.



The young woman and her twin sister Romina were arrested after taking part in the anti-government protests that engulfed the nation in January.

Imprisoned in the notoriously abusiveIranian jail, Taraneh has developed a severe ear infection from an untreated head injury that is now affecting her balance, her cousin reveals.



The young detainee is “keeping her spirits up” but “there are days she breaks down in tears,” Masoud Nourmohammadi told BBC News Persian.

Both sisters were visited in jail by their mother, who was horrified to see their battered faces, skin-bare scalps, and barely audible voices.



While Romina was spared the death penalty, her twin sister is one of six women sentenced to death over January’s protests, according to the UN’s human rights rapporteur for Iran, Mai Sato.

The sisters’ lawyers have reportedly submitted a complaint alleging they were tortured and sexually abused during interrogation.



But the investigation into their claims are being overseen by one of the very officials they accuse of torture.

The young women were still in high school when they were snatched from their beds by the IRGC in February.

Romina has been given a 25-year prison sentence.

Taraneh has been sentenced to death for her participation in the demonstrations, with her forced statements reportedly used as the primary evidence in the trial.

She reportedly confessed under the threat that her sister would be raped in front of her if she refused.



Amnesty International called the charges against the twins “politically motivated”.

While as men bear the brunt, the Islamic Republic is increasingly handing down death sentences to women protesters at a rate not witnessed in decades.

Earlier this week an Iranian singer received 74 lashes after she performed without a hijab.

Parastoo Ahmadi, 29, was branded “obscene and vulgar” by the warped Iranian regime following a 2024 performance at the at the historic Deir-e Gachin Caravanserai.

The singer and four crew members were flogged in Qom on Monday in what human rights groups have called a “crime against humanity”.



They were officially charged with offending public decency by producing and publishing obscene and immoral content online.

As well as the lashing, the group of five were sentenced to a two-year ban on artistic and musical activity plus a two-year travel ban.

Violence against women is running rampant in Iran.

On November 18, Sadaf Haghbin, 23, was shot dead at her own birthday party in the northern province of Gilan.

Her former boyfriend was reportedly behind the killing after she refused to marry him, according to Iranian news outlet Khabaronline.



Just days earlier, the body of 16-year-old schoolgirl Sogand Sayyadi was discovered in the courtyard of her apartment block in Kermanshah.

The youngster had desperately warned school staff that her father would hurt or even kill her if she was sent home with him.

Her dad, Kioumars Sayyadi, had allegedly been summoned to the school after staff discovered she was in contact with a prospective suitor he disapproved of.

He allegedly battered his daughter in front of horrified classmates and teachers.

The vicious assault reportedly continued outside the school, where he repeatedly slammed her head against a wall.



More recently a pregnant Iranian teen was allegedly murdered by her own parents after the forced her to swallow dozens of pills before beating and suffocating her.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Helia Fattahi, 19, had told her family just days earlier that she was two months pregnant following a relationship with a young man.

Human rights groups Hengaw and Hana have branded the teenager’s death a so-called “honour” killing.

News.title: Hero Ukrainian gymnast, 10, who lost leg in Russian missile strike dreams of Paralympic glory
News.content:
Next

HERO gymnast Sasha Paskal, 10, takes a big step closer to her Olympic dream after losing a leg in a Russian missile strike in Ukraine.

War survivor Sasha told children “don’t be afraid and follow your goals” on an inspirational visit to London.



She said: “Don’t be afraid, don’t be negative. You have to always follow your goals.”

She added: “My dream is to go to the Paralympics in Brisbane in 2032 and compete in gymnastics for Ukraine.”



A split second changed Sasha’s childhood when a missile hit yards from where she was walking when she was only six years old.

She told The Sun: “I will never forget the moment it happened. I was walking outside with my mother when a missile hit the building next to us and I was trapped under concrete and rubble. It was so painful.”

Doctors were unable to save her leg but she was walking within a month after it was surgically amputated in 2022.

A few weeks later she was dancing again.

Sasha visited London as a guest of the Rinat Akhmetov Foundation, a charity founded by Ukraine’s richest man, which has also bought her family a car and a home.

Sasha said: “Our car was destroyed by the same missile strike. We use the car all the time to get from home to gymnastics training.”



The Ukrainian billionaire Akhmetov owns Ukraine’s Shakhtar Donetsk football club.

They borrowed Chelsea’s Stamford Bridge ground on Wednesday as their home ground was captured by Russia in 2014.

Sasha said her favourite sights were Big Ben, Tower Bridge and the legendary Harry Potter platform 9 and 3/4 at Kings Cross Station.



Asked if she had a message for tyrant Putin, Sasha said: “I would ask him to stop this war.”

News.title: Labour should stop celebrating falling migration when fed-up Brits are fleeing the country
News.content:
British exodus







Next

LABOUR ministers are patting themselves on the back over net migration tumbling to a 30-year low.

It’s welcome news that the headline figure has finally dipped below 100,000.



But look behind the spin and you’ll see the drop is largely down to fed-up Brits packing their bags for a better life abroad.

Official figures show 137,000 fewer British nationals living here, replaced by 258,000 non-Europeans – plus 68,000 asylum seekers.



Meanwhile, any modest fall in new arrivals owes far more to the tough visa reforms rushed through by Rishi Sunak’s Tories before Labour won power.

The reason the Government was able to do this?

The Brexit vote Andy Burnham is desperate to reverse.

Don’t expect the numbers to stay low in the long-term, either.

Under his so-called “reset” deal, the figures will be swelled by 100,000 Europeans aged up to 31 who are taking advantage of the PM’s “youth experience scheme”.

Cost of Brussels

ANDY Burnham boasts his Brexit reset will save Britain cash — yet he’s keeping quiet about the eye-watering bill.



The true price of the PM’s cosy Brussels love-in will sting taxpayers for tens of millions of pounds for the privilege of accepting their rules.

Before Eurocrats lift a single border check on our food and drink exports, we’ll be forced to cough up a massive surcharge.

Not content with surrendering our right to set our own food laws, Burnham has signed a blank cheque ­— committing Britain to member-style “operational contributions” plus a four per cent added fee for not being an EU member state.

Burnham laughingly calls handing power back to Brussels the “Cutting Costs Bill”.

It’s no joke when food producers warn it won’t save consumers a penny.



No remorse

SHAMELESS paedophile Huw Edwards clearly has no remorse.

Most people convicted of crimes as sickening as his would hang their heads in shame, keep a low profile and spend the rest of their lives trying to atone.

But not Edwards. Instead of hiding away in disgrace, the former TV newscaster will spend an hour whingeing about his “fall from grace”… back on prime-time TV.

This is a predator who dodged jail in 2024 despite hoarding 41 vile child abuse images, including ones of kids as young as seven.

He hasn’t had the decency to pay back the £200,000 in BBC salary he pocketed after his arrest.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Yet he has the breathtaking arrogance to appear before Channel 4 cameras from rural Wales, and moan about HIS “difficulties”.

Viewers will see through this self-pitying attempt to rebuild his reputation.

News.title: Why is Black Friday called Black Friday? Everything you need to know about the shopping bonanza
News.content:
Next

BLACK Friday is almost upon us once again, with Brits ready to flock to stores for Christmas bargains.

The history of the term has long been disputed though, here, we explain what it’s all about.

Why is Black Friday called Black Friday?

The story behind the name Black Friday is disputed.



Some say that the day is so named as it is the day retailers “move into the black”, meaning they can cover their costs through the years whilst also slashing prices for the sales.



Historically, in UK Black Friday referred to the Friday before Christmas, when extra pressure was put on the police and emergency services, due to festive celebrations.

But since 2014, Black Friday has come to refer to the massive shopping sales event.

Black Friday always falls on the Friday following the Thanksgiving holiday in the USA, and is considered of the Christmas shopping season.



Now, in the UK, retailers including Amazon, John Lewis, and Sainsbury’s offer discounts on Black Friday.

What is Black Friday?

In a bid to attract shoppers in the run-up to Christmas, retailers offer majorly discounted prices on products, throughout the Black Friday weekend.

However, Black Friday has grown into a two-week shopping event, as retailers compete to attract customers.

Many deals will be available online, so shoppers can avoid the long lines and crowded high-streets.



Most Brits shop for Black Friday bargains online, but some prefer to visit physical shops.

This has previously caused chaos on shop floors.

News.title: Labour’s 1.5million homes pledge branded ‘fantasy’ as housebuilding hits ten-year low
News.content:
Next

LABOUR’s housing pledge was branded a “fantasy” last night as the number of new homes fell to a ten-year low.

Just 203,690 homes were added to England’s housing stock in 2025/26 – down two per cent on the previous year, official figures show.



It deals a fresh blow to Labour’s promise to deliver 1.5 million new homes by the end of this Parliament.

Some 300,000 homes a year would need to be delivered on average to hit the target.



Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has already admitted there is only a slim chance of meeting the pledge amid rising construction costs and the fallout from the Iran war.

Sam Richards, of campaign group Britain Remade, said the target was “looking like a fantasy”, adding: “Ministers cannot hide behind global events as an excuse for their failure to deliver.”



A Housing Department spokesman insisted the Government was “not giving up” on its target.

Prices of new-build homes will be slashed by up to £50,000 through a proposed Tory war on red tape.

Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith is vowing a blitz on bureaucracy and Net Zero regulations to halt low growth.

Proposals also include backing a third Heathrow runway and scrapping a £1.5billion grocery packaging tax to ease the cost of the weekly shop.



Mr Griffith said: “No one else is coming to save our economy. Only we can inject reality, tell the hard truths and make this a country we are proud to hand on to the next generation.”

The £50,000 price cut for new builds will partly come from scrapping rules such as the Future Homes Standard on reducing carbon emissions.

They make developers include low-carbon technology, such as heat pumps or district heat networks.

News.title: ‘Loud boom’ heard as flight declares emergency over Scotland and emergency crews race to Edinburgh Airport
News.content:
Next

A SCOTTISH flight declared an emergency after a deafening bang was heard above a major city.

An EasyJet plane bound for Gatwick left Edinburgh at around 9pm on Thursday night, but shortly after take-off, local residents reported hearing a loud ‘explosion’ overhead.



It is understood the sound, captured on doorbell camera footage which has been shared across social media, indicated an engine failure.

The Airbus A321neo issued a 7700squawk notice, which is code for a general emergency, not long after leaving the ground, as it was approaching Livingston.



The Aircraft Communications Addressing and Reporting System (ACARS) issued warnings of an engine stall and high exhaust gas temperatures.

The plane’s left engine was reportedly shut down when the aircraft remained at around 5,000 feet.

Emergency crews, including cops and fire crews rushed to the area, and sealed off several roads.

The aircraft circled the area several times before landing safely at Edinburgh Airport.

An EasyJet spokesperson said: “Flight EZY816 from Edinburgh to London Gatwick was required to return to Edinburgh due to a technical issue.

“The flight landed normally and was met by emergency services in line with procedures and a precautionary measure only.



“A replacement aircraft has been arranged to operate the flight to London Gatwick this evening.

“The safety and wellbeing of customers and crew is always easyJet’s highest priority and easyJet operates its fleet of aircraft in strict compliance with manufacturers’ guidelines.”

News.title: Meghan Markle’s Christmas menu with sweet handwritten note to guests revealed
News.content:
Meghan Markle’s Christmas menu with sweet handwritten note to guests revealed

In a new foodie magazine feature, Meghan has revealed what she likes to have on the menu for guests over the festive season, and the 'little touches' that can make celebrations feel all the most special

View 4 Images Meghan Markle in 'With Love, Meghan: Holiday Celebration' which aired on Netflix in 2025 (Image: Jake Rosenberg/Netflix)

Meghan Markle has shared details of her Christmas preparations as she, Prince Harry, and their children are due to spend their festive festive season back in the UK in more than six years.

‌



‌



The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have spent the last six years living in the United States after leaving their working royal roles in 2020.

‌



In an upcoming foodie magazine feature, Meghan has revealed what she likes to have on the menu for guests over the festive season, and the 'little touches' that can make celebrations feel all the most special.

‌



The Duchess said she stocks the kitchen with breakfast provisions such as bagels, berries, yogurt, smoked salmon, and capers. She then leaves a handwritten note inviting them to help themselves.

And when she's the guest, rather than host, she enjoys creating homemade treats as a sweet thank you, like a batch of honey-roasted spiced nuts or a blackberry pound cake that can double as breakfast the following morning.

View 4 Images The With Love, Meghan Christmas special on Netflix from 2025 (Image: Netflix)

‌



The Duchess doesn't scrimp on presentation either, as she says using a little kitchen twine, a length of ribbon, or a sprig of rosemary to decorate the gift can add a crucial thoughtful touch.

‌



The upcoming winter issue of Bon Appétit features her recipes, with Meghan telling the magazine: “I still believe little touches are all you need to make something ordinary feel special, especially when you're having loved ones over.”

She adds: “It doesn't have to be over the top.”

‌



Meghan added that she likes to lay the table a day in advance, freeing herself up to actually enjoy the company of her guests when they arrive.

For anyone staying with her overnight, she says she likes to programme the coffee machine to brew before they wake up so they can rise to the smell of freshly brewed coffee, reports Vogue on the magazine feature .

‌



View 4 Images Meghan in a promo for her As Ever brand's Christmas collection (Image: As Ever)

For those who didn't catch last year's Christmas instalment of the Duchess's Netflix show, With Love, Meghan, the special episode saw her making personalized advent calendars for her children. She also decorating her Christmas tree with slices of fig, and preparing cacio e pepe gougères with restaurateur Will Guidara.

‌



Her companion lifestyle brand, As Ever, has leaned further into the art of gifting, too. Earlier this autumn, Meghan marked the launch of its latest holiday collection with a sweet video of her five-year-old daughter, Princess Lilibet, helping her make raspberry jam.

Rumours were circulating that they would be heading back to the states for Christmas and were planning to spend the season with Meghan’s mother, Doria Ragland.

‌



View 4 Images Meghan Markle admires her Christmas advent calendar (Image: @aseverofficial/instagram)

‌



However, now, the pair look set to spend Christmas in the Cotswolds, with Doria flying over to Britain instead, reports say.

A source reportedly said Meghan wants to keep things simple after their big relocation and her father's recent arrest.

‌



The Sussexes plan to spend Thanksgiving and Christmas in the Cotswolds with Meghan's mother, reports Marie Claire.

Meghan’s father, Thomas Markle Sr was arrested and charged with one count of possession of child pornography. Meghan made a statement addressing the allegations against her father.

‌



Thomas Markle Sr has denied any wrongdoing. An insider told People that the Duchess wants a stress-free holiday season.

The source reportedly added: “Traveling back and forth would be too much for everyone.”

They said: “She [Meghan] doesn’t want to add any more pressure right now.”

Article continues below

Meghan and Harry’s young children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet have also had to adapt to the move across the pond.

The young children have both started at British schools and Prince Harry has spoken about how his children are adapting to the culture change after living the vast majority of their young lives in America.

News.title: High-speed ferry crashes in Hong Kong with dozens injured
News.content:
High-speed ferry crashes in Hong Kong with dozens injured

Authorities are continuing rescue efforts in Hong Kong, after a ferry bound for Shenzhen crashed into a floating dry dock, injuring more than 20 people

View Image The ferry which crashed into the Hong Kong dry dock

Two dozen people have been injured after a high-speed ferry collided with a floating dock in Hong Kong, police said. Four of the injured are in a serious condition.

‌



‌



Hong Kong Police said the incident took place at 9:25am local time on Friday morning (November 27). It’s thought the passenger ferry hit the floating dry dock near the Tsing Yi oil depot, reports the South China Morning Post.

‌



Reports suggest 15 ambulances were sent to the scene, and emergency workers are continuing to rescue efforts as of 12:15pm local time. Injured passengers were taken to land before being sent to Princess Margaret Hospital and Yan Chai Hospital, a spokesperson for the Hong Kong government added.

‌



The ferry had left Sheung Wan and was bound for Shekou, in Shenzhen, HK01 news also reported. After the crash, the boat was towed away.

Hong Kong was a British territory until 1997, when it became a special administrative region of China.

News.title: Tributes to 'sweet' mum, 38 who died after 'walking into plane propeller'
News.content:
Tributes to 'sweet' mum, 38 who died after 'walking into plane propeller'

Despite emergency service attempts to save her life, the 'kindest' and 'sweet' Christina Blake was declared dead at the scene at just 38 after she 'walked into the airplane’s propeller while it was stationary'

View 3 Images Christina Blake died Tuesday after walking into a plane’s propeller blades (Image: Katherine Faye/Facebook)

A " sweet sister" and mum-of-two died after walking into a plane propeller at an airport, leading to an outpouring of grief and touching tributes after her horrific death.

‌



‌



Family members have remembered her as having "the biggest heart" as they say her death was a "terrible way to go".

‌



Christina Blake, 38, walked into the propeller of a Taylorcraft F19 aircraft that had landed just before 5pm on Tuesday at Big Lake Airport in South Central Alaska, the New York Post reports.

‌



Christina had been driving a vehicle on the airport taxiway as the single-engine aircraft landed.

View 3 Images Christina Blake has been remembered as a ‘sweet sister’ (Image: Katherine Faye/Facebook)

“While the plane was stopped and waiting for the vehicle to move off the taxiway, Blake exited the vehicle, approached the running aircraft, and walked into the airplane’s propeller while it was stationary,” Alaska State Troopers said.

‌



“Despite lifesaving efforts by first responders, the female was declared deceased at the scene.”

Blake had gestured towards the pilot of the aircraft before walking into the propeller, Department of Public Safety spokesman Austin McDaniel told Anchorage Daily News.

‌



View 3 Images Katherine Faye posted tribute photos of her and sisters Christina Blake (Image: Katherine Faye/Facebook)

However, Blake does not appear to have links to the airport or the pilot, McDaniel added, and troopers do not believe she intentionally walked into the blades.

‌



McDaniel added that the pilot had switched off the engine to try to stop the propeller as Blake headed towards the aircraft.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

‌



“You will always be in my heart sweet sister of mine,” Katherine Faye wrote on Facebook with heartwarming photos of her sibling. “Give mom and grandma a hug for me, I’ll be with you all one day.”

The pictures show the duo growing up over the years, having fun on trips and embracing loved ones.

‌



Christina's aunt, Laura Blake, has said that her niece was a mum-of-two with a “big heart.”

“She was the kindest and had a big heart,” she said. “She was just always really sweet.”

Article continues below

Speaking of her niece’s horrific death, the heartbroken aunt said, “It’s really tragic, that’s a terrible way to go.”

News.title: Zelensky questions Trump's 'strange' friendship with Putin after bizarre change to NATO statement
News.content:
Zelensky questions Trump's 'strange' friendship with Putin after bizarre change to NATO statement

Donald Trump has repeatedly boasted that Vladimir Putin is his "friend". He has even gone as far as changing a joint statement with NATO to include blame on Ukraine.

View 5 Images Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump have not always seen eye-to-eye (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has questioned Donald Trump's relationship with Russian leader Vladimir Putin after the US President made a bizarre change to his statement from a meeting with NATO leaders.

‌



‌



Last week, Trump boasted that Putin was his "friend" in a remarkable exchange with the Russian president on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China. Trump appeared to be in beaming as he entered a room and spotted Putin waiting for him on November 20. Pointing towards Putin, Trump said: "Who's he? He's my friend." The pair then burst into laughter.

‌



Trump continued his flattery in a post on Truth Social on Saturday, again describing his Russian counterpart as "my friend".

‌



View 5 Images Trump and Putin met on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China (Image: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Pool Sputni)

In response, Zelensky told the BBC in an interview: "Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange."

Zelenskyy continued: "He [Putin] is an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be."

‌



The Ukrainian leader's comments come after Trump sprung a surprise on NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte after the two met in Florida as part of the latest push to end the war between Ukraine and Russia.

View 5 Images Zelenskyy questioned Trump's relationship with Putin during an interview (Image: BBC)

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

Following the Wednesday meeting, the men said they had "discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible," as per a joint statement shared by both the White House and NATO.

‌



Trump subsequently took to Truth Social to change the statement to read as "Russia and Ukraine" must avoid such actions.

View 5 Images Rutte and Trump have met several times this year (file image) (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



A NATO official told Politico that the original missive was the officially agreed statement between the two sides, signalling Trump had later amended the statement unilaterally.

Trump has long boasted he could quickly broker an end to war, but has so far been unsuccessful. Now, tensions appear to be heating up between Trump and Zelenskyy.

‌



Last month, Trump claimed that Russia "has been fine on Ukraine" and blamed his Ukrainian counterpart for the increasing death toll in the war. He also suggested he would be open to attending a summit on the conflict without Kyiv representatives and told reporters at the time: "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much."

View 5 Images In the past, Zelensky said he had been "betrayed" by Trump (Image: BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI, AFP via Getty Images)

Article continues below

Zelensky has also gone as far as saying he had been "betrayed" by Trump after a key part of his country's defences against Russia went down last month. He claimed that Trump and his ally Elon Musk deliberately blocked Ukraine's access to Starlink overnight after the Ukrainian military faced slowdowns in speed and put the country at risk of Russian attacks.

Earlier this month, Trump also teased a "big agreement" with Vladimir Putin after White House meeting on the war. Mr Trump met at the White House with a Russian envoy who was on the premises for an event with First Lady Melania Trump at the time. He did not meet with visiting Ukrainian officials who also were on hand.

News.title: Burnham bounce continues as Labour secure 'huge' red wall by-election victory
News.content:
Burnham bounce continues as Labour secure 'huge' red wall by-election victory

Labour has claimed a big win in Harpurhey following the sad passing of Pat Karney, holding on to the north Manchester seat with comfortable by-election victory.

View 2 Images The Burnham bounce appears real in the north (Image: NurPhoto, NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Labour has beaten Reform in a red wall by-election by a 'huge margin'. The party defended a council seat in Manchester with a 'resounding victory'.

‌



‌



Labour 'took a kicking' in May's council elections, haemorrhaging seats to the Greens and Reform UK. However, Andy Burnham coming in as Prime Minister appears to have improved the party's fortunes in traditionally Labour-voting areas as Thursday night's (November 26) win was its third Greater Manchester by-election victory in a matter of weeks.

‌



The vote in Harpurhey was triggered by the death off former Councillor Pat Karney aged 78 last month who served the area for nearly 50 years. Abdul Sarfraz, 26, won the race comfortably, reports the Manchester Evening News.

‌



The Labour man collected 1,016 votes, far ahead of Reform UK's candidate Ian Carter in second with 366. Manchester council leader Garry Bridges said it was a 'huge' and 'resounding' victory for Labour.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

‌



He said: "This by-election was called after the really sad loss of Pat Karney, he was such a giant of Manchester politics and of Labour politics in the city for so long, and we really wanted to do him proud and keep his legacy going. People have really started to come back to Labour in big numbers and it's a massive vote of confidence in us in the city.

View 2 Images New Harpurhey Councillor Abdul Sarfraz, 26, for Labour (Image: LDRS)

‌



"Last May was really tough and to be honest Labour deserved a bit of a kicking and it got one, and it took the message loud and clear about what needed to change, and it started to change straight away. It just shows if you offer people hope and something exciting they want to believe in, that things can be better, then they will vote for it."

Coun Sarfraz said his top priorities include 'being visible in the area' and listening to what matters to people. Harpurhey is one of Manchester's most deprived neighbourhoods.

Article continues below

A recent report by Manchester council revealed that children born to families in the area and other deprived communities can expect to live up to eight years less than kids born to families in the city's most affluent corners. Cllr Sarfraz said Manchester Labour are 'tackling' the housing crisis, and are 'taking steps to solve homelessness' in the city.

Labour are comfortably in control of Manchester council as it stands, with 63 seats. The Greens are the biggest opposition group at the town hall with 21 councillors, next to seven Reform UK members, four Lib Dems, and one independent.

News.title: Devastating tribute to Mississippi plane crash victims who were flying home for Thanksgiving
News.content:
Devastating tribute to Mississippi plane crash victims who were flying home for Thanksgiving

The rest of their families have issued a heartbreaking tribute saying 'they died doing what they loved: celebrating the start of a wonderful holiday season with a fishing trip together, before heading home to be with the rest of our family'

View 3 Images Michael Knox, Arlyn Knox, Charles Holden Knox, and Truett Knox pose for a photo. They were among six victims killed in a plane crash near Horn Island. (Image: Facebook / Arlyn Knox)

A heartbreaking tribute has been shared to the six family members who all died in a Mississippi plane crash as they were flying home from a fishing trip to be with their loved ones for Thanksgiving.

‌



‌



Pilot Brent Stokes, 50, received a warning from an air traffic controller that he was facing treacherous weather conditions before his plane, carrying his entire family, fatally plummeted into the sea near Horn Island on Tuesday afternoon.

‌



The father was piloting a single-engine Cessna 210L, with his son Hunter Stokes, 16, sister Arlyn Knox, 43, brother-in-law Michael Knox, 43, and their sons Charles Holden Knox, 12, and Truett Knox, 10, onboard. All of them tragically died in the crash.

‌



Brent received a warning from air traffic control of heavy rains and adverse weather as he piloted the aircraft over the coast.

Officials said the pilot did not report any issues when he took off from New Orleans and never made a distress call, the Daily Mail has reported. But officials added that he was warned of 'precipitation and adverse weather in the area' by an air traffic controller at Gulfport-Biloxi International Airport moments before the crash.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

‌



View 3 Images Michael Knox, left, Arlyn Knox, Charles Holden Knox and Truett Knox have now been identified as among those killed in a plane crash near Horn Island (Image: Facebook / Arlyn Knox)

Brent was the president of a marine contracting company based in Fort Myers, continue the Daily Mail. According to the firm's website, he was an 'avid fisherman and life time boater.'

‌



Arlyn and Michael Knox, meanwhile, were the founders of Knox Technologies, a Fort Myers-based IT firm they set up in 2012.

A statement released by their families on Wednesday read: "They died doing what they loved: celebrating the start of a wonderful holiday season with a fishing trip together, before heading home to be with the rest of our family.

‌



"In the middle of our grief, we are holding on to that, and to how much love they gave us and how much love surrounds us now. We will carry them with us always."

Turning Point USA, a conservative youth organisation founded by political and media figure Charlie Kirk, said it was 'heartbroken' by the death of Hunter Stokes, who it described as the president of its Fort Myers High School chapter.

‌



The Mail reports that the organisation posted a statement on X, saying: "Hunter was a young patriot who loved his country and led by example."

The Knox boys both attended St. Francis Xavier Catholic School. Its principal John Gulley said following the families' deaths: "These children and their family have been a part of the St. Francis Xavier Catholic School community for several generations, and their loss will be irreplaceable.

‌



"As a community and a school, we will endeavour to honour their memory and cherish their lives by continuing to "Be Like Christ" to one another every day and never forget the light and love they shared with us.'

"In this time of Thanksgiving, we pray with thanks for our loved ones, and we pray for those suffering and processing this tragic loss," Gulley added.

‌



View 3 Images Michael Knox, left, and Arlyn Knox are among six family members killed when their plane crashed off the Mississippi coast. (Image: Facebook / Arlyn Knox)

Investigators say the plane left New Orleans Lakefront Airport in Louisiana just after 2pm and was headed toward Florida when it lost contact with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) at around 3.45pm.

‌



According to FlightRadar24, it was scheduled to land just before 7pm at Fort Myers Page Field Airport.

The FAA said that the plane began falling at around 10,000ft per minute roughly 30 minutes into the flight.

‌



About two hours later, the US Coast Guard confirmed that it found multiple pieces of debris, including the plane cabin, three life jackets and a life raft near Horn Island, but there were no signs of the passengers.

The search concluded 'when divers from the Mississippi Department of Marine Resources (MDMR) located the remains of all six individuals within the fuselage of the aircraft.'

Article continues below

The National Transportation Safety Board is leading the investigation into the cause of the crash, with the FAA assisting.

According to FAA data, the Cessna was owned by a Cape Coral-based company called EAB Services LLC.

News.title: Britain’s favourite Christmas carol named as much-loved 19th century ballad
News.content:
Britain’s favourite Christmas carol named as much-loved 19th century ballad

Silent Night took 42% in a nationwide poll about Christmas carols with O Come, All Ye Faithful in second place with 25%, butthe survey found the tradition of carol singing has declined

View Image A group of friends sing Christmas carols (Image: Trinity Mirror)

Silent Night is Britain’s favourite Christmas carol, a survey has found.

‌



‌



The 19th century ballad took 42% in a nationwide poll with O Come, All Ye Faithful in second place with 25%.

‌



The survey also found eight in 10 of us believe carol singing has declined in recent years. Of the 2,015 participants in the Postcode Lottery study, 65% wanted to see more carol singers on their street.

‌



Almost six in 10 (57%) said they still prefer traditional carols to festive pop songs from artists such as Wham!, Slade and Mariah Carey. Away in a Manger and Hark! The Herald Angels Sing both brought in 23% of the carols’ vote share.

UK weather maps show exact time snow is forecast tomorrow amid -2C cold snap READ MORE :

Heartwarming story behind couple's spectacular Christmas lights display READ MORE :

Legend has it Silent Night was written to replace a midnight mass after mice had put a church organ out of action by nibbling through the bellows at St Nicholas Church in Obendorf, Austria, and was first performed on Christmas Eve in 1818.

‌



With no time to fix the organ, priest Father Joseph Mohr asked friend Franz Gruber to compose music to accompany a poem he had written, Stille Nacht, Heilige Nacht, and it was arranged for choir and guitar. It was first translated into English in 1863 and was sung in the trenches during the Christmas truce of 1914.

The carol has since been translated into about 300 languages and dialects, and has Unesco Intangible Cultural Heritage status.

Article continues below

David Miller, of the Postcode Lottery, said: “Christmas is all about bringing people together, and nothing does that quite like a festive sing-a-long. Our research shows we still love these traditions.

News.title: Tragedy as fell-runner Jenny Hall, 23, found dead after five-day search
News.content:
A woman whose disappearance triggered a five-day search has been found to have died from a medication overdose, a coroner has ruled.

Jenny Hall, 23, was last seen leaving her home on February 18, 2025. A major search across the Durham dales was launched after her red Ford Focus was discovered on the B6278 between Stanhope and Eggleston in County Durham.

Ms Hall's body was found on 23 February that year. At Crook Coroners' Court today, area coroner Crispin Oliver said: "I have had to think very hard about this and to balance things - which I have found particularly difficult in this case."

He concluded: "Jenny did take a substantial overdose while in a highly distressed state. She probably did not have a settled determination to end her own life, but did so recklessly as to the consequences."

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 3 Images Durham Police's expert teams with specialist equipment searched for Jenny Hal (Image: Durham Constabulary)

Mr Oliver spoke of how he had to weigh up "highly persuasive" toxicology evidence against the absence of proof regarding Ms Hall's intentions - noting that she appeared to be a young woman with a "lot to live for", including a close-knit family and a loving partner, reports Chronicle Live.

Mr Oliver had previously heard evidence that Ms Hall's medical cause of death was attributed to a combination of paracetamol and other medication found in her system. The coroner also received evidence from Durham Constabulary's Det Insp Peter Lonsdale, who headed the CID investigation into Ms Hall's disappearance.

Det Insp Lonsdale said he believed, based on the manner in which Ms Hall was discovered, that she had been using the torch on her Garmin smartwatch. He told the court: "She had a Garmin fell-runner's watch with a torch and I believe she had been using it to guide herself or using the torch [from her watch] to find her key."

Speaking on behalf of her family, Ms Hall's sister Helen told the coroner they did not believe her intention had been suicide. She said: "As a family we do not feel that would have been her intent and we would more lean towards this having been due to an accidental or unintentional overdose."

View 3 Images Ms Hall with her fellow runners (Image: Facebook)

Ms Hall, from Tow Law, County Durgham, was spotted by a police helicopter pilot on the Sunday morning, following an extensive search that had been severely hampered by adverse weather conditions in the days prior. The last confirmed sighting of Ms Hall alive was dashcam footage recorded in her car, which ceased when the engine was switched off at around 5.24pm.

She had earlier driven around the local area after telling her father Stephen she was heading out to the shops.

Home Office pathologist Dr Sam Hoggard informed the court that a toxicology report revealed she had significantly elevated levels of paracetamol and other medication, for recently diagnosed ADHD, in her system at the likely time of her death. Ms Hall, a qualified accountant, had been "extremely fit", the court heard.

Recapping Dr Hoggard's report, the coroner said: "You have described a 6 foot 1, 23-year-old woman who, physically, is basically an athlete, she was an extremely physical fit young person."

Mr Hoggard confirmed there had been "no evidence that Jenny had drowned or been assaulted". Discussing the toxicology results, he added that the levels of both paracetamol and other medication both fell "within the potentially fatal range".

He then agreed with coroner Mr Oliver, who stated: "It seems like the effects of one or both drugs has caused Ms Hall to collapse suddenly."

In her evidence, Ms Hall's parents described her as having been "ambitious and motivated". She had recently departed from her role as an accountant in Bishop Auckland, though the court heard from Ms Hall's mother Karen, who said at the time she "did not believe this had affected her greatly as she was ambitious" and was "considering several options" regarding her future career.

Durham Constabulary police search adviser Sgt Richard Liddell told the court about the extensive search operation for Ms Hall. Describing how she was discovered during a brief respite in appalling weather conditions, he said: "On day five I noticed there was a potential opportunity [for the police helicopter] - they had a period of time where they could finish the search of an area they had been unable to do so previously. The tactical flight commander was able to spot Jenny by eyeball from about 1,000 feet."

Speaking about the enormous level of support for the search effort, he added: "We had at one stage 120 mountain rescue volunteers from 20 different mountain rescue teams."

He noted that all police officers "not on business as usual duties" had also been deployed at various points during the operation.

News.title: UK to pay 'participation' fee to deliver EU deals
News.content:
The UK will pay a "participation fee" to the EU as part of the deals agreed by Andy Burnham, according to legal documents.

The surcharge will go towards the running costs of EU agencies and systems required to deliver two of the agreements unveiled by the prime minister last week.

It will be paid in addition to a contribution towards costs that broadly mirrors how EU members contribute to the bloc's shared budget, the documents show.

The government has sought to contrast the financial costs of the deals against their overall effect on the economy, which it estimates will receive an eventual boost by billions a year due to increased trade.

The government is yet to publish an estimate of overall additional costs, but officials said they expected them to be in the low tens of millions per year and "massively outweighed" by predicted economic gains.

British ministers had already said they were prepared to pay towards administrative costs required to implement deals to re-link the UK to the EU's carbon trading regime, and align Britain with the EU's food standards.

Now, details of how the payments will be calculated have been revealed in treaties to deliver the two agreements, which are meant to take effect during 2028.

Legal text for a third agreement agreed last week, on youth visas for 18 to 31 year olds, is expected to be published in the coming days.

News.title: Met Police ruined my life, says Kenyan man wrongly sentenced over attack on UK couple
News.content:
In April 2023, Kenya's High Court quashed Kololo's conviction, because of doubts over the prosecution's evidence. This followed years of work by the legal charity Reprieve and a Kenyan lawyer, Alfred Olaba, who represented him for free.

They were supported by Judith Tebbutt, who believed Kololo was innocent. In an interview with the BBC in 2022, she said he had been scapegoated by Scotland Yard.

"He was not there on the night. He was not part of the group that held me. They've put this man in prison without any real evidence."

More than three years after his release, Kololo says he is still living with the effects of his torture and decade in prison. As we walk the narrow streets of Lamu's old town, his thin frame moves stiffly. He is on edge. "My mind is not good," he says. "I have not recovered."

He remembers being kept in a filthy, bedbug-ridden cell with up to eight other inmates, which he thought he would never leave. Twice he contracted tuberculosis and nearly died.

Kololo is now too frail to do the woodcutting he once relied on to make a living. He tries to grow enough to eat on the land around his home, but erratic rain makes it difficult.

"I have nothing. On the days I get food, I eat, and on the days I don't, I endure."

He lives alone in a mud hut. His wife divorced him after he went to prison, and their children went to live with his mother. They dropped out of school because the family could not pay the fees. Kololo says they were not allowed to visit him in prison. When he was released, they barely remembered him, especially his youngest.

"They were too young. Only now are they starting to regain the memory that 'this is our father who disappeared'," he says. "If it weren't for my mother, my children might have died."

For much of our time together, Kololo is remarkably upbeat. He trusts that his lawyers and God will deliver him justice. But when we talk about the Met, his demeanour shifts.

"I am extremely angry with the police," he says. "I'm also angry with the Kenyan Police. They collaborated to incriminate me. What [Hibberd] said destroyed my entire life and my children's lives."

The Met has not apologised to Kololo or admitted wrongdoing. The force is contesting his compensation claim, which his lawyers say could take years to resolve.

"These people falsely accused me. Do I not deserve something?" he asks.

The Met told the BBC that neither they nor Hibberd wanted to comment on Kololo's claim, but it said: "Our thoughts are with Mr Kololo, Mrs Tebbutt, her family and all those who have been affected by this terrible crime. The Metropolitan Police remains committed to supporting the Kenyan authorities in any way that may be possible, in order to get justice for Mrs Tebbutt and her late husband."

Preetha Gopalan, Reprieve's head of UK litigation, describes the Met's behaviour in Kololo's case as "egregious".

"They've spent 10 years trying to evade accountability in every way possible, now dragging him through the courts," she says. "It's possible for them to do the right thing, but they are unwilling, and so this ordeal continues to haunt Kololo and his family."

"Even if I get a billion shillings, I will never be the same," Kololo says. "But if I get the justice I deserve, I can help my children and take care of myself when I am an old man."

News.title: NHS boss warns of 'horrible spike' in flu as hospital admissions surge
News.content:
Speaking at the NHS Alliance autumn conference, Sir Jim said he was asked to wear a mask for the first time in years during a hospital visit, saying it was "a bit of a shock".

"I think we have more beds occupied with flu than we did this time last year, as we're just about going to that horrible spike in flu," he said.

According to the UKHSA, almost 9.5 million people under the age of 65 in clinical risk groups - including those with lung conditions, kidney or liver disease and diabetes - are eligible for the flu jab.

However, only 34% had received a flu vaccine up to 22 November, leaving almost 7 million without vital protection.

Sir Jim also condemned corridor care in hospitals saying that it had become "embedded" in some parts of the health service.

"It's not something any of us would want for our families, our mothers, our aunties, uncles â whether it's from a safety point of view, or more importantly from a personal dignity point of view," he said, adding there was a need to get a grip and eliminate it.

Sir Ciaran Devane, chief executive of the NHS Alliance, representing employers, said: "While the flu season is clearly hitting earlier this year and could add to the strain on NHS services heading into another difficult winter, we are yet to see how or when it will peak.

"The NHS has already had to deal with the challenge of heatwaves this summer, so this could pile yet more pressure on already squeezed services."

UKHSA flu lead Dr Suzanna McDonald urged people to get vaccinated, saying thousands of people die from the flu every year.

Flu levels are expected to increase further as Christmas approaches and people start socialising indoors more.

McDonald also called on those who are ill with respiratory symptoms to practise good hand hygiene by washing hands with warm soapy water, cough and sneeze into elbow or into a tissue, and to stay at home in bed and avoid anyone at much higher risk from catching diseases.

Meanwhile, it emerged that just a little over a third of toddlers in England have had a vaccine so far this autumn on the NHS.

Two and three-year-olds can have the vaccine, given as a nasal spray, for free at pharmacies.

But the UKHSA said just 37% of those eligible had taken up the offer.

School age children usually have the vaccine at school, with a catch-up available in pharmacies until 1 December for those who missed it.

McDonald said: "Please don't dismiss the importance of a flu vaccine for your children.

"It will help keep them out of hospital and even save lives."

This time last year an early increase in flu cases caused real concern across the NHS.

The virus was spreading sooner than expected and the fear was that the numbers would continue climbing right through the always challenging Christmas and New Year period.

As it happened the outbreak peaked early and the bleakest predictions did not become reality.

This time hospital admissions with flu patients are a little higher than 12 months ago after another early surge materialised.

Once again, officials do not know when the peak might be reached.

Adding to the challenges is an increase over the last year in patient numbers with a range of illnesses and conditions, partly explained by the ageing population. That means even more pressure on hospitals and their staff.

A bad flu winter could create significant problems.

News.title: Drug rape husband says wife 'would have been terrified', court hears
News.content:
Warning: This article contains distressing content

A husband who admits drugging and raping his wife with strangers has told a court that if she had woken during the abuse, she would have been "terrified".

The defendant, who has admitted multiple sexual offences dating back to 2004, said he drugged his wife so she would be unaware of the abuse by him and other men.

He changed his pleas earlier this year and admitted offences including rape, sexual assault and administering a substance with intent to commit a sexual offence, as well as inviting 13 other men to take part in the abuse.

Nine of those men have pleaded not guilty to sexual offences against the woman and are standing trial at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court.

The husband, who cannot be named to protect his wife's right to anonymity, entered the witness box to give evidence for the prosecution.

The court has heard that the man, who is in his 60s, filmed and photographed his offending as his wife lay "out of it" on their bed before sharing the material online.

Prosecutors say that, by 2023 at the latest, he had begun inviting other men to the couple's home in Stockport, Greater Manchester, where it is alleged they sexually abused her while she was unconscious.

Asked by prosecutor Louise Oakley KC why he was now telling the truth, he said: "So the court knows what happened. So my wife knows and my children know.

"I am here to tell the truth and give my account of what actually happened."

He told jurors he had drugged his wife so she would be unaware of the abuse by him and other men.

"She would never agree to do any of this," he said. "She would have been terrified and scream."

Following his guilty pleas in September, the husband gave police a written statement detailing his offending.

He told the jury the process had been "very difficult" because of the "guilt and shame" he felt and the "pain" he had caused his wife.

He accepted responsibility for his actions and for facilitating contact between other men and his wife.

Asked whether she had ever consented to what happened to her, he replied: "Never."

He said his wife did not know any of the men he invited to the house and had never spoken to them.

News.title: MoD has no email addresses for about half of its reservists
News.content:
The Ministry of Defence (MoD) is urging reservists to update their contact details, after it has emerged it does not have email addresses for about half of them.

The UK has an estimated 95,000 members in its strategic reserve force, which is made up of veterans who can be recalled in exceptional circumstances, but the MoD said it has only been able to send letters to around 50,000.

Open letters have been published on the ministry's website encouraging others to "reconnect".

On Thursday Defence Secretary Wes Streeting confirmed that the MoD had written to ex-military personnel to check their contact details and skills against the backdrop of a rising "threat environment".

His comments were made after The Times and the Telegraph reported that reservists who previously served in the Armed Forces had received letters telling them to prepare to be called up for war.

Streeting told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that this meant should they ever be needed "either for a national disaster here at home or for a more serious threat or conflict elsewhere" then they would "know where our strategic reserve is" and what their skills were.

"I want the country to be alert, not alarmed," he said.

The defence secretary also reiterated the importance of keeping "up to date" with reservists, and ensuring they had access to "further development opportunities".

On the MoD's website, the ministry said it was re-engaging with reservists due to a "more dangerous and unpredictable security environment."

It emphasised that the threshold for being recalled is high and reservists would not be used to fill routine staffing shortages in peacetime.

"It may be considered for serious national emergencies, warlike operations, preparations for war or a major crisis that requires additional military capability," it said.

Earlier this year, former Defence Secretary Lord Robertson said officials were failing to maintain records of military veterans who were entering the reserves.

"The Ministry of Defence at the present moment doesn't even know where most of them are," he said in April.

"So we need to round up those who are available and fit and willing to be able to do it."

Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton has made similar comments, warning in January that the UK did not have "an effective system of tracking and engaging" personnel after they had left the Armed Forces.

News.title: Huntingdon train attacker found guilty of all 14 counts of attempted murder
News.content:
A knifeman has been found guilty of attempting to murder 14 people, including 10 on board a train to London.

Passengers on the Doncaster to King's Cross service fought off Anthony Williams, 33, with a frying pan and a toaster as the attack unfolded on 1 November 2025.

Some hid in toilets and bike racks before the driver was forced to make an unscheduled stop in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, where Williams was arrested by armed police.

As well as the train attacks, Williams, of Langford Road, Peterborough, was found guilty of attempting to murder four other people in separate incidents and will be sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court on 4 and 5 February.

Jurors deliberated for 15 hours and 53 minutes before delivering seven guilty verdicts, and then returned an hour later to give the final seven.

The judge, Mr Justice Calver KC, said the victims handled themselves with "great dignity throughout" the trial.

Aside from the attack on the LNER train, Williams also attempted to murder a boy and two men in Peterborough on 31 October 2025, and then a teenager on a DLR train in east London hours later.

The defendant, who appeared at court via a video link from a secure hospital, showed little emotion as each verdict was delivered.

Reacting to the verdicts, Ben Samples, of the Crown Prosecution Service, said: "The fact that nobody was killed in his rampage is down to the courage, quick thinking and good fortune of the people he attacked."

News.title: From £250 job to £9,000 bill: Inside the rogue trader networks scamming customers at scale
News.content:
Organised networks of rogue plumbers and electricians have been scamming people on a large scale, a BBC investigation has found.

Nessar Khawaja, who used the online name ThatGuyNess, regularly posted TikTok videos showing his work as a plumber, explaining how he made thousands of pounds from "desperate" customers, and recruiting online to expand his network.

"Me and my team, we're top of the food chain," he said in one video.

The investigation found the 23-year-old is a key figure within an organised group that is systematically ripping off customers and teaching others to do the same.

The BBC put these allegations to Khawaja in writing. He denied any wrongdoing and said his social media posts were intended as light-hearted comedy that did not reflect how he operated in practice.

In a recorded phone call, Khawaja insisted he was an entertainer, was joking and that the BBC had "taken things out of context".

In another video, Khawaja made claims he had electricians working for him who made more than Â£40,000 a month.

"I've got 100-120 engineers. Imagine how much money I am making them and making from them," he said.

One of Khawaja's associates told an undercover BBC journalist during a secretly-recorded recruitment call that engineers working for them had to hand over 60% from every job to the network.

After being approached for comment, TikTok said it banned the account for "breaching its rules on fraud and scams".

News.title: Victorian railway station left untouched for 70 years goes on sale with suitcase still inside
News.content:
A Victorian-era railway station is up for sale at Â£135,000 after being left empty for more than 70 years.

Holland Arms station in Pentre Berw was the second stop on the defunct Anglesey Central Railway line that ran from the village of Gaerwen to the port town of Amlwch.

Opened to the public on 12 March 1865, the station has been disused for decades after closing in 1952 and bears relics of its past, including rusted signal lamps and a cobweb-covered suitcase.

However, its estate agent said the property has the potential to be transformed into something "truly individual", including a home, subject to planning permission.

"Today, the building offers the chance to preserve a fascinating part of the island's railway history while exploring its future potential," said estate agents William and Goodwin.

The company called it a "rare opportunity" to own a piece of Anglesey's heritage, as the building retains a number of its original Victorian features, including a ticket office and male and female waiting rooms - reflecting the era's social conventions.

News.title: UK net migration at lowest level since 1997 as asylum claims also fall
News.content:
The prime minister went on to say: "I'm not going to say all of the work is done, and I don't want to appear complacent, but I think we're finally as a country getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see."

The underlying official statistics show that an estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the figures showed that Labour had "delivered" after Conservative failures - but Chris Philp, her Tory shadow, said restrictions introduced by his party before the 2024 General Election were behind the falls.

The 77,000 figure is also the first time the UK has seen net migration in the tens of thousands since former PM David Cameron's controversial pledge 16 years ago to reach such a level.

The biggest factors in Thursday's record low were falls in the arrivals of people coming from outside Europe in three major categories of migration: The number of people coming to the UK to work fell by 45,000, asylum claims fell by 19,000 and the total number of students fell by 33,000.

These number had been expected to fall because of the tightening of visas rules that began under the previous Conservative government which was then continued by Labour from July 2024.

The effect of those policies, plus emigration from the UK, has meant that while net migration had already begun to fall, it more than halved in the last 12 months alone.

Mahmood said the figures showed the government had "restored control".

"We have brought net migration to 77,000, down 92% from its peak under the Conservatives," she said. "Where they failed, we have delivered for the British people."

This is a reference to the so-called "Boriswave" after Brexit. When the UK left the EU and its freedom of movement rules, Boris Johnson's government allowed in many more people to work and study from other parts of the world.

That led to the record-breaking arrivals in the year to March 2023. Johnson's successor, Rishi Sunak, introduced major restrictions on visas in the last months of his government.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the falls were a result of those changes.

In a post on X, he called for an "annual legally binding inward migration cap, set by Parliament, at far lower levels".

Dr Ben Brindle of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, an impartial expert body, said: "We are entering an unusual period where immigration has come down and may still have further to fall - but we still have relatively high emigration, at least for the time being.

"Most of those emigrants are non-citizens, including people who arrived a few years ago when immigration was very high. That could push the net migration figures down even further next year, but the downwards blip is unlikely to last forever."

News.title: Mandelson kept shares as ambassador despite conflict of interest fears, documents show
News.content:
Lord Mandelson still held shares in his lobbying company eight months after becoming US ambassador, despite government concens about conflicts of interest, newly released documents show.

The peer was sacked as ambassador last year by Sir Keir Starmer following revelations about the extent of his relationship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

This 85-page release is the third since MPs voted to publish documents aiming to reveal behind-the scenes-discussions about how he was appointed to the role.

The documents were previously withheld due to the Metropolitan Police investigation into allegations Lord Mandelson had passed market-sensitive government information to Epstein.

Sir Olly Robbins was sacked as head of the Foreign Office by Sir Keir Starmer during the scandal when it emerged Lord Mandelson had been granted clearance for the role despite concerns being raised by vetting officials.

The newly released documents highlight that Lord Mandelson was able to keep his shares in Global Counsel, the lobbying company he co-founded, while serving as ambassador to Washington.

They reveal civil servants' concerns about the risk of perceived conflict of interest.

But selling the shares was clearly not a condition of him taking up the role.

Part of that is because of the desire in Sir Keir's government at the time to have Lord Mandelson in Washington as quickly as possible.

That is exemplified in an email from Sir Olly, saying a process to police Mandelson's conflicts of interest could be "up and running in a light touch way".

Another factor is selling shares in a private company like Global Counsel, which advised high-profile clients including Chinese-owned TikTok, US tech firm Palantir and pharmaceutical firm GSK. requires finding a new buyer or selling them back to the company.

But the documents also reveal Lord Mandelson had not sold his shares back to Global Counsel because their offer was not the "fair value". Another attempt to sell to a different buyer fell through.

The result was Mandelson kept his shares, and while in office tried to set up a meeting between Global Counsel and a key Donald Trump advisor, as well as taking the firm's advice on a speech on Britain's role in the world.

Lord Mandelson remained a shareholder until February 2026, the same month the company went into administration.

News.title: Burnham joined by former PMs at Widdecombe service
News.content:
Andy Burnham was joined by former prime ministers as he attended a memorial service for the late politician Ann Widdecombe.

Hundreds gathered for the Service of Remembrance at Westminster Cathedral on Thursday afternoon, including David Cameron, Liz Truss, Boris Johnson and Rishi Sunak.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage and deputy leader Richard Tice, along with former Conservative Chancellor Philip Hammond and Speaker of the House of Commons Sir Lindsay Hoyle, were also in attendance.

Bishop James Curry, the Auxiliary Bishop of Westminster, led the service after the Archbishop of Westminster, Richard Moth, was taken to hospital earlier.

Smith said: "It has been a privilege to be the CMO of Scotland for the last six-and-a-half years, but it has become very clear to me that the nature and purpose of the role is not generally understood.

"Like many colleagues across the health system, those years of the pandemic and afterwards have taken their toll.

He added: "No-one in public life is unaccountable. I am confident, however, that the review initiated by the cabinet secretary will show that I provided my advice in relation to Grampian hepatobiliary service consistent with the role of the chief medical officer."

Dominiczak was appointed as the Scottish government's chief health scientist in July 2022 and is regius professor of medicine at the University of Glasgow.

Constance said: "Dame Anna has played a key role in driving medical innovation in her time as chief scientist and she brings a wealth of clinical experience to the role of interim chief medical officer.
