Fernandes' crazy strike looked like it would be the United winner, thus handing Mauricio Pochettino his first win in just his second game. But a howler from Senne Lammens would ultimately allow Sporting to equalise late in the day as the goalkeeper's personal struggles continued.

He failed to catch a routine cross despite being under minimal pressure, and as he dropped the ball it fell at the feet of Luis Suarez, who tucked home into an empty net from close range. Despite the blunder, Fernandes was keen not to point fingers.

‌



He said: "It’s part of football, mistakes are part of football, and from that, you get goals. But, obviously, it’s not an individual sport, so everyone has to take the blame for everything we do good and everything we do bad.

View 2 Images The moment where Bruno Fernandes created his divot was pinpointed post-match (Image: TNT Sports)

‌



"I think the main thing and the most important thing is to understand we need to be together, in the good and in the bad moments, and it’s not going to change the belief we have in each other."

United had to endure their fair share of frustration on the night. They saw two goals disallowed - the first for an alleged foul by Youri Tielemans before Amad slotted home. Pochettino refused to answer with words when quizzed on that decision post-match.

He also saw a third goal chalked off for a foul by Patrick Dorgu on the Sporting goalkeeper with VAR advising that the potential winner be ruled out.

Sports.title: Paris Fury retracts Tyson schizophrenia claim
Sports.content:
Paris Fury says Tyson did not receive a diagnosis of schizophrenia; Netflix documentary has now been updated; The British Boxing Board of Control indicated it would look into comments about a schizophrenia diagnosis and could deny Fury a licence to face Anthony Joshua on December 11

Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua: Paris Fury retracts claim her husband has been diagnosed with schizophrenia

Tyson Fury has previously spoken about his struggles with mental health

Paris Fury has retracted her claim that husband Tyson Fury was diagnosed with schizophrenia.

A new Netflix documentary explores Tyson Fury's experiences of depression, anxiety and bipolar disorder, which became particularly acute after his unified heavyweight championship victory over Wladimir Klitschko in 2015.

Paris Fury made the comments about schizophrenia in an initial version of the documentary. Netflix said it has worked to "update" the footage in light of her clarification.

She has now said: "I want to clarify a statement I made in the original version of the Tyson Fury documentary. I recalled a conversation from many years ago when discussing Tyson's condition and I used the word 'schizophrenic'. Whilst Tyson did show some symptoms associated with schizophrenia, he doesn't have this condition and has never received a diagnosis.

"Mental health is complex, and it isn't always easy to find the right words, especially when you're living it with someone you love. I'm so proud of Tyson for really opening up in this documentary and want to say thank you for all the support we've received as a family."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player A look inside Tyson Fury's training camp ahead of his December 11 showdown with Anthony Joshua

Earlier on Thursday, the British Boxing Board of Control (BBBoC) indicated that it was investigating the comments and could deny Fury a licence to face Anthony Joshua in Cardiff on December 11 if he was deemed unfit to fight.

Sky Sports News has contacted the BBBoC to clarify if an investigation is ongoing after Paris Fury's retraction.

A spokesperson for Netflix said: "Following new information shared by the family relating to Tyson's official mental health diagnosis, we have worked alongside them to update the documentary accordingly ahead of launch."

After his victory over Klitschko, Fury revealed he had struggled with drug and alcohol addiction and had gained weight.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua come together in a face-off ahead of their fight on December 11

He was admitted to hospital in June 2016 with a suspected heart attack, and revealed that while in hospital he had heard voices in his head.

"Words can't explain the darkness I was in," Fury said during the Netflix documentary.

"It was like a living version of the pits of hell.

"I thought I would end up in a padded room with the door locked, and that scared me so much.

"The anxiety was crippling me. I just could not overcome it and that's when I went and saw the psychiatrist down in London. She asked me a gazillion questions, and I ticked all the boxes. Depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder."

The NHS says schizophrenia is a long-term mental health illness that is a form of psychosis.

Those suffering from the condition may, at times, be unable to distinguish their own thoughts from reality. Symptoms can include hallucinations and delusions.

The NHS describes bipolar disorder as a mental health issue where a person can experience extreme changes in their mood.

If you've been affected by anything discussed in this article, support is available; please visit Sky Viewer Support.

If you are worried about your mental health, get advice and support through your GP or call the NHS on 111.

Sports.title: Duran scores late Celtic winner to keep Europa League hopes alive
Sports.content:
Camilo Duran came off the bench to keep Celtic's Europa League hopes alive with a vital win against Torreense.

The Colombian striker peeled away to the back post to meet a cross from fellow substitute James Forrest, guiding a downward header into the net in the 85th minute.

Duran's 15th goal of the season secured a 2-1 victory over the Portuguese second-tier side and moved Celtic on to six points in the Europa League. His latest decisive contribution follows a match-winning double off the bench in the Hoops' comeback victory over Besiktas last time out.

Image: Torreense's Javi Vazquez (L) turned a cross from Celtic's Jota into his own net

Celtic took the lead in the ninth minute when Javi Vazquez turned Jota's cross into his own net, with Hyun-jun Yang lurking behind him.

However, the Portuguese Cup winners hit back 10 minutes later after some hesitant defending from the visitors. Alex Alfaro rattled the crossbar with a 22-yard effort, but neither Kieran Tierney nor Colby Donovan could deal with the resulting loose balls, allowing Haiti international Dany Jean to volley home the equaliser.

Celtic dominated possession after the break but struggled to create clear-cut opportunities until Duran's late intervention secured all three points.

The Hoops' attention now turns to Hearts on Sunday, live on Sky Sports, as they look to remain top of the Scottish Premiership.

Their next Europa League match is away to Omonia Nicosia on December 10.

Key moments from Campo Manuel Marques

2: CLOSE! Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain sends in a corner, it's flicked on by Liam Scales but Hyun-jun Yang can't knock the ball in before it's cleared.

9: GOAL CELTIC! Javi Vazquez tries to clear Jota's cross but turns it into his own net.

19: GOAL TORREENSE! Alex Alfaro's effort rattles the underside of the bar, Celtic fail to make a clearance and Dany Jean fires in the equaliser.

33: SAVE! Jota's powerful strike is pushed over the bar by Adriel.

36: OFF THE LINE! More awful defending from Celtic, but Liam Scales manages to head the ball clear.

47: SAVE! Jota tries to chip the ball over the goalkeeper but he manages to pluck the ball out of the air.

53: BLOCK! Jota is continuing to cause problems for the hosts as he sends in a cross for Kieran Tierney, which is headed behind.

61: CLOSE! Jean looks to squeeze in a shot at the near post, but it's just wide.

69: CHANCE! A misplaced pass from Oliver Sorensen lets Musa Drammeh get a shot away. Thankfully for Celtic it's wide.

70: LET OFF FOR CELTIC! Trouble at the back again gives Drammeh space to get a shot away, but the former Hearts striker is inches wide.

84: GOAL CELTIC! Camilo Duran rises at the back post to head in James Forrest's cross. Celtic are back ahead.

Positives but also problems

Jota looked back to his best despite not scoring or providing an assist.

In his first European appearance for Celtic since 2025, the winger was a pest for the Portuguese side until he was replaced by James Forrest.

Image: James Forrest set up the winner as he matched Scott Brown's record of 127 European appearances for Celtic

He created chances with some brilliant crossing with one turned in by Vazquez for the opening goal.

Then there is Camilo Duran.

He has been sensational since arriving in the summer and he saved Celtic again.

But it was far from a perfect performance in Portugal.

Image: Striker Kasper Hogh once again failed to score for Celtic

Once again, slack defending and individual errors proved costly, allowing Torreense to remain well in the game.

Record signing Kasper Hogh started, but once again did not score. He is lacking in confidence, but how long do you stick with a striker who is not putting the ball in the net?

O'Neill: 'From an almost impossible position, we have hope'

Image: Celtic manager Martin O'Neill (L) celebrates with Camilo Duran

Celtic manager Martin O'Neill on TNT Sports:

"I'm just delighted to have won, it keeps us going if nothing else. We've got six points on the board and we've still a couple of games to go.

"From an almost impossible position, having lost the first three games, we've given ourselves some hope.

"Three points tonight were of vital importance. There's lots we can still do to improve our game."

Asked about Camilo Duran, he added: "He's just a magnificent footballer.

"15 goals and we're not into December, he's been flying. He's a terrific player, and that's two games he's come up big for us."

Jota 'enjoying life' as he returns to best

Celtic winger Jota speaking to TNT Sports after his first European appearance for almost two years:

Image: Jota was added to Celtic's Europa League squad after Mika Baur's injury

"It was a long road and I did my maximum to be as fit as possible.

"Right now, it's all about enjoying life. No expectations, just be professional and having the responsibility of being a Celtic player.

"It wasn't easy. I think we just had to stick with our plan and in the end it worked out, that's the most important thing.

"We must believe [Celtic can qualify]. Every game is a different battle, we know what to do."

Sports.title: Bears stun Lions with TD in final seconds of NFL Thanksgiving epic
Sports.content:
The Chicago Bears scored the game-winning touchdown with just three seconds remaining to secure a stunning 39-35 comeback win over the Detroit Lions on Thanksgiving and claim first place in the NFC North.

Rome Odunze's second TD - a sensational toe-tap grab in the back of the end zone - clinched the victory and deny Detroit, who had led by 11 earlier in the fourth quarter after Jahmyr Gibbs ran in his third score of the game from 70 yards out.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Detroit Lions' Jahmyr Gibbs scored an incredible 70-yard Touchdown during their game against the Chicago Bears

Chicago's lead secured right at the death was the first lead change in a game they've been involved with since they trailed the Carolina Panthers 7-0 in the first quarter of their opening game of the season. They had trailed the Lions for 53 minutes and 31 seconds of this match.

The Bears' dramatic win nudges them into solo first in the fiercely-fought NFC North, at 9-2 on the season, while the Lions drop to 8-3 with a first loss in seven.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Chicago Bears' Rome Odunze scored the game-winning touchdown during their Thanksgiving match against the Detroit Lions

It also improves Chicago's record in the division to 1-2, with Detroit now 2-1, which could prove crucial should any potential playoff tiebreakers be necessary to separate the two teams - who meet again on the penultimate week of the season - or the Minnesota Vikings (7-3) and Green Bay Packers (6-5).

The game was initially slow to ignite, with only a Lions field goal to show from the first quarter, before Gibbs' first score to start the second lit the blue touchpaper.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Dan Campbell's call to take the safety pays off, as the Lions then follow that up with a touchdown from Sam LaPorta

The Lions continued to lead thereafter, until the Bears came roaring back in the final quarter. Caleb Williams firstly located Odunze deep down the field for a 41-yard TD, the QB ran in the resulting two-point play to cut the score to three, before Jared Goff threw an interception on the next series.

Chicago turned the ball over on downs, failing to convert on 4th and 3 just inside Detroit territory, but they got the ball back with just over two minutes to go, and this time marched down the field before Williams linked up with Odunze again for the game winner with seconds remaining.

Williams finished with 345 yards passing and those two scoring strikes to Odunze, while Bears running back D'Andre Swift had 162 yards from scrimmage and a touchdown. Gibbs had 20 carries for a massive 205 yards and three TDs for the Lions but it didn't prove to be enough.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports NFL's Ndamukong Suh and Jason Bell ate their Thanksgiving turkey live but one pundit was left far from impressed

Stats leaders

Bears:

Passing: Caleb Williams, 30/44, 345 yards, 2 TDs

Caleb Williams, 30/44, 345 yards, 2 TDs Rushing: D'Andre Swift, 9 carries, 65 yards, 1 TD

D'Andre Swift, 9 carries, 65 yards, 1 TD Receiving: D'Andre Swift, 7 catches, 97 yards

D'Andre Swift, 7 catches, 97 yards Rome Odunze, 6 catches, 87 yards, 2 TDs

Image: Rome Odunze pulls off the game-winning touchdown grab for the Chicago Bears in the closing seconds

Lions:

Passing: Jared Goff, 25/36, 313 yards, 1 TD, 1 INT

Jared Goff, 25/36, 313 yards, 1 TD, 1 INT Rushing: Jahmyr Gibbs, 21 carries, 205 yards, 3 TDs

Jahmyr Gibbs, 21 carries, 205 yards, 3 TDs Receiving: Amon-Ra St. Brown, 7 catches, 146 yards

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Jason Bell and Ndamukong Suh react to the recent accusations Aaron Rodgers made about Mike McCarthy

How the Bears roared back on Thanksgiving

After the Lions' first quarter field goal, they failed to add further points on the back of a Colston Loveland fumble, but they would find the end zone early in the second - Gibbs from down at the goal line - as the Bears offense was slow to fire.

Chicago finally sparked into life in the second and tied the game up at 10-10 with the first of two Kyle Monangai scores.

Detroit were back in front by the half, up 19-10, after a bizarre sequence saw them first awarded a safety as a Bears player deliberately batted a fumbled football out of the end zone, before Goff found Sam LaPorta for an 11-yard TD.

A second Gibbs touchdown was sandwiched in between scores for Monangai and Swift in the third quarter, while Jake Bates' second field goal put the Lions 29-24 up early in the fourth.

Image: D'Andre Swift found the end zone with a big 30-yard touchdown run in the third quarter

Gibbs only added to that advantage as he completed his hat-trick of TDs with the best of the bunch, breaking loose from 70 yards out but the game was far from over, with Willams and Odunze answering back almost immediately.

After Chicago failed to capitalise on Goff's interception, Detroit missed the chance to ice the game when opting against a 50-yard field goal try as they went for it on 4th and 4 from the Bears 33-yard-line.

Stopped short, Chicago got the ball back to pave the way for Williams and Odunze's dramatic, game-winning connection in the closing seconds.

Sports.title: NZ skipper Latham laughs off Pant dominating local cricket under false name
Sports.content:
New Zealand captain Tom Latham has laughed off India's Rishabh Pant dominating a local Christchurch cricket match under a false name, a day before their second Test.

On Monday, Daryl Mitchell and Glenn Phillips held firm for 43 overs to earn the Black Caps a hard-fought draw in Wellington after India posted a record score of 720-9d.

Pant scored 128 in that Test, with the second Test between the sides beginning on Thursday at Hagley Oval.

Yet, footage has since emerged of Pant playing for club side Open House Swingers against The Chosen Ones on Wednesday, scoring 54 off 21 balls under the name 'Stan Stan' to seal a 16-run victory.

In an interview with The New Zealand Herald, Open House player Mohammad Safi said he had seen Pant on an electric bike in the city and asked if he would play, due to his club team being a player short.

"Did he play?! How'd he go?" Latham said at his New Zealand press conference. "That's brilliant!

"It's great. He's obviously a real character of the game, is Rishabh.

Image: New Zealand's captain Tom Latham (right) leads his side into the second Test after a gritty draw in the first Test

"It's great for him to be giving his experience back to LMS (Last Man Standing) teams!"

Pant has scored 3,853 runs in his 53 Tests for India, averaging just below of 45.

The 29-year-old also boasts a strike-rate of 74.43, which is bettered only by Virender Sehwag and Kapil Dev among players to have scored more than 2,000 Test runs for India.

Sports.title: Frank earns first Palace win with late comeback against Sociedad
Sports.content:
Thomas Frank earned his first win as Crystal Palace manager, coming from behind to beat Real Sociedad 2-1 in the Europa League.

The Dane lost his opening game to Coventry at the weekend, but saw the heart and fight he will need from his side as they picked up their second win in the competition this season.

For 70 minutes, Sociedad dominated at Selhurst Park, with Dean Henderson needed to make a string of saves. They finally made the breakthrough when Chelsea loanee Mamadou Sarr tapped home from Job Ochieng's cross.

But the game turned out of nowhere as Crystal Palace were awarded a penalty and Jon Martin was sent off. He picked up a second yellow card for holding Jean-Philippe Mateta round the middle, with the striker expertly dispatching the spot kick to level for the Eagles.

Image: Jean-Philippe Mateta proved influential in masterminding Crystal Palace's comeback victory over Real Sociedad

The confidence surged in the hosts - backed by the famous atmosphere at Selhurst Park - and it was a well-worked second that put them ahead.

Yeremy Pino's cross was cleared to Jorgen Strand Larsen at the back post, who hit an overhead kick. It wasn't on target, but it did bobble into the six-yard box for the incoming Dwight McNeil, who slid to poke home.

Image: Jon Martin was sent off for Real Sociedad

Crystal Palace could have wrapped up the points in a topsy-turvy end after they were awarded another penalty. Carlos Soler was penalised for handball, but Pino's effort was well-saved by Unai Marrero.

The win catapults Crystal Palace into 12th place in the league phase table, just two from the top eight, and gives them a huge boost ahead of another key clash against Hull on Super Sunday. Real Sociedad have slid down into 27th.

Crystal Palace

Hull City Sunday 29th November 1:00pm Kick off 2:05pm

Key moments from Selhurst Park...

35: SAVE! Dean Henderson has to be alert as Goncalo Guedes strikes, but the goalkeeper is down to push it away.

38: SAVE! A wonderful pass from Mikel Oyarzabal to release Guedes, but his shot is pushed away by Henderson.

45: ALMOST! A Chris Richards long throw is pinged into the box, Axel Disasi nods it on for Jean-Philippe Mateta - but the Frenchman's own header goes wide.

52: SAVE! OVER! Henderson pushes away Gorrotxategi's shot before the rebound is skied into the stands.

Image: Jean-Philippe Mateta scored Crystal Palace's equaliser as they beat Real Sociedad

67: GOAL! Sarr taps home after Ochieng's low pass.

71: PENALTY CRYSTAL PALACE! RED CARD! Martin has his arms wrapped around Mateta for far too long and picks up a second yellow card.

73: GOAL! Mateta fires home the penalty to level for Crystal Palace.

82: GOAL! McNeil turns home from Strand Larsen's overhead kick to put the Eagles ahead.

90: PENALTY! Crystal Palace are awarded a second penalty for a Soler handball, but Pino has his effort saved.

90+7: SAVE! Henderson pushes away a shot from Oskarsson to keep Sociedad from a late leveller.

Frank hopes Europa win can be turning point in Palace's season

Image: Thomas Frank applauds the fans after winning his first game as Crystal Palace manager

Crystal Palace manager Thomas Frank to TNT Sport on if the win can be a turning point: "I surely hope so. You can't underestimate a win, what that gives the group, what they're feeling.

"I think there was more positives than negatives from this performance, but still a lot we need to work on, and to keep working on.

"It's a fantastic feeling to get the win in every aspect here at home and in the circumstances that it's a season that hasn't been living up to everything we expected, so the confidence is maybe not at the highest.

"The ability to come from 1-0 behind and then go to win the game, the mentality and the belief in the players was really good.

"We're playing a very good team, they're fifth in LaLiga, they're very good on the ball. Not everything was perfect in the first half, but the willingness to suffer together and defend together was there, that was good, then we built a little bit more into the second half."

McNeil: Frank has bought energy and confidence

Crystal Palace goalscorer Dwight McNeil to TNT Sport on what Frank has bought to the club: "It's like an energy, a belief. He keeps telling us how good as players we are, but now we're just putting it out on the pitch and we did that tonight.

"We knew it was going to be a tough game but we stuck in there, especially going down 1-0 and then the big man [Mateta] scoring to get us back into the game and then we go on from there."

In response, Frank said: "It's easy to bring energy and the confidence, but what really moves the needle is that you get over the line and get some wins.

"In the last five minutes, I think we all almost were about to get a heart attack because it went both ways, back-to-back. That's also part of the confidence and also we should have controlled that game against 10, but it's football, it's emotions, it's everything."

Flashes of the 'old' Crystal Palace in Europa win

Analysis from Sky Sports' Charlotte Marsh: "Perhaps one of the most surprising aspects of Crystal Palace this season has been a lack of fight and desire.

"Under Pierre Sage, the team looked disjointed and out of sorts. You did not always see the same determination and sheer-mindedness that has seen the Eagles achieve beyond their wildest dreams over the last few years.

"But we saw that again on Thursday - the Palace of last season, of 'old' perhaps, is still there. To come from behind against a team of Real Sociedad's quality is impressive, and it hinged on one moment. Some fans might say it is about time things started turning in Palace's favour this season.

"They had certainly ridden their luck until that point. Frank very quickly must eradicate the mistakes in and out of possession. Too many sloppy moments allowed Sociedad onto the ball and to have a shot. They were certainly victims of their own lack of precision - Palace might not be so fortunate next time.

"But what the final 20 minutes and result will bring them is a huge boost in confidence that must be channelled towards the Premier League. Frank said in his pre-match press conference that he knows he will be judged on league results and he's right - now it's time to start getting some."

What's next?

Sports.title: Bakole: Late-notice Wilder fight not like Parker | 'I like danger!'
Sports.content:
Martin Bakole explained his decision to step in as a replacement opponent for Deontay Wilder on the Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua undercard next month.

After Jai Opetaia withdrew from his December 11 bout with former heavyweight world champion Wilder, Bakole came in to take his place on the Principality Stadium bill.

He insists it is a very different scenario to his short-notice assignment against Joseph Parker last year.

Bakole came in to box Parker for the WBO Interim title, landing in Riyadh just a day before the fight. Parker promptly put him down heavily and stopped him in their second round.

For this fight with Wilder though he's had more warning. He was training in Las Vegas to box on the same bill, albeit originally for a much lower-level opponent.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of Joseph Parker's spectacular knockout victory against Martin Bakole

"When I heard Wilder doesn't have an opponent, his opponent cancelled, they proposed me and I said why not? I'm ready to give a big fight," Bakole told Sky Sports. "Why not jump from a comeback fight to a big fight?

"I was surprised they mentioned my name and I said yes," he added. "I'm ready to come back again because I want to take over now the heavyweight division.

"I don't see Deontay beating me. He doesn't have the strength I have.

"I don't see any danger because I like danger, I like to impose myself.

"I'm ready and prepared for him."

That wasn't the case for Parker when he took that fight. "I was out in the Congo on holiday, I jumped in," Bakole said.

"In that fight I was giving Joseph Parker a hard time in the first round but because I was not fit and my head was not moving, he landed a punch. But I don't regret that fight. It's just part of my story.

"That was something to save the card."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Here's why no-one wants to fight Martin Bakole

While Bakole has been training in Las Vegas, he will still have long-time coach Billy Nelson in his corner for the fight.

"I came here to learn something new. I was getting ready for everyone," Bakole said. "Everything has changed [with his preparation], conditioning, nutrition."

He believes victory over Wilder will lead him to a world title shot next year.

"Of course," Bakole said. "That's why I wanted to change everything because I know next year, with my team, with His Excellency's [Saudi financier Turki Alalshikh] help, I will get a world title next year."

Sports.title: Eckert: Time to 'close the chapter' on Spygate ahead of Boro reunion
Sports.content:
"I think we've experienced a little bit more in the last 12 months than normal."

It may be the understatement of the century, but it's not a huge surprise considering Tonda Eckert is a relatively understated man.

The storm of 'Spygate' is over, but the aftershock is still being felt. Southampton are sixth in the table, seven points behind leaders Middlesbrough ahead of their reunion on Friday night - live on Sky Sports.

Were it not for the four-point deduction, the gap would be smaller. Were it not for the entire controversy, the Saints would possibly be in the Premier League right now.

Eckert knows he broke the rules, and is thankful for the club and the support-base for backing him. Something that wouldn't have been easy after the ignominy of being kicked out of the play-offs.

"There have been some points, especially over the summer, where I think the club has made a commitment that not many clubs would have made," he admits.

"I'm very grateful, first of all, for the opportunity to step up in the first place, but also for the support over the summer. Obviously, that goes from everyone in the building to our supporters.

"This summer has been the biggest test we can possibly have in terms of the relationship between a football club and a fan base, and a manager and a fan base. I think the supporters have been great. It's been a tough period for them.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Tonda Eckert says he's relieved the FA's investigation into last season's spying controversy has concluded

"Towards the end of last season, it was difficult to process for everyone because of the process we used. I would have wanted to address the supporters a little earlier, so it took almost two weeks before I got to speak to them.

"From there on, I think the commitment has been very clear. It started with the football club and some players who committed to the project.

"You could just sense, the closer we got to the season, that everyone wanted to leave that behind and show what we are about as a football club and how much joy we bring when we go on the pitch. We felt that throughout the summer and on the first day of training.

"To come out of that situation with new strength just shows what this football club is about. Now it's for us to look forward and make sure that we continue to do that.

"There was still some uncertainty for the first block of games, and you just need to find a way, for me and obviously for everyone else in the football club, to put that to the side. As soon as the season starts, you need to perform.

"Then, obviously, to close that chapter finally, we needed a decision from the club. I think that's helped us to close that chapter."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Last month, Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert said it's time to move on after he was handed a six-week ban suspended until the end of next season over the Spygate scandal

The uncertainty came from the FA investigation, which wasn't resolved until October. In the end he was given a fine and a suspended six-week ban.

"Obviously, it's never easy to work on a daily basis if you have some uncertainty, and that's not just for me," he says. "I think it's the same for everyone at the football club.

"But I think we found a way, even in the first block of games, to perform. There's always something going on in football, sometimes a little bit bigger and sometimes not as big, but you need to push that to the side and make sure you find a way to perform.

"Once the decision came, I think it was important for everyone that we could finally close that."

For Eckert and Southampton it is just about points on the board, now. Trying to make up the deficit they were dealt at the start of the season.

"Obviously, if you could choose, no one would choose to start the season on minus four points," he says. "That's what it is. I think we are strong enough to make our way forward in the table.

"You shouldn't underestimate us coming from behind. We've shown that we are able to chase teams down, and that's the job for this year.

"It's been important for us to get some points on the board early in the season. We are still not where we want to be towards the end, so we need to make sure we continue."

Last week, Southampton handed Eckert, still just 33, a contract extension until 2029. They clearly feel he is their man to get them back to where they want to be.

"I think we've always been very open with our ambitions," he says. "There's no point in hiding that.

"I think the conditions are there to go up. It's never easy, but it's for us now to finish the job."

Sports.title: Taylor and Lewis suffer five straight defeats on Modus Super Series return
Sports.content:
Phil 'The Power' Taylor and Adrian Lewis suffered five losses from five matches for England at Thursday's Modus Super Series International Pairs Tournament in Portsmouth.

Taylor, now 66, retired from the competitive circuit in 2018, five years after claiming his 16th and final world title. However, the 16-time world champion returned to action to partner his long-time friend Lewis for the tournament.

Their opening match on Thursday saw them face Scotland's John Henderson and Robert Thornton, with the England pair suffering a narrow 4-3 defeat.

Things failed to improve in their second outing, as Taylor and Lewis were beaten 4-2 by Sweden's Andreas Harrysson and Anton Ostlund.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Taylor takes his first dart at double and checks out 84 in his competitive comeback in Modus Super Series International

A shock 4-3 defeat to unheralded Swiss duo Ansh Sood and Marcel Walpen followed, before Taylor and Lewis suffered a fourth consecutive loss, going down 4-1 to Germany's Daniel Klose and Liam Maendl-Lawrance.

Their fifth and final group-stage outing saw England take a 2-1 lead against Denmark, the only other side in their pool yet to record a victory. However, Ivan Springborg Poulsen and Andreas Toft Jorgensen responded by winning the next three legs in succession to condemn the English pair to a 4-2 defeat and a fifth straight loss.

Taylor revealed in September that the opportunity to partner Lewis was enough to tempt him back to the oche, although his return is not expected to signal a permanent comeback.

The 16-time world champion, who recently underwent successful hip replacement surgery, previously enjoyed considerable success alongside Lewis, with the pair winning four World Cup of Darts titles together.

The Modus Super Series International Pairs Tournament continues in Portsmouth until November 28.

Sports.title: OLIVER HOLT: The day Tyson Fury threatened to have me 'annihilated' and my 'jaw broken' after I published his disturbing views on paedophilia, homosexuality and Satan - and the signs of his mental health struggles that were already there
Sports.content:
OLIVER HOLT: The day Tyson Fury threatened to have me 'annihilated' and my 'jaw broken' after I published his disturbing views on paedophilia, homosexuality and Satan - and the signs of his mental health struggles that were already there

Oliver Holt Chief Sports Writer

As the build-up to his eagerly awaited fight with Anthony Joshua in Cardiff next month gathers pace, a new Netflix documentary about Tyson Fury will hit our screens on Friday. There is, apparently, no mention of the backdated two-year doping ban he served between December 2015 and December 2017, which is disappointing but predictable.

There is another episode that I would wager ended up on the cutting room floor, too. In November 2015, a few days before Fury beat Wladimir Klitschko for the world heavyweight title, the fight that changed his life for better and for worse, he gave an interview to Kugan Cassius of the popular iFLTV channel.

Fury and his entourage – including his brother, Shane, and one of his team, 'Cliff' – were in the thick of fight week but when Cassius asked the Gypsy King about the controversy that had followed an interview he had done with me in The Mail on Sunday a couple of weeks earlier, and mentioned my name, Fury’s expression changed.

‘Oliver “The W**kstain” Holt?’ Fury said, with the beginnings of a grin. ‘He tried his best to get me in trouble and it didn’t work, did it? So I’m not really too bothered what he does or anybody else like him. Men meet before mountains, don’t they?

‘And when they do, see Big Shane there, have a look at Big Shane, 6ft 6in and 25 stone, he’s going to break his jaw completely with one straight right hand. I’m not going to do it because I’ll get in trouble but the big fella there will annihilate him.

‘So Oliver, take a good look at him because that’s the face you’re going to see before you hit the deck. And that’s the face (gesturing towards Cliff) you’re going to see when he’s jumping up and down on your head. What are you going to do him, Cliff?’

‘I’m going to f**k him up,’ said Cliff.

I interviewed Tyson Fury back in November 2015, and the boxer caused outrage by conflating homosexuality and paedophilia

A few weeks later Fury beat Wladimir Klitschko in Germany to win the world heavyweight title

I did not want to be blasé but I did not take the threats too seriously. The Mail asked if I wanted to get the police involved and I declined. I took the threats as a mixture of bravado, bullying and slapstick. Boxing’s a rough trade and this was a long way from its outer borders. Fury’s nods to retribution felt more performative than sinister.

I was also aware by then that Fury’s mental health was in a precarious state. It is claimed in this new documentary that a few months after the threats he made to me, he was diagnosed with anxiety, depression, OCD, ADHD, bipolar disorder and schizophrenia.

Some years earlier, he had told the journalist Don McRae: ‘One minute I'm over the moon and the next minute, I feel like getting in my car and running it into a wall at a hundred miles an hour.’

And when we had talked a few weeks before the Klitschko fight, in an interview arranged at a hotel at Bolton Wanderers’ stadium, the base for his training camp, Fury had spoken in a stream of consciousness. He was hugely engaging and fascinating, too, but some of the things he said were disturbing as well as provocative.

‘We live in an evil world,’ he said that day. He spoke breathlessly and with the kind of troubled intensity that has never left him. ‘The devil is very strong at the minute, very strong, and I believe the end is near. The Bible tells me the end is near. The world tells me the end is near. Just a short few years away, I reckon, from being finished.

‘Abusing the planet, the wars in the Middle East, the famines, the earthquakes, the natural disasters, all these things were talked about 2,000 years ago. Prophesised. So now it’s all coming true…

‘There are only three things that need to be accomplished before the devil comes home: one of them is homosexuality being legal in countries, one of them is abortion and the other one’s paedophilia. Who would have thought in the 50s and 60s that those first two would be legalised?

‘When I say paedophiles can be made legal, that sounds like crazy talk doesn’t it? But back in the 50s and early 60s, for them first two to be made legal would have been looked on as a crazy man again. If I would have told you 120 years ago, that a 1,000-ton aeroplane is going to float through the sky, a piece of steel – ludicrous.

‘When Christopher Columbus said the world was round, he’s an idiot. All these things that happen in the world, wise men already know they’re going to happen and they see what they really are.

Fury on his way to a victory over Klitschko - who, he told me, was a devil-worshipper - that changed his life for better and for worse

Fury was incensed by the fact I reported what he had said in our interview in Bolton

‘Foolish people follow the system, get caught up in media news, what the government wants you to believe and all the higher powers want you to believe and go down the same path as all the sheep in the cattle market.’

And so it went on. Fury said that Klitschko was a devil-worshipper. ‘They are involved in bigger circles and stuff like that and they do magic tricks and whatever,’ he said. ‘All these rock stars and singers and these famous people, it is common knowledge that they are all involved in an occult group of Satan-worshippers and all that sort of stuff.’

Some of it felt like an extreme attempt to promote the fight with Klitschko. Fury was not box-office back then. He was on the margins. He was regarded as a talented, quirky curiosity but promoters were not quite sure what to do with the then-27-year-old. He had sublime skills but he was not an explosive fighter.

All that was about to change. The interview – and particularly his comments conflating homosexuality and paedophilia – caused outrage. He claimed, initially, that I had misquoted him but then the Mail on Sunday published the transcript of the conversation. He stopped claiming he had been misquoted.

He doubled down. He said he imagined Olympic champion heptathlete Jessica Ennis-Hill ‘slaps up good’ and that he believed ‘a woman's best place is in the kitchen and on her back’. There were demands he be removed from the shortlist for BBC Sports Personality of the Year, demands which the BBC resisted.

If the signs of his struggles with his mental health were already there before he produced a masterful performance to beat Klitschko in Dusseldorf in November 2015, his own version of shocking the world, the documentary charts Fury’s psychological and physical decline in the two years after it.

If Fury’s fight against Joshua next month feels like a natural end for what has become a remarkable career, the documentary paints a picture of that momentous victory over Klitschko 11 years ago as almost the beginning of the end.

It claims that triumph cast Fury into a pit of self-loathing and despair that contributed to him being diagnosed with schizophrenia several months later. He had started to hear voices in his head, he told Louis Theroux, in a podcast timed to coincide with the film’s release.

Fury poses for Daily Mail Sport at our 2015 interview

Fury will fight Anthony Joshua on December 11 in one of the most eagerly awaited Battles of Britain of all time

He suffered from cruel delusions that his wife, Paris, his dad and his best friend were involved in a plot to kill him. The revelations are such that, even though the alleged diagnosis is more than a decade old, they have prompted some disquiet about the fighter’s welfare and whether Fury should be allowed in the ring to face Joshua.

The Netflix documentary addresses some of this but skips over his ban for use of the anabolic steroid nandrolone and his former connections with management and promotions company MTK Global, whose boss was suspected Irish crime lord Daniel Kinahan.

‘I do like him,’ documentary-maker Lucy Wilcox told the media ahead of the film’s release. ‘He’s gentle, he’s quite camp, quite feminine. Not everyone’s gonna like Tyson, but I wanted people to understand him.

‘I wanted to understand him, because I wasn’t sure if I liked him. He’s not sexist, he’s not homophobic. But when you question him on certain things, he doubles down, like my kids would.’

A bizarre twist last night saw Paris claim her husband has not actually been diagnosed with schizophrenia — despite her saying so in the documentary — but it is undeniable that Fury has struggled with his mental health.

His openness in discussing it will have helped many people to confront their own issues and to attempt to get help for them. Fury deserves, and has been given, much praise for that.

It is also undeniable that Fury has caused a lot of a pain to others. And we are talking about the type of pain that goes beyond the kind he inflicts with his fists inside the ring.

The Netflix documentary presents the arc of his career as a redemption story but that is only partly true. If his openness about mental health has helped some people, his cruel comments about homosexuality and his casual misogyny will have caused hurt and pain in the lives of countless others and legitimised similar attitudes in the minds of the more impressionable of his fans.

In the decade and more since I spoke to him at what was then the Macron Stadium in Bolton, I have tried several times to arrange another interview, all without success. Frank Warren, his highly respected promoter, interceded on my behalf some years ago but to no avail.

In the decade and more since I spoke to him in Bolton, I have tried several times to arrange another interview, all without success

I don’t blame Fury for that. He can speak to whoever he wants and in the past few years, it has become unfashionably inconvenient to mention, or even to acknowledge the drugs ban and his links to Kinahan. It gets in the way of the redemption story and redemption sells better than a reality that is not quite so clear-cut.

The truth is that much of what Fury says and does is unsettling. It is the way he is and it is the way he wants it to be. He is a compelling talker, a conspiracy theorist, a man who wears a hat saying ‘Donald Trump for Prime Minister’ but he is not an urbane man. He is charismatic but it is not an easy charisma.

The worry – and he has admitted this himself – is that he will miss the discipline of boxing and training for fights when his career comes to an end. He is 38 now and he has enough money to last several lifetimes but no amount of money can buy him the peace that he finds through the purpose that boxing brings him.

It is the same for many sportsmen when it is over. They miss the lights. They miss the attention. They miss the focus. Fury has always been smart enough to recognise that there is a form of dependence there for him. Maybe that explains the fact there is an uneasy watchfulness about him. He prides himself on being awkward.

‘Awkwardness to the utmost, highest level,’ he said in that interview in Bolton in 2015. ‘Whatever is conventional, I am the opposite. If you want to walk in a straight line, I am going to walk in zig-zags. If you want to throw a one-two, I’ll throw a two-one. I don’t want to be an ordinary person. Because if you are ordinary, you do ordinary things.’

Sports.title: Pascal Gross interview: Brighton isn't a nice stepping stone club anymore. We're a big club who need to be ruthless - we can win every game
Sports.content:
Before Pascal Gross returned for his second spell at Brighton last January, he sat down for a rather frank conversation with manager Fabian Hurzeler. It was time, he suggested, for the club to take the next step. ‘There were some games in the past where we went (away to big teams) and you're not sure you can really do it,’ Gross tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘But we should now have a mindset that we can win every game. I really believe in that. We have the players. That’s what I said. ‘People say we are nice club and, yeah, maybe we are. But on the pitch, it was time to be ruthless. Time to kill games, be a big club. That’s what this is about now.’ Gross may feel his ambition has been vindicated, at least in part. Brighton sit second in the Premier League table, despite a disappointment at Hull last weekend that saw them lose a game they had dominated at the death. Gross, 35, ended that one on his knees in his own penalty area, having tried in vain to stop Oli McBurnie sliding in Hull’s second goal. ‘That felt really, really bad,’ he says. ‘Maybe today (Tuesday) is the first day I am starting to feel a bit better about it. I would be more worried if we didn’t create chances. We did. We just didn’t score.’ ‘On the pitch, it was time to be ruthless,' Pascal Gross tells Daily Mail Sport. 'Time to kill games, be a big club. That’s what this is about now’ Brighton sit second in the Premier League table, despite a disappointment at Hull last weekend that saw them lose a game they had dominated at the death Before Gross returned for his second spell at Brighton last January, he sat down for a rather frank conversation with manager Fabian Hurzeler

Your browser does not support iframes.

Brighton are six points behind leaders Arsenal – who they have already beaten 3-0 at the Amex – but are the Premier League’s top scorers by a distance, with 26. Gross, the German who returned to Sussex after a short spell at Borussia Dortmund, has created an astonishing 31 chances for his team. That puts him only two behind the best in the country this term, his friend and Germany team-mate Florian Wirtz. The debate about Wirtz’s value or otherwise to Liverpool has swirled around the country since he arrived at Liverpool in the summer of 2025 for £116million. The conversation even reached Brighton’s training ground. ‘Jamie Redknapp was there and he asked me all about it just a couple weeks ago,’ Gross explains. ‘I just told him: "He's too good not to prove himself." People here still don't know how good he is, but they will. He's a complete package and he knows I support him a lot. ‘Football is a team sport. It’s not ever on one person. Also, nobody should forget just how difficult and different the Premier League is when you first come.’ Gross knows this well. He smiles at the mention of his own first English away game – a 2-0 defeat at Leicester in August 2017 that brings to mind the Patrice Evra quote about his first experience of playing in England being akin to ‘an afternoon spent in a washing machine’. ‘I was on the floor so much that day that I looked like a little child,’ Gross recalls. ‘It was just all too physical. I knew I had to improve fast, play faster. My decision-making had to be quicker. ‘My father called me after and said I wouldn’t last three weeks if I played like that again. But I already knew. Going home that day, I really questioned a lot of things. But that’s just how hard it is when you come to the Premier League.’ Gross had a brutal introduction to the Premier League in 2017, but it was a reminder of the level he needed to reach Gross fires in Brighton's equaliser at Old Trafford in the Carabao Cup back in September. The Seagulls trailed 2-0 but fought back brilliantly to dump out Man United Brighton players Luka Vuskovic and Groß visit local independent restaurant Riddle & Finns to support American Express' Shop Small campaign The Hull game was Gross' 300th in a Brighton shirt, and he is perhaps playing at a higher level than ever with four goals and four assists in the first 11 league games this season, as well as a goal in the Carabao Cup win at Manchester United. On an official club podcast, former striker and team-mate Glenn Murray labelled him Brighton's best-ever player, and last week he signed a new contract keeping him on the south coast until the end of next season. Signed by Chris Hughton from Bundesliga side Ingolstadt after the Seagulls' promotion to the top division a little over nine years ago, Gross has had an inside view of the most successful period in the club’s history. During his time, Brighton have sold enough players for big profit to make a pretty good Premier League XI – Robert Sanchez, Ben White, Jan Paul van Hecke, Marc Cucurella, Moises Caicedo, Alexis Mac Allister, Leandro Trossard and Joao Pedro get you most of the way there, for a total transfer taking of £424m. Gross suspects there will be more over time. Equally, he feels the days of players using Brighton as a stepping stone to the next level are gone. A lack of commitment soon gets sniffed out, he says. ‘There have been players who saw it like that,’ he explains. ‘And they couldn't even get in our team because they came with the wrong mindset. If you don't have the right mentality, you don't want to work every day, you can't get in the Brighton team. ‘And if you do come with the right mentality and you push every day, and the team is doing well, I always say that good things will come for everybody – for the club, for the coaches, for the players. ‘I love the club, and we have big potential. There will always be players that move on. But I think the players who come here now, they know we are bigger than a jumping club. We're a big club in the Premier League. We have been there almost 10 years and are improving all the time.’ Gross thought hard before first leaving Germany for England. He visited Brighton’s training ground twice before making his decision and, once he had, dug down into the individual statistics of the players who would soon be team-mates. Gross (right) has seen a huge change at Brighton since joining from Bundesliga side Ingolstadt, where he played under former Southampton manager Ralph Hasenhuttl (left) Brighton's form this season has been inspired by a prolific attack, with their 26 Premier League goals by far the most in the division They have progressed season on season despite the departure of a host of star players for big money, including Alexis Mac Allister (right) to Liverpool for £35m in 2023 Having married and had two children in Sussex, Gross has the club in his heart and soul now. We meet to talk at beachfront restaurant Riddle & Finns as part of American Express’s Shop Small campaign, encouraging people to support local business. During his spell at Dortmund – who he adored as a boy – Gross watched every Brighton game on TV. But it may not have been this way. There was a time, in pre-season 2020, when former Brighton manager Graham Potter told Gross he could leave. ‘That was hard to take,’ Gross says. ‘I asked him if there was no chance at all of me playing. I needed to know if he saw me as, like, No17 or 18 in the squad so that whatever I did, I wouldn't play. Or in his mind was I 12, 13 or 14? ‘Then I figured I could work my way back into the team because I would always back myself to prove the manager wrong. We lost a lot of games and eventually, I came back into the team.’ Gross’s approach back then was to train as well and as hard as he could. Murray recalls that his attitude stood out. ‘It wasn’t my team-mates’ fault I wasn’t playing,’ explains Gross. ‘Why would I take it out on them? That wouldn’t make sense.’ Culture is often discussed in modern football but it’s just a new word for an old truth: unhappy football teams tend to fail. ‘There are days when you see, maybe, that the way we play gives an opponent frustration and you can see bad body language,’ Gross says. ‘That's where I sense we have them. ‘It wasn’t my team-mates’ fault I wasn’t playing,’ explains Gross, pictured celebrating the win at Man City with Jack Hinshelwood. ‘Why would I take it out on them? That wouldn’t make sense’ 'If you don't have the right mentality, you don't want to work every day, you can't get in the Brighton team' 'Players who come here now, they know we are bigger than a jumping club. We're a big club in the Premier League' ‘But there are also teams who maybe struggle but they are still together and they're still fighting and you see a group of guys who can still be hard to beat. That’s about culture. It’s important and I think we value that here.’ As part of Brighton’s leadership group, Gross speaks regularly to manager and compatriot Hurzeler. His personal creed is that confidence should never bleed into arrogance – ‘I just hate that’ – and he believes that Hurzeler, known to rub the occasional manager up the wrong way, is on the right side of the line. ‘He is pushing, pushing,’ Gross says with a smile. ‘He has so much passion for the job, he puts so much work into it. He wants to challenge, he wants to think differently. ‘He doesn't want to think: “Everything is nice." He really wants to push himself and us. And that balance is a really fine balance. He's trying to stretch the limit and I think that's good.’ Pascal Gross is supporting American Express Shop Small, which aims to support small businesses by encouraging the nation to back their local high street on Small Business Saturday and beyond. This year, American Express is investing £1million in new Shop Small grants, offering 100 independent UK businesses £10,000 each to help them grow, innovate and invest in their future. Visit go.amex/shopsmalluk

Sports.title: 'I've got the same mentality as when I was five years old': Rugby's global superstar ANTOINE DUPONT opens up on fame, France's 'exciting' showdown with South Africa - and England's 'impressive' revival
Sports.content:
'I've got the same mentality as when I was five years old': Rugby's global superstar ANTOINE DUPONT opens up on fame, France's 'exciting' showdown with South Africa - and England's 'impressive' revival

It is a peculiar feeling to be in the presence of rugby greatness.

Spend even a short amount of time with the likes of Martin Johnson, Dan Carter, Richie McCaw, Jonny Wilkinson or Sir Gareth Edwards, and the sense that they have achieved something extraordinary in their chosen field radiates from them.

With England’s World Cup-winning captain Johnson, it comes from his sheer presence. The giant stature and steely gaze. The late Jonah Lomu was a similarly imposing figure.

His fellow All Blacks Carter and McCaw possess a film star-like pizazz. For Edwards, it is a regality, the glories of yesteryear unspoken.

In the case of Antoine Dupont, undoubtedly worthy of being compared to these greats, it is slightly different. Small in stature at less than 6ft, France’s captain does not dominate a room physically.

He is softly spoken too, either in his native tongue or his impressively well-spoken English. A non-sports fan might not immediately pick him out as a superstar.

But when he steps between the white lines, Dupont becomes a gladiator – a man capable of otherworldly feats. He has proved that once again this month, producing a string of mesmeric individual displays to lead France into Sunday’s Nations Championship final with South Africa.

Antoine Dupont's France and Siya Kolisi's South Africa will meet at Twickenham on Sunday to decide the winner of the Nations Championship

Dupont may not be the tallest of rugby's all-time greats, but he becomes a gladiator on the pitch

Dupont is one of rugby’s true global icons, a man of whom France expects so much. Fortunately for them, Dupont invariably delivers – and plans on doing so again as Les Bleus bid to win a cross-hemisphere competition for the first time in their history.

‘I’ve been used to having this kind of pressure on my rugby, but also outside the pitch, for the last five or six years,’ he tells Daily Mail Sport.

‘I've learned how to deal with it and to keep the passion. It's the same as what's been driving me since my first year playing rugby when I was five years old. Then, I just wanted to be on the rugby field with a ball in my hands. I try to keep this same mentality now. Honestly, I just live my life normally.

‘I walk the dog. I have a coffee. I’m very lucky because my family lives just one hour from Toulouse (where Dupont plays his club rugby). It’s very important for me to spend time with them and my childhood friends. It’s the simple things when you have the opportunity to think about something other than rugby.’

Dupont's glittering career so far... and he's only 30! Six Nations titles: 3 (2022, 2025, 2026) Six Nations grand slams: 1 (2022) TOP14 wins: 6 (2019, 2021, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026) European Champions Cups: 2 (2021, 2024) Olympic golds: 1 (2024, in rugby sevens) World Rugby men’s 15s player of the year: 1 (2021) World Rugby men’s sevens player of the year: 1 (2024) Player of the Six Nations: 3 (2020, 2022, 2023) European player of the year: 2 (2021, 2024)

Dupont turned 30 a few weeks ago. A Nations Championship winner’s medal would add to his impressive CV – one which already contains a dozen major honours.

A second straight victory over South Africa is his latest target. Dupont played a starring role when France beat the back-to-back world champions in a compelling match in Paris earlier this month.

‘This is a new competition and for us to play a final in an international competition, is a great challenge – a first,’ says Dupont. ‘South Africa are probably the best team at the moment, so it's very exciting for us.

'Obviously, we have some good memories of the last game, but we can trust the Springboks to be strong in big moments. They’ve proved it for the last few years, so I think it will be even harder to win on Sunday.’

Dupont also had words of praise for England’s performances this autumn, particularly in their record win over New Zealand.

‘They were very impressive. In the last game, I found them in very good shape,’ he adds. ‘It was very hard for the All Blacks to stop their offensive line. So, we will have a lot of work to do during the Six Nations. It’s good to see the northern teams in good shape.’

In the 2025 Six Nations, Dupont suffered the second serious knee injury of his career – one which kept him out until December of last year. He returned better than ever, leading a French side weakened by injury issues of their own to a string of successes. Fabien Galthie, the French coach, has used a mammoth 50 players across the summer and autumn windows.

When his team beat South Africa earlier this month, he was without 25 men, including many of his leading lights. Led by the effervescent Dupont, his team still downed the Springboks in what was a battle for the ages.

A similar game is expected in the final. A win would take France top of World Rugby’s rankings for only the second time in their history.

Dupont has returned better than ever since his knee injury during the 2025 Six Nations

France have already beaten South Africa this month, in a 21-19 thriller in Paris

Dupont's relationship with Miss Universe winner Iris Mittenaere is the source of plenty of media attention in his homeland

‘This tournament has shown the depth of the players in France,’ says Dupont, whose high-profile relationship with Iris Mittenaere, a model, television presenter and former Miss France and Miss Universe winner, is big news in his homeland.

‘We know French players play a lot of games every year and it's hard to have the best players in the best shape all the time. So, we were a bit worried at the beginning of the competition. We had to go on our summer tour without the players from the TOP14 finalists, which is probably crazy for other countries.

'This is our situation in France. It's very uncommon. But we have to deal with it. We are very proud for the team to finish first in the northern hemisphere after this very demanding competition. It's a huge thing. I feel very good.

'When I finished the last Six Nations, I was so tired. And with our calendar, it's very hard to rest. I had to finish my season, but it wasn't an easy task for me. The summer break helped me a lot to have some rest and to prepare well for the beginning of the TOP14 and to be in my best shape in November and hopefully for the end of the season.’

Including an Olympic gold in sevens, Dupont has won almost everything rugby has to offer. If he lifts the inaugural Nations Championship, the only thing left outstanding will be a World Cup. South Africa knocked France out of their own global showpiece in 2023. Galthie and France have vowed to go 'all in' on their latest Springbok clash, with a trophy on the line.

‘There are not a lot of players in our team today who played in the quarter-final in 2023,’ says Dupont. ‘Obviously, we have some bad memories of the result. But it's a different story, different context, and we're really focused on 2027. This weekend will be a huge step on the way.’

Sports.title: Former world champion boxer known as 'Beefy' denies punching hotel concierge 'and attacking man as he lay on the floor'
Sports.content:
Former world champion boxer known as 'Beefy' denies punching hotel concierge 'and attacking man as he lay on the floor'

Former world champion boxer Liam Smith has denied attacking a man at a luxury apartment block.

Smith, 38, who held the WBO light-middleweight title from 2015 to 2016, allegedly punched the concierge worker outside the Blade, in Manchester city centre.

The alleged attack, on September 13, is said to have happened as the man lay on the floor and he suffered facial injuries that needed hospital treatment.

The fighter - nicknamed 'Beefy' - appeared at Manchester Crown Court on Thursday and denied charges of causing grievous bodily harm with intent and inflicting grievous bodily harm.

He did not enter a plea to a public order charge of racially aggravated behaviour over alleged 'racist words' he used prior to the alleged attack.

Smith was granted bail with conditions not to contact the complainant, and not to enter Manchester, unless to attend court, or for appointments with his solicitor.

He's due to face trial on March 15, 2028.

Smith, now of Formby in Sefton, was due to make a comeback in a fight on 4 September in Finland, but pulled out due to a calf injury, according to reports.

Former world champion boxer Liam Smith has denied attacking a man at a luxury apartment block

Smith, 38, who held the WBO light-middleweight title from 2015 to 2016, allegedly punched the concierge worker outside the Blade, in Manchester city centre

He is one of four Liverpool brothers who all boxed professionally and all won titles at British level and has fought some of the biggest names in the sport including a defeat to Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez.

Smith won the vacant WBO light-middleweight world title in October 2015 when he stopped American John Thompson in Manchester and successfully defended the belt twice before losing it to Mexican superstar Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez the following year.

A former Commonwealth and British champion, Smith compiled a record of 33 wins, four defeats and one draw across a professional career spanning almost two decades.

More recently he fought British rival Chris Eubank Jr twice, defeating him in the first fight in January 2023, before suffering a defeat in the rematch eight months later.

Sports.title: Inside Arsenal's tifo culture: how the Emirates banner at last year's PSG semi-final that fell flat led to fans taking control.... as they prepare to unveil new design for Sunday's showdown with Man City
Sports.content:
Tifos are back at the Emirates. Those loud, passionate designs which last season galvanised Arsenal en route to a first Premier League title in 22 years return on Sunday for the visit of Manchester City.

An emotionally-charged fixture between the title holders and the team found guilty of the majority of 115 breaches of the league’s financial rules by an independent commission (which is being appealed by Man City) awaits.

Still, it can be revealed that Sunday’s display will be more restrained than initially considered.

Daily Mail Sport understands that a supporter-led group, established by the Arsenal Advisory Board (AAB) last season, initially raised an idea with Arsenal of referencing Man City’s charges in the tifo. However, following consultation with the club, collectively the idea was dropped.

Instead the tifo will be done ‘in the Arsenal way to inspire the fanbase’, a source says. They added: ‘It will galvanise and charge the fans in the right way.’

These matters can often be delicate. For example, it’s understood a debate was had over the north London derby tifo ahead of Arsenal vs Tottenham in November 2025 at the Emirates, which involved a montage of club icons from past and present. And at the very top, positioned deliberately, sat Sol Campbell.

Sol Campbell, perched atop this Arsenal tifo for the derby game against Tottenham last season, moved between the clubs in a highly contentious transfer in 2001

What Arsenal offered on that PSG night in 2025 caused embarrassment – a solitary white cannon on a red backdrop

His 2001 move from Spurs to the Gunners remains one of the rivalry’s deepest fault lines. Arsenal initially thought it could be too provocative but proceeded as the group were adamant on the imagery.

The reception when the tifo unveiled was immediate. The players felt it. The supporters felt it. Thierry Henry himself shared the image on social media with a simple verdict: ‘What a tifo! Thank you, Gooners!’

As revealed in the book 22 Years: The Inside Story of Arsenal’s Title-Winning Season, later in the season Mikel Arteta met up with the creators to say thank you and gifted each of them a signed, framed picture of the Tottenham tifo. Stuart MacFarlane, the club’s chief photographer, was also there to take pictures of the group alongside Arteta. The Spaniard privately values the energy these displays create and embraces them.

It’s understood Arteta checks the tifo designs before they are finalised. Much work goes into creating them, as reflected in the final proposal for Sunday’s tifo which had to be confirmed and sent to the manufacturers nearly three weeks before matchday.

The artwork is printed on a square shape canvas which is then cut out and backed onto a paper-like material. That is cable-tied to a huge rectangular netting and tied to the roof with further cables and ropes.

The design along with the attached apparatus weighs around a couple of hundred kilograms, which is a serious amount. The lightweight fabric also has to be fire retardant and meet weight restrictions.

The work involved in putting the tifo together has seen volunteers invited to the Hale End academy this Friday to cable tie the tifo and get the design laid out on an indoor pitch.

Budgets have to be met, too, for the group are allocated an undisclosed amount to cover tifos for the whole season. Blowing the budget on one or two displays would rule out further spectacles later in the season.

The latest design builds on a growing trend which Arsenal began to grasp just over a year ago, the mission to properly create tifos initially starting in April 2025. Arsenal had unveiled their own tifo ahead of a Champions League semi-final first leg against Paris Saint-Germain — the first to be draped from the Emirates Stadium’s roof in the arena’s history.

For those confused by the term ‘tifo’, it stems from the Italian word tifosi, meaning passionate supporters. The designs are an attempt to galvanise fans, building an atmosphere with powerful messaging and provocative imagery to unsettle opponents.

Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta checks the tifo designs before they are unveiled

What Arsenal offered on that PSG night was widely mocked – a solitary white cannon on a red backdrop. That was it. A sterile design for one of the biggest European nights the Emirates had ever hosted, at that time.

It’s understood a club-produced design had been used over a fan-led alternative, mainly because there was limited time between the proposal and the game itself.

The episode proved to be a pivotal turning point, led by the AAB.

The AAB is the club’s formal fan-engagement body, created in 2021 following the backlash over Arsenal’s involvement in the wretched European Super League plot — a breakaway competition set to feature 12 of Europe’s leading clubs. The subsequent supporter anger forced Arsenal to improve their communication with fans.

After the PSG tifo disappointment, the AAB helped create a new group for the start of the 2025–26 season focused on creating tifos. Arsenal wanted to learn from the error, and this was their way of putting fans back in control.

It’s worked. The outcome resulted in a slew of eye-catching displays in the previous campaign from Campbell to Leandro Trossard’s eye-goggles celebration for the ‘history in our sights’ tifo ahead of the Champions League quarter-final second leg against Sporting Lisbon — or the ‘over land and sea’ design with a huge ship for the semi-final second leg against Atletico Madrid.

By softening the parameters and letting fan representatives into the inner sanctum, Arsenal have utilised a marginal gain Arteta had craved ever since he took charge seven years ago — make the Emirates a fortress.

While there was an initial temptation from the AAB to reference Man City’s guilty verdict in Sunday’s tifo, the overall message will be unmistakably clear: Arsenal are now in charge.
