World.title: Gérard Depardieu to stand trial for alleged rape of actress in 2018, court rules
World.content:
French film actor GÃ©rard Depardieu is to stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, a Paris appeals court has confirmed.

Arnould, who was 22 at the time, had reported the alleged rape several days after going to his house in Paris to rehearse a play.

She has waived her right to anonymity and her lawyer said Thursday's ruling was a "first" and the forthcoming trial would be historic.

Depardieu, 77, had contested his indictment on two counts of rape. In a letter published in Le Figaro in 2023, Depardieu strongly denied Arnould's allegations, saying "there was never any coercion or violence between us".

Depardieu was for decades a leading figure in French and international cinema for roles in Green Card, The Man in the Iron Mask and the Asterix films. He was awarded France's LÃ©gion d'honneur in 1996.

But in recent years a series of allegations have been made against him over his conduct on film sets and elsewhere in the wake of France's #MeToo movement, known as balance ton porc (call out your pig).

Last year, he was given an 18-month suspended jail term after he was found guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set in Paris in May. He was also placed on the sex offenders register and ordered to pay compensation.

He dropped his appeal against the ruling last week and offered "sincere apologies" for his behaviour on the set of director Jean Becker's 2021 film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters).

Depardieu had been a friend of Charlotte Arnould's father and on 7 August 2018 she had gone to his home, where much of what happened was captured on the actor's own CCTV.

Arnould's case was initially dismissed for insufficient evidence, but after she filed a civil complaint, a judicial investigation was opened in the summer of 2020.

Speaking outside the Paris appeal court on Thursday, her lawyer Carine Durrieu Diebolt said the ruling was a victory for her client for whom it was "genuinely a relief".

The appeal court said that while Depardieu should stand trial for what took place on that day, he would not be tried for a further alleged rape at a hotel six days later.

Depardieu's lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski told reporters that court had partly ruled in his favour: "As soon as we get the ruling, we will look into the possibility of appealing to the Court of Cassation."

Meanwhile, Depardieu is under a separate investigation alongside French author Michel Houellebecq for "allegations of a sexual nature".

French authorities confirmed their inquiry last week, following reports of an alleged "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line.

World.title: Diesel tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes capsizes near Ibiza, killing one
World.content:
An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has capsized off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have said.

The Med Emre, a Malta-flagged vessel, was carrying 17 crew members who were all rescued. However seven were taken to hospital and one was later pronounced dead, Balearic Islands emergency services confirmed.

The six crew receiving treatment reportedly suffered minor injuries, such as hypothermia, Spanish media reports.

The possible environmental damage is being assessed by a plane and Spain's pollution control vessel, Clara Campoamor, which is owned by the country's national maritime rescue service.

"There is still little information available about a possible fuel spill," Balearic Islands' President Marga Prohens wrote on X.

Elena Delgado, maritime captain of Valencia, told news agency AFP that a small slick that had formed around the boat had "disappeared".

"The situation is stabilised," she said, adding that further inspections would be carried out on Friday morning.

Earlier, regional emergencies director Pablo GÃ¡rriz said the tanker had not completely sunk, as had originally been reported. The vessel remains partially submerged.

The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia. It is unclear what caused the sinking.

The chemical tanker was en route from Algeciras, in southern Spain, to Barcelona in the north-east.

World.title: Lawmaker woos challenger after Appeal Court victory
World.content:
The Court of Appeal in Abuja has dismissed an appeal challenging the election of Yusuf Gagdi, a member of the House of Representatives representing Pankshin/Kanke/Kanam Federal Constituency of Plateau State.

The appellate court, sitting on Thursday, dismissed the appeal filed by John Gozhak against Mr Gagdi. It also partially allowed a separate appeal filed by the APC, according to a statement issued by Mr Gagdi.

The ruling followed an earlier judgement of the Federal High Court in Jos, which had ruled in favour of the lawmaker.

Reacting to the decision, Mr Gagdi described the judgment as a victory for democracy and the people of Pankshin, Kanke, and Kanam, urging his supporters to avoid triumphalism and embrace reconciliation.

He said the outcome should not deepen political divisions in the constituency, insisting that the dispute was a contest between political actors and should not turn them into enemies.

“Political contests may place us on different sides, but they must never make us enemies. Beyond every aspiration lies a greater obligation: the peace, unity and development of our constituency,” he said.

The lawmaker also invited Mr Gozhak and others who opposed him during the legal process to work together for the constituency’s development.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“I extend my hand of fellowship to Hon. Dr John Tongshinen Gozhak and everyone with whom we have differed during this process. Let us embrace reconciliation, join the winning team and work together in the interest of Pankshin, Kanke and Kanam,” he added.

The legal dispute dates back to the APC primary election for the constituency ahead of the 2027 general elections.

The party initially announced Mr Gozhak as the winner of the primary conducted in May 2026. However, the APC subsequently reversed the announcement, declaring Mr Gagdi the winner and dismissing the earlier result as unauthorised.

Dissatisfied with the development, Mr Gozhak approached the Federal High Court in Jos, challenging Mr Gagdi’s emergence as the party’s candidate.

In the suit marked FHC/J/CS/39/2026, he asked the court to determine whether the primary election complied with the Electoral Act and the APC’s guidelines. He also sought orders setting aside Mr Gagdi’s nomination and recognising him as the party’s candidate.

However, on 17 September, Judge Sharon Tanko struck out the suit, holding that Mr Gozhak had relied on provisions of the Electoral Act 2022, which had been repealed and replaced by the Electoral Act 2026.

The court consequently declined jurisdiction to determine the substantive claims. The judgment did not determine all the allegations surrounding the conduct of the APC primary.

Thursday’s Court of Appeal decision represents another development in the prolonged dispute over the APC ticket, with Mr Gagdi now announcing the dismissal of Mr Gozhak’s appeal.

In his statement, the lawmaker also urged his supporters not to use the judgement as an opportunity to attack or ridicule political opponents.

“I urge you to celebrate with decorum, humility and respect for democracy. Let there be no insults, provocation or humiliation of anyone,” he said.

He added that the outcome should strengthen efforts to unite the constituency rather than create further divisions.

Gagdi congratulates Lalong

In a related development, Mr Gagdi congratulated former Plateau State Governor and Senator representing Plateau South, Simon Lalong, on a Federal High Court judgement delivered on Wednesday.

According to Mr Gagdi, the court affirmed Mr Lalong’s nomination as the APC candidate for Plateau South Senatorial District.

He described the ruling as a significant victory for the former governor and his supporters, wishing him continued strength in his service to the people.

Mr Gagdi also thanked the APC leadership, his legal team, party stakeholders and supporters for their roles throughout the legal proceedings.

He acknowledged the judiciary’s role in resolving political disputes through lawful processes, saying the outcome carried a responsibility to unite the people and deliver development.

“Our victory carries a responsibility: to unite our people, deepen service and deliver progress. With renewed resolve, we move forward together,” he said.

World.title: 2027 Polls: INEC to deploy electronic checks to prevent result manipulation
World.content:
The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) says it has introduced an electronic version of the polling unit result sheet, designed to prevent discrepancies between results recorded manually and those uploaded to its result viewing portal ahead of the 2027 general election.

The commission said the new system, which operates alongside the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS), would block the upload of results where figures entered electronically do not tally with information on the physical Form EC8A.

INEC’s Director of Voter Education and Publicity, Victoria Eta-Messi, disclosed this on Thursday during an X Space conversation organised by Yiaga Africa, titled ‘Testing BVAS, Testing IReV, Testing Trust: What INEC Must Get Right’.

She said the electronic result sheet identified as EEC8A was introduced as an accountability mechanism to address concerns about the integrity of results uploaded to the INEC Result Viewing Portal (IReV).

Under the arrangement, polling officials must enter the figures recorded on the physical Form EC8A into the electronic version on the BVAS. The system checks the entries against accreditation figures and other relevant information before permitting the results to be uploaded.

“We saw that there were also other mischievous attempts by poll officials, where at the backend you would see things that were far from being an election result. So the EEC8A has been input into the BVAS, which now allows you to input the data on the EEC8A physically, and it must match your accreditation figures as well. It helps you to correct yourself,” she said.

Ms Eta-Messi explained that where discrepancies are detected, the system would prevent the upload and allow officials to review and correct genuine mistakes before proceeding.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“So, it will block you if your entries are not correct. That is one of the major reasons why the EEC8A was introduced, to self-correct you and also to ensure that anyone who is trying to be mischievous will not get away with it,” she said.

The commission’s planned nationwide mock accreditation and result management exercise on Saturday, 28 November, will test the system’s functionality ahead of the 2027 elections.

Testing the system after 2023 failures

The exercise comes against the backdrop of controversies surrounding the electronic transmission of presidential election results during the 2023 general election, which significantly weakened public confidence in INEC’s electoral technology.

During the 2023 elections, the commission’s failure to upload presidential election results to IReV in real time triggered widespread criticism and questions about its commitment to transparency.

Ms Eta-Messi said the commission had acknowledged the technical challenges encountered during the elections and explained that the volume of data generated by the presidential election contributed to the failure.

She said the mock exercise would allow INEC to test whether its infrastructure could accommodate election data on a nationwide scale, unlike previous off-cycle elections, which generated smaller volumes of information.

“The commission wants to conduct a mock exercise so that we will test the system to be sure that it has the capacity to take on the data that it receives at a national level ahead of the election,” she said.

She added that identifying technical problems before the main election would give the commission time to address them.

“We should discover the gap now rather than being taken by surprise on election day,” she said, explaining that the commission would rather identify and resolve problems during the mock exercise than encounter them during the general election.

According to the INEC official, the exercise will cover 17,676 polling units across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), with mock accreditation, voting, counting, and electronic transmission of results.

According to Ms Eta-Messi, the exercise will use dummy ballots and fictitious political party names rather than the actual names of political parties.

Polling, she said, is scheduled to begin at 8:30 a.m. and end at 2:30 p.m as voters in the selected polling units are expected to present their Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) for accreditation before participating in the mock voting exercise.

Lawyer questions INEC’s explanation

However, the commission’s explanation did little to address concerns raised by lawyer and social commentator Inibehe Effiong, who questioned its credibility as an explanation for the 2023 IReV failure.

Mr Effiong argued that the commission had taken too long to adequately explain what happened during the 2023 elections, noting that its handling of the controversy contributed to public distrust.

“I heard the explanation, the familiar one, yet not satisfactory to some of us,” he said.

He faulted the commission for failing to address public concerns promptly after the 2023 elections, recalling what he described as the former INEC chairman’s arrogance when the issue was raised at the National Collation Centre.

He also rejected the explanation that the failure resulted from inadequate testing of the system at the scale of a national election.

“I do not accept the explanation that the reason why INEC failed was that there was no mock test or accreditation at the level with the kind of spread that they want to experiment now. I do not have any scientific basis to support this explanation,” he said.

Mr Effiong maintained that IReV remained fundamental to electoral transparency because it allows citizens to scrutinise polling unit results independently.

“The reason why IReV is so fundamental is that it is what I call a self-censoring device. It is a self-censoring technology. It is a technology that allows the commission to fact-check itself,” he said.

He urged INEC to give Nigerians clear assurances that the technology would work in 2027 and to explain contingency arrangements in the event of another failure.

He also questioned provisions in the Electoral Act that allow the use of physical result forms where electronic transmission fails, arguing that the commission must demonstrate how it would guarantee transparency under such circumstances.

Voters’ register remains a concern

A PREMIUM TIMES journalist, Qosim Suleiman, also identified the results transmission process and the integrity of the voters’ register as major concerns ahead of the 2027 elections.

He said although BVAS had recorded considerable success in voter accreditation, public concerns following the 2023 elections were largely centred on the failure to upload results transparently.

“From my understanding and reporting, and talking to people, the BVAS is not exactly the major concern for people. It is in a way, but not exactly the major concern,” he said.

Mr Suleiman said the commission’s planned exercise would be meaningful if it tested the entire results management and transmission process rather than focusing mainly on accreditation.

He also questioned INEC’s handling of irregular registrations discovered during the recent voter registration exercise, noting that some questionable profiles remained visible on the online register despite assurances that the commission had begun a clean-up.

He said the continued presence of questionable entries raised concerns about the extent of the commission’s efforts to sanitise the register.

Responding to the concerns, INEC’s Resident Electoral Commissioner in Edo State, Obo Effanga, said the commission had removed several irregular registrations identified during the display of the provisional voters’ register.

He explained that the register initially contained more than 103 million entries following the registration exercise conducted between August 2025 and July 2026.

However, after Nigerians submitted complaints and observations during the claims and objections process, the commission reduced the figure to slightly above 100 million.

Mr Effanga said some irregularities included fictitious names, duplicate photographs, and multiple registrations, some of which had remained in the register for years because of limitations in the technology the commission had previously deployed.

He said the commission had also identified suspicious registrations arising from the introduction of online voter registration.

The REC maintained that even where an irregular registration had resulted in the issuance of a PVC, the holder would not be allowed to vote if the person’s name had been removed from the final register.

“If you have a PVC and your name is not on the voters’ register, you cannot vote,” he said.

He added that the final register would be published on 15 December.

Mr Effanga also disclosed that INEC had postponed its planned nationwide voter revalidation exercise until after the 2027 general election because of its proximity to the polls.

Election officials also under scrutiny

Beyond the technology, participants at the discussion warned that the competence of election officials would be equally important in determining the credibility of the 2027 elections.

Akindeji Aromaye, senior media associate at Enough is Enough Nigeria, said the commission needed to demonstrate that its personnel could properly operate BVAS, authenticate voters and complete result sheets under actual election conditions.

He cited observations from the 2026 off-cycle governorship elections in Osun and Ekiti, where observers reportedly documented officials struggling with biometric accreditation and completing Form EC8A properly.

He said discussing BVAS and IReV without considering the people who operate them overlooks an important part of the electoral process.

“Sometimes we discuss BVAS and IReV as though the technology operates independently, and it actually doesn’t,” he said.

Mr Aromaye said the mock exercise should assess whether election officials could perform their responsibilities correctly under pressure, rather than establish the number of personnel recruited or trained.

He added that the exercise should also test the support system available to officials when they encounter technical difficulties.

“It should not only test whether the devices work. It should also test whether the support system responds effectively when they encounter problems,” he said.

He further called for clearer communication from INEC on the procedures officials must follow when equipment malfunctions or other problems arise at polling units.

Yiaga Africa to deploy 300 observers

Meanwhile, the Executive Director of Yiaga Africa, Samson Itodo, said the organisation would deploy 300 observers to monitor the mock exercise.

He said the observers would assess the performance of BVAS and IReV, while the organisation would also deploy its election results analysis dashboard to monitor the process.

Mr Itodo said the exercise would provide an opportunity to assess whether the commission could identify and address weaknesses before the general election.

“Let us overwhelm the system and test whether this system that INEC has created will be functional,” he said.

He added that Yiaga Africa would publish its findings and subsequently convene another X Space discussion to assess the exercise, identify gaps and examine lessons for the 2027 elections.

Mr Itodo urged Nigerians in the selected polling units to participate in the exercise and share their experiences with civil society organisations.

He said the commission must remain open to scrutiny, adding that Nigerians and civil society organisations should continue to hold it accountable.

World.title: Beyond extractive banking (1): Who bears the risk of Nigeria’s industrialisation?, By Dipo Baruwa
World.content:
Nigeria has largely socialised the responsibility for industrial development while privatising much of its risk. Government expects commercial banks and entrepreneurs to carry substantial parts of the risks associated with productive transformation, while government itself competes for the same pool of domestic capital by offering relatively attractive, comparatively low-risk sovereign instruments.

This then begs a more fundamental question: is Nigeria truly aspiring to become a socio-economically developed and industrialised economy, or have industrialisation policies gradually become little more than recurrent aspirations — sing-songs of development announced to signal intent while the broader political-economic system continues to work against their achievement?

This is not an accusation directed at the current leadership of the country. The contradiction predates it. Successive governments have progressively constructed a fiscal, monetary and financial architecture whose incentives frequently run against the country’s stated industrial ambitions. The structure has become so deeply embedded that each succeeding government inherits not merely a policy problem, but an institutional system that has become increasingly difficult to reengineer.

Beyond Blaming the Banks

Lately, I have been thinking and writing about Nigeria’s financial system. I had provocatively described it as “the new extractive industry” — not because banks and financial institutions produce nothing of value, nor because their operators are uniquely responsible for the problem, but because much of the system increasingly appears structured to extract value from economic activity rather than deliberately participate in building the productive capabilities from which sustainable value can be created.

It would be convenient to blame the banks.

Their profits are visible. Their charges are visible. Their appetite for government securities is visible. And their lending rates to productive enterprises can appear almost irreconcilable with the country’s industrial aspirations.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

And have I not done some of that in my recent articles?

Surely, I have placed a significant part of the burden for Nigeria’s inability to domestically mobilise adequate long-term capital for industrial development at the doorstep of the commercial banks.

But, as in many aspects of life, one tree does not make a forest.

Looking purely at the operations of commercial banks as an explanation for Nigeria’s industrial-development difficulties will inevitably produce an incomplete diagnosis.

Commercial banks are commercially minded institutions. We should expect them to respond rationally to the incentives placed before them. The bigger question, therefore, is not simply what the banks are doing, but what kind of financial behaviour the Nigerian political economy rewards.

Follow the Incentives

Let us reason through it together.

If Nigeria asks its financial system to perform two potentially competing functions simultaneously — finance a government with substantial borrowing requirements at attractive risk-adjusted returns, while also providing affordable, patient and long-term capital for industrial transformation — which direction should we reasonably expect commercially driven financial institutions to favour?

The answer is hardly mysterious. Capital will tend towards the activity offering the more attractive return relative to the risk being assumed.

A bank considering a government security does not ordinarily need to evaluate whether a factory has adequate electricity, whether imported machinery will become prohibitively expensive after another exchange-rate movement, whether a manufacturer’s customers will continue to afford its products, whether poor transport infrastructure will raise distribution costs, or whether an industrial borrower will remain viable five or ten years into the future.

Lending to productive enterprise requires considerably more work and considerably more risk-bearing. The bank must assess the business, monitor the borrower, evaluate collateral, price sectoral risk, account for macroeconomic uncertainty and retain capital against the possibility of default. These are cost-bearing activities with substantial attendant risks.

And in an economy where the insurance industry remains relatively shallow, commercial lenders cannot rely upon a sufficiently deep risk-transfer ecosystem to absorb many of the uncertainties surrounding productive investment.

Commercial banks are consequently being asked not only to provide credit, but to carry substantial portions of the risks surrounding productive activity while simultaneously performing the economy-stimulating role that policymakers expect of them.

Government borrowing, by comparison, presents a substantially different risk proposition. That makes sovereign instruments attractive not only to commercial banks, but also to pension funds, institutional investors and portfolio investors.

Recent capital-flow patterns reinforce the logic: where attractive risk-adjusted returns are available in liquid financial instruments, capital responds accordingly. The problem, therefore, is not simply that banks prefer government securities. The more important question is: why has the system made that preference so commercially rational?

Monetary Policy Compounds the Problem

And then there is the monetary-policy environment within which banks are expected to perform this developmental responsibility. In September 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria reduced the Monetary Policy Rate to 23 per cent, while retaining a 45 per cent Cash Reserve Requirement for Deposit Money Banks.

The CRR matters in this discussion. A substantial portion of applicable deposits mobilised by commercial banks is effectively sterilised with the central bank. This serves legitimate monetary-policy purposes, particularly liquidity management and inflation control, but it also affects the volume and cost of funds available for intermediation.

Banks therefore operate within a system in which a substantial portion of deposits is immobilised, the monetary-policy benchmark remains high, sovereign securities provide attractive alternatives, and productive enterprises simultaneously require long-tenor financing at affordable rates.

In August 2026, the average prime lending rate stood at about 17.86 per cent, while the average maximum lending rate was approximately 29.20 per cent. Contrast this with Treasury-bill rates of around 15.5 to 15.9 per cent in September.

Why should a commercially rational institution take substantially greater manufacturing risk — conduct project appraisal, monitor production, assess collateral, absorb default uncertainty and lock capital away for years — if government securities can provide comparatively attractive returns with substantially lower borrower-specific risk?

That is the contradiction.

Intervention Is Not the Same as Architecture

Government recognises the financing problem. That is why it establishes intervention programmes, development-finance institutions and concessional lending schemes. But the scale tells its own story.

As of January 2025, commercial-bank credit outstanding to Nigeria’s manufacturing sector stood at approximately ₦8.31 trillion, representing about 14.18 per cent of total sectoral credit. This is the stock of manufacturing credit outstanding at a point in time, not new lending in January.

Now juxtapose that with the Federal Government’s ₦75 billion Manufacturing Sector Fund, administered through the Bank of Industry. By December 2024, only about ₦28.53 billion had been disbursed to 42 manufacturing companies nationwide.

The two figures are not directly comparable: one is a stock of commercial-bank credit, while the other is disbursement from a specific intervention programme. But even with that qualification, the relative scale remains instructive.

We place enormous expectations upon commercial banks to finance industrial activity while the specialised public mechanisms designed to address market failures in industrial finance remain modest relative to the financing needs of the productive economy.

And therein lies the danger of confusing intervention with system design. A ₦75 billion manufacturing fund may be useful. A 9 per cent concessional facility may help some firms. But intervention programmes cannot indefinitely compensate for a much larger financial architecture whose underlying incentives continue to push capital towards safer and more immediately rewarding uses.

We may therefore be addressing the price of finance without sufficiently addressing the architecture of risk. And this, I increasingly think, is where Nigeria’s industrial-financing conversation has been wrongly framed.

The Question Beneath the Interest Rate

Whenever manufacturers complain about finance, our first question usually tends to be: How do we reduce interest rates? But perhaps the more fundamental question should be: Who is expected to bear the risks that make productive lending expensive in the first place?

Industrialisation has never been risk-free. Factories operate in uncertain markets. Technology can fail. Infrastructure may be inadequate. Exchange rates fluctuate. Suppliers may be weak. Skills may not yet exist locally. Returns from major industrial investments may take years to materialise. Someone must carry those risks.

The question is: who?

And if government is genuinely serious about industrial transformation, that question can no longer be left primarily to entrepreneurs and commercial banks. That is where the discussion must go next.

Because Nigeria’s industrial-financing problem may not ultimately be about whether the banks are sufficiently patriotic, sufficiently generous or even sufficiently development-oriented.

It may be about whether we have built a financial system in which productive risk can actually be shared, transferred, insured and made financeable.

That is the subject of the second part.

Dipo Baruwa is a business climate development analyst.

World.title: ‘Politics must not block national development’ — Shettima tells Anambrarains
World.content:
Vice President Kashim Shettima has said partisan politics must never stand in the way of national development, adding that the administration of President Bola Tinubu is committed to the progress and prosperity of all states, irrespective of political affiliation.

He said the collective responsibility of improving Nigerians’ living conditions transcends party loyalties, and he charged governors and local government chairmen to translate increased revenues accruing to them into tangible benefits for citizens.

VP Shettima stated this on Thursday in Awka, Anambra State, where he commissioned the Ekwulobia Flyover Complex, Tower of Light, Shopping Mall, and ancillary structures executed by Governor Charles Soludo’s administration.

Insisting that the revenue windfall from the Tinubu administration’s economic reforms must be translated into visible, everyday relief for Nigerians, he explained that the reforms were designed to strengthen the financial capacity of all tiers of government, irrespective of political affiliations.

He said, “The increased revenues available to our states and local governments offer their leaders greater scope to discharge their responsibilities. The success of a governor, irrespective of political affiliation, is an outcome in which the federal government has a stake.

“However, the increase in revenue would count for little if it failed to improve the living conditions of our people. We often overlook this dimension of our federal system.

“Many of the responsibilities that touch the daily lives of our citizens fall within the concurrent and residual powers of the states and the statutory functions of our local government councils. The resources available to each tier of government must ultimately translate into better public services and opportunities for the citizen.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Shettima commended Governor Soludo for prioritising infrastructure that addresses the social and commercial needs of the people, underscoring the importance of strategic public investments in driving productivity, reducing the cost of doing business and stimulating economic growth.

“Anambra State is a model of commercial enterprise, having produced some of the nation’s most enduring businesses and resourceful entrepreneurs. What such a people ask of government is the infrastructure that allows their ambitions to travel beyond the boundaries of their home. Every hour saved in transit is an hour returned to the business of earning a living,” he stated.

The vice president maintained that the enduring measure of leadership is the impact of government policies, programmes and projects on the lives of citizens rather than the political fortunes of those in office.

“Politics may bring us into office, but history remembers us for how we govern. The security of our political stations can never measure our success. We govern in the fullest sense when our programmes, policies and projects offer the people a reason to believe in the purpose of government,” he added.

On behalf of President Tinubu, VP Shettima congratulated Governor Soludo and the people of Anambra State, assuring them of the federal government’s continued support for developing the state’s commercial and industrial potential.

In his remarks, Mr Soludo thanked the traditional worshippers in Ekwulobia for agreeing to relocate a shrine within the project site, recalling how some property owners initially resisted the flyover but now appreciate its benefits.

The governor disclosed that over 100 roads, an innovation district and several urban renewal projects across Awka, Nnewi, Onitsha, Okpoko and other communities were ready for commissioning.

Also speaking, the Mayor of Aguata Local Government Area, Kingsley Ezeagu, described the vice president’s visit as significant, noting that the reinforced pillar supporting the flyover symbolised Nigeria’s unity and strength.

He reaffirmed the state’s commitment to strengthening its relationship with the federal government, saying, “Anambra State, with my governor, is yours. We don’t have anywhere else to go; we don’t have anyone else to talk to. We only have you and our dear president.”

Giving an overview of the project, Ifeanyi Okoma, an engineer, explained that the convergence of two major federal highways, a sprawling market and a busy interstate motor park at a single junction had created severe traffic congestion in Ekwulobia, necessitating the construction of the flyover.

He added that the project involved relocating the market and taxi loading bay away from the intersection, as well as erosion control works.

On his part, a community leader and Chairman of Jezco Group of Companies, Joseph Ezeokafor, who spoke in Hausa, commended VP Shettima for his longstanding support for Ndigbo living and doing business in Northern Nigeria.

“I would like to greet you specially because you have been our master, even in Maiduguri and anywhere in the North. You have been helping Igbos. So we want to thank you,” he said.

Meanwhile, at a separate town hall meeting with traditional rulers, town union leaders, women and youth leaders in Isuofia, Governor Soludo’s country home, the vice president called for stronger political cooperation across ethnic, geographical and party lines, insisting that national unity must be anchored in fairness, inclusion and equal opportunities for all Nigerians.

Traditional rulers and community representatives from the state’s 179 communities attended the town hall meeting.

According to the VP, President Tinubu has approved an economic free trade zone license for the Anambra Aerotropolis Mixed Industrial City, which will further strengthen the state’s investment prospects.

He explained that the license would provide eligible businesses operating within the development with tax concessions and other duty-free incentives, helping to attract investment and support industrial growth.

Acknowledging the enormous contributions of Ndigbo to Nigeria’s economic development, Mr Shettima said their entrepreneurial ingenuity, industrial capacity and resourcefulness remain integral to the nation’s prosperity.

“Nations are held together by the confidence of their constituent peoples that they belong, that their voices matter and that their aspirations are legitimate. We must never allow the circumstances of our past or the differences of our politics to diminish our sense of common destiny,” he said.

Reiterating the Tinubu administration’s commitment to developing the South-east, VP Shettima highlighted the establishment of the South-east Development Commission (SEDC), with a budget provision of N250 billion, as a strategic institutional intervention to accelerate regional reconstruction and industrialisation.

He also listed the rehabilitation of the First Niger Bridge, construction of access roads to the Second Niger Bridge, reconstruction of the Enugu-Onitsha Expressway and approval of the Oba-Nnewi-Uga-Okigwe and Otuocha-Anam-Ibaji roads among federal interventions in the region.

The vice president cited the appointment of Bianca Odumegwu-Ojukwu, a member of the All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA), as minister of foreign affairs as a demonstration of President Tinubu’s commitment to inclusive governance beyond partisan considerations.

Mr Shettima recalled that former President Muhammadu Buhari contested the presidential election with two prominent Igbo sons, Chuba Okadigbo in 2003 and Edwin Ume-Ezeoke in 2007, before eventually emerging as President in 2015 after forming a broader national coalition.

“The history of our democracy demonstrates the importance of building bridges across geographical, ethnic and political boundaries,” he stated.

Mr Shettima also commended Governor Soludo for his constructive engagement with the federal government despite differences in political affiliation, emphasising that partisan considerations must never override the people’s collective interests.

He affirmed the legitimacy of the political aspirations of Ndigbo, including their aspiration to occupy the highest office in the country.

“The aspiration of Ndigbo to occupy the highest office in the land is legitimate. No section of this country has a monopoly on leadership, and no Nigerian should consider himself a permanent outsider. Our democracy must remain an open space for dialogue, coalition-building and the pursuit of legitimate political aspirations,” the vice president said.

Ahead of the 2027 general election, Mr Shettima said President Tinubu would present his administration’s record of performance to Nigerians as he seeks a renewed mandate, stressing that the collective responsibility of building a secure, prosperous and inclusive nation must transcend electoral contests.

Community leaders at the town hall meeting included the Chairman of the Anambra State Council of Traditional Rulers and traditional ruler of Obosi, Chidubem Iweka; President-General of the Anambra State Town Unions Council (Men’s Wing), Vin Dike; President-General of the Women’s Wing, Blessing Onuigwe; and President-General of the Youth Wing, Comrade Ken Okoli.

Stanley Nkwocha
