World.title: When a policy meant to protect tenants becomes a signal to double rents: The Enugu Tenancy Bill dilemma, By David Okelue Ugwunta
World.content:
As some landlords seek to double rents in anticipation of a law designed to protect tenants, one question becomes unavoidable: If the House of Assembly passes a law to protect citizens, but its announcement is followed by actions that expose those same citizens to even greater hardship, and the government has no immediate response, who exactly protects the citizens?

There is an uncomfortable irony unfolding around Enugu State’s proposed tenancy reforms. On the 17th day of November, the Enugu State House of Assembly passed an amendment to the state’s Landlord and Tenant Law. Sponsored by Honourable Okey Mbah, the bill responds to genuine problems: the rising cost of securing accommodation, arbitrary rent increases, and extra charges that can make a property far more expensive than its advertised rent.

As reported, the bill requires landlords to wait four years before increasing rent, with an increase capped at 2 per cent of the prevailing rent. Up to 10 per cent is allowed where qualifying renovation has been undertaken. The bill also proposes controls on agency, legal and caution fees, a bond-account arrangement for refundable caution deposits, and stronger safeguards against unlawful eviction. It awaits the governor’s assent, so none of these protections is yet in force.

The objective to protect tenants from exploitation is understandable. Reports describe how cut-throat fees by agents, lawyers, and rents by landlords have been aggravating the housing crisis in the state, making regulation of Enugu’s rental market necessary.

Yet the announcement appears to have coincided with a troubling response. I have encountered several recent cases in which landlords sought rent increases of as much as 100 per cent, apparently in anticipation of the proposed restrictions. These are individual cases, not evidence of a statewide pattern. They raise a serious question about how some parts of the rent market may be responding, but they do not establish what the costs of landlords are or what increase would be justified.

Signalling theory helps explain the dilemma. In economics and finance, signalling describes how an announcement conveys information and shapes other actors’ expectations and decisions. The Landlord-Tenant Amendment Bill 2026 signals stronger protection against arbitrary increases. Some landlords appear to have read the announcement of its passage as notice that their window to reset rents was closing. Their anticipatory increases, driven by a wish to secure higher rents before the cap takes effect, or probably by fears of inflation, or both, fall on tenants now, while the statutory protection is not yet in force.

Anticipatory rent increases are therefore only the first of three channels separating a well-meant bill from improved tenant welfare. Others are possible effects on rental supply and maintenance if the cap does not reflect relevant costs, and an enforcement gap between the law on paper and in practice.

The October 2026 inflation data underline wider cost pressures. The reported national inflation of 14.06 per cent and Enugu’s state-level rate at 22.81 per cent year-on-year provide context for the debate. Consumer price inflation is not a direct measure of an individual landlord’s costs or of rents. It is an indicator of broad price pressure, not proof of any particular landlord’s expenses or the basis for a particular rent increase.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

A ceiling without enforcement offers little protection. Enugu should designate a lead complaints authority by law, with a named responsible ministry or agency and clear coordination with the Attorney-General’s office, the Ministry of Housing / Housing Corporation and the body administering the bond account. Tenants should be able to report unlawful charges, improper increases, and eviction threats by telephone, in person and online.

Consider an illustration in which these annual rates persist for four years. At 14.06 per cent, the general price level would rise by about 69 per cent; at Enugu’s 22.81 per cent, it would rise by about 127 per cent; all compounded annually. A landlord charging ₦1 million a year who kept the rent unchanged for four years would need about ₦1.69 million or ₦2.27 million, respectively, to preserve the original rent’s purchasing power against those general price changes. In comparison, a single 2 per cent increase after the four-year period would bring the rent to ₦1.02 million. These calculations assume constant inflation and do not forecast rents, measure property-specific costs or establish a fair rent adjustment.

The figures illustrate how a fixed ceiling could diverge from general price movements if inflation remained high. They may help explain why a landlord expecting a long freeze could have an incentive to seek an increase before the restriction takes effect. Nevertheless, an incentive is not proof that a particular landlord faces those costs, and the illustrative 69–127 per cent change in the general price level does not justify a 100 per cent rent increase. Such a demand must be assessed on its facts and under applicable law. Tenants with few alternatives will definitely bear the immediate burden.

A balanced assessment must also recognise that property ownership ties up capital and carries maintenance, repair, insurance, tax and rate costs that may rise. International evidence cautions against assuming that rent caps automatically produce affordable housing. A widely cited study of San Francisco’s 1994 rent-control expansion found lower displacement among protected incumbent tenants. It also estimated that landlords of newly covered properties reduced the rental supply of affected units by 15 per cent, through conversion, sale to owner-occupiers or redevelopment, and that this supply response contributed to a 5.1 per cent rise in citywide rents. These estimates reflect a particular US policy, housing market and regulatory setting, so they are not a forecast for Enugu. The lesson is to pair tenant protection with measures that sustain rental supply and maintenance, and to monitor the effects locally.

Enugu could consider three measures:

Close the transition gap. The final law should state its commencement date and explain how the four-year period applies to existing tenancies. California offers a design lesson, though its framework cannot simply be transplanted. The state’s Tenant Protection Act (AB 1482) th March 2019, although the law became operative on 1st January 2020. For Enugu, protection of tenants can come at different levels of legal risk. Prospective steps carry the least: a standstill from assent to commencement, public guidance and a complaints desk. A tribunal could review unusually large post-announcement increases, so none becomes the four-year baseline. A retrospective reference date, such as the second reading on 11 March 2026 public hearing on 26 March 2026 California’s lookback

Replace the flat ceiling with a transparent formula. A fixed 2 per cent after four years is predictable but does not respond to conditions, and during sustained inflation it could cut landlords’ real rental income. Full indexation could shift too much risk to tenants. Oregon, for example, sets an annual maximum under a statutory formula of 7 per cent plus CPI, subject to a 10 per cent ceiling for specified tenancies Build an enforcement and complaints system. A ceiling without enforcement offers little protection. Enugu should designate a lead complaints authority by law, with a named responsible ministry or agency and clear coordination with the Attorney-General’s office, the Ministry of Housing / Housing Corporation and the body administering the bond account. Tenants should be able to report unlawful charges, improper increases, and eviction threats by telephone, in person and online. The authority should publish procedures, referral routes and response times. The state should also consider a specialised tenancy track in magistrates’ courts across the three urban local government areas, with a statutory timeline, and powers to order refunds where authorised by law. Written tenancy agreements and rent receipts would make disputes easier to resolve and give government better market data.

The real test of this bill will be whether it creates a fair and predictable rental market that protects tenants without unfairly undermining landlords’ legitimate interests or discouraging investment in housing. It must anticipate possible side effects, provide credible enforcement and ensure that the burden of transition does not fall on the people it is meant to protect. Tenant protection must be economically sustainable, legally enforceable and institutionally accountable.

The state should publish quarterly performance data, anchored by a first-year baseline survey. These are proposed accountability measures, not provisions of the bill. The complaints authority should report complaints by category, referrals, median time to first response and resolution, cases resolved within 30 days, and unresolved cases and outcomes, protecting personal information. A target such as resolving 80 per cent within 30 days could follow once baseline data show what is feasible. The housing agency should report registered tenancies or written agreements against baseline, and the courts tenancy cases filed, disposed of, time taken and orders made, including unlawful increases reversed. The state should also track median urban rents against inflation and rental supply, including new construction, conversions and landlord exit. Published methods and results would help spot problems early and separate individual cases from broader trends.

The Enugu House of Assembly deserves credit for confronting a genuine problem. Good intentions, however, are not enough. Policymaking requires an understanding of incentives, behavioural responses and unintended consequences.

The real test of this bill will be whether it creates a fair and predictable rental market that protects tenants without unfairly undermining landlords’ legitimate interests or discouraging investment in housing. It must anticipate possible side effects, provide credible enforcement and ensure that the burden of transition does not fall on the people it is meant to protect. Tenant protection must be economically sustainable, legally enforceable and institutionally accountable.

Government should not merely legislate for the behaviour it wants; it must also anticipate the behaviour its policies may encourage.

As some landlords seek to double rents in anticipation of a law designed to protect tenants, one question becomes unavoidable: If the House of Assembly passes a law to protect citizens, but its announcement is followed by actions that expose those same citizens to even greater hardship, and the government has no immediate response, who exactly protects the citizens?

David Okelue Ugwunta, a public policy and economic planning specialist, is a senior adviser (Economic) with Thoughts and Mace Advisory.

World.title: Delta Killings: PANDEF urges trial of ringleaders, seeks govt aid to bereaved families
World.content:
The Pan Niger Delta Forum (PANDEF) has called on the Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu, and the Director-General of the State Security Service (SSS), Adeola Ajayi, to investigate the violent attack that claimed six lives during a campaign rally of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) in Delta State.

PANDEF also urged the security agencies to immediately arrest and prosecute those responsible for the attack on the NDC campaign rally at Uduere Community in Ughelli North Local Government Area of the state.

The apex socio-political organisation representing Nigeria’s South-South geopolitical zone made the demands in separate petitions addressed to the IGP and the SSS director-general, dated 24 November and signed by its National Chairman, Godknows Igali.

“Arising from the foregoing, PANDEF strongly urges your respective organisations, working in concert with other relevant agencies within the national security architecture, to undertake a comprehensive, impartial and thorough investigation into the circumstances surrounding the reported violence at the Ughelli rally.

“It is imperative that all those who masterminded, instigated, sponsored or directly participated in these acts be identified and brought to justice in accordance with the law,” the petition reads.

The attack occurred on Monday when armed men disrupted a campaign tour of Uduere Community by Ovie Omo-Agege, a former deputy Senate president and the NDC candidate for Delta Central Senatorial District in the 2027 elections.

The Nigeria Police Force subsequently confirmed that six people were killed and several others injured in the violence.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Delta State Governor, Sheriff Oborevwori, condemned the incident and ordered the arrest of those responsible.

The NDC presidential candidate, Peter Obi, has also visited the families of the slain party members to commiserate with them.

Demand for support

PANDEF also urged the federal government, relevant agencies and the Delta State Government to provide financial and other forms of assistance to the families of those killed in the attack.

The group further called for adequate medical attention and support for those injured during the violence.

“We also call on the federal government, the relevant federal agencies and the Delta State Government to urgently explore appropriate measures to provide succour and support to the families of those who reportedly lost their lives, whose lives have been cut short under such tragic circumstances.

“We further urge that adequate medical and other necessary assistance be extended to the injured to facilitate their full recovery,” it said.

PANDEF also warned against political thuggery, violence, and the intimidation of voters in the South-South region, stressing the need to protect democratic participation and ensure peaceful political activities.

World.title: Temple, BOS Africa spotlight Nigeria’s sports business potential at Lagos event
World.content:
Sports industry executives, entrepreneurs and professionals have called for better funding, infrastructure, stronger partnerships and improved organisation to unlock Nigeria’s sporting potential and build a sustainable sports economy.

The call was made at KINETIC, an executive sports business mixer organised by the Business of Sports Institute (BOS) Africa in partnership with The Temple Company, in Lagos on Wednesday.

The event brought together professionals from different sectors of the sports industry, including finance, law, media, engineering, sports management, marketing, broadcasting and technology, for discussions on investment opportunities, collaboration and the commercial development of sports in Nigeria.

The gathering, held at The Temple Company, Victoria Island, was designed to encourage networking and connect people whose businesses and expertise could contribute to the sports industry’s growth.

Speaking at the event, Beverley Agbakoba-Onyejianya, founder and academic director of BOS Africa, said Nigeria’s sporting potential remained largely untapped because of gaps in capacity, funding, infrastructure, and a lack of sufficient opportunities for collaboration.

She said the country has the talent and enthusiasm for sports but has yet to develop an industry that can generate adequate employment and sustainable commercial opportunities for professionals across the value chain.

“We are a sporting nation, and we are a vibrant nation. We’re a footballing nation, actually. But we still don’t provide enough jobs. It’s just not a sustainable industry as it ought to be when you compare it to, say, England, France,” she said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mrs Agbakoba-Onyejianya, however, said Nigeria should develop its sports industry in a manner that reflects its culture, identity and peculiar circumstances rather than merely attempting to replicate Western models.

She said KINETIC was conceived to bring professionals from different sectors together to encourage meaningful conversations, strengthen relationships and explore opportunities for collaboration.

“We want finance to talk to the agents. We want the agents to talk to the telecoms people. We want us all to communicate more so we can do more in this industry,” she said.

Sports business education

Mrs Agbakoba-Onyejianya said her motivation for establishing BOS Africa was the shortage of accessible and quality sports business education in Nigeria, particularly programmes that prepare people for commercially driven careers in the industry.

She said while some universities offer sports-related programmes, the country still lacks sufficient specialised training opportunities to meet the demands of its growing sporting ecosystem.

The initiative, she said, was intended to provide a flexible, accessible and affordable platform for people seeking to develop careers in sports business.

Mrs Agbakoba-Onyejianya, a sports lawyer with more than two decades of professional experience spanning Nigeria and the United Kingdom, founded Lagos Tigers Football Club, a grassroots football academy, and contributed to the development of Nigeria’s National Sports Policy.

She is also a FIFA mediator and serves on international sports dispute-resolution and governance panels.

She said the mixer showed the value of bringing professionals together outside their usual business environments, and expressed hope that the initiative would grow into a regular platform for industry engagement.

“Imagine having this platform on a massive scale, where media, finance, broadcasting, engineering, legal and other sectors come together, connected by sports. That way, we grow the economy, contribute to the GDP, do more projects through collaboration and literally create a domino effect,” she said.

Nigeria’s sporting potential

During a panel discussion moderated by Telema Davies, managing partner of DMPartners, participants expressed differing views on whether Nigeria could be regarded as a serious sporting nation, despite its abundance of talent.

Aderoju Ope-Ajayi, chairperson of the Lagos State Aquatic Association and head of strategy and business transformation at MTN MoMo PSB, questioned Nigeria’s commitment to developing its athletes, pointing to the country’s inability to consistently identify, nurture and adequately represent promising talents.

She said she was often amazed by the level of talent available, particularly among young athletes who break national records but do not receive the support needed to progress to international competitions.

“Nigeria is not a serious sporting nation. We have so much potential, but we are just not doing enough”, she said.

Ms Ope-Ajayi also highlighted the challenges of accessing sporting facilities, noting that the shortage of suitable infrastructure had forced some organisers and development programmes to depend on privately owned schools and other facilities.

She said sponsorship was also difficult to secure, with some companies supporting sporting initiatives out of goodwill rather than through clearly defined long-term commercial objectives.

Folake Shasanya, managing partner of Aesura Group, a strategic capital advisory firm, agreed that Nigeria’s sporting potential was undermined by inadequate structures.

She said young athletes often demonstrate exceptional ability but lack the systems needed to sustain their development and translate their performances into success at major international competitions.

Ms Shasanya cited Nigeria’s recent achievements at the Youth Olympic Games as evidence of the country’s potential, arguing that greater attention to athlete development, organisation and investment could help produce more consistent performances across sporting disciplines.

Jouko Gorissen, founder of Next Level Global Recruiting, said Nigeria could be described as a sporting nation in terms of its population, talent and enthusiasm but has yet to establish the structures needed to make sports a sustainable business.

He said countries such as the United States had developed stronger sports systems through investments in facilities, coaching, education, safeguarding and commercial opportunities.

Mr Gorissen said Nigeria’s sports industry remained overly dependent on athletes as its principal commercial assets, a model he described as unsustainable in the long term.

He argued that the country needed to develop the professionals, institutions and businesses that support athletes and sporting competitions, rather than focusing almost exclusively on the players.

Infrastructure, investment and commercial opportunities

Opeyemi Babalola, an engineer who also serves as founder and managing director of Webber Engineering, said Nigeria had the talent to compete internationally but was held back by politics, inadequate infrastructure, and poor management of sporting facilities.

He said government ownership of many facilities created challenges for commercial operators, particularly when political activities or other government priorities affected access.

The discussion also examined the commercial potential of sporting facilities, including opportunities for private investment, improved management and alternative revenue streams.

Mr Babalola argued that naming rights, a common commercial arrangement in international sports, could provide additional revenue for facilities, but said Nigeria sometimes missed such opportunities by prioritising commemorative naming conventions.

He suggested that sports infrastructure could be better positioned to attract commercial investment through naming rights and other sponsorship arrangements, while still recognising national figures and sporting heroes.

Seun Akinbolu, founder and co-founder of The Athletics School Games and Pan-Africa School Games, also highlighted funding and infrastructure challenges facing sports development.

She said establishing individual facilities could be expensive and difficult to sustain, suggesting partnerships as a more viable route for organisations seeking to expand sporting opportunities.

The concerns raised at KINETIC mirror wider challenges identified in Nigeria’s sports development plans, including inadequate investment, infrastructure deficits and the need for greater private-sector participation.

Nigeria’s National Development Plan has identified limited funding, uneven access to facilities and poor infrastructure as constraints to the sector’s growth, while emphasising the need for public-private partnerships to unlock its economic potential.

The federal government has also been exploring alternative financing models for sports infrastructure, including plans announced in October by the National Sports Commission to mobilise a N1 trillion fund to rehabilitate facilities and attract private investment.

Terfa Tilley-Gyado, President & CEO, The Temple Company & Ogidi Studios, said the partnership with BOS Africa was driven by the belief that African sports needed more than talent and passion to thrive.

He said the continent’s athletes were increasingly competing worldwide but remained underrepresented by African professionals in areas such as management, agency, sports nutrition, law, and other specialist services.

He said KINETIC was an attempt to begin building the relationships and professional networks necessary to address the gap.

“This is just the first, as Amaka said. And there will be many more,” he said, encouraging participants to explore BOS Africa’s training programmes and opportunities to develop their expertise in the sports industry.

The organisers said KINETIC was expected to become a recurring gathering, providing a platform for professionals to connect, exchange ideas and develop partnerships capable of strengthening Africa’s sports business ecosystem.

World.title: How ISWAP uses drones, satellite technology to sustain insurgency in Lake Chad – Report
World.content:
Nearly two decades after the Boko Haram insurgency began in Nigeria, the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) has transformed into a resilient, tech-enabled organisation driven by an adaptive ecosystem of commercial drones, satellite communications, and localised weapons fabrication.

That is the core finding of a major new research report published today by the Institute for Security Studies (ISS), titled “Wiring the insurgency: Inside ISWAP’s adaptive technology programme.”

Drawing on interviews with ex-Boko Haram fighters, who recently defected and security insiders, the report, launched in Abuja on Thursday, reveals how the insurgent group has systematically modified ordinary commercial and digital tools to enhance its intelligence gathering, propaganda operations, and combat capabilities.

Unlike other insurgent groups backed directly by foreign states, ISWAP relies on the broader Islamic State global network for technical guidance and financial backing. Equipment and funds reach the group through transnational supply lines, the report found.

Cash and items such as Starlink and Thuraya satellite communication devices – initially registered in Dubai – are channelled from the United Arab Emirates through currency exchange operators in Kano, Nigeria, and secondary routes in N’Djamena, Chad.

Highlighting the scale of these communications, an ex-fighter noted: “We have our own laptops, and we use Thuraya and Starlink … the number of the Thuraya is uncountable.”

These supplies are smuggled into Lake Chad Basin territories hidden inside bundles of fabrics and food via transit hubs like Geidam, according to the report.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

ISWAP’s manufacturing capacity has evolved from an early, improvised tradition sparked by the 2013 raid on the Government Technical College in Bama, where equipment was looted to build initial workshops, into purpose-built workshops on Lake Chad islands that produce specialised explosives and fit commercial DJI drones with IEDs.

To protect these operations, the group enforces strict operational security measures, including banning local SIM cards across its bases, restricting smartphone use among fighters, and utilising satellite Wi-Fi to bypass government telecom shutdowns.

The report contrasts ISWAP’s structured approach with its rival faction, Jama’tu Ahlis Sunna Lidda’awati wal-Jihad (JAS). While ISWAP maintains a disciplined, professionalised organisation backed by IS central, JAS operates via a comparatively loose structure.

Pointing to the stark organisational gap between the two factions, an ex-fighter dismissively described JAS’s media as “nothing organised.”

Furthermore, while ISWAP focuses heavily on military base attacks to capture weapons through its ghanimah pricing system, which pays fighters for weapons captured from the military and surrendered to the group, JAS relies more heavily on civilian predation and older illicit camel-riding arms corridors running from Sudan.

The research also underscores ISWAP’s sophisticated organisational structure, including the Ilan, a media department that coordinates real-time propaganda and manages back-channel messaging with journalists. At the community level, the group relies on the rijal–awam network, embedding covert agents into civilian populations to gather intelligence, handle logistics, and project parallel governance.

While state militaries and the Multinational Joint Task Force (MNJTF) have increasingly deployed counter-drone measures, such as handheld jammers and specialised radar training, the report warns that slow procurement processes and reactive strategies continue to hamper national and regional security responses.

Furthermore, the study cautions that while empirical evidence of frontier artificial intelligence (AI) adoption as operational infrastructure remains unconfirmed, ISWAP’s rapid innovation cycle means counterinsurgency planners must look ahead before AI becomes an active threat.

“This work is an output of our Disrupting Armed Groups’ Operational Governance project, which seeks to draw on primary research to reveal core elements of ISWAP’s enabling ecosystem as evidence to inform understanding and responses by counterinsurgency planners,” said the author Taiwo Adebayo.

The report urges a multi-stakeholder response, recommending that counterinsurgency actors systematically use defector intelligence, strengthen amphibious and naval operations in the Lake Chad Basin, clamp down on transnational currency exchange networks that facilitate illicit financing, and engage satellite communication providers to monitor device diversion in conflict zones.

World.title: How 6 were burnt to death, 12 injured in Lagos road accident
World.content:
The accident scene.

By Esther Onyegbulam, Matthew Johnson & Patrick Chidubem

Six persons were burnt to death, while 12 others sustained varying degrees of burns yesterday after a commercial vehicle caught fire at Magbon, along the Lagos-Badagry Expressway.

The Lagos State Fire and Rescue Service, which confirmed the incident, said the victims comprised two females and four males, all adults. It added that the 12 injured persons were rescued and taken to Badagry General Hospital for medical attention.

However, an eyewitness account shared in a video gave a different initial account of the tragedy, claiming that many people were feared dead, with only two occupants, reportedly the driver and another passenger, surviving the incident.

According to the eyewitness, the accident occurred between 8am and 9am and involved a commercial bus travelling from Mile 2 towards Badagry. The incident reportedly happened shortly after Checking Point Bus Stop, before the Black Signboard axis of the expressway.

The eyewitness account indicated that the vehicle caught fire, resulting in multiple casualties. However, the initial casualty figures could not be independently verified.

In its official account, the Controller-General of the Lagos State Fire and Rescue Service, Margaret Adeseye, said the agency received a distress call at 8:44am, while firefighters from its Badagry station arrived at the scene at 9:13am.

According to Adeseye, “Preliminary information gathered during the investigation indicated that the driver reportedly had an additional five litres of fuel stored inside the vehicle, intending to refuel the vehicle’s tank.

The presence of the extra fuel is suspected to have contributed to the intensity of the fire.

“Tragically, six persons, comprising two females and four males, all adults, were involved in the incident. All six victims were burnt beyond recognition,” the statement said.

Vanguard News

World.title: Sexual violence: UK, Mirabel Centre push for stronger protection, Justice for survivors
World.content:
Itoro Eze-Anaba

*Mrs Sanwo-Olu hails centre’s 10,000-Survivor Care Milestone

By Henry Ojelu

THE United Kingdom and the Mirabel Centre have called for stronger protection, sustained support and access to justice for survivors of sexual and gender-based violence in Nigeria.

The British Deputy High Commissioner in Lagos, Mr Jonny Baxter, and founder of the Mirabel Centre, Itoro Eze-Anaba, made the call on Thursday at a reception and panel discussion in Lagos to mark the centre’s milestone of supporting more than 10,000 survivors of sexual violence.

The event, held as part of the 2026 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence, also featured the launch of the centre’s publication, The Survivor Experience: A Voice That Matters.

Speaking on the theme, “A Milestone of Care, A Call for Sustained Support & Justice,” Baxter said the achievement deserved celebration but stressed that sexual violence remained a serious issue requiring sustained attention and commitment.

He said: “We want to celebrate 10,000 survivors, but we also want to ensure that many more people are able to access the professional support and services they need.”

Baxter emphasised the importance of placing survivors’ experiences at the centre of interventions, saying their voices were essential to understanding their challenges and improving access to support and justice.

He reaffirmed the UK’s commitment to ending violence against women and girls through development partnerships and collaboration with governments and civil society organisations.

He also disclosed that the UK would soon host an international summit on technology-facilitated gender-based violence, noting that emerging forms of abuse required new approaches and solutions.

Earlier, Eze-Anaba acknowledged the contributions of the British Council, the Department for International Development and the British High Commission to the establishment and growth of the centre.

She said the British High Commission funded the centre’s first three years and continued to support its work through partnerships and advocacy opportunities.

Describing the milestone as more than a numerical achievement, she said the centre remained committed to delivering services with dignity and respect.

“Today is not about public relations for the Mirabel Centre. It is about the services we provide and how those services are shared in a dignified manner for survivors,” she said.

Eze-Anaba said the centre regularly sought feedback from survivors and had engaged an independent consultant to assess its services, identify gaps and recommend improvements.

She thanked the centre’s partners and funders, assuring that it would continue to provide compassionate care where survivors’ voices mattered.

Sanwo-Olu Hails Centre’s Milestone

Meanwhile, Lagos State First Lady, Mrs Ibijoke Sanwo-Olu, has commended the Mirabel Centre for supporting more than 10,000 survivors of sexual violence, describing the achievement as a significant contribution to the fight against gender-based violence.

Sanwo-Olu, who launched the publication, The Survivor Experience: A Voice That Matters, announced the donation of five copies each to all primary healthcare centres in Lagos State. She said support for survivors should extend beyond medical treatment and court proceedings to include counselling, continuous care and interventions to help them rebuild their lives.

According to her, survivors need sustained support to heal and live better lives, while prevention should receive as much attention as treatment and rehabilitation.

The First Lady said she had championed advocacy against gender-based violence through partnerships with government and non-governmental organisations, including the establishment of an inter-ministerial stakeholders’ committee in 2020.

She also called for greater efforts to educate children from an early age to reject violence and respect others.

Vanguard News

World.title: 18.3m children out of school: Stakeholders demand urgent action
World.content:
… NGE challenges govt, media, private sector as UNICEF warns on first 1,000 days

By Chioma Obinna & Juliet Umeh

Media leaders, government officials and development partners yesterday called for urgent action to address Nigeria’s child welfare and education challenges, raising concern over the 18.3 million children out of school in the country.



They warned that poverty, insecurity, displacement, poor learning conditions and inadequate investment in maternal and child healthcare were undermining the survival, development and future of millions of Nigerian children.



The stakeholders spoke at the 2026 World Children’s Day High-Level Media Symposium in Lagos, organised by UNICEF Nigeria in partnership with the Nigerian Guild of Editors, NGE, and the Diamond Awards for Media Excellence, DAME.



In his opening address, President of the NGE, Mr Eze Anaba, challenged government, media organisations, community leaders and the private sector to take responsibility for the growing number of children without access to education.



Citing a UNICEF report that put the number of out-of-school children at 18.3 million, Anaba said: “It’s our collective responsibility to ask why. In a country of about 200 and something million people and 18 million plus of that population is on the streets, not going to school. It’s not only alarming. It’s a collective responsibility.”



He questioned whether stakeholders were doing enough to address the crisis, asking: “Have we reminded government? Community leaders, have they done their part? Has the media done enough? The private sector, has it done enough?”



Anaba also raised concerns over the location of some public schools close to bus stops, motor parks and train stations, warning that such environments could expose children to negative influences at a critical stage of their development.



He said children’s welfare must not be treated as an annual talking point without measurable commitments.

“It is not enough for us to be episodic. Every year we come and remind ourselves that look, we have to build a future for the kids. Last year, on this same programme, I made a commitment on behalf of my newspaper that Vanguard would do more. Have we done enough?” he asked.



He called for an action plan spelling out what government, media organisations, businesses and other stakeholders would do to improve children’s lives.



Speaking, UNICEF Representative in Nigeria, Wafaa Saeed, called for sustained investment in children, particularly during the first 1,000 days of life, warning that neglect during this period could have lifelong consequences.

“You cannot pause a baby’s brain development while waiting for economic recovery. From conception to age two, 80 percent of human brain growth occurs, making investment in the first 1,000 days critical to a child’s survival, development and future,” Saeed said.

She urged journalists to go beyond reporting statistics and highlight the experiences of vulnerable children and families.

“Statistics only matter when they move us to protect the child behind the number. We need the media to humanize the numbers, keep children in the headlines year-round and spotlight the solutions that are working across Nigeria,” she said.

In her keynote address, Lagos State First Lady, Dr Claudiana Ibijoke Sanwo-Olu, said supporting mothers and investing early in children were essential to building a healthier and better-educated generation.

She said the Babajide Sanwo-Olu administration remained committed to inclusive child development and gender-responsive governance, ensuring that every child, irrespective of gender, had the opportunity to realise his or her potential.

On the proposed review of the Lagos State Child’s Rights Law 2015, she said: “As we undertake the review of the Child’s Rights Law 2015, we have before us a unique opportunity to strengthen our legal and institutional framework in ways that respond to emerging realities while safeguarding the best interests of every child.”

Providing further insight into the child health situation, Permanent Secretary, Lagos State Primary Health Care Board, Dr Ibrahim Akinwunmi-Mustafa, said Nigeria had made progress in reducing under-five mortality but continued to face serious challenges in newborn survival and childhood malnutrition.

“Under-five deaths have fallen from 132 to 110 per 1,000 live births since 2018. But newborn deaths have barely moved, and four in ten Nigerian children are still stunted.”

He disclosed that child stunting in Lagos was about 17 per cent, compared with 40 per cent nationally, while an estimated 120,000 to 130,000 children in the state had never received a single vaccine.

“Most of them live in our informal settlements, riverine communities and fast-growing areas,” he said.

Mustafa called for stronger primary healthcare financing, investment in frontline health workers and improved access to antenatal care, nutrition counselling, immunisation and birth registration.

He also urged journalists to support public health campaigns, counter misinformation and hold government and other stakeholders accountable.

“To our friends in the media: you are partners in this work, not spectators,” he said.

Also speaking, the Director of Corporate Communications and Corporate Social Responsibility at Airtel Nigeria, Adefemi Adeniran, said a child’s background, economic circumstances or developmental differences should not determine his or her future.

“Neither the economic circumstances of a child’s parent, background nor their developmental differences should determine a child’s prospects in life. Keeping them alive is our fundamental obligation. Enabling them to learn is our collective responsibility. Creating conditions for them to thrive must be our shared ambition,” he said.

Also the DAME Trustee, Mr. Lanre Idowu, said the partnership between UNICEF, NGE and DAME was helping to strengthen child-rights journalism through training, access to credible evidence, field visits and recognition of excellent reporting.

On his part, UNICEF Nigeria Goodwill Ambassador and musician, Cobhams Asuquo, highlighted the role of music in communicating messages about child survival and development.

“Music is a powerful tool. It can take an important message beyond the statistics and help people connect with the real lives and experiences behind it. With the First 1,000 Days of Life song, we wanted families and communities to understand that what we do for a child from the very beginning, the nutrition, care and support we provide, can shape that child’s future,” he said.

Children also participated in the discussions, questioning decision-makers on how they would ensure that poverty, gender, disability and family circumstances did not deny any child access to healthcare, education and protection.

Their performances, including “The First 1,000 Days of Life” and “I Am a Nigerian Child,” reinforced the importance of including children’s voices in decisions affecting their future.

The symposium coincided with UNICEF’s 80th anniversary, with participants renewing calls for sustained government leadership, adequate financing, private sector investment, community participation and media accountability to secure a better future for Nigerian children.

World.title: 2027 Election: IBB, Abdulsalami endorse Tinubu — Gbajabiamila
World.content:
File: General Ibrahim Babangida, retd. (right) and General Abdulsalami Abubakar, retd.

By Johnbosco Agbakwuru

ABUJA — Chief of Staff to the President, Femi Gbajabiamila, has said former Military President, General Ibrahim Babangida (retd), has endorsed President Bola Tinubu, ahead of the 2027 elections.

This comes as former Head of State, General Abdulsalami Abubakar (retd), also assessed Tinubu’s stewardship positively, saying: “So far, so good. I think the President has done a good job.”

Gbajabiamila said both former leaders spoke yesterday when he led a presidential delegation to their residences in Minna, the Niger State capital.

Speaking to journalists after a closed-door meeting with Babangida, Gbajabiamila said the former military President was impressed with Tinubu’s performance and had reaffirmed his support for the President.

He said: “These are two personalities that you cannot write the history of Nigeria without them occupying very major chapters in that history book.

“He is very happy with what Mr President is doing. He is very happy with his work, and he continues to support him and wishes him all the very best and the best of luck in the forthcoming elections,” he added.

According to Gbajabiamila, Abubakar, speaking on behalf of the National Peace Committee, said: “I want to pray for Nigeria so that we can have a peaceful election, because I keep saying, on behalf of the National Peace Committee, that we need peace in the country.

“Without peace, there will be no country, and if there is no country, there wouldn’t be an election. So, I am praying to our people that they should please give peace a chance, so that we can have a peaceful election,” Abubakar added.

Gbajabiamila said Tinubu directed the visit after returning from Borno State on Wednesday to ascertain the wellbeing of the former leaders and report back to him.

He said the President had wanted to maintain regular communication with the former leaders but had been constrained by official engagements, including campaign trips across the country.

Gbajabiamila also said Tinubu asked him to discuss other matters privately during the visit but declined to disclose the details.

Abubakar thanked Tinubu for maintaining contact with the former leaders despite his campaign activities and the demands of governance.

“I want to thank him for this simple act of remembering us, despite the period of campaigning. He still remembers us, that we are still here in Minna,” he said.

He also appreciated the President for the support extended to him during his medical trip abroad.

He added that Tinubu had also asked Vice-President Kashim Shettima to check on him during the BRICS meeting in India.

Abubakar said his health had improved considerably and that Babangida was also doing well.

The delegation included the Minister of Information and National Orientation, Alhaji Mohammed Idris; Special Adviser to the President on Policy and Coordination, Hadiza Bala-Usman; former Minister of State for Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction, Yusuf Sununu; and former Minister of Transportation, Sa’idu Alkali.

World.title: 2027: Opposition alliances ‘ll fail again, Fashola declares at APC Lagos rally
World.content:
File: Babatunde Fashola

AHEAD of 2027 general elections, former Governor of Lagos State and former Minister of Works and Housing, Babatunde Fashola, has declared that emerging opposition coalitions will suffer the same fate as past failed alliances in Nigeria’s political history.

​Fashola made the assertion yesterday while speaking as the Chief Host at the Babatunde Raji Fashola, BRF Support Group (BRFSG) Campaign kick-off rally, held at the National Stadium in Surulere, Lagos, where he also launched a grassroots mobilisation drive aimed at building a 10,000-strong volunteer base to secure the re-election of President Bola Tinubu and the election of Lagos State Deputy Governor, Dr. Kadri Obafemi Hamzat, as the state’s next governor scheduled for January 16 and February 6, 2027, respectively.

The initiative is designed to establish a volunteer-based mobilisation structure across communities, markets, streets and households ahead of the presidential and governorship elections

​ Contrasting the APC 2013 political merger with ongoing talks among rival parties, Fashola, addressing the mammoth crowd of party stalwarts, former heads of service, lawmakers, and students in Lagos, maintained that historical coalitions in 1964, 1983, and 1999 all collapsed without winning the presidency.

He dismissed critics who once labeled the APC’s founding blocs as “strange bedfellows,” noting that while the ruling party has consolidated, the opposition has fragmented.

​ “This APC was and remains the only merger that has happened in the history of Nigeria’s political parliament. All of the alliances you have seen on the horizon now will fail too, with your votes,” Fashola told the gathering.Those who see conflict in their party and run away, don’t trust them. They will leave you when things are tough.They don’t stand for anything; they will fall for everything,” he warned.

​​“The intention is to achieve a volunteer party base of 10,000 people, working from now all through to election day, knocking doors, carrying the message of our party, explaining what our party has done, explaining what the candidates have done, explaining what the government has done,” Fashola stated.

​ ​Highlighting the APC’s track record in governance, Fashola pointed to major infrastructure milestones, including: the Lekki Deep Sea Port, the Second Niger Bridge, the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway, and the Lagos-Ibadan Railway, as proof of the party’s commitment to long-term economic growth over short-term savings.

Hamzat rallies Lagos APC supporters

​The governorship candidate, Hamzat, on his address launched a spirited defence of the ruling party’s governance record, contrasting the APC’s development “blueprint” against what he described as the opposition’s “manifesto of grievances.”

​Addressing the gathering, Hamzat urged APC canvassers to take a bold, fact-based message to voters ahead of the 2027 general elections. He emphasized that the upcoming polls are consequential for both Lagos State and Nigeria’s ongoing economic reforms.

​ Taking a swipe at rival political parties, Hamzat accused opposition figures of peddling falsehoods and backtracking on policies they once championed, specifically referencing the removal of the fuel subsidy.

Equipping party faithful for door-to-door campaigns, Hamzat outlined key achievements of the Babajide Sanwo-Olu administration and President Tinubu’s federal government, noting that Lagos has domesticated the Electricity Act signed by President Tinubu, enabling the state to participate in power generation, transmission, and distribution.

​Expressing concern over low voter turnout in previous cycles, Hamzat challenged residents to match the state’s high voter registration numbers at the ballot box.

World.title: Stay away from our state, Imo APC tells Wike
World.content:
File image of Wike.

The All Progressives Congress, APC, in Imo State, has declared that the state is not available for political manipulation or interference by the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, FCT, Nyesom Wike.

Read Also: ‘I’m done with Rivers, FCT; give me Imo, Kwara to deliver’ – Wike tells Tinubu

It vowed to resist any attempt to import what it described as his controversial political tactics into the state ahead of the 2027 general elections.

The party made its position known in a statement yesterday by its State Publicity Secretary, Onwuasoanya Jones in reaction to alleged Wike’s recent claim that he had concluded arrangements to secure electoral victories for President Bola Tinubu and the APC in the forthcoming elections.

Wike was also reported to have offered to undertake additional political assignments for the President, including delivering other states for the APC.

Reacting, the Imo APC dismissed the minister’s claims, contending that he should not assume that his political activities could determine the electoral fortunes of the party in different states.

The statement particularly faulted Wike for reportedly suggesting that Imo State and another APC-controlled state had political problems requiring his intervention.

“We would have ignored the politically displaced errand boy, like we always do, but for the fact that we deem this particular statement of his a direct affront on the President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria and the electoral integrity of our dear party, the APC,” the statement declared.

The party accused the FCT minister of attempting to portray President Tinubu as politically dependent on individuals outside the APC to secure electoral victories, insisting that the party enjoys its own grassroots support and political structure.

It also faulted Wike’s reported assertion that he had already secured victory for the APC in the FCT and Rivers State, describing such declarations, made weeks before the elections, as disrespectful to democratic principles and the electorate.

According to the statement, “our party, the All Progressives Congress, has immense regard for the Nigerian people and would not encourage actions and utterances that tend to cast the Nigerian electorate as irrelevant in the determination of their political future.”

The Imo APC further accused Wike of taking advantage of the party’s political goodwill to sustain his relevance while allegedly making disparaging remarks about some of its leaders.

It challenged the minister to demonstrate his political influence by campaigning for his own party, the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), rather than making claims about delivering APC victories.

On the political situation in Imo State, the party maintained that its activities were progressing without difficulty and expressed confidence in its preparations for the 2027 elections.

It said its mobilisation efforts across the state were ongoing, adding that it expected Imo voters to participate in the forthcoming elections scheduled for January 16 and February 6, 2027, as stated in the release.

The statement also alleged that Wike had deployed political associates and emissaries to Imo State with financial inducements in an attempt to create divisions within the APC. However, the party did not provide specific details or independent evidence to substantiate the allegation.

Describing the alleged moves as an attempt to introduce godfatherism, political intimidation and electoral manipulation into the state, the APC said it had warned those reportedly involved against such activities.

Vanguard News

World.title: Community attacked 24 times by bandits wants exit from Kaduna
World.content:
For the people of Kurmin Wali community in Afogo Ward, Kajuru Local Government Area of Kaduna State, incessant attacks by bandits have made them start thinking of relocating to where they could find peace.

The simple desire to sleep peacefully in their homes has become an increasingly distant dream.

For years, residents have lived under the agony of armed attacks, abductions and ransom demands, with the community reportedly attacked by bandits 24 times.

As a result, many families are not only battling the fear of being kidnapped but also hunger, poverty and the emotional burden of having their loved ones in captivity.

Some residents say they have reached the end of their endurance and are contemplating leaving their ancestral homes in search of safety elsewhere.

“We are leaving. We have sold our food to pay ransom. We are hungry and traumatised,” a resident lamented, describing the devastating consequences of repeated attacks on the farming community.

The latest attack occurred on Sunday, November 15, when armed men invaded the community and abducted 12 residents, renewing fears among villagers that another round of suffering had begun.

For the people of Kurmin Wali, however, the incident was not just another attack. It was the 24th time, according to residents, that the community had suffered attacks and abductions by armed criminals.

The repeated incidents have left families emotionally drained, with some struggling to raise money for the release of relatives while others have been forced to sell food and other possessions to meet ransom demands.

For a community largely dependent on subsistence farming, the situation has become particularly unbearable. The people who should be preparing their farms and harvesting food to feed their families are instead preoccupied with the desperate search for money to secure the freedom of their loved ones.

The Village Head, Isiaku Danazumi, said the community was exhausted by the persistent attacks and appealed to Governor Uba Sani to fulfil his earlier promise to facilitate the establishment of a military base in the area.

“They have attacked and kidnapped our people 24 times. Each time they come, the community is thrown into fear and trauma. Even me, I am not feeling well as we speak,” he said.

The traditional ruler said the community had endured so much that residents were beginning to question how much longer they could continue living under such circumstances.

“We are tired. We cannot continue like this. Where can we go again? How can we abandon our ancestral home because of this?” he asked.

Beyond the physical danger, the repeated attacks have inflicted deep psychological wounds on the villagers, who live with the uncertainty of whether their relatives will return home safely or whether another invasion will occur.

Danazumi said residents had identified a recurring route allegedly used by the attackers, particularly the forest corridor linking Maro and Rijana.

According to him, the attackers have repeatedly approached the community through Maro, with residents suspecting that the criminals operate from the Rijana axis through adjoining forests.

He recalled that Governor Uba Sani had promised to facilitate the establishment of a military base in the area following the mass abduction of worshippers during the Easter period earlier this year.

“We are making a strong appeal to our Governor, Uba Sani, to speed up the military base he promised us earlier in the year when several of our people were abducted during the Easter celebration,” the village head pleaded.

He described the proposed military base as an urgent necessity, saying the community could no longer cope with the financial and emotional consequences of repeated ransom payments.

“A military base around here is the only solution for now. We are tired of paying ransom. We are just an agrarian community that farms with hoes and cutlasses,” he said.

The village head further disclosed that some residents were still being held captive despite efforts by their families and the community to raise money for their release.

“We have our people in their custody. We have raised ransom, and up till now, they have not freed them,” he added.

The plight of Kurmin Wali is part of the wider security challenges confronting rural communities, particularly settlements located close to forest corridors suspected to be used by armed groups.

Rijana, along the Kaduna-Abuja Expressway in Kachia Local Government Area, has repeatedly featured in accounts of kidnapping incidents in the state.

In January 2026, following the abduction of 177 worshippers from churches in Kurmin Wali, Governor Uba Sani identified Rijana as a major security concern and called for the establishment of a military base close to the affected community.

In May 2026, eight farmers abducted near Kankomi village were reportedly released from a bandits’ camp in Rijana Forest after spending weeks in captivity.

For the people of Kurmin Wali, however, the statistics of attacks, abductions and ransom payments represent something much more painful than security figures.

They represent families separated from loved ones, farmers deprived of their livelihoods, children growing up in fear and households forced to sell the food meant to sustain them.

As another painful chapter unfolds following the November 15 attack, the residents are left with a desperate question: how long must they continue to live this way before they can sleep peacefully in their own homes?

For a people whose lives revolve around farming, family and their ancestral land, leaving may become the only option they believe is left. But for now, they are appealing for protection before fear and hunger finally drive them away.

Vanguard News

World.title: Security chiefs hail IGP Disu for suspending declaration of Obaigbena, others wanted
World.content:
IGP Olatunji Disu

By Emma Nnadozie

THE police order suspending the wanted declaration on Arise TV owner, Mr. Nduka Obaigbena and seven others over alleged assassination attempt by Assistant Inspector-General of Police, Olohundare Jimoh, has elicited reactions from some security chiefs in the country, who said that the wanted declaration was done without due process.

One of the security chiefs who spoke with Vanguard, said: “It was misappropriate and procedurally flawed” and showered encomiums on the Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu, for his quick response by suspending the wanted declaration

The Assistant Inspector-General of Police, Zone 2, Onikan, Lagos, Olohundare Jimoh, last Tuesday, declared Chairman of Arise News and This Day Media Group, Chief Nduka Obaigbena, Managing Director of Nestoil, Dr. Ernest Azudialu-Obiejesi, and seven others wanted over an alleged threat to the life of First Bank Managing Director, Olusegun Alebiosu in a crowed press conference in Lagos.

He said the declaration followed an investigation into the delivery of a parcel containing two rounds of 7.62mm live ammunition to Alebiosu’s residence in Lagos.

However, in a swift reaction two days later, the IGP, through the Force Public Relations Officer, FPRO, Ani Iniedu suspended the wanted declaration against the suspects and stated that the case has been transferred to the Force Intelligence Department, FID, Abuja, for a thorough and impartial investigation.

He also directed the nine individuals to report to the FID, at the Force headquarters , Abuja, between November 26 and 30, 2026.

In his reaction, the Director-General of the Institute of Security, Nigeria at the University of Lagos, Mr. Adebayo Akinade, said that the Zone 2 declaration was “misappropriate and procedurally flawed. The IGP’s suspension and transfer to Force Intelligence Department was correct, strategic and has restored public confidence.”

Former Director with the Department of State Service, DSS, and currently a security consultant, Mr. Mike Ejiofor, said: “The IGP has the superior order on such matters. When a subordinate makes a mistake, the IGP is in a position to correct it. So, I do not see any conflict in the matter.”

In his response the Chairman/Chief Executive Officer of Perfect Security Services Limited, Dr. Patrick Uwagbale saw the incident as “part of a system that is not in order. A good society will do something according to the rules. Even if the allegation is true or not, it is unheard of that someone as IGP would be on seat and a subordinate had the audacity to take such a decision on such a high profile incident without authorisation from the IGP who ordinarily should have the last say on such a matter. This type of behaviour clearly shows that our system is not healthy. “Something is wrong somewhere. There is a gap somewhere. I wholly support the decision of the IGP to suspend the declaration by his subordinate.”

Recall also that The Chairman of This Day Newspapers and Arise, Nduka Obaigbena also denied that he has been declared wanted by the Nigeria Police Force, following a petition by the bank Chief. In a statement by his office in Ikoyi, Lagos, he described the reports as a “desperate smear campaign,” insisting that neither the police nor any other law enforcement agency had invited him for questioning.

World.title: Lost in translation? Nando’s has a message for France
World.content:
Nando's has poked fun at France ahead of the Nations Championship finals this weekend. Images via X

Nando’s has made a cheeky dig at France ahead of the Springboks’ performance in the Nations Championship finale, which takes place on Sunday, 30 November.

The clash will mark the second time the countries have faced each other in recent weeks, following their showdown in Paris earlier this month, which South Africa lost.

This weekend, the rugby rivals will compete for the inaugural title at the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham.



NANDO’S MOCKS FRANCE WITH SPRINGBOKS SUPPORT

On its Instagram and Facebook pages, Nando’s showed its loyalty and support to the Springboks when it posted: “France, Uya kusiqonda ngeCawe”,

The Xhosa statement was a message to the French rugby team, translated as: “You will understand us on Sunday.”

It was also an ode to Springbok assistant coach Mzwandile Stick, who addressed a media conference earlier this week in his mother tongue, Xhosa. The move was frowned upon by international media, despite Xhosa being one of South Africa’s official languages.



It is believed to have been made in a bid to avoid misunderstanding, particularly on the back of Springbok coach Rassie Erasmus’s matchday suspension following his comments about the duties of match officials during the match against France in Paris earlier this month.

MATCH DETAILS

The Springboks will face France in the inaugural Nations Championship final on Sunday, 29 November 2026, at Allianz Stadium in Twickenham, London.



Kick-off is scheduled for 18:40 South African time.

South African viewers can watch the match live on SuperSport Rugby, which is open to all DStv subscribers as part of its OpenTime promotion.

Meanwhile, Springbok coach Rassie will host another watch-along party, which will stream from his hotel room.

World.title: ‘I’m a size 34’: Miss SA Tiyani responds to body-shamers
World.content:
Miss South Africa 2026 Tiyani Makamu has responded to social media trolls who have criticised her appearance with body-shaming comments about her weight.

The 27-year-old PR and Corporate Communications graduate was crowned earlier this month in a pageant finale at the Sandton Convention Centre.

Many critics questioned the new management, new direction of the pageant and even its makeshift crown, which quickly went viral on social media.



MISS SA TIYANI MAKAMU RESPONDS TO BODY-SHAMERS

Speaking to SABC talk show, Daily Thetha, Miss SA Tiyani Makamu spoke about being body-shamed on social media after her crowning.

She shared: “Now I’m a size 34…I’m a 27-year-old woman, and I’ve dealt with a lot of my insecurities, and there is no conversation people can have outside of me that I haven’t had with myself.

“Going onto the Miss SA platform, I was fully aware of what I was opening myself up to. There was a lot of self-counselling, unspoken conversations I’ve had with myself”.



Tiyani, who revealed that she was severely underweight as a teen, continued: “It’s not to say that when I go through things that it doesn’t sting a little, but I need to go back to higher ground and understand that I’m here now.

“There’s also caution now because of the platform that I hold”.

VIEWS ON THAT CROWN

Tiyani Makamu also shared that she was unfazed about the social media backlash to the Miss SA crown



According to pageant organisers, the item placed on Tiyani’s head during the finale was “temporary”, as they have planned to invite designers to contribute towards the finished product.

World.title: Tatjana Smith embraces ‘new family’
World.content:
Tatjana Smith on representing the Netherlands. Images via IG

Tatjana Smith has shared her excitement about representing the Netherlands as a professional swimmer, given her Dutch ancestry.

Earlier this month, the Olympic swimmer revealed that she would be representing the European country, to which she has dual citizenship.

The gold-medallist shared that finances, sustainability and support were key motives for switching her sporting nationality.



TATJANA SMITH EXCITED ABOUT DUTCH SPORTING CHAPTER

In an Instagram post, Tatjana Smith shared her excitement at her new chapter, joining Team Netherlands.

In a clip, the 29-year-old introduced herself to her new Dutch followers, sharing a look at her own Dutch upbringing and heritage.

Tatjana revealed that she had deep roots in the Netherlands, where her father, Rene Schoenmaker, was born and raised.



She shared: “Joining a new team and becoming part of a new swimming family is something I dont take for granted”

A few days earlier, Tatjana shared a post about how her Christian faith had affirmed her career move.

“Grateful for where I’ve been, at peace with where I am, and trusting Him with everything that’s still ahead”, she shared.



NOT ‘RUNNING AWAY’

Not long after announcing her decision to switch sporting nationalities, Tatjana Smith reflected on representing South Africa as a professional swimmer. She also responded to her critics who questioned her new allegiance to the Netherland.

Posting a montage of her career highlights on her social media platforms, Tatjana shared: “11 years being part of Team SA. One flag. Countless sacrifices. Four Olympic medals. World Championship medals. Commonwealth medals. African Championship medals.



“Years of dedication, commitment and pride in wearing the green and gold”

She continued: “Giving up when things get difficult doesn’t produce a journey like this. And running away when things get tough? I think 11 years tells a different story”.

Tatjana – whose gold and silver Olympic medals will remain SA accolades – added: “Forever grateful for the privilege of representing South Africa”.



FIRST RACE AFTER NATIONALITY SWITCH

Tatjana Smith will make her debut for the Netherlands at the World Aquatics Short Course Swimming Championships in Beijing, China, from 1–6 December 2026.

Instead of wearing green and gold, she will be wearing as she swims alongside her former South African colleagues.

World.title: Table Mountain introduces online-only ticketing ahead of festive season
World.content:
Visitors to Table Mountain can no longer buy the standard and Fast Track Cableway tickets from the onsite ticket office. Image: Pexels

The Table Mountain Aerial Cableway Company (TMACC) has made changes to the way visitors can buy tickets.

With the festive season just around the corner, those who visit the popular Capetonian landmark will have to purchase tickets online rather than buy them from the Lower Station Ticket Office. Through this switch, this will drastically reduce visitor queue lengths.

Let’s unpack this new change:



TABLE MOUNTAIN: NEW TICKETING RULES

From Tuesday, 15 December 2026, you can no longer buy the standard and Fast Track Cableway tickets from the onsite ticket office.

Instead, you will need to buy these tickets via authorised online booking channels before you arrive.

These channels include:

Webtickets

World.title: ‘Why am I alive?’: Derick Hougaard shares emotional update
World.content:
Former Springbok Derick Hougaard has shared an emotional update about his state of mind. His Facebook post comes a few months after the rugby player, fondly known as the “Liefling van Loftus”, revealed that he was in “big trouble” and facing financial hardships.

Since then, fans have rallied to show him support with kind words and by donating to his GoFundMe campaign.

Since hanging up his boots in 2015, Derick has suffered significant personal setbacks, including substance addiction, failed relationships and a series of health issues.



On his Facebook account, Derick Hougaard posted a lengthy message reflecting on his life. This included going through significant lows, in which he relied on his Christian faith to guide him through

“But God, you stayed with me through the night. In the hospital all night alone. I was weak and full of fear. But a faithful voice was always there. Your grace carried me home when I could not stand alone. Through the storms and the darkness, You led all the way. Grace held my hand. When I couldn’t understand…Through it all, You never left my side.

“There were seasons of confusion where my prayers were lost in spaces… When the world said I was hopeless… You rewrote my whole story and showed me where I belong”.



Derick Hougaard also hinted at a 2023 biography of his life.

He continued: “There was even a book written about me that I didn’t have a say or input. And not everything is true. Will I ever have the guts to tell my side of my life, or will I forgive and go to the grave with it?

“Jesus, why am I alive? You have a plan for me greater than what many people see. Because you saved me when I could have been dead.



Derick ended the post on a positive note, hinting at a “comeback”.

“Thank you to the person who stands by me. You know who you are. You don’t want credit, and I respect that. For everyone who relishes in another’s sorrow, I just want to say: the further you fall, the greater the comeback. And bigger is your testimony in Jesus’ name.

“Thank you to everyone who believes in me and prays and made me who I am today. See you soon in a town near you”.



RUGBY HERO TO BOOZE AND PILL ADDICT

Derick Hougaard’s stint as a Springbok player was cut short due to multiple head injuries. He had just 8 test caps for the national team.

However, the flyhalf had a decorated career as a Bulls player – where he was known as the “Liefling van Loftus” – playing over 100 matches in total, including 43 Super Rugby caps and 68 Currie Cup appearances for the team between 2002 and 2008.

In 2003, the star athlete suffered a significant blow to the head during the Rugby World Cup. This, after he was knocked out by Samoa’s Brian Lima in a brutal yet legal tackle, according to SA Rugby.



In the 2023 KykNET docuseries Hougaard: Liefling van Loftus, Derick admitted to heavy drinking and dependency on sleeping pills and pain medication.

He also claimed he had spiralled into a deep depression after his rugby career was cut short.

In the self-titled 2023 biography Derick Hougaard, author Brendan Nel wrote about the player’s long history of addiction.



An excerpt from an interview in the book reflected on Derick’s struggle to adapt to life after rugby.

He said, “This is one of the biggest gaps in my life. I always knew rugby was my passion, yes. But you don’t realise how big a role it plays in your life until you lose it. You don’t realise how big a void it will cause when you are no longer actively involved in it.”

Derick then again admitted to his addiction struggles: “It takes a man to ask for help or to admit that you need help. There are ugly and difficult times behind me, especially when I mix the pills and booze.”

World.title: Carling Knockout Cup final: Pirates, Chiefs off to Durban!
World.content:
The Moses Mabhida Stadium will host the 2026 Carling Knockout Cup final despite concerns surrounding a major rugby fixture scheduled in Durban on the same day.

The iconic Durban venue was among the options being considered by the PSL to host the highly-anticipated final between Kaizer Chiefs and Orlando Pirates on Saturday, 12 December 2026.

However, the scheduling presented an interesting challenge, with the Hollywoodbets Sharks also set to host Welsh outfit Scarlets in an EPCR Challenge Cup encounter at Kings Park Stadium on the same evening.



The encounter between The Sharks and Scarlets is at 19:30 while the Pirates and Chiefs match is scheduled for 15:30.

The two venues are approximately two kilometres apart, raising potential concerns about traffic congestion, crowd movement and security arrangements.

Carling Knockout Cup final between Orlando Pirates and Kaizer Chiefs in durban

Despite the potential logistical headache, Moses Mabhida Stadium was always in the conversation as the PSL considered the best venue for what promises to be one of the biggest football matches on the South African sporting calendar.

The situation had also attracted interest from Cape Town, with DHL Stadium expressing its willingness to host the Soweto Derby final.

The City of Cape Town had reportedly backed its bid with an estimated R4 million.

However, hosting the final in Durban would give local football supporters another opportunity to witness the country’s biggest football rivalry at a stadium that has previously staged more than one Soweto Derby game.



Interestingly, South African sporting authorities have previously adjusted major fixtures to avoid clashes with other events.

In April 2026, the Soweto Derby between Chiefs and Pirates was moved from 25 to 26 April because of the Ultra Music Festival at Nasrec.

With two major sporting events potentially competing for space in Durban on 12 December, the PSL’s final decision is regarded as crucial.

World.title: Moya pledges coalition unity as Tshwane’s new government takes shape
World.content:
PRETORIA - The City of Tshwane’s new coalition government is taking shape following Nasiphi Moya’s re-election as mayor.

The EFF’s Omphile Maotwe was elected deputy mayor, while the ANC’s Naeem Patel was elected Speaker of Council.

Moya has pledged to maintain cooperation among coalition partners despite their differing political interests and priorities.

Addressing councillors, she thanked the parties that had formed the governing coalition for their support and willingness to share the responsibility of running the capital.

“The past two years have taught me a great deal about coalition government. We come from different political traditions, with different perspectives and priorities. Yet we have demonstrated how much can be achieved when we listen to one another, respect our differences and find common ground.

“I commit myself to approaching our partnership in that same spirit.”

World.title: Who gets the mayor's chain? All eyes on eThekwini council
World.content:
DURBAN – The political battle for control of eThekwini Municipality comes to a head on Friday as newly elected councillors return to the Durban Exhibition Centre to elect the metro’s new leadership.

The high-stakes council sitting follows Tuesday’s adjournment, which was intended to give political parties more time to conclude coalition negotiations and find common ground on the municipality’s leadership.

However, competing political interests and ongoing behind-the-scenes negotiations have left the race for the mayoral chain far from settled.

The MK Party emerged as the biggest vote-getter in the local government elections but fell short of securing an outright majority, leaving the party needing support from other political formations to take control of the metro.

World.title: Marie-Antoinette's 'nipple bowl' auctioned for record $3.1 million
World.content:
PARIS - A rare porcelain cup in the shape of a woman's breast which once belonged to French Queen Marie-Antoinette fetched a record 2.9 million euros ($3.1 million) at auction on Thursday.

Complete with a moulded pink-tinged ceramic nipple, the late 18th-century masterpiece from the renowned Sèvres porcelain factory was thought lost for two centuries before its chance rediscovery in the inventory of the Meyer Gallery in Paris.

The "jatte-teton", meaning nipple bowl, was one of four such pieces which King Louis XVI once ordered for Marie-Antoinette's dairy creamery at the royal residence in Rambouillet, southwest of the capital.

The Austrian-born royal was notorious for her extravagant spending, contributing to the souring of public opinion against the monarchy ahead of her execution by guillotine in October 1793 at the age of 37.

Hôtel Drouot, which auctioned off the shapely china, said the 2.9-million fee was a record for a Sèvres porcelain under the hammer.

The auctioneer, which had estimated that the nipple bowl would sell between one and two million euros, did not reveal who had managed to get their hands on the extravagant piece.

Both Hôtel Drouot and the Coutau-Bégarie house, which organised the sale, decided to donate part of the auction's proceeds to the Pink Ribbon breast cancer charity.

World.title: Nations Championship Final: three key Springboks v France head-to-heads
World.content:
Ever present in both scrum-half and fly-half channels, Dupont has been in outstanding form, marshalling his team to the 21-19 victory over South Africa earlier this month.

Reinach, a speedster with a nose for the line and known for his intelligent game management, partners Manie Libbok at half-back, the pair having also started the 2023 World Cup quarter-final when the Boks beat France 29-28 on home turf.

"We've taken a good look at ourselves, and we've gone through the games carefully and identified our shortcomings, and we're ready to correct that," said Reinach, who spent five seasons in France with Montpellier.

"We'll definitely be better this weekend."
