World.title: Powerful storms disrupt holiday travel, as Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is postponed
World.content:
Powerful storms disrupt holiday travel, as Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is postponed

toggle caption i Adam Gray/Getty Images

Tens of millions of people are bracing for delays at airports and highways across the country on Thursday, as powerful storms across the United States threatened to disrupt travel for the Thanksgiving holiday.

On the West Coast, high tides have flooded streets along California's shorelines and knocked off a part of Pacifica Pier. The floods have also prompted evacuation warnings. On the East Coast, authorities are preparing to weather the impact of a storm making its way up into New England from the southeast with strong winds and heavy rain. Snow was also forecast in parts of the Midwest.

toggle caption i Mario Tama/Getty Images

Some 81.5 million people in the U.S. are expected to travel for the holiday between Thursday and Monday, according to AAA .

Sponsor Message

Hundreds of flights had already been cancelled or delayed by early morning Thursday, particularly on the East Coast, where authorities have warned people to stay home as the storm barrels through. The majority of people are expected to travel by car for the holidays, and the winter weather could affect their plans due to visibility issues on the road.

toggle caption i DANIEL SLIM/AFP via Getty Images

Richard Bann, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service Weather Prediction Center, told NPR that the East Coast storm remained the main concern, calling it a "multi-hazard" storm.

"It's going to be getting better organized as we go through the day, and it'll be spreading a considerable amount of wind, heavy rain. The real concern with this thing is going to be coastal flooding," Bann said.

Meteorologist Matthew Cappucci with The Washington Post and MyRadar told NPR the storm's magnitude at this time of the year was "unusual."

"We would expect this in deep winter," Cappucci said.

The storm in the East Coast, however, is expected to mostly clear out by Saturday, easing weekend travel for those returning from Thanksgiving gatherings.

Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade in New York City delayed

Beyond travel, several Thanksgiving parades have also been affected by severe weather.

Sponsor Message

The incoming storm is expected to cause high winds in New York City, prompting Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Wednesday to delay the city's famous Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade. Organizers were already inflating the iconic giant balloons for the parade on Wednesday when officials announced the decision.

toggle caption i Adam Gray/Getty Images

The parade, which is now expected to take place on Saturday, will be the city's 100th, and while it was cancelled before during World War II, this is the first time that it's been postponed in the last century.

The parade's organizers said it took two years to prepare the elaborate celebration, which includes over 11,000 participants and volunteers, thousands of high school marching band musicians from across the country and hundreds of balloon handlers. In previous years, up to 2 million spectators have attended the parade.

"Safety is and will always remain our top priority, and this will be a heavy storm," Mamdani told reporters.

toggle caption i Adam Gray/Getty Images

He urged the city's residents to prepare for extreme weather conditions. He said the city expected sustained winds between 30 and 40 mph and possible gusts as high as 65 mph, with resulting floods and flash floods.

"Generation after generation has watched Spongebob and Spiderman soar down our streets and has taken in Garfield floating down 6th Avenue. And I know this change of plans will cause inconveniences," Mamdani said. "Yet safety has to come first."

Philadelphia also grounded all balloons for its parade this year due to winds.

Steve Kastenbaum contributed reporting for this story.

World.title: Ford says he wouldn't hesitate to shoot a home invader, encourages Ontarians to 'fight back'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said he wants to see legal changes after a number of recent home invasions. Ford urged people to fight back and said he wouldn't hesitate to shoot a home invader: 'I'll blow the guy right through the front door.'

Ontario Premier Doug Ford says he wants to see legal changes to address a spate of home invasions, and in the meantime is advising people to "use anything you can to protect your family."

Ford says he is a legal gun owner and wouldn't hesitate to use it on someone trying to break into his home, advising people without guns to use knives or baseball bats to protect themselves and their children.

"I encourage people to use whatever tool they have to fight back," Ford told reporters at Queen's Park on Thursday. "Not hide, but fight back."

"Someone comes through my door with a gun and a knife and starts shooting it up, I'll blow the guy right through the front door. You'll look like Swiss cheese by the time he's done."

The premier was reacting to the fatal shooting of a 39-year-old musician during an overnight home invasion in an affluent midtown Toronto neighbourhood on Wednesday.

It happened nearly a month after a violent home invasion and shooting in the Bridle Path neighbourhood left a family of four adults injured.

WATCH | Victim in fatal home invasion was Toronto musician: Victim in fatal home invasion was Toronto musician | Duration closed caption 2:41 Police have identified the victim of a shooting during a home invasion in midtown Toronto Wednesday as Michael Eckert, 39. As CBC’s Dale Manucdoc explains, police are seeking at least one suspect.

Police suggest contacting 911 first

Toronto police said in a Wednesday news conference that people facing home intruders should contact 911 first.

"The Toronto Police Service provides the very best that it can in terms of public safety services," said Det. Sgt. Alan Bartlett. "I would encourage people to contact 911 to tell people what is happening."

Green Party Leader Mike Schreiner said he trusts police.

"I would call 911 and make sure my family is safe and allow the police to do their job," he said. "I think it's incredibly dangerous to suggest to people that they should be shooting other people."

NDP Leader Marit Stiles said Ford should be looking for ways to ensure people feel safe in their own homes, not telling them to arm themselves in order to protect their families.

"Doug Ford, he's really good at writing letters and coming out with outrageous statements, but the truth is that he can control some things in the province of Ontario," she said.

"For example, we have absolutely overloaded courts right now in the province of Ontario. We are letting the bad guys out too soon because of these packed courts, and he can do something about that and refuses to take responsibility.

"He has the power as the premier of Ontario to be able to protect Ontarians, and instead he's saying, 'You're all on your own. Protect yourselves.' That is unacceptable."

Past comments on Ford's take on crime

It's not the first time the premier has advocated for a violent approach to crime.

At an unrelated news conference in June of last year, Ford told a story about masked men who had tried to steal a vehicle overnight from his home, saying that if they came back, he would "take care" of them better than the police.

At the same news conference, he said a man charged by York Regional Police for allegedly shooting a gun in the air during an attempted vehicle theft deserved a medal.

A few months later, the premier spoke about threatening to beat up a Home Depot shoplifter.

Earlier this year, he said a York Region resident who shot and injured an alleged home invader "should have shot him a couple more times."

"Congratulations," he said. "I'm glad you shot the guy."

WATCH | Ontario Premier Doug Ford praises homeowner who shot intruder: Ontario Premier Doug Ford praises homeowner who shot intruder | Duration closed caption 2:06 Ontario Premier Doug Ford congratulated the homeowner who shot and injured an alleged home invader north of Toronto, saying he 'should have shot him a couple more times, as far as I'm concerned.' Opposition leaders denounced the comments as irresponsible.

Premier calls for legal change on federal level

Ford says he is directing his attorney general and solicitor general to look at legal changes that could bring the province "right up to the edge" of so-called castle law.

Ford has previously mused about introducing the castle doctrine, laws in some U.S. states that allow people to use reasonable force, sometimes including lethal force, to protect themselves in their homes.

Attorney General Doug Downey says there are already rules around self defence, but that they will examine whether the line is in the right spot.

Ford also called on the federal government to strengthen bail laws and increase mandatory jail time for violent offenders, which federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre echoed.

"This unfortunately has become an all-too-common story," he said in Ottawa. "Canadians are literally afraid to go to sleep at night."

The federal government's Bail and Sentencing Reform Act, or Bill C-14, received royal assent in June. It makes over 80 changes to the Criminal Code, Youth Criminal Justice Act and the National Defence Act to make bail and sentencing laws tougher for repeat and violent offenders.

Meanwhile, criminal lawyers and justice advocates have said that the changes could put more pressure on an already backlogged court system while doing little to address the factors that lead people to commit crimes.

Home invasions hit a 10-year high in 2024, before dropping in 2025 and then rising again at the beginning of this year in Toronto, according to CBC News analysis of Toronto police data. Affluent areas with large detached houses and driveways were among the hardest hit.

World.title: KDgate for Montreal mayor continues with website mocking Kraft Dinner comments
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The controversy over her Kraft Dinner comments is sticking to Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada.

The City of Montreal unveiled a budget that featured a property tax average increase of 9.8 per cent — about three times the inflation rate – on Tuesday.

The budget is due to be adopted in mid-December.

But an ill-timed Kraft Dinner comparison over budget choices has been haunting the mayor, giving rise to a website created by a Montreal software developer presenting the city budget on KD boxes.

There was also a protest outside city hall Thursday afternoon.

The landing page for the website, kdgate.ca, alludes to the mayor's comments. (Submitted by kdgate.ca)

Martinez Ferrada’s comments during an interview with French-language media outlet Quatre95, a personal finance site, following the budget rollout compared creating a municipal budget to decisions taken at home.

"We're going through every service to see what we can save. It's like when you make your personal budget: if you know you'll have less money one year, then, you have to make choices," she said.

"Sometimes, you'll have to eat a little more Kraft Dinner because you can't afford filet mignon."

WATCH | Protesters gathered to eat KD outside Montreal city hall: 'We can’t even afford Kraft Dinner': Montrealers protest mayor’s KD comments amid tax hikes | Duration closed caption 2:31 Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada is being flamed online after a comment she made in an interview Tuesday when discussing the city’s budget — which includes a historic residential property tax hike of nearly 10 per cent. Montrealers gathered to eat Kraft Dinner outside city hall on Thursday to mock the mayor’s comment, which they say was out of touch.

The comments were walked back by Martinez Ferrada on Wednesday morning in an Instagram story where she described the comparison as “clumsy.”

"What I meant was that when we make choices, the city is the same as when we make personal choices," she said.

But not before it unleashed a torrent of backlash on social media, framing her remarks as out of touch with the reality of Montrealers dealing with higher cost-of-living.

The website, kdgate.ca, includes a rundown of the city budget listed in a way that mirrors the nutritional facts on the back of a food item. (Submitted by kdgate.ca)

On Thursday morning, a website, kdgate.ca, was published outlining a municipal budget in the form of nutritional information on the packaging of the popular comfort food.

Niko Draca, the Montrealer behind the site, told CBC News about what prompted him to create it.

"I saw a lot of outrage over the comment and I wanted to turn it into something positive and really get people looking at this data," Draca said.

"These documents are usually quite long and dry, so I figured a fun way to visualize could help, basically using the KD comment as a hook."

Protesting tax hike, mayor's comments

Meanwhile, a crowd gathered in front of Montreal’s city hall Thursday evening to cook boxed macaroni and cheese, some Kraft and some not, to protest the mayor's tax hike and comments.

There were portable stoves, roiling water, elbow pasta and waving signs chastising the mayor. Other people held up enlarged printouts of the famous blue Kraft Dinner box.

Sam Bélanger was among those in attendance. Speaking to CBC News as metal was clanged, drums were banged and voices rang in the background, he called the mayor’s comments unacceptable.

“I feel like she’s totally disconnected from the reality of most people in Montreal, in Quebec and in Canada — the situation with rent and food and everything we saw since the pandemic,” he said. “Everyone is feeling that pain.”

Protesters held up signs Thursday afternoon that chastised Montreal's mayor and highlighted the rising cost of living in the city. (CBC)

He said the municipal budget has nothing to do with personal budgeting. While Montreal leadership is spending tens of millions, he said he’s not even thinking about filet mignon because “I can’t afford that.”

Meghan Henderson attended the event as well, and was enjoying some President’s Choice macaroni and cheese freshly cooked from the box. She said it’s tasty, but she’s feeling bitter.

“We’re just not really happy with how the city is being run,” she said.

“I was pretty peeved by the election results initially and I guess I had a feeling things would go this way. It doesn't feel like she’s really working for us or trying to make our lives better in any way.”

Rex Beckett, holding a homemade sign, said she attended the event to express her frustration over the property tax increase that will trickle down to renters like her.

At the same time, she said there are empty housing and commercial spaces during a crisis, and the homeless population is growing every day.

“How could you be that tone deaf? Who is eating filet mignon? We’re eating lentils and rice."

World.title: N.L. apologizes, says it now accepts Innu history dates back more than 300 years
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

“I don’t know if I thought this news would ever come, honestly,” said Grand Chief Jodi Ashini live on Facebook on Thursday. She read a letter Premier Tony Wakeham had sent her in which he apologized and said he regretted past tensions when the province refused to acknowledge that Innu had been in the province longer than 300 years.

The Grand Chief of the Innu Nation says Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham has apologized following a months-long controversy over the Innu's history in Labrador.

"Newfoundland and Labrador accepts the position that the history of the Innu in Labrador goes back to the time of immemorial, prior to the arrival of Europeans," Jodie Ashini said on a Facebook livestream Thursday.

Ashini was reading a letter written to her by Wakeham dated Thursday.

The controversy has been making headlines since June, and boiled over when it was revealed that, according to the Innu, the province's archaeology office only considered the history of the Innu to go back 300 years — which Ashini has called "a theory."

The tension between Ashini and Wakeham boiled over in September, when Ashini walked out of a meeting with Wakeham and later committed that the Innu Nation would not vote to support the new Churchill River deal with Quebec unless the province changed its tune on the Innu's history.

The pair held a nearly three-hour meeting earlier this month. Wakeham had previously committed to an independent audit of Innu records held by the archaeology office.

“I regret the length of time the controversy around the 300-year issue has taken to resolve. I apologize for the problems which arose from the province's position," Wakeham's letter, shared with CBC News, said.

WATCH | Breaking down the dispute between the N.L. government and the Innu Nation: Why is the Innu Nation upset with the N.L. government? | Duration closed caption 8:03 A conflict has erupted between the Innu Nation, The Rooms provincial museum and the provincial archaeology office over the First Nation's history and a planned exhibit. The CBC’s Leila Beaudoin takes this look at Innu history and what could be prompting the controversy.

Speaking with reporters late Thursday afternoon, Wakeham said he had an emotional conversation with Ashini on Wednesday.

"To be brutally honest, it was emotional for both of us," Wakeham said.

"It caused me a lot of grief … trying to get to the bottom and understand all of it. And yeah, it was a lot of grief, I think, especially for the Innu Nation."

Federal clarification was what N.L. needed to hear: Wakeham

Wakeham was hesitant to take a stance on the timeline in the months during the dispute, often saying he wanted to wait to get the facts before making a judgment.

On Thursday, Wakeham told reporters he got those facts in October.

As part of land claim negotiations between the Innu, the provincial government and the federal government — which have been ongoing since 1977 — Wakeham said the federal government clarified that Innu have history in Labrador since time immemorial.

Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham says the federal government clarifying to the province that the Innu have been in Labrador since time immemorial was what he needed to be able to move forward in addressing the wrongs felt by the Innu Nation. (Terry Roberts/CBC)

Following that clarification, Wakeham said he felt comfortable to move forward.

"Clearly, I don't see as a province how Newfoundland and Labrador cannot be on the same side as the federal government in acknowledging the Innu. And I spoke to the Grand Chief about that," Wakeham said.

"[I] apologized for the length of time that it had taken and regret the grief that it had caused the Innu Nation.”

Ashini wiped away tears several times throughout the livestream, expressing thanks for the support from "every single Innu."

“I don’t know if I thought this news would ever come, honestly,” Ashini said.

“I’m proud to bring you this letter that our history will forever be recognized that we were here longer than 300 years … and they’re not going to erase our grandparents and they’re forever marked."

Wakeham said he hopes the province and the Innu Nation can continue to work toward reconciliation.

"It was important for me to try to mend that relationship. None of us want to be at odds, and I think for both myself and Minister [Lela] Evans, that was important."

World.title: Defence minister 'very concerned' after Poilievre claims constituent's job was threatened
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Defence Minister David McGuinty says he's asked his deputy to raise concerns about a Wainwright, Alta., nurse's job being threatened after she was photographed with Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre.

The minister told MPs on the House defence committee that the issue was brought up with the government contractor that employs the nurse, but beyond that there is little more that he could do at this point.

"This is a matter of privity of contract between her and her employer, which is a contractor to the federal government. So obviously you can imagine I can't involve myself in that private sector contract," he said.

"I did ask my deputy to speak to the company involved to at least raise the issue. It was raised."

WATCH | Minister agrees with Poilievre on concerns about threats made against constituent: Defence minister agrees with Poilievre on concerns about threats made against constituent | Duration closed caption 2:54 In a House of Commons committee on Thursday, National Defence Minister David McGuinty said his department looked into Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre's point of privilege raised in the House of Commons Wednesday evening, when he said a constituent's job was threatened after she met with him.

In an unusual speech in the House of Commons on Wednesday evening, Poilievre said his parliamentary privilege is being breached because of the incident.

Last month, Maureen Carpenter — a nurse who helped treat soldiers burned in the CFB Wainwright fire — was photographed speaking to Poilievre following the tragic incident that killed five soldiers and wounded 38 others on Oct. 17. Poilievre said she is under contract with Calian Health, a government contractor.

"Maureen spoke to me on base, with the permission of the unit commander. I had the permission of the base commander to be there. She talked about caring for our men and women on the shift that night, that horrendous night," said Poilievre.

An online post from Oct. 20 shows Poilievre meeting with medical staff at CFB Wainwright Health Services. Online comments identify the woman in the photo as Carpenter, which was confirmed by Poilievre's office.

This photo of nurse Maureen Carpenter was posted online by Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre on Oct. 20. (Pierre Poilievre/Facebook)

The base is part of Poilievre's federal riding of Battle River-Crowfoot.

He said, following the meeting, Carpenter was subject to a complaint and threatened — told by her boss that if her term contract was not already coming to an end, she would be put under the microscope by the company's legal department.

McGuinty said during the committee meeting that he agrees with Poilievre "that constituents should always feel free — and MPs should always be able to speak to their constituents."

"I've been on this file, on this issue, because I'm very concerned. It's not right that a member of Parliament should not be able to speak to a constituent."

Now that Poilievre has raised the matter as a point of privilege, the minister said he needs to wait for the Speaker's ruling as well.

"I can't cross a certain other line, which is the question of, now, this claim that Mr. Poilievre's own privileges have been affected. That's now residing with the Speaker and I'm hoping for a good outcome in terms of the decision there."

McGuinty said he has been in contact with Carpenter's brother.

CBC News has reached out to Calian Health and Carpenter for comment but has not yet received a response.

World.title: Residents skate the streets as freezing rain blankets Fort St. John, B.C.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Chris Boehm didn't let hazardous weather keep him indoors Thursday morning.

After freezing rain coated the streets of Fort St. John in northeast B.C., he decided to strap on his skates and take a spin around his neighbourhood.

"I saw a couple people skate by our house, I'm like, what the heck, I've never done this in my lifetime. I'm 50 years old, now I've done it," he said.

He wasn't alone. Around the city people took out their sleds, skates and hockey sticks to take advantage of the unusual conditions.

WATCH | Skating the streets of Fort St. John: Residents skate and sled the icy roads of Fort St. John | Duration 0:40 Adverse driving conditions didn't stop people from using the roads for other modes of transportation.

"It was super fun, I felt like a kid again," said Leann Muggeridge, whose kids stayed home from school after bus runs were cancelled due to the slippery streets.

She said the roads were surprisingly smooth, likely due to a lack of snow, while Boehm said it was as if they had been flooded specifically for skating.

Throughout the morning, highway warnings were posted encouraging people not to drive unless absolutely necessary. The City of Fort St. John also urged people to avoid unnecessary travel as crews worked to clear and sand main routes.

Muggeridge didn't mind the delays.

"I know we have our ups and downs ... but I feel like when something like this happens you'll see even adults, their personalities come out," she said.

World.title: A Boston man won $1M US in the lottery. Days later, ICE arrested him
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales held an oversized cheque for $1 million US and smiled in the photo posted Saturday by the Massachusetts State Lottery.

Local media described the Boston man as "all smiles," reporting that he planned to save and invest his winnings after matching 11 words on a $10 US scratch ticket. Lottery officials said it was the first puzzle he'd ever scratched.

A few days later, his photo was posted online again — but this time, by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which said it had arrested the "illegal alien from El Salvador" on Tuesday. Now, Velasquez-Morales will remain in ICE custody until he's removed from the U.S., the agency said in a news release.

The ticket "ultimately led to his arrest," ICE said, without elaborating how. CBC News has reached out to ICE and not yet heard back. Velasquez-Morales does not yet appear on ICE's Online Detainee Locator System, where members of the public can search for people held in the agency's custody.

“Looks like his luck ran out,” said ICE public affairs assistant director Micah Bock in the news release.

On Nov. 24, ICE Boston arrested Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales, an illegal alien from El Salvador, during operations in East Boston, Mass. Velasquez-Morales entered the United States illegally on May 15, 2013. He was ordered removed by an immigration judge on April 24, 2014. https://t.co/YieIbY7afF —EROBoston

"Welcome to the ERO [enforcement and removal operations] Boston lottery! Where illegal aliens and sanctuary politicians are out of luck, and the law-abiding citizens of New England are always the winners!" ICE Boston posted on X.

It's unclear if Velasquez-Morales has legal representation. CBC News has reached out to several Boston-area immigration lawyers and not yet heard back.

A woman identifying herself as Velasquez-Morales's sister-in-law wrote on Facebook Wednesday asking for respect and empathy for him, his wife and children.

"There is a family waiting for him," she wrote in Spanish.

Another woman identifying herself as Velasquez-Morales's older sister commented on the same post, writing her wishes that he would soon be back home with his family.

CBC News has reached out to both women for comment and not yet heard back.

A photo of Ariel Velasquez-Morales posted by ICE in a new release on Nov. 25, announcing that ICE Boston had arrested the man a day prior. (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement)

Can you win the lottery if you're not a citizen?

Velasquez-Morales illegally entered the U.S. in 2013 through the Texas border, according to ICE. An immigration judge ordered him removed in 2014, the press release noted, but "he illegally remained in the country."

While ICE posted on social media that "th e rights and privileges reserved for American citizens are for American citizens," state lotteries typically do not require citizenship or residency — if you meet the age requirement and are physically present in a participating jurisdiction when buying the ticket, you can play.

CBC News has reached out to the Massachusetts State Lottery and has not yet heard back. But its website help desk notes that anyone age 18 and up who is physically present in the state can buy lottery tickets at retail locations and win prizes. The Boston Globe reports that the lottery also doesn't require winners to have social security numbers, but that non-resident winners often face higher federal taxes on their winnings.

Some U.S. states allow lottery winners to remain anonymous no matter the amount, others depend on how much a person win, but many — including Massachusetts — do not let winners claim prizes anonymously.

"The Massachusetts State Lottery treats a winner’s name, town and prize as public information and releases them," explains the Massachusetts Legal Resources website.

WATCH | ICE arrests passengers boarding plane in Seattle: 'They're taking my dad:' Masked ICE agents arrest passengers at Seattle airport | Duration closed caption 2:00 New video showing masked, plainclothes ICE officers detaining Sofia Hernandez Mejia and her father, Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport is sparking backlash from various politicians and protesters. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security says Mendoza overstayed his visa and will be deported to Mexico.

"The lottery’s position, and the state’s, is that publicity is part of the game: It demonstrates that real people win, and it deters fraud in the claiming process."

Michael Baker, a Massachusetts attorney who works with lottery winners, told the Boston Globe that immigrants may not realize how much exposure winning the lottery can bring them.

"I’m sure people, when they play, they’re not expecting being at risk of being arrested," he told the media outlet.

World.title: Yukon power infrastructure project now at Carney's Major Projects Office
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The number-one item on Yukon Premier Currie Dixon's wishlist has materialized: federal support for a major power infrastructure project in the territory.

Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Thursday the Whitehorse Power Centres project has been referred to the federal Major Projects Office.

The announcement came after a day of meetings between the prime minister, Yukon Premier Currie Dixon and First Nations leaders in Whitehorse. Before the visit, Dixon said his top priority was talking with Carney about the territory's electrical grid.

"The Yukon is growing, and reliable, affordable electricity is essential to building our future," Dixon said in a news release Thursday night. He added federal support gives the Yukon a chance to double its electricity grid.

The Whitehorse Power Centres project, which will now see a federal investment of up to $73 million, includes two new thermal power plants, a new electrical substation and transmission infrastructure in Whitehorse. It will add 15 megawatts of capacity to the grid by 2028, a number that should eventually expand to 150 megawatts in later phases of the project.

A news release from the Prime Minister's Office states the Major Projects Office will help Yukon assess necessary upgrades to accommodate stress on its power grids as a result of the project.

It said the office will also look at opportunities for Indigenous partners to participate in the energy sector, including through potential equity ownership.

Yukon Energy has said the plants are a necessity right now as the grid is under increasing strain. Last winter, the territory almost maxed out its power capacity during a particularly nasty cold snap, prompting warnings from officials of possible rolling blackouts — though it never actually came to that.

This winter, the territory and City of Whitehorse have said they have a plan to prevent that risk from happening again, by selecting buildings to temporarily disconnect from the grid at times of peak energy demand.

The power project in question was identified in the federal budget earlier this month, but Thursday is the first time the federal government has released a figure for how much funding it intends to apply to it.

The Major Projects Office was established to speed up permitting for projects considered to be in the national interest. Other northern projects include the Mackenzie Valley Highway and Taltson hydro expansion in the N.W.T., and the Grays Bay Port and Road Project in Nunavut.

World.title: This birdwatching expert tracked down every single bird in Grand Theft Auto VI
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Getting tired of slinging drugs, stealing cars and running from the cops in Grand Theft Auto VI? You can always give birdwatching a try.

When the news dropped a week before its release that arguably the most anticipated video game of the decade would feature 62 bird species to log, birdwatching expert Nick Lund took notice — and vowed to be the first to find them all.

"I've played video games my whole life, but I'm a birder first and foremost," he told CBC's As it Happens.

"It's not often in real life that I get to rob a bank and then look at some parrots on the way out as I'm escaping."

In the smash-hit release from Rockstar Games, players can alternate between the perspectives of characters Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos as they roam a fictionalized Miami and south Florida.

As with previous games in the series, the central plotline dives into the criminal underworld. But for those who want to take their time with the crime, players can do chores, buy flowers — or go looking for avian species from roseate spoonbills to house sparrows.

Birders working to fill out their GTA VI wildlife checklists should know something I just found out: THERE’S A ZOO https://t.co/2xN0joPKcR —TheBirdist

Players can simply use in-game binoculars to look at a bird and the game automatically logs its information. Other forms of wildlife can also be logged, adding another dimension for completionists.

For Lund, the most tantalizing illegal activity the game offers isn’t smuggling or high-speed chases: it’s being able to pull his car to a screeching halt in the middle of an intersection just so he can get out and look at a cool bird in the sky.

"[It’s] something that as a real life birder I’ve wanted to do my entire life," said Lund, who lives in Maine and works for a state conservation organization.

Nick Lund, who has been birding for more than 20 years, says the birding experience in GTA VI is surprisingly accurate. (Nick Lund)

'Actual species you'd find in south Florida'

Not only do the birds in GTA VI look accurate enough for most to be identified without binoculars, Lund said, but you also have to trek to their habitats to find them.

"It's set in a fictional version of south Florida and I've birded in Florida a lot. And so I was actually able to use my experience in real Florida to figure out where to go to find birds in fake Florida GTA," he said.

Wading birds and herons creep through the game's version of the Everglades. Sanderlings and terns are found flitting around the beaches. Birds known to be in the north of Florida are found in the northern part of the game’s map, while bird populations that make Miami their home in real life, including tropical birds, are also found in the heart of the game’s city.

But there’s a few hiccups.

"There’s a whole bunch of whooping cranes around," Lund said. "It's a very rare bird that lives mostly in Texas."

Golden eagles are also a common sight in the game, despite being rarely spotted in south Florida.

incredibly healthy populations of critically-endangered Whooping Cranes across Vice City. Huge if true. https://t.co/doe6oMOvBX —TheBirdist

Overall, though, the game "does a great job of presenting actual species that you’d find in south Florida," Lund said.

Before the game’s release it was reported there would be 62 bird species to find — a fraction of the real number found in Florida — but the official in-game compendium only includes 60 slots for gamers to log their birds.

Lund said he’s found 63 in total so far, including three not listed in the official bird count. He’s since written a guide to the game’s birds for Audubon magazine .

He isn’t the only GTA player going gaga for gulls — many have taken to social media to share their birding excitement. One user on X suggested players "make a GTATwitter Birdwatching club!"

WATCH | Inside the buzz around Grand Theft Auto VI: What makes the release of Grand Theft Auto VI so special? | Duration closed caption 4:29 It's been 13 years since the last Grand Theft Auto game came out and a lot has changed in the video game industry since then. Video game developer Jason Kapalka joins the CBC's Dan Burritt to discuss the hype surrounding Grand Theft Auto VI and how it could save the game industry, which has been going through brutal rounds of layoffs.

"It's really wild that birding is such a prominent part of such a huge cultural phenomenon," said Kyle Horner, an engagement co-ordinator at Birds Canada.

He noted that some other games, like Rockstar’s Red Dead Redemption 2, have included birding, and said he hopes it catches on.

"Hopefully people who enjoy it in the game maybe take it up in real life. Maybe they realize there's birds outside in their own world that they can go and explore, too."

Considering the game is for entertainment and not for education, "they really nailed it," Horner added.

Players can use the in-game binoculars to automatically log birds. (Rockstar Games/Grand Theft Auto VI)

Lund doesn’t know if he was actually the first player to find all the birds, but a designer from Rockstar gave their seal of approval.

World.title: The bizarre twists and turns of Colombia’s supermarket hostage siege
World.content:
Blackout drunk kidnappers, false statements by De La Espriella, and bogus accusations against hostages leave a trail of chaos and doubt.

Shortly after 76 hostages were liberated from the Exito Supermarket in Cartagena, Colombia, corporate media broadcast a video of two of the men they claimed were involved in the attack.

​The two men, Carlos Tapia and Daniel Díaz, appeared in handcuffs, being escorted by police from the scene of a tense 18-hour standoff between criminals and police.

The media, with information from President Abelardo de la Espriella, suggested that Tapia and Diaz were two of four surviving members of the gang that attacked the supermarket.

​De la Espriella praised the operation he said “came off perfectly,” and released a video of himself mocking two different men, who police say were the actual kidnappers, together with one more person who was killed in the operation.

The president also released a video of himself making demands into a walkie-talkie, falsely claiming that he was in charge of negotiations with the hostage-takers.

According to the indictment from the Prosecutor’s Office, all negotiations and communications with the three hostage takers were handled by Colombia’s anti-kidnapping police unit, the GAULA.

​Tapia and Díaz were released by police just a few hours later, and cleared of any wrongdoing after police confirmed the men were hostages rather than hostage-takers. De la Espriella confirmed shortly afterwards that the men were innocent of any crimes.

​The two men have since both spoken with Colombian media, in interviews in which both men claimed they were mocked by De la Espriella and treated badly by police before being cleared.

​A third man, Edgar Díaz, was also falsely accused by police. He released a video to social media as well, claiming that not only was he mocked and verbally abused by the President, but also robbed of a gold chain by police. Diaz says he was leaving a gym where he works as a personal trainer, in the same mall as the Exito, when he was grabbed by men who appeared to be armed.

The stories of the falsely accused hostages aren’t the only odd parts of the official story surrounding the stand-off between 3 nominally armed men and hundreds of marines, police, snipers, helicopters, and riot police in the city of Cali.

​One of the hostage-takers was killed by police when they entered the supermarket around 1 a.m., after the hostage-takers missed a deadline of 12:30 to release all hostages.

​According to police, the three men attempted to rob an armored car transporting money around 8 a.m., but the car had already left by the time the men arrived. For unclear reasons, the three decided to take nearly 100 people hostage in the Exito supermarket instead, which is part of the same “mega-mall” where the men allegedly intended to carry out the hijacking.

​Two of the men carried long guns that, again according to police, were “traumatic weapons” (similar to Airsoft rifles, the weapons fire foam bullets meant to be non-lethal), and one was armed with another that resembled a shotgun.

Early in the morning, before the men blocked windows in the supermarket, Colombian media captured one of the men from a distance clad in black tactical clothing, body armor, and what appeared to be a heavy steel helmet with a facemask.

​Many of those who were held hostage, speaking with media, said the men were drinking heavily throughout the day, with one witness going as far as to say they were “blind drunk” by the end of the day.

​Workers at the Éxito, who were also taken hostage, said the men set up large speakers, blasted music, and demanded to be given bottles of whisky.

​The two men who survived the police assault that liberated the hostages were asleep when police entered the Éxito, likely why they survived, according to multiple witnesses.

​Confusing matters even further, the wife of the man who was reportedly killed by police, Javier Humberto Muñetón Zapata, had spent the previous 14 hours speaking with local media in Cartagena, looking for her husband, who she believed to be among the hostages.

​She says they lived nearby and went to the mall every day, and that her husband had a membership at the same gym where Diaz works. She claims she began searching for her husband, who had promised to drive her to work and bring pastries from the supermarket, after he suddenly stopped replying to texts.

​She showed Blue Radio a text message at 8:12 a.m. from her husband that said, “Okay, I’m going to pop into Éxito, and I’ll pick you up right away.”

​She claims that her husband ran a small business, regularly drove her to work, and has no criminal record — a fact that has since been confirmed by Cartgena’s mayor. She has made multiple statements to the media asking for clarification and more information, claiming he could not have been involved in any crimes.

Early statements by police, shortly after the hostage situation began to unfold, put the number of hostages at 50. After two releases of hostages by the nominal gunmen, police stated they believed 20 hostages remained as evening approached.

​Shortly after the operation to enter the Éxito, police released details about their raid, claiming that they had “drilled holes in the walls and inserted cameras,” allowing them to identify the kidnappers and estimate the number of hostages.

​They also stated they had men on the roof, in the warehouse of the supermarket, and stationed at the interior entrance to the Éxito, which connects to the mega-mall.

​But more than 70 hostages remained when the raid was successfully carried out.

The attackers claimed in a letter to authorities that if the store was entered by police they would detonate explosives placed near the entrances, killing the hostages.

Police later revealed there were no explosives, and the men were bluffing.

​The two men who were captured alive (and reportedly asleep), Juan Camilo Torres Manco, 33, and Jhon Albeiro Mejía Blandón, 44, are both from Antioquia and have previous convictions for “violent” crimes, according to police.

​Both men appeared intoxicated in videos shortly after they were captured. De la Espriella released a video in which he berates the two men, telling them, “You thought you could just kidnap people and get away with it? Welcome to the miracle country.”

​The bizarre details of the event, as well as misreporting by the media, inaccurate and even contradictory statements by police throughout the day, and general confusion, led some critics of De le Espriella to claim the entire event was staged.

De la Espriella’s efforts to insert himself into the situation, and false claims made by the president, worsened that dynamic.

​There is no evidence currently to support those claims, but with a story that is just straight-up strange, we can see how some people came to that conclusion.

World.title: Colombia’s special forces liberate hostages from Cartagena supermarket
World.content:
Colombia’s security forces liberated some 20 people who were held hostage inside a supermarket in the northern city of Cartagena after a 15-hour stand-off.

The operation ended a tense situation that began around 8AM on Tuesday when the armed kidnappers entered the Exito supermarket in La Castellano, a residential neighborhood.

According to President Abelardo de la Espriella, who led the liberation operation, the kidnappers meant to rob an armored car that had already left with the proceeds of the day before.

The kidnappers subsequently kidnapped a group of 30 people, and demanded COP7billion ($2 million) and the possibility to escape the supermarket.

Throughout the day, at least five of the hostages were released from the supermarket cafeteria, whose windows had been covered with papers. One video showed a row of hostages sitting behind the window.

Riot police was deployed around midnight after family members and onlookers became restless.

The situation took a quick turn after 1PM when explosions were heard and special forces entered the building.

The security forces killed one of the kidnappers and detained the remaining four, De la Espriella said in a social media video.

Images that were shared on social media showed special police forces securing the Exito’s cafeteria and removing the paper from the windows.

De la Espriella said that all the hostages were released in an “extraordinary joint operation between the National Police and the military forces.”

One agent would have been injured in the rescue operation, reported Caracol Radio.

The kidnappers “were given the opportunity to surrender and release the hostages, but they rejected that opportunity, so we took decisive action,” said the president.

In the morning, the prosecution said the kidnappers’ arms and explosives were fake and former hostages said the hostage takers spent most of the day getting drunk.

World.title: 22 injured after car bomb strikes central Colombia governor’s office
World.content:
Twenty-two people were reportedly injured and more than 80 buildings were damaged in a car bomb attack on the Governor’s Office of Meta in Villavicencio, central Colombia.

According to Meta’s Security Secretary, Franklin Olivos, the car that exploded carried approximately 100 kilograms of explosives and caused damage to buildings that were located more than 100 meters away from the blast.

Among the injured are five private security guards. One of them needed surgery, according to his employer.

Olivos blamed the attack on the 39th Front, a unit of the FARC dissident group EMC, which has opposed the peace process that started 10 years ago on Tuesday and controls large swathes of jungle territory in the south of Colombia.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said that “narcoterrorism is desperate because we are confronting it head-on. It seeks to intimidate us and force us to back down so we seek another sham peace process.”

De la Espriella, an opponent of the peace process, has been advertising an “iron fist” policy against organized crime and illegal armed groups.

The president’s alleged offensive has failed to produce any results and guerrilla groups have continued to attack State security forces and infrastructure.

World.title: Colombia strips key critics of security details
World.content:
Colombia’s National Protection Unit (UNP) has withdrawn the security details of journalist Daniel Coronell, a major critic of President Abelardo de la Espriella, after vowing to protect the freedom of the press.

Coronell’s local security detail was removed because he lives in the United States, which would make it impossible for the UNP to reassess his protection plan.

The Miami-based journalist frequently travels to Colombia for his work and was in Bogota to receive a lifetime achievement award from the national journalism prize.

While receiving the prize, Coronell sharply criticized De la Espriella for promoting self-promotion over governance. using state resources to censor critics, restricting public information to “friendly media,” and leveraging a history of aggressive lawsuits against reporters.

The journalist’s criticism triggered a clash with Interior Minister Alejandro Ordoñez, who accused Coronell of being angry for having State subsidies pulled.

After press freedom foundation FLIP responded to defend Coronell, Ordoñez claimed that “the freedom of the press enjoys full protection and guarantees from the government.”

We value and defend freedom of the press as a cornerstone of democracy. The press is free, but it is also responsible. It is not a license to abuse, slander, defame, fabricate stories, spread misinformation, or engage in politics. Nor is it a license to destroy democracy or its institutions with lies. Interior Minister Alejandro Ordoñez

Coronell played a key role in Colombian journalism since the late 1980’s and was forced to flee Colombia in 2005 after reports on the ties of former President Alvaro Uribe and paramilitary groups escalated death threats.

The journalist currently works with Noticias Uno and Caracol Radio, and has more than 700,000 subscribers on YouTube.

The UNP previously stripped former President Gustavo Petro and former presidential candidate Claudia Lopez of their security details.

World.title: Illegal armed group carries out first urban drone attack: three injured in northeast Colombia
World.content:
A couple and their 18-month-old baby were injured in a drone attack on a police station in Cucuta, the first major city to be struck from the sky by guerrilla explosives.

The attack damaged more than 60 homes near the Norte de Santander Police Department in the Tasajero neighborhood in the north of the regional capital, the province’s security secretary, George Quintero, told press.

As of now, the situation is as follows: more than 60 damaged homes located just 20 meters from the police headquarters, and three people injured. Security secretary George Quintero

The homes were hit because the police department’s signal-jamming systems reportedly caused the drones to miss their target.

An unknown number of drones were able to reach the interior of the Police Department’s compound, leaving only minor damage.

Guerrilla group ELN has been carrying out multiple drone attacks in Catatumbo, a nearby region with major coca cultivations, and exercises control in the peripheral slums of Cucuta.

The group was accused of attacking the same police department with home-made mortars in August. This attack injured seven policemen.

In a response to the guerrilla attack, President Abelardo de la Espriella in October ordered the militarization of the border city, which has been struggling with security issues for years.

De la Espriella vowed that he “will not allow narco-terrorism to continue sowing fear and threatening families” in Cucuta and the surrounding Norte de Santander province.

According to the authorities, the militarization of the city sought to “strengthen territorial control, protect citizens, and confront” the illegal armed groups that operate in and around Cucuta.

The president’s offensive against illegal armed groups and organized crime has been hampered by an increase in the use of drones that are equipped with explosives.

All kinds of illegal armed groups use the relatively new technology to push back the authorities from areas under their control.

World.title: Colombia asks X to suspend Petro’s social media account
World.content:
Colombia’s communications ministry said Sunday that it had requested social media platform X to suspend former President Gustavo Petro for “possible incitement to violence.”

In a statement that was published of X, the ministry said it reported Petro’s account to X’s Public Affairs, Safety, and Rules Enforcement Team.

According to the statement, the request to suspend the leftist former president, who has more than 9 million followers, was due to a November 21 post in which Petro asked “the people of Colombia to demand Abelardo’s resignation now.”

Petro has been trying to promote popular opposition against De la Espriella, who he has called an illegitimate president.

According to the ministry, Petro’s call to “take action in the streets” could constitute a call for violence against the government.

In a response, the former president said the De la Espriella administration sought to impose censorship on him, which is “expressly prohibited by the Constitution.”

The ministry’s request “demonstrates the extent of the current government’s illegitimacy,” added Petro.

The former president is now the leader of the Historic Pact (PH) opposition party and has actively been promoting a general strike in response to his successor’s controversial policy decisions.

Petro is a member of the PH’s more radical wing and can still count on a significant following among Colombia’s population.

World.title: De la Espriella calls on US to prosecute Petro in response to call to “resign now”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the US Justice Department to “investigate, prosecute and hopefully jail former President Gustavo Petro after the latter called on the people to “rise up” and “restore real democracy.”

De la Espriella addressed the nation at the end of a day of anti-government marches that mobilized tens of thousands of people throughout Colombia.

Petro led the march in Cali and called on his supporters to “rise up,” call a general strike and force the president to “leave now,” less than four months after De la Espriella took office.

Reiterating fraud accusations and the president’s business ties to paramilitary warlords and drug traffickers, the former president told the crowd that “it is not about waiting until 2030; an illegitimate government must leave now.”

A government whose policy goes against the people must leave now. A government whose policy builds hunger and death for the people of Colombia must leave now. Life must be restored, democracy must be restored, and the slogan “Abelardo, resign now!” must become the slogan of the majority of the Colombian people. An agreement will eventually be made to transition back so that the Constitution of Colombia and the laws in favor of the Colombian people prevail. But from here on out—and that is why we must move to a national strike, that is why we must move to a general strike—within the people’s right of expression and decision, an illegitimate government that goes against the interests of the Colombian population must leave now. Gustavo Petro

De la Espriella told Petro that he would never accept they “attack democracy, promote a coup d’état or attempt to destroy Colombia, just as he did when he was a guerrilla fighter.”

The president claimed that the former President and congressional opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “have no moral authority whatsoever. However, as I tell you, I will not accept them attacking democracy, attacking institutionality, or promoting a coup d’état in an attempt to destroy Colombia.”

De la Espriella repeated his threat to extradite his predecessor if requested to do so by the administration of his ally, US President Donald Trump.

I make a direct call to the judicial authorities of the United States so that investigations related to acts of corruption, drug trafficking, or any other criminal conduct move forward with full rigor and the independence of the judicial system in the United States. Petro’s government was a criminal enterprise, and international laws and provisions were violated. The United States has jurisdiction to investigate him, prosecute him, and hopefully imprison him. Let the North American justice system act, let the whole truth be known, let the evidence be examined, and let those found responsible answer before the law without regard for anything other than the application of the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president has tried to criminalize the opposition and the former government ever since taking office in August without much success.

World.title: Vast Majority of Women Suffer Violence Without Reporting It
World.content:
Actress Samantha Ruth Prabhu is participating in a campaign to end violence against women in India. Globally, only a very small percentage of women seek help or report the physical or sexual violence they have experienced to the authorities, and legal cases often fail to result in convictions or sentences. Image: UN Women India

By IPS Correspondent

HAVANA TIMES – Only seven percent of women who experience physical or sexual violence report it to the police, and barely 23 percent seek help from family members, their communities or authorities, according to a UN Women report released on Monday, November 23.

The study by the United Nations agency, based on data from 54 countries, estimated that worldwide, 840 million women and girls – nearly one in three – have experienced physical or sexual violence at some point in their lives.

Published ahead of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, November 25, the report notes that even when women decide to come forward, justice is far from guaranteed.

Sexual violence crimes are among the least likely to result in a conviction.

Sima Bahous, executive director of UN Women, said that “too many justice systems around the world are failing women and girls who experience violence. Cases go unreported, trials fail to move forward, and rulings go unenforced.”

“Justice cannot be achieved when women and girls have no access to it or when the law fails to protect them. We must work to ensure that justice systems fulfill their fundamental responsibilities to protect survivors, uphold their rights and prosecute perpetrators,” she added.

The UN Women study reveals a system in which silence is the norm, accountability is the exception, and perpetrators are far more likely to go unpunished than women are to obtain justice.

Many women remain silent, not by choice, but to protect themselves from the risks associated with speaking out. That is why barely seven percent of victims report acts of physical or sexual violence to the police, despite it being one of the most widespread human rights violations.

Women who report abuse may lose their homes, their children and their income. They may face abandonment by their families, exclusion from their communities and threats from the perpetrators they identify.

When women decide to come forward – sometimes years after the crimes were committed – they are all too often punished for speaking out and blamed for having waited. Some are murdered by their abusers simply for seeking help.

The number of women survivors of violence seeking help is declining in most countries that track such data.

In Asia, according to UN Women, only 16 percent of survivors seek help. In Africa, the figure is 31 percent, and in Latin America and the Caribbean, 40 percent.

In European Union countries, while 64 percent of survivors speak about the assault with someone close to them, only 14 percent go to the police.

According to research cited in the report, between 63 and 97 percent of complaints worldwide do not result in a conviction. Cases get lost in the justice system; survivors are subjected to repeated questioning and intimidating situations, and perpetrators may never be brought to trial.

All too often, perpetrators in positions of power are never convicted of the crimes they commit, fostering a culture of impunity.

The same pattern is repeated in the digital sphere. Only 25 percent of women involved in public life who experienced online violence filed a complaint with the police.

It is not the perpetrators who are penalized, but the women, who are silenced and excluded from digital spaces and prevented from exercising their right to participate freely in public life.

Against this backdrop, Bahous stated that “progress is possible. Today there is greater recognition of violence against women and girls, more laws protecting survivors, and more perpetrators behind bars.”

She emphasized that “the protections women have today are the result of the struggles of generations who dared to speak out. Now we must honor their courage by delivering justice, ensuring that every law provides safety, every promise translates into protection, and every word into action.”

“Until every woman and every girl can live free from violence, without fear and without having to prove that she deserves to be believed,” the UN official added.

The theme of this year’s International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women is “UNiTE to End Violence against Women and Girls.”

First published in Spanish by IPS and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

World.title: Cuban Regime Punishes Jailed Journalist Henry Constantin
World.content:
and also his partner with three months without visits

Although authorities allege a violation of prison regulations, the journalist interprets the measure as further retaliation against her and her partner/ Facebook

HAVANA TIMES – Alejandra García denounces that prison authorities sanctioned her for trying to deliver water, food, and books to the journalist, who has been imprisoned since September.

Cuban authorities have added a new measure of punishment against independent journalist Henry Constantín, director of La Hora de Cuba, who has been imprisoned in Camagüey since September 16. This time, the sanction falls on his partner, fellow journalist Alejandra García, whom the Kilo 7 prison administration has banned from visiting him for three months for attempting to deliver drinking water, food, and books. The items never even made it into the prison.

The complaint was published by La Hora de Cuba in a video in which actress and independent journalist Iris Mariño interviews García about what happened. According to her testimony, she received a call from prison officials asking her to come in on Thursday, November 19. After waiting several hours without being seen, she was told to return the next day. On Friday, she was informed that her visits to Constantín were suspended for three months.

The alleged reason given by the authorities was that she had tried to deliver items to the inmate outside of designated visiting hours. García explained that the water, food, and books were rejected by the officials. Despite this, the prison administration decided to impose a sanction that will keep her separated from her partner for three months.

“Another injustice is being committed right now,” La Hora de Cuba reported when publishing the testimony. “Everything has been arbitrary, everything is unjust; it has all been pressure, aggression, and threats,” García stated.

The new measure adds to a series of incidents denouced since the journalist’s arrest. He was initially accused of disobeying a police summons, which he maintains he did attend. After being detained at Villa María Luisa, the State Security headquarters in Camagüey, he was transferred on September 24 to Kilo 7, where he remains in pretrial detention.

Since then, his defense has denounced obstacles to accessing the court file, procedural delays, and the refusal to modify the precautionary measure. A habeas corpus petition filed to challenge the illegality of his detention was rejected.

The persecution denounced by his family and friends is not limited to the legal proceedings. On October 15, Constantín was sent to solitary confinement after officials claimed to have found a homemade knife among his belongings. The journalist denied that the weapon was his and maintained that it had been deliberately planted to frame him.

In addition to the accusations, there are complaints about his conditions of confinement.

In a statement published by his own media outlet , García questioned the circumstances of the search and claimed that no fingerprints had been taken from the object. The incident resulted in 15 days of isolation and a second criminal case for alleged disorderly conduct and possession of weapons in prison facilities.

In addition to the accusations, there are also complaints about his prison conditions. García stated that Constantín had lost about eight pounds and was being pressured to leave Cuba. She also reported that he was not receiving all the medications and food sent by his family.

The journalist described hygiene problems, the presence of mosquitoes and bedbugs, as well as difficulties accessing drinking water. In an article published after her first conjugal visit , held on November 12, she recounted the conditions of the cellblock and reported that prison authorities had threatened her because of her writings about Constantine’s imprisonment.

The ban on visits comes, therefore, after García made those allegations public. Although the authorities cite a violation of prison regulations, the journalist interprets the measure as further retaliation against her and her partner.

Constantin’s imprisonment comes amid a repressive escalation against the independent Cuban press.

The legal situation also appears to be stalled. According to García, Constantín’s lawyer informed him that the case for disobedience is now before the Camagüey Municipal Court, under the abbreviated procedure. However, a trial date has not yet been set.

The case has prompted statements from international organizations. The Inter-American Press Association (IAPA), whose Committee on Freedom of the Press and Information Constantín serves as regional vice president for Cuba, demanded his release and described his imprisonment as extremely serious. Reporters Without Borders and the Committee to Protect Journalists have also called for his freedom, while the Cuban Observatory for Human Rights has requested guarantees for his physical and psychological well-being.

Constantín’s imprisonment comes amid a repressive escalation against the independent Cuban press, marked in recent months by arrests, interrogations, threats of imprisonment, and restrictions on movement. In November alone, police detained reporters Adelth Bonne and Camila Acosta, while Yoani Sánchez, director of 14ymedio , was held for nine hours by State Security.

More recently, Acosta denounced that the authorities intend to charge her with assault . The Inter-American Press Association (IAPA) had already warned in October about the intensification of police and judicial harassment against those who practice journalism outside of official media outlets, in a country where the independent press still lacks legal recognition.

Translated by Translating Cuba.

World.title: Havana Weather for November 26 to December 2
World.content:
Photo at a Havana bakery by Juan Suarez

Change in weather in western Cuba with rain followed by a drop in temperatures, bringing cooler conditions toward the weekend…

By Adrian Fuentes

HAVANA TIMES – The approach of a trough and the advance of a cooler air mass over western Cuba will bring an increase in rainfall in Havana over the coming hours, followed by a slight drop in temperatures toward the end of the week.

In the capital, rain and thunderstorms were expected to continue on Wednesday the 25th. A cold front will arrive between Wednesday night and the early hours of Thursday the 26th. Beginning Thursday, rainfall will gradually decrease, with partly cloudy skies and cooler conditions. Stable weather will prevail on Friday the 27th and Saturday the 28th, with temperatures slightly below normal for this time of year. Starting Sunday the 29th, temperatures will gradually rise again, although variable cloud cover will persist.

Winds will be from the southwest and west before and during the passage of the system, subsequently shifting to the northwest and north at speeds of between 15 and 30 kilometers per hour, with potentially stronger gusts associated with thunderstorms. Relative humidity will remain high during the first half of the forecast period, potentially exceeding 90% during rainfall, before decreasing slightly toward the weekend. Maximum temperatures will range between 24 and 29°C (75 and 84°F), with the lowest expected on Friday and Saturday, while the lows will range between 20 and 23°C (68 and 73°F). Sea surface temperatures will remain at 26 and 27°C (79 and 81°F).

According to the National Hurricane Center, the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season recorded 10 named storms and only one hurricane (Isaias), with activity well below average. No additional tropical cyclone development is expected in the basin before the official end of the season on November 30, and there are no active systems posing a threat to Cuba.
