World.title: Anti-Feminism as an Electoral Force for Brazil’s Far Right
World.content:
Newly elected state legislator Eduarda Campopiano, a young rising star of Brazil’s far right, at an election campaign event in São Paulo in October. Fighting feminism is the main rallying cry of this new lawmaker, who rose to fame as a social media influencer. Photo: Rafa Neddermeyer / Agência Brasil

By Mario Osava (IPS)

HAVANA TIMES – At just 23 years of age, anti-feminist activist Eduarda Campopiano is Brazil’s new electoral sensation, espousing a cause that has become a powerful electoral rallying cry for the far right.

She received 1,956,238 votes to win a seat in the São Paulo State Legislative Assembly, presenting herself as “the greatest enemy of feminists” in that southeastern Brazilian state.

In the October 4th general elections, only two men surpassed her in the number of votes received: Nikolas Ferreira and Lucas Pavanato, both from the same far-right Liberal Party (PL) as Campopiano. The two male candidates received more than three million votes each to win seats as federal deputies in the states of Minas Gerais and São Paulo, respectively.

Another candidate who is also a leading anti-feminist crusader is Ana Campagnolo from Brazil’s southern state of Santa Catarina. Campagnolo was elected to that state legislature with a record 387,522 votes. The 36-year-old historian wrote the book Feminism, Perversion and Subversion, which seeks to provide a theoretical foundation for anti-feminism.

In percentage terms, she was Brazil’s most-voted candidate, securing 9.07% of the valid votes (out of an extensive list of candidates) in her state, which has 8.3 million inhabitants. Meanwhile, Campopiano received 8.4% of the valid votes a field of 20 candidates in São Paulo, the country’s most populous state, with 44.2 million inhabitants.

The presidential, federal and state legislative, and gubernatorial elections held in October resulted in a 21% increase in female representation in both the national legislatures and in the 26 states plus the Federal District of Brasília, according to electoral authorities.

The number of women elected to legislative bodies rose from 308 in 2022, to 373 in October.

The most significant increase was seen in Brazil’s senate, where two-thirds of its 81 seats were up for grabs. Of the 54 newly elected or reelected senators, 12 are women, three times the number in 2022, when only one-third of the seats were contested.

In the 513-member Chamber of Deputies, the number of female representatives will increase from 90 to 109, a rise of 21.1%.

The new legislatures will be inaugurated on February 1, 2027, while governors will take office on January 6, and reelected president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, will be sworn in a day earlier.

A demonstration by the Mujeres Vivas [“Women Alive”] movement in Rio de Janeiro in July 2026, urging both chambers of Congress to approve a law against misogyny and femicide. It now appears unlikely that any legislation against gender-based violence will be approved by Brazil’s new Congress, dominated by far-right forces. Photo: Tomaz Silva / Agência Brasil

The rise of the far right a blow to feminism

However, the far right was the political force that made the greatest gains in both legislative chambers. The Liberal Party, which encompasses most of the extremists, will have three new female senators, increasing its number of female deputies from 17 to 22. Its congressional delegations will occupy 28 of total 81 Senate seats, and 121 of 513 seats in the Chamber of Deputies.

These figures dampened feminists’ celebrations over the increase in the number of women in the legislative branch. Moreover, conservatives as a whole strengthened their majority in the bicameral National Congress.

There are fears of a rollback of some hard-won women’s rights, given that the PL’s far right, known as Bolsonaristas for their allegiance to former President Jair Bolsonaro, has allies in other parties considered right-wing or center-right.

The strong presence and mobilization of women on the far right is nothing new. It occurred during the years of of “historical fascism in Germany and Italy,” as well as in Spain with the “blue women” of the Civil War (1936–1939), and in Portugal under the dictatorship of António de Oliveira Salazar (1933–1968), recalls Sonia Correa, coordinator of the Sexuality Policy Watch.

In Brazil, the so-called Integralismo movement, a far-right group of the 1930s, had a broad female base. In 1964, a series of demonstrations called the “March of the Family with God for Liberty”, spearheaded by women, paved the way for the military coup that same year and served as an example for similar mobilizations in the United States and Chile, the researcher added.

From the grassroots to leadership

“One difference is that in historical fascism, women were mainly in the movement’s grassroots, or served as mid-level cadres in the Italian Fascist Party, the Nazi hierarchy, the Spanish Falangist movement and the rise of Portuguese dictator Salazar. Today, they are leaders, aspiring to and attaining leadership positions,” Corrêa explained.

The winners of the 2024 European Parliament elections included Marine Le Pen (France), Giorgia Meloni (Italy) and Alice Weidel (Germany), far-right figures who subsequently won other victories, she noted.

In Brazil, conservative women such as Damares Alves, minister of Women, Family and Human Rights during Jair Bolsonaro’s administration (2019–2023), have risen to prominence, along with deputies Bia Kicis (Brasília) and Caroline De Toni (Santa Catarina), elected in 2018 and reelected in 2022.

All three will now hold Senate seats: Alves was elected in 2022 and the other two in October 2026. Together they make up the female leadership within the Bolsonarista movement, alongside the former president’s wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who was also elected senator for Brasília.

Alves, the former minister and now senator, is not a member of the Liberal Party like the other three, but rather of the Republicans Party, an example of how Bolsonaro supporters are spread across several right-wing political organizations.

One similarity between the women recruited by historical fascism and those on the far right today is that both have benefited from feminist struggles begun in the 19th century, and spearheaded by progressive movements, Corrêa pointed out.

“The reactionary women aligned with the fascist camp today are clear beneficiaries of what is known as the fourth wave of feminism – that of my generation – in terms of access to the workforce, education and, above all, political participation,” she said in an interview with IPS in Rio de Janeiro.

Ana Campagnolo, the newly elected state legislator from Santa Catarina and an active proponent of Brazilian anti-feminism, at a hearing in the City Council of Itajaí, a city of 302,000 inhabitants and an important export port in southern Brazil. Photo: Davi Spuldaro / Itajaí City Hall

A backwards step for civilization

In Brazil’s specific case, one significant aspect of the rise in women’s anti-feminism, alongside the macho far right, is “the expansion of fundamentalist evangelical sects, whose main audience is women, especially poor women,” she stressed.

“Ultra-Catholicism” also contributes to shaping this political current, but “evangelical Christianity creates a favorable environment, not only because of its economic dimension, the so-called prosperity theology and its emphasis on entrepreneurship, but also because of its agendas concerning sexuality,” the researcher emphasized.

“Gender and sexuality issues are not peripheral. They are not merely moral issues or a smokescreen to deceive people but long-standing central pillars of the political project of the reactionary camp, as well as of the new right,” she clarified.

Far-right women deny the benefits of feminism. Ana Campagnolo, for example, attributes women’s suffrage, which was not introduced in Brazil until 1932, not to feminist struggles but to a concession made by men. Only those who held power could extend that right to others, she argues in her public statements.

Campopiano, the youngest star of the Bolsonarista movement and a follower of Campagnolo, rose to popularity as a social media influencer by espousing thoroughly backward-looking ideas, going so far as to claim that the Christian conversion of Indigenous peoples prevented them from continuing to practice cannibalism and burying children alive.

In her view, femicide is an invention, and it is not enough to eliminate the legality of abortion in cases of rape or when the mother’s life is at risk, both of which have been legal in Brazil since 1940; rather, abortion must be made “unthinkable,” unacceptable under any circumstances.

She opposes racial quotas for admission to universities, public service and other activities, and advocates expanding the right to carry firearms, including for women, as a way to defend themselves against violence.

Campopiano dropped out of her political science studies in her second year at a private university and acknowledged having been an “agnostic” until the age of 20, when she converted to Catholicism.

In addition to social media, she spread her beliefs through a traditional radio network. In 2024, she was elected to the City Council of Praia Grande, a city of 371,000 inhabitants located 77 kilometers from São Paulo. This marked the beginning of her precocious political career, and another example of how Brazil’s far right is renewing its leadership.

“There is an obvious contradiction in women occupying positions of political power thanks to rights historically won by feminist movements, while at the same time rejecting feminism and advocating social roles of submission and devotion to the domestic sphere for other women,” warned Leticia Vella, a lawyer and sustainability director of the Feminist Collective for Sexuality and Health.

But exposing these contradictions and debating the meaning of feminism is not enough. “We need to understand how anti-feminist narratives manage to connect with women’s anxieties, expectations and aspirations, and how to build alternative narratives based on those experiences,” she acknowledged in remarks to IPS from Brasília.

A major challenge is changing the way a segment of the population perceives feminism, which requires reassessing strategies for communication, mobilization and dialogue with society, Leticia Vella concluded.

First published in Spanish by IPS and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

World.title: The Grocery Combo: Cuba’s Pantry Is Paid for Abroad
World.content:
Products paid for abroad and delivered to homes.

By Safie M. Gonzalez

HAVANA TIMES – On an iron chair and a blue sofa with worn upholstery, survival is displayed in plastic. A tray of thirty eggs, bottles of cooking oil, bags of powdered milk, Yeya pasta, Rios rice and canned goods form a pyramid that, at first glance, looks like a middle-class family’s groceries for the month. To one side sits the coveted La Excelencia toilet paper, Fox detergent and Coolwhite soap. On the floor, green mesh bags reveal malanga, sweet potatoes and plantains.

This is not the bounty from a miraculous ration store, nor the result of a carefully planned shopping trip to a local market. It is a supermarket package paid for abroad.

The transaction did not take place in Havana. It happened through a screen in Miami, Madrid or Santiago de Chile. A click, a credit card, a Zelle transfer or a cash payment at a shipping agency. Across the sea, a relative or friend put together the package, selected the brands and paid in foreign currency so that, days later, a “mule” or a delivery truck would drop off this shipment of food and hygiene products at the doorstep of a Cuban home.

This is the new anatomy of Cuba’s basic basket of goods: a household economy no longer governed by state salaries, but by the wallets of the diaspora and the exchange rate.

The Luxury of Basic Necessities

This type of grocery combo package is a barometer of the crisis. A decade ago, a shipment from abroad usually included clothes, shoes, perfumes or household appliances. Today, the priorities are eggs, cooking oil and toilet paper. The diaspora has become the de facto “Ministry of Food” for thousands of households, sending what cannot be guaranteed locally.

The irony lies in the brands. Products such as Yeya rice or La Excelencia toilet paper are notorious among Cuban consumers for their poor quality or local packaging processes. Yet when included in a package paid for abroad, they acquire the status of a privilege. Having a pantry stocked with these products means having a relative who makes sacrifices, working overtime abroad to ensure that detergent or powdered milk does not run out back on the island.

The Divide of Plastic and Cardboard

This reality also illustrates the social inequality eating away at the island. While packages of pasta and canned goods pile up in some households, in others survival depends on the informal market, where prices are beyond people’s reach.

The grocery package paid for abroad is a lifeline, but also a marker of social class. For those who receive it, it offers the peace of mind of knowing that their protein and hygiene needs are covered for a month. For those who have no one abroad, it is a reminder of their economic isolation. In Cuba today, family solidarity crosses oceans, but it also leaves many stranded on the shore.

The Business of Survival

Behind this domestic scene lies a commercial machinery. Shipping agencies have perfected the model of grocery packages known as “combos” (Combo A, Combo B, Executive Combo). They offer emigrants the convenience of choosing a preassembled package—with eggs, grains, cooking oil and hygiene products—and paying for it securely.

This model has transformed consumption. Families in Cuba no longer ask for what they need; they adapt to what the package offers. Standardization has turned grocery shopping into a lottery in which those who pay get to choose, and those who receive make do with what they get.

In the middle of the living room, the package waits to be unpacked. Every can, every roll of toilet paper is a reminder of distance and of love packaged for delivery. But it is also evidence of a country where daily survival has been outsourced abroad, and where a packet of detergent or a simple bag of root vegetables and plantains has become the most precious of treasures.

Read more from the diary of Safie M. González aquí en Havana Times.

World.title: Earth exceeds 2C of warming for seven consecutive days for the first time
World.content:
Earth exceeds 2C of warming for seven consecutive days for the first time

27th Friday, November 2026 - 04:35 UTC Full article

The record coincides with the failure of the UN COP31 climate summit in the Turkish city of Antalya, which ended on November 22 without a main political agreement

The planet's average temperature exceeded pre-industrial levels by more than 2C for seven consecutive days, something that had never happened before, the Copernicus Climate Change Service, the European Earth observation programme, has confirmed. On Monday, November 23, the largest daily anomaly ever measured was also recorded: 2.25C above the 1850-1900 period.

The 2C threshold was reached on ten days in November — the 3rd, 4th, 13th and from the 18th to the 24th — seven of them consecutively. On November 23, the global average temperature was also 1.34C above the 1991-2020 average. These are not the highest absolute temperatures, which usually occur in July and August, but the largest deviation from normal for this time of year. Until now, 2C had been exceeded on only two days in November 2023 and four in February 2024. The data are preliminary, although Copernicus does not expect changes of more than 0.02C.

Exceeding that threshold for a few days is not the same as breaching the 2015 Paris Agreement, which aims to limit warming to 1.5C and keep it well below 2C, measured as an average over many years. “While this does not mean the long-term 2C threshold set by the Paris Agreement has been exceeded, it is a clear preview of where our climate is heading,” warned Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. “El Niño is temporary; the underlying warming caused by greenhouse gas emissions will persist unless we reduce those emissions.”

Copernicus considers it very likely that 2026 will end as the second-warmest year on record, with a 20% chance of equalling or surpassing 2024, and expects it to be the second calendar year in which warming exceeds 1.5C. Its director, Carlo Buontempo, has warned that there is a fairly high chance of at least one year exceeding 2C before 2030.

The record coincides with the failure of the UN COP31 climate summit in the Turkish city of Antalya, which ended on November 22 without a main political agreement after several oil-producing countries refused to allow the final text to mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.

World.title: Lula picks banker Luiz Carlos Trabuco to run the Finance Ministry in his fourth term
World.content:
Lula picks banker Luiz Carlos Trabuco to run the Finance Ministry in his fourth term

27th Friday, November 2026 - 04:30 UTC Full article

Trabuco, who comes from a humble background and has been a personal friend of Lula for years, has worked at Bradesco, the country's second-largest private bank, since the age of 17

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has chosen banker Luiz Carlos Trabuco, 75, chairman of Banco Bradesco's board, as finance minister for his fourth term, which begins on January 5. Trabuco accepted the post on Thursday night, according to the magazine Veja, although the appointment has not yet been officially announced.

He is the first known name in the new cabinet, which reflects the importance of the task ahead, including implementing the fiscal adjustment. Trabuco, who comes from a humble background and has been a personal friend of Lula for years, has worked at Bradesco, the country's second-largest private bank, since the age of 17.

Markets welcomed the news. The São Paulo stock exchange rose 6% on Thursday, its biggest gain since Lula's re-election on October 25. Over the past month the index had lost 18% of its value and the real had fallen 15% against the dollar, amid investor distrust over the public finances. Last week the Central Bank sold US$1 billion from its reserves to curb the rise of the US currency.

Congress has just approved the government's spending containment plan, with savings of about 60 billion reais, around US$10.6 billion, and the government has pledged to maintain the social benefits Lula announced at the end of the campaign. Public debt has risen sharply during the current term, the fiscal deficit is around 9% of gross domestic product and the benchmark interest rate stands at 13.75%, one of the highest in the world. Last week the Finance Ministry cut its 2027 growth forecast to 1.8%.

The ministry was led for almost the entire current term by Fernando Haddad, of the Workers' Party. According to Reuters, Lula plans to announce a first batch of ministers next week, on his return from the Mercosur summit in Montevideo.

World.title: Milei becomes the first head of state to visit Alliana in Paraguay after Peña's fall
World.content:
Milei becomes the first head of state to visit Alliana in Paraguay after Peña's fall

26th Thursday, November 2026 - 22:33 UTC Full article

Milei and Alliana in Asunción

Argentine President Javier Milei travelled to Asunción on Thursday to back Paraguayan President Pedro Alliana, becoming the first foreign head of state he has received since replacing Santiago Peña, who was removed from office and jailed over the collapse of Ueno Bank. The same day, Paraguayan prosecutors said they had detected funds from the bank in Argentina.

Argentine President Javier Milei travelled to Asunción on Thursday to back Paraguayan President Pedro Alliana, becoming the first foreign head of state he has received since replacing Santiago Peña, who was removed from office and jailed over the collapse of Ueno Bank. The same day, Paraguayan prosecutors said they had detected funds from the bank in Argentina.

Milei was received with honours at the López Palace, the seat of Paraguay's government. “Welcome to Paraguay, President Milei! May this visit allow us to keep building a future of prosperity for our brotherly peoples,” Alliana wrote on social media, highlighting that the two countries are united by “the affection of two peoples who have grown up together”.

Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno, who accompanied Milei, gave a press conference with his Paraguayan counterpart, Rubén Ramírez, whom he described as a “friend”. Quirno said the two governments have long shared “the ideas of freedom and the protection of private property”, and that Buenos Aires had offered its cooperation in dealing with the crisis caused by the collapse of Ueno Bank, which left almost three million savers without access to their deposits.

Paraguay's deputy prosecutor for international affairs, Manuel Doldán, told ABC Cardinal radio that “some funds” from Ueno had been detected in Argentina, so Argentine authorities had been asked to freeze assets and property linked to the bank, and a formal request for cooperation had been sent. “We are requesting the identification of bank and financial accounts, corporate, accounting and asset documents, which will also allow us to see how the financial ecosystems were handled there,” he said.

The visit coincided with an intense legislative day in Argentina. The Chamber of Deputies passed into law the reform of the Central Bank's charter by 141 votes in favour, none against and 99 abstentions, a week after the session scheduled to approve it collapsed for lack of quorum. The reform bans the bank from printing money to finance the Treasury and strengthens the tenure of its authorities. Deputies then moved on to debate the 2027 budget, while the Senate discussed suspending next year's open primary elections, known as PASO.

Milei and Alliana will meet again next week in Montevideo at the Mercosur summit of heads of state, together with the host, Yamandú Orsi, and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Relations between Argentina and Brazil are at their lowest point: this week Brasília permanently withdrew its ambassador from Buenos Aires and decided not to invite Milei to Lula's inauguration, after Quirno cast doubt on Brazil's electoral process.

World.title: Edmundo González announces his return to Venezuela after more than two years in exile in Spain
World.content:
Edmundo González announces his return to Venezuela after more than two years in exile in Spain

26th Thursday, November 2026 - 22:31 UTC Full article

Venezuelan opposition leader Edmundo González

Venezuelan opposition leader Edmundo González, a candidate in the July 2024 presidential election, announced on Thursday that he will soon return to Venezuela, after more than two years in exile in Spain, to take part on December 5 in the pilgrimage of the Virgin of Coromoto, the country's patron saint, in the city of Guanare.

Venezuelan opposition leader Edmundo González, a candidate in the July 2024 presidential election, announced on Thursday that he will soon return to Venezuela, after more than two years in exile in Spain, to take part on December 5 in the pilgrimage of the Virgin of Coromoto, the country's patron saint, in the city of Guanare.

“I will soon be in Venezuela to accompany the pilgrimage of our patron saint, the Virgin of Coromoto. What better time to return? After so long away from home, I am moved to think that I will be with you again,” González wrote on X. He said he had “much to thank Venezuelans, Spain” and his family for.

Opposition leader María Corina Machado had announced his return the day before at an event at the Central University of Venezuela. “He will be here soon,” she said. González replaced Machado as candidate in 2024 after the authorities barred her from running. The opposition claims González won, citing the tally sheets it collected, while the National Electoral Council proclaimed Nicolás Maduro the winner without publishing detailed results.

González left Venezuela in September 2024, with an arrest warrant against him, after negotiations with siblings Jorge and Delcy Rodríguez held at the Spanish embassy in Caracas. His son-in-law was detained for more than a year and released in early 2026.

He will return to a very different country, after Maduro's removal from power in the January 3 US military operation. Delcy Rodríguez has since governed as acting president and has promised elections under a renewed electoral authority, though without setting a date. Machado returned to Venezuela after ten months abroad, and in recent weeks close aides such as her adviser Carlos Blanco and her campaign chief, Magalli Meda, have also come back.

González's return coincides with a rapprochement between Rodríguez's government and Washington: last week US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth signed a military cooperation agreement with Venezuela in Caracas.

World.title: Storms on both US coasts leave 840,000 without power and disrupt Thanksgiving travel
World.content:
Storms on both US coasts leave 840,000 without power and disrupt Thanksgiving travel

26th Thursday, November 2026 - 22:30 UTC Full article

Flooding caused by the storm in the United States

Severe storms battered the east and west coasts of the United States on Thursday, Thanksgiving Day, the busiest travel holiday of the year, leaving more than 840,000 customers without power, hundreds of flights cancelled and the traditional Macy's parade in New York postponed, the BBC reported.

Severe storms battered the east and west coasts of the United States on Thursday, Thanksgiving Day, the busiest travel holiday of the year, leaving more than 840,000 customers without power, hundreds of flights cancelled and the traditional Macy's parade in New York postponed, the BBC reported.

On the east coast, a storm was moving north with wind gusts of 70 to 80 miles per hour in Virginia. Pennsylvania, with more than 180,000 customers without power, Maryland, with 173,000, and Virginia, with 167,000, were the states worst hit by outages, which also reached Missouri and Illinois. In Maryland, firefighters rescued several people trapped in homes crushed by falling trees, and the water utility WSSC asked nearly two million customers to limit use to essential needs because of power cuts at its treatment plants. Local meteorologists described it as the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington, where most runways at Reagan National Airport were flooded.

More than 400 flights were cancelled and about 1,700 delayed on Thursday, according to FlightAware. Some 81.5 million Americans were expected to travel at least 50 miles during the holiday week, according to the motoring association AAA, in what Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy described as “the Super Bowl of US air travel”. Authorities temporarily closed the Chesapeake Bay Bridge because of the wind.

In New York, the Macy's parade, celebrating its 100th edition this year, was postponed until Saturday. “It will be a heavy storm,” warned Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who said gusts could reach 65 miles per hour. “Safety is, and will always remain, our top priority,” he said. In Philadelphia, the parade was replaced by a television-only show.

On the west coast, king tides, which could reach 8 feet over the weekend, flooded homes in Pacifica, south of San Francisco, and Amtrak cancelled coastal services between Irvine and San Diego. According to the BBC, the tides are being strengthened by the strongest El Niño on record.

The eastern storm is expected to move out into the Atlantic on Friday. The bad weather is the second major blow to US air travel in two weeks, after a failure in air traffic control communications forced a nationwide ground stop on November 13.

World.title: Falklands’ Legislative Chair Jack Ford met Minister Uma Kumaran
World.content:
Falklands’ Legislative Chair Jack Ford met Minister Uma Kumaran

26th Thursday, November 2026 - 05:34 UTC Full article

Minister Kumaran and MLA Ford at her FCDO Office

UK Minister for the Overseas Territories Uma Kumaran met with MLA Jack Ford, Chair of the Falkland Islands Legislative Assembly, in the framework of the Joint Ministerial Council.

The bilateral meeting took place at the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) at the start of the annual JMC, Monday 23 November, which brings together UK ministers and elected leaders from the British Overseas Territories.

The meeting occurred during a heightened diplomatic push by Argentina regarding hydrocarbon exploration (specifically the Sea Lion oil project) and recent rhetoric from Buenos Aires, which Kumaran has publicly criticized in Parliament.

According to a brief release MLA Ford thanked the UK government for its continued support over recent months as the Falkland Islands delegation kicked off a week of diplomatic talks in London.

Ahead of and during the summit, both Kumaran and Ford reiterated the UK's commitment to the Falkland Islanders' right to self-determination, referencing the 2013 referendum.

The Falklands’ delegation al JMC is headed by MLA Chair and includes Governor Colin Martin-Reynolds, Richards Hyslop, FIGO Representative to the UK government and Europe, Michael Betts from FIGO and Will Bateman FIGO PR.

World.title: Brazil withdraws its ambassador to Argentina and will not invite Milei to Lula's inauguration
World.content:
Brazil withdraws its ambassador to Argentina and will not invite Milei to Lula's inauguration

26th Thursday, November 2026 - 04:45 UTC Full article

Lula and Milei

Brazil's government has decided to permanently withdraw its ambassador in Buenos Aires, Julio Bitelli, and will not invite Argentine President Javier Milei to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's inauguration on January 5, the Brazilian news site UOL and other outlets citing official sources reported. The decision comes after Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno cast doubt on the electoral process in which Lula was re-elected on October 25.

Brazil's government has decided to permanently withdraw its ambassador in Buenos Aires, Julio Bitelli, and will not invite Argentine President Javier Milei to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's inauguration on January 5, the Brazilian news site UOL and other outlets citing official sources reported. The decision comes after Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno cast doubt on the electoral process in which Lula was re-elected on October 25.

Bitelli had been recalled for consultations in July, after Milei insulted Lula at a Flávio Bolsonaro campaign event in Brazil. He will now not return to his post, and the embassy will be run by a chargé d'affaires, downgrading the level of representation without breaking off diplomatic relations. According to the Brazilian press, Lula's government had been waiting for a gesture from Buenos Aires before considering his return, and it plans to invite other Argentine political leaders to the inauguration.

The trigger was Quirno's remarks on a television programme at the weekend, when he was asked why Milei had not congratulated Lula. “There were situations within the electoral process that in some way cast doubt on the whole situation,” he said. He later added: “The one who recognises the election result is the Brazilian electoral court itself. So whether we say yes or no doesn't change the result.” Brazil's Superior Electoral Court declared Lula the winner, ahead of Flávio Bolsonaro by about four million votes, and no evidence of irregularities has been presented. Asked about the terms Milei has used for Lula, Quirno replied: “They are not insults, they are descriptions.”

The Argentine government acknowledges ideological differences between the two presidents but says it has chosen not to bring them into the diplomatic sphere, and Quirno said bilateral trade has not been affected. Brazilian diplomatic sources quoted by El País, however, say the persistent attacks show Milei's government “has no intention of dealing with bilateral issues seriously”.

Relations between Mercosur's two main partners are at their lowest point in decades. During the Brazilian campaign, Milei posted on social media: “I hope his latest dirty campaign trick doesn't include stealing the election.” After the run-off, Flávio Bolsonaro did not concede defeat and left Brazil via Argentina for the United States. When Milei took office in December 2023, Lula was invited and sent his foreign minister in his place.

The two presidents are due to meet on December 4 in Montevideo at the Mercosur summit of heads of state, at which Uruguay will hand over the bloc's pro tempore presidency.

World.title: Colombia drops its bid to join the BRICS bank in a new shift towards the United States
World.content:
Colombia drops its bid to join the BRICS bank in a new shift towards the United States

26th Thursday, November 2026 - 04:42 UTC Full article

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella

The government of Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has abandoned Colombia's process of joining the New Development Bank, the financial arm of the BRICS group of emerging economies, which his predecessor Gustavo Petro began in 2025. The decision adds to other changes in Colombian foreign policy, now more closely aligned with the United States and Israel.

The government of Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has abandoned Colombia's process of joining the New Development Bank, the financial arm of the BRICS group of emerging economies, which his predecessor Gustavo Petro began in 2025. The decision adds to other changes in Colombian foreign policy, now more closely aligned with the United States and Israel.

In a statement released on Wednesday night, the Foreign Ministry headed by Omar Bula said Colombia “will not continue the actions aimed at securing such membership” of the group founded by Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa and of its bank. The text adds that the government will seek financing from “other multilateral organisations” for its 2026-2030 National Development Plan, but does not explain the reasons for the decision.

Petro applied to join the bank in Shanghai on May 16, 2025, shortly after bringing Colombia into China's Belt and Road Initiative. On June 19, the bank's president, former Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff, announced its approval, which the board of governors ratified in July. Because the bank's founding agreement is a treaty, ratification required a law from the Colombian Congress. The government submitted the bill on November 25, 2025, but it never came to a vote, and Colombia was listed as an observer in the process of joining.

Since taking office, De la Espriella has recognised Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, opened Colombia's embassy in Jerusalem and withdrawn the country from the Hague Group, a coalition of countries critical of Israel's offensive in Gaza. According to the Colombian newspaper Portafolio, Donald Trump's nominee for ambassador in Bogotá, Nathaniel Morris, told the US Senate that De la Espriella had expressed his intention to take the country out of the Belt and Road Initiative, something the Colombian government has not confirmed.

The decision reflects the weight of the United States, which buys almost three in every ten dollars of Colombia's exports, according to the statistics agency DANE. China, however, has been the country's main supplier since 2021: between January and September, Colombia bought US$17.833 billion of goods from China, 26.7% more than a year earlier, against US$13.995 billion from the United States.

World.title: Guanajuato quadruples its wine exports through June, and ranks third among Mexico’s wine-exporting states
World.content:
Wine exports from the central state of Guanajuato in Mexico’s El Bajío region have hit a record high, with 315.8% growth in the first six months of 2026 compared to the same period last year.

According to Mexico’s trade agency Cofoce (the Coordinator for the Promotion of Foreign Trade), Guanajuato sold abroad US $231,300 worth of wine in the year’s first half, exceeding its previous record total for that period in 2023. It was also four times higher than the state’s total in that period in 2025.

Within the state, the UNESCO World Heritage Site of San Miguel de Allende and the historic city of Dolores Hidalgo led export transactions during the period.

The United States is Guanajuato’s largest international market by far, accounting for more than 99% of the state’s wine exports. According to Cofoce, during the first half of the year, that 99% purchase by the U.S. totaled $229,000 worth of wine, representing a 313.6% increase compared to the previous year.

Though perhaps the fastest-growing wine market, Guanajuato makes up just a small part of Mexico’s national wine industry, which has seen modest growth since last year. During the first half of 2026, Mexico as a whole recorded exports of wine and vermouth totaling approximately US $4.2 million, up 2.7% compared to the same period in 2025.

The value of exports from Guanajuato accounted for only about 5.4% of the national total, though the state’s growth rate was significantly higher than the country’s average. In fact, Guanajuato’s performance placed the state as the country’s third-largest exporter of wine and vermouth, trailing only Mexico City and Baja California.

Cofoce reported wine from Guanajuato was also sold to France, a country historically recognized for its high-quality wine. However, no figures were shared on sales volume.

Beyond global sales, Guanajuato’s wine production is gaining international recognition. At the 2026 Concours Mondial de Bruxelles, wines from Guanajuato earned 52 international awards. Guanajuato ranked second among Mexican states in total awards, just behind Baja California, home of the renowned Valle de Guadalupe wine region.

The award-winning wines come from 13 vineyards located across five municipalities: San Miguel de Allende, Dolores Hidalgo, San Felipe, Comonfort and León.

With reports from Conexión Turística and Expansión

World.title: Why El Chapo Isidro’s arrest may not bring peace to Sinaloa
World.content:
Listen to this article

Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, a cartel kingpin known as “El Chapo Isidro,” was arrested by the Mexican Army last Friday night.

His capture in Guasave, Sinaloa, triggered an immediate and very violent reaction, with cartel operatives setting up narco-blockades and engaging in gun battles with military forces.

But what will be the longer-term consequences of the arrest of a man who was considered one of Sinaloa’s most powerful traffickers?

Will the capture of one of the FBI’s 10 most-wanted fugitives lead to more violence in Sinaloa, a state already reeling from more than two years of Sinaloa Cartel infighting?

Two security experts, Víctor Sánchez Valdés and David Saucedo, believe it could.

To better understand their views, it is worth recalling who El Chapo Isidro is.

Meza Flores, 44, is the alleged leader of the Guasave Cartel, also known as Los Mazatlecos. His criminal group grew out of the Beltrán Leyva Organization.

After Meza Flores’ arrest, the Ministry of National Defense said that he was “the boss of the Beltrán Leyva criminal organization” and an ally of the “Mayos” faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which is also known as the Cártel del Pacífico, or Pacific Cartel.

His alliance with the Mayos faction, led by the son of imprisoned drug lord Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, is especially significant because his arrest could weaken the partnership as that faction continues to wage a bloody war against the “Chapitos” wing of the Sinaloa Cartel, which is headed by sons of convicted cartel kingpin Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán.

Could violence spike in Sinaloa?

Sánchez Valdés, a researcher at the Autonomous University of Coahuila, told the news outlet Infobae that the arrest of Meza Flores could cause an increase in violence in Sinaloa if the Chapitos faction seeks to take advantage of the weakening of the Mayos faction to seize control of territory held by the Mayos and their allies.

He said that the most likely scenario is that the Chapitos will try to “regain territory, seize other municipalities” from the Mayos and the Guasave Cartel, whose stronghold is in northern Sinaloa.

“Who knows how much success they’ll have,” Sánchez said.

As a result of the Chapitos’ predicted offensive, the epicenter of cartel fighting in Sinaloa could shift from the south of the state to the north, where Meza Flores held sway, according to Sánchez.

He said that the arrest of El Chapo Isidro is “obviously an achievement,” but added: “I don’t think this will lead to peace in Sinaloa, at least not in the short term.”

In a written analysis shared with the news website Animal Político, Saucedo said that the arrest of Meza Flores could benefit the Chapitos in their ongoing battle with the Mayos.

“The blow to the structure of ‘El Chapo Isidro’ provides respite to the rearguard of the Chapitos, which for months has been hit by assaults from cells of hitmen that set out from Guamúchil and Angostura [in northern Sinaloa] to attack various strongholds of the sons of ‘Chapo’ Guzmán,” he said.

Saucedo also said that Meza Flores’ capture triggers a period of uncertainty for the Guasave Cartel. He said that the criminal group could be temporarily weakened as a result of the arrest. He also said that disputes over the cartel’s leadership could arise, potentially leading to an increase in violence.

Saucedo said that the arrest of Meza Flores doesn’t mean that the Guasave Cartel will break its alliance with the Mayos, led by Ismael “El Mayito Flaco” Zambada Sicairos. However, it could “pause” its participation in the war between the Mayos and the Chapitos, he said.

For his part, Sánchez said there is no sign of any “crack” that could break the alliance between the Guasave Cartel and the Mayos.

Who will succeed ‘El Chapo Isidro’ as leader of the Guasave Cartel?

Among seven other alleged criminals arrested during the military operation in Guasave last Friday was Meza Flores’ cousin, Germán Rolando Gálvez Meza, identified by federal authorities as the Beltrán Leyva Organization’s second-in-command.

Consequently, Gálvez is not in a position to succeed El Chapo Isidro as leader of the Guasave Cartel.

While he flagged the possibility of a dispute over the cartel’s leadership, Saucedo said that another scenario is that Meza Flores could name a successor from prison. He said that person could be a relative or close associate of El Chapo Isidro.

Associates of the detained capo include Óscar Manuel Gastélum Iribe, a man known as “El Músico” (The Musician), and the brothers Mario Germán and Amberto Beltrán Araujo.

Sánchez said the Guasave Cartel is maintaining operations “through” Gastélum and the Beltrán Araujo brothers. Infobae reported earlier this week that Gastélum — who is accused of terrorism, drug and firearm offenses in the United States — is considered the most likely successor, followed by the Beltrán Araujo brothers.

Saucedo said that the arrest of Meza Flores doesn’t mean that the Guasave Cartel is going to disappear. He said that criminal, political, police and business networks that support the organization remain in place.

“What … [authorities] do is capture high-profile kingpins — the leaders — but they don’t dismantle the entire organization,” Saucedo told the Associated Press.

“They arrested the No. 1 and No. 2 [of the Guasave Cartel], but the entire network of hit men, street-level drug dealers, businesses and political and police connections remains intact,” he said.

Saucedo also said that the arrest of El Chapo Isidro was “a product of pressure from the United States,” which frequently urges Mexico to do more to combat cartels and the drugs they ship to the U.S.

García Harfuch: Capture of Meza Flores doesn’t mean his criminal group is ‘dismantled’

On Monday, Federal Security Minister Omar García Harfuch acknowledged that the capture of Meza Flores doesn’t spell the end for his criminal group.

“There are still a number of other significant individuals who were associates of this detained suspect. We cannot say that [the cartel] has been dismantled,” he said.

Other criminal organizations, including Mexico’s two most powerful cartels, have survived the capture of their leaders. The Jalisco New Generation Cartel lost its leader in February when the Mexican Army fatally wounded Nemesio “El Mencho” Oseguera Cervantes in an operation in Jalisco.

The Sinaloa Cartel has lost its two most notorious leaders: El Chapo Guzmán, who was captured in Los Mochis, Sinaloa, in January 2016 around six months after he escaped from the Altiplano federal prison in México state, and El Mayo Zambada, who was arrested in the United States in July 2024 after he was kidnapped by one of El Chapo’s sons and forced onto a plane that flew him to New Mexico. Both men are serving life sentences in U.S. prisons.

It remains to be seen whether Meza Flores will be extradited to the United States to face drug trafficking and other charges. President Sheinbaum said on Thursday that the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) and the federal government’s Security Cabinet have to assess what’s in Mexico’s best interests.

“What’s better for the country? … The Attorney General’s Office and the Security Cabinet will have to determine that in a manner that guarantees peace and security in the country,” she said.

Meza Flores, who is currently being held at the Altiplano prison, is scheduled to face an initial court hearing this Saturday.

With reports from Infobae and Animal Político

World.title: Mexico’s National Anthropology Museum tops list of best 100 museums in the world
World.content:
Mexico’s National Museum of Anthropology — which broke its all-time attendance record last year — has now topped the Prado in Madrid, the Hermitage in St. Petersburg, Russia, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York to be named the world’s best museum.

Worth a Journey, a travel-ranking publication based in Munich, Germany, has placed the 62-year-old museum No. 1 on its World’s 100 Best Museums list for 2026-27.

Never mind that the awarding travel guide has cautioned that the Mexico City institution offers “many labels only in Spanish.”

The Prado took second, followed by Denmark’s Louisiana Museum of Modern Art, with the Hermitage and Vienna’s Kunsthistorisches Museum rounding out the top five. The Met in New York City was 10th, while the Louvre in Paris came in at 31st.

Two other Mexican museums made the list, which includes museums from 37 countries: the Desert Museum in Saltillo at No. 78 and the Amparo Museum in Puebla at No. 82. The top 100 was released Oct. 27.

Highlights at the National Museum of Anthropology, as listed by Worth a Journey, include the 12-foot-across Aztec Sun Stone, the eye-popping Mexica gallery and the El Paraguas (The Umbrella) courtyard fountain.

The guide recommends at least three hours to visit the site — which covers more than 45,000 square meters and has 16 permanent exhibit halls — though it suggests dedicating a full day. It also notes that Sundays are more crowded due to free admission for Mexicans.

Worth a Journey has compiled 39 worldwide 100-best lists in categories that include travel, nature, culture and architecture, and food and drink. Overall, the lists cover some 3,900 venues in 142 countries.

Mexico also had the No. 1 archaeological site, the ancient Maya city of Calakmul, deep in the jungle on the Yucatán Peninsula. Overall, Mexico has 64 places on 22 of the 39 lists.

Worth a Journey says it uses an algorithm and on-site visits to compile its lists, that it takes no nominations and that it does not charge a fee to be listed.

“This recognition also honors the INAH teams that study, preserve and share our heritage,” Culture Secretary Claudia Curiel de Icaza said in a release this week from INAH, the National Institute of Anthropology and History.

Over the past 18 months, the museum has also won the Princess of Asturias Award for Concord and received a UNESCO maximum protection Blue Shield designation — a first in Latin America and the Caribbean.

The museum, which opened in 1964, drew a record 5.04 million visitors in 2025, up from 3.78 million in 2024.

However, according to INAH statistics through October, the museum is down about 5.8% from last year’s pace, with roughly 3.89 million visitors in the first 10 months of 2026 compared to 4.13 million over the same span last year.

With reports from CNN Español, Ciudad de México Secreta and PR Newswire

World.title: Customs seizes 18 million counterfeit cigarettes in Michoacán port city
World.content:
Federal authorities seized more than 18 million counterfeit cigarettes at a customs office in the port city of Lázaro Cárdenas, Michoacán, earlier this week.

In a Wednesday social media post, the Security Cabinet said Navy, Security Ministry and Customs personnel seized the illicit cargo during a physical inspection, which revealed the suspected counterfeit nature of the material.

In a press release, the Security Cabinet said routine inspection of a container uncovered 861 packages containing 10,332,000 cigarettes, and customs officers recognized irregularities related to intellectual property rights.

In a second operation, stemming from “risk analysis and merchandise inspection procedures,” customs officials located 834 packages containing 8,340,000 cigarettes originating from Singapore.

In both cases, the merchandise was secured and placed under the custody of the corresponding bonded warehouse. Both the cigarettes and the containers are now in the hands of the Federal Attorney General’s Office, while legal procedures are carried out to determine the origin of the illicit cargo.

The port of Lázaro Cárdenas, one of the main commercial entry points on the Mexican Pacific coast, has become a priority focus of surveillance for the Navy and customs authorities due to the recurring entry of illicit merchandise from Asia.

Counterfeit cigarettes now account for one in four cigarettes consumed in Mexico and have become a serious problem fueled by Asian smuggling and tax evasion.

Although they appear legal at first glance, they are far more harmful to health because they are manufactured clandestinely with waste materials and without any sanitary controls, operating completely outside the law.

Of the nearly 40 billion cigarettes sold in Mexico last year, nearly 9.2 billion — or 23.3% — were illegal cigarettes, according to a study commissioned by Philip Morris International and released in April

The study, conducted by KPMG and entitled “Illicit Cigarette Consumption in Latin America and Canada,” revealed that Mexico accounts for over 15% of illicit cigarettes globally. At the same time, counterfeit cigarettes are being smuggled from Mexico to Costa Rica and Colombia.

The illicit trade represents a tax loss of US $1.3 billion for Mexico, the study found. It also calculated a tax loss of US $8.5 billion for the region as a whole.

KPMG said that while Mexico’s legal domestic cigarette consumption fell from 34 billion in 2021 to 30 billion in 2025, illegal consumption rose from 7.02 billion to 9.19 billion cigarettes in that same four-year period.

With reports from El Universal, Aristegui Noticias, Forbes México and Once Noticias

World.title: León Zoo temporarily closes after bird flu outbreak spreads to mammals
World.content:
The zoo in León, Guanajuato, temporarily closed its doors to the public this week amid an avian influenza outbreak that has killed birds and at least two mammals.

Officials believe migratory birds may have introduced the virus to the zoo, located in the northeast of León, Guanajuato’s largest city.

Zoo León announced its decision to close in a statement and a video message posted to social media.

REFUERZA ZOOLEÓN MEDIDAS PREVENTIVAS ANTE PRESENCIA DE INFLUENZA AVIAR https://t.co/zKC7n8gmzK — Zooleon (@zooleon) November 25, 2026

“In accordance with the recommendations of both the federal Health Ministry and the state Health Ministry, we have taken the decision to temporarily close the León Zoo to the public starting Wednesday, Nov. 25,” the zoo’s director Diana Karen Casillas said on Tuesday.

Casillas said that the decision to close the zoo is a “preventative measure” related to two cases of avian influenza (also known as bird flu) in mammals.

Avian flu was confirmed in a spider monkey and a tigrillo (a small wild cat) that died at the zoo. The deaths of three geese, two wild ducks and a vulture at the zoo were reported earlier this month.

Casillas said that the aim of the temporary closure — which is expected to last 21 days — is to “strengthen” measures aimed at stopping the spread of the disease. She said migratory birds brought avian flu to the zoo.

“I want to stress that this situation is not exclusive to the León zoo,” Casillas said.

“It can happen at any site that keeps wild animals,” she said.

In its statement, Zoo León said that specialized zoo staff will continue feeding, monitoring and providing veterinary care to animals during the temporary closure. Casillas said in an interview that zoo personnel who work closely with animals use protective equipment.

Fifteen workers developed flu-like symptoms after exposure to migratory birds with avian influenza, but to date none have tested positive for the disease, according to Guanajuato Health Minister Gabriel Cortéz Alcalá.

The zoo thanked the public for its understanding during the temporary closure, and said that taking timely action is “essential to prevent infections, protect public health and safeguard animal life.”

The zoo said its reopening will depend on how “the health situation” develops and on assessments by the relevant authorities.

With reports from El Universal, La Jornada and AFP

World.title: MND Local San Miguel de Allende: Court rulings, highway upgrades and mobile pet care
World.content:
A recent bullfight in San Miguel de Allende‘s 19th-century bullring prompted a court challenge; a second Starbucks location has opened; the second phase of a federal highway reconstruction is underway and local companion animals now have mobile access to a relatively new form of therapy. Read on for the details.

Legal challenge to local bullfight fails to persuade court

A recent judicial ruling denied a lawsuit challenging a Nov. 13 bullfight at the Plaza de Toros Oriente on Calle Recreo in San Miguel. That event went ahead, with another scheduled for Nov. 27 at the same site and by the same promotion company, Toluca-based Redondeles.

The plaintiffs, Animal Heroes and PETA Latino, had asked the court to prevent the use of instruments in the bullring that can injure the bulls. Although their request for a temporary injunction was denied, a final ruling on the merits of the case is still under consideration.

Bullfighting — and cockfighting — in Mexico has come under increasing scrutiny in recent years as opponents seek to outlaw wounding or killing the bulls and ban the events completely. Last year, Mexico City prohibited the killing of bulls and the use of sharp objects such as swords or knives that could injure them.

The practice of so-called “violence-free bullfighting” or “bloodless bullfighting” has already been adopted in other areas of the country, while the states of Coahuila, Guerrero, Michoacán, Quintana Roo, Sinaloa and Sonora have banned bullfighting altogether.

A recently approved federal law aims to prohibit animal mistreatment across the country, but individual states are in charge of regulating bullfighting and cockfighting. However, the new federal law gives states one year to adopt regulations in alignment with it, which could strengthen implementation and regulation.

According to a March 2025 poll, conducted by Enkoll for El País and W Radio, 72% of Mexicans are opposed to bullfighting and view it as animal abuse.

Second Starbucks outlet opens east of San Miguel

After having just one Starbucks location since 2008 — on Calle Canal in Centro across from the Jardín — San Miguel now has a second. The new outlet, Starbucks La Pilarica, just opened on Carretera a Querétaro near Zirándaro east of the city.

The building features two stories, a big parking lot and a drive-thru area. Coffee drinks, bulk coffee, a selection of food options and various types of Starbucks-branded merchandise are available inside.

Mexico City-based restaurant operator Alsea began partnering with Starbucks on licensing agreements in 2002 and recently extended the agreement, giving it exclusive operating rights through 2046.

Alsea currently has 976 Starbucks locations in Mexico and additional ones across 11 other countries. The Mexican locations are operated by its wholly owned subsidiary, Café Sirena, and are not owned by Starbucks.

Work continues on highway to Dolores Hidalgo

Continuing construction on Federal Highway 51 from San Miguel to Dolores Hidalgo will turn a two-lane stretch over the train tracks into a four-lane highway with an overpass. A sign announcing the additional work recently appeared, and workers have also been seen there.

Construction initially started in September 2023 to modernize about 30 kilometers of the highway, known as Bulevar de la Libertad. The second stage reportedly will address about 3 kilometers near La Cieneguita and take about eight months to complete.

Guanajuato Governor Libia García Muñoz Ledo said this second phase will mean an investment of 271.7 million pesos (US $14.23 million) and will include a bike path, four lanes and an overpass over the railroad tracks.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Libia Dennise (@libiadennise)

At the inauguration of the second phase last week, the governor said the work will strengthen the connection between the two cities in Guanajuato state with the highest level of tourist and economic activity.

“This project will unite San Miguel de Allende and Dolores Hidalgo, two cities that are economic and tourist powerhouses of Guanajuato and Mexico,” she said.

Mobile hyperbaric oxygen therapy available for local pets

Those with companion animals in San Miguel and nearby areas now have access to a type of cutting-edge therapy for veterinary use. San Miguel-based Hipervet Bajío has purchased a mobile van equipped with a hyperbaric oxygen therapy machine and is making it available in conjunction with Petvet.

The machines provide dogs and cats — and potentially other animals that can fit inside — with 1.5-hour therapy sessions during which they breathe 100% oxygen. This increases blood oxygen and helps the animals heal faster after surgery, counteracts infection and reduces swelling.

Daniel Medina, owner of Hipervet Bajío, said he bought the machine after his 10-year-old dog, Lula, suddenly stopped walking due to painful nerve compression in her back. After hyperbaric treatment in Mexico City, he said she now walks, jumps, plays and “looks like 6 years old.”

Dr. Zazil Morales, a Petvet veterinarian, said another dog treated with the therapy couldn’t stand, walk or eat by herself but now is able to do all of those things.

“Normally, what happens with inflammation is (that) without enough oxygen, the cells start to die because there are not enough nutrients,” she said, adding, “Hyperbaric treatment has a lot of uses.”

There’s another mobile van offering the therapy in Mexico City, Medina said, but that one and the one in San Miguel are the only ones he’s aware of in Mexico.

“It’s still very new for a lot of people,” he said.

Cathy Siegner is an independent journalist based in San Miguel and Montana. She has journalism degrees from the University of Oregon and Northwestern University.

World.title: Sheinbaum calls foul after DEA announces Sinaloa Cartel tip line: Thursday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🚨 Sheinbaum calls DEA tip lines US “interference” in Mexico: The president said it is “clear that this is a matter of interference” after DEA Administrator Terry Cole announced “dedicated tip lines” for information on cartels and corrupt officials, starting with Sinaloa. “Imagine if the [Mexican] Ministry of Security and Citizen Protection opened a WhatsApp to report corruption in the United States,” she said.

The president said it is “clear that this is a matter of interference” after DEA Administrator Terry Cole announced “dedicated tip lines” for information on cartels and corrupt officials, starting with Sinaloa. “Imagine if the [Mexican] Ministry of Security and Citizen Protection opened a WhatsApp to report corruption in the United States,” she said. 🔍 “The DEA has a lot to do in its country”: Sheinbaum said the agency’s first task should be investigating corruption in the U.S. linked to organized crime.

Sheinbaum said the agency’s first task should be investigating corruption in the U.S. linked to organized crime. ⚖️ Security Cabinet and FGR to decide where “El Chapo Isidro” faces justice: Asked whether Fausto Isidro Meza Flores should be sent to the U.S. or tried in Mexico, the president said the decision must guarantee “peace and security in the country.” The FGR said the U.S. has requested his extradition and that he faces an initial court hearing on Saturday.

Asked whether Fausto Isidro Meza Flores should be sent to the U.S. or tried in Mexico, the president said the decision must guarantee “peace and security in the country.” The FGR said the U.S. has requested his extradition and that he faces an initial court hearing on Saturday. 🇪🇸 Spain hasn’t responded to Mexico’s extradition request for Inés Gómez Mont: Sheinbaum said she is asking Spain to “apply Spanish justice and the extradition treaty” in the case of the former TV host who was deported from the U.S. this week. She said it is “fully proven” that Gómez Mont and her former husband laundered money over a period of years.

Why today’s mañanera matters

The Mexican government has collaborated closely with the Trump administration on security matters, but President Sheinbaum has made it clear that there are certain lines the U.S. must not cross — including military intervention and unilateral operations — and that Mexico’s sovereignty must be respected.

Sheinbaum pushed back on that front during her Thursday press conference, after the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) announced a tip line to collect information on cartel activity and government corruption in Sinaloa.

Sheinbaum responded to the development by once again accusing the U.S. government of interference in Mexican affairs. She has accused the U.S. government of interference on repeated occasions this year, citing the CIA’s alleged participation in a drug lab raid in Chihuahua in April and U.S. charges against Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya and other current and former officials for alleged collusion with the Sinaloa Cartel.

Her latest allegation of U.S. interference came just six days after the Mexican military captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, a drug lord known as “El Chapo Isidro,” in an operation in Sinaloa that used U.S. intelligence.

Sheinbaum spoke about Meza Flores’ case at today’s mañanera in response to a question about where the suspect should face justice. The 44-year-old faces drug trafficking and other charges in both Mexico and the United States.

Sheinbaum: ‘It’s clear that this is a matter of interference’

Sheinbaum responded Thursday to the DEA’s Wednesday night announcement that it had established dedicated tip lines to receive information regarding members and associates of designated Foreign Terrorist Organizations (FTOs) — i.e. drug cartels; corrupt government officials providing material support to designated FTOs; and criminal networks and individuals laundering money to finance narcoterrorism.

“Your information matters. Your identity and safety matter,” DEA Administrator Terry Cole wrote in a social media post that included a WhatsApp and Signal number, a Threema ID and a DEA email address that members of the public can use to provide information to the DEA.

The @DEAHQ has established dedicated tip lines to receive information regarding: Members and associates of designated Foreign Terrorist Organizations (FTOs).

Corrupt government officials providing material support to designated FTOs.

Criminal networks and individuals laundering money to finance narcoterrorism. Your information matters. Your identity and safety matter. If you have information, connect with the DEA through the designated reporting channels. Confidential and anonymous reporting is available. For Sinaloa: WhatsApp and Signal: +1-858-298-5670, Threema ID: PTJ4HS3J, MFSinaloaTipLine@dea.gov Together, we can expose corruption, disrupt financial networks, dismantle narcoterrorist organizations, and protect our communities.

@CarlosLoret @aristeguicnn @lopezdoriga @jorgeramosnews @Adela_Micha @CiroGomezL @azucenau @PaolaRojas @beltrandelrio @El_Universal_Mx @Reforma @Milenio @Excelsior Numbers for Jalisco/CJNG will be posted tomorrow . — DEA Terry Cole (@DEATerryCole) November 26, 2026

Cole said that the contact details are “for Sinaloa,” indicating they could be used to share information on the Sinaloa Cartel and officials in the northern state.

“Together, we can expose corruption, disrupt financial networks, dismantle narcoterrorist organizations, and protect our communities,” he wrote.

“Numbers for Jalisco/CJNG will be posted tomorrow,” Cole said, referring to the Jalisco New Generation Cartel.

A reporter asked the president Thursday morning what her government’s position was on Cole’s announcement about the establishment of tip lines allowing citizens to report people “linked to the Sinaloa Cartel.”

“Imagine if the [Mexican] Ministry of Security and Citizen Protection opened a WhatsApp to report corruption in the United States,” Sheinbaum said.

“How would the U.S. government view that?” she asked.

“It’s clear that this is a matter of interference,” Sheinbaum said.

“… The DEA has a lot to do in its country,” she added, seemingly questioning the agency’s focus on Mexico.

“The first thing it should be doing is investigating corruption in the United States linked to organized crime or what they call terrorist groups,” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum: FGR and Security Cabinet will decide where ‘El Chapo Isidro’ faces justice

A reporter asked the president whether “El Chapo Isidro” should be sent to the United States or face trial in Mexico.

Sheinbaum said that the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) and the federal government’s Security Cabinet have to assess what’s in Mexico’s best interests.

“What’s better for the country? … The Attorney General’s Office and the Security Cabinet will have to determine that in a manner that guarantees peace and security in the country,” she said.

In a statement on Tuesday, the FGR noted that the United States has requested Meza Flores’ extradition.

#FGRInforma https://t.co/0gf8s5Qg3F — FGR México (@FGRMexico) November 25, 2026

“The diplomatic request originated in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia and seeks to prosecute this person in that country for offenses that correspond under Mexican law to criminal association, crimes against health [drug trafficking] and violations of the Federal Firearms and Explosives Law,” the FGR said.

It said that “the procedure and formalities” set out in the bilateral extradition treaty, “along with diplomatic timelines, will determine whether his extradition is viable.”

The FGR noted that Meza Flores is scheduled to face an initial court hearing this Saturday.

Sheinbaum says Spain hasn’t responded to Mexico’s request for the extradition of Inés Gómez Mont

A reporter asked the president whether the Spanish government had responded to Mexico’s request for the extradition of Inés Gómez Mont, a former Mexican television host who was deported to Spain this week after she was released from immigration detention in the United States. Gómez Mont, who was arrested in Florida last month for overstaying her U.S. visa, is wanted in Mexico for alleged tax fraud and embezzlement.

Sheinbaum said that as far as she was aware the Spanish government hasn’t responded to Mexico’s extradition request.

Asked how Mexico can ensure Gómez Mont doesn’t leave Spain to avoid extradition, Sheinbaum said her administration is asking the Spanish government to “apply Spanish justice and the extradition treaty.”

She said it is “fully proven” that Gómez Mont and her former husband, Víctor Manuel Álvarez Puga, laundered money over a period of years.

“We hope there is a response from the Spanish government,” Sheinbaum said.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: First winter storm brings bitter cold along with rain and snow to central and northwest Mexico
World.content:
Listen to this article

The first cold snap of the 2026-2027 season is forecast to bring not only low temperatures but also very heavy to intense rainfall to western, central and southern portions of the country, possibly even dumping snow on the outskirts of Mexico City

Cold Front No. 8 features a mass of cold air with temperatures dropping as low as –10 degrees Celsius, as well as sleet, rain and strong wind gusts of up to 100 km/h.

Hoy, la primera #TormentaInvernal de la temporada ocasionará #Lluvias intensas en #Sinaloa, #Nayarit, #Jalisco, #Colima, #Michoacán y #Guanajuato. Más información en ⬇️

https://t.co/bnFZCrT68N https://t.co/9DO466MCaz — CONAGUA Clima (@conagua_clima) November 26, 2026

The National Meteorological Service (SMN) says a polar trough accompanied by polar and subtropical jet streams has been crossing from western Mexico beginning Thursday, giving rise to the season’s first winter storm.

The SMN warns of intense localized rains in areas of Sinaloa, Nayarit, Jalisco, Colima, Michoacán and Guanajuato, and very heavy rains in Durango, Zacatecas, Aguascalientes and Querétaro. Additionally, snow and sleet are forecast for mountainous areas of Jalisco, Colima and Michoacán on Thursday night.

The cold front and the Arctic air mass associated with it will also maintain cold conditions in northern, eastern, central and southeastern Mexico. It will likely generate a “Norte” event with gusts of 90 to 100 km/h in the Isthmus and Gulf of Tehuantepec, and gusts of 40 to 60 km/h on the coasts of Tamaulipas, Veracruz, Tabasco, Campeche, Yucatán and Quintana Roo, decreasing Thursday afternoon.

By Friday, the storm will have moved across western Mexico, and torrential downpours are forecast for Michoacán and Guerrero, while intense rain is expected in Jalisco, Colima, Guanajuato and México state.

A significant drop in temperature (0 to 5 degrees Celsius) is also expected in the states of the Northern Plateau and the Central Plateau, along with the possibility of snow or sleet in mountainous areas of Jalisco, Colima and Michoacán.

These conditions will extend overnight Friday to areas higher than 2,800 meters above sea level in central Mexico (Guanajuato, Querétaro, Hidalgo, México state, Tlaxcala, Puebla, Morelos and Mexico City), with the likelihood of snow and sleet in the mountains surrounding the Valley of Mexico.

By Saturday, the SMN projects the storm to bring torrential downpours to Guerrero and Oaxaca, and intense rain to Puebla. Very heavy rains on Saturday are expected in México state, Morelos, Michoacán, Mexico City, Tlaxcala and Veracruz.

With reports from Vanguardia, El Economista, LópezDoriga.com

World.title: Lula Allies Welcome Banker as Finance Chief
World.content:
Backers call it a signal of fiscal discipline, and critics call it a bank in the ministry. The data say interest rates will fall only slowly.

The Finance Ministry building in Brasília, the post Adolfo Sachsida is reported to be favoured for (Photo: Agência Senado, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Finance Ministry: Brazil

Brazil’s political and business establishment lined up on Thursday 26 November 2026 behind President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s choice of Luiz Carlos Trabuco, chairman of Bradesco, one of Brazil’s biggest private banks, as finance minister. Praise came from the vice-president, the leader of the Senate and the sitting minister, while lawmakers on the left and the right raised pointed doubts.

The split matters to investors abroad because the next steps on interest rates and the budget now depend on one banker’s credibility. The central bank’s rate committee, known as Copom, meets on 8 and 9 December.

Key Facts Who. Government allies and congressional leaders back Lula’s finance pick, Bradesco chairman Luiz Carlos Trabuco.

What. Backers see lower rates and a tighter budget; some left-wing lawmakers fear a banker’s influence.

Where. Brazil, where the benchmark Selic interest rate stands at 13.75% a year.

When. Announced Thursday 26 November 2026; he starts in 2027, with no date given.

As of. 27 November 2026, 04:00 GMT

Backers call it a signal of fiscal discipline, and critics call it a bank in the ministry. The data say interest rates will fall only slowly.

The presidential office, known as the Planalto, said in a note that Trabuco accepted Lula’s invitation and will lead the Finance Ministry from 2027. It gave no start date.

Trabuco has worked at Bradesco since he was 17 and is a member of the Conselhão, the president’s advisory council on economic and social development. The stock market welcomed the news, with the Ibovespa, Brazil’s main stock index, rising more than 6% on Thursday.

WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Vice-President Geraldo Alckmin called the choice “an excellent piece of news for Brazil” and said Trabuco “has the preparation, experience and public spirit” for the job (translated from Portuguese). Senate president Davi Alcolumbre said he received the choice with great optimism.

Dario Durigan, the sitting finance minister, said a country “moves well when led with seriousness and ethics” (translated). He will hand over the ministry when Trabuco takes office in 2027.

The Doubts on Left and Right

Lindbergh Farias, a deputy from Rio de Janeiro for Lula’s Workers’ Party (PT), wrote on social media that the first thing that came to mind was “the Joaquim Levy moment” and that he hoped history would not repeat itself. Levy was the banker who ran the ministry under President Dilma Rousseff in 2015 and left in December of that year as the economy slid into recession.

Flávio Bolsonaro, a senator of the conservative Liberal Party (PL), accused Lula of an electoral swindle. He said Lula had become a “Faria Limer”, a jibe at Avenida Faria Lima, the São Paulo street that houses the financial industry.

File photo. A ministry building on the Esplanada dos Ministérios, the government avenue in Brasília, in 2022. Foto: Jefferson Rudy/Agência Senado

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Brazil finance minister Email address Follow

What the Numbers Allow

The central bank’s benchmark Selic rate has stood at 13.75% a year since at least 1 October, according to the bank’s own data series. In the central bank’s weekly Focus survey of about 145 market economists, dated 19 November, the median forecast was no change by the end of 2026 and 13.00% for the end of 2027.

That is only 0.75 percentage points of cuts over a year, far less than the hopes in the political statements. The same survey expects a primary deficit of 0.4% of gross domestic product in 2027, meaning the budget before interest payments would still show a gap.

For readers in the United States, the link is the cost of borrowing. A smaller deficit lowers the government’s borrowing need, and the central bank can then cut its rate with less fear of inflation.

The real strengthened on the day, with the central bank’s official rate at R$5.74 to the dollar (about US$0.17 per real) on 26 November, from R$5.88 the day before. Bradesco’s New York-listed shares, which trade as BBD, did not trade that day because US markets were closed for Thanksgiving.

The next dated step is the Copom decision on Wednesday 9 December, due that evening. Trabuco’s plan for the 2027 budget is the larger test, and he has not yet set it out in public.

Who backs Trabuco’s appointment?

The vice-president, the Senate leader and the sitting finance minister welcomed it. Their statements are praise, not policy commitments.

World.title: Paraguay Spots Ueno Bank Activity in US
World.content:
Paraguay’s search for the money behind its failed Ueno Bank now also involves the US financial system. So far that is a possibility, not a US case.

The Palacio de Justicia in Asunción, seat of Paraguay's judiciary. Photo: FF MM, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Crime and Justice: Paraguay

Paraguayan prosecutors say they have detected money movements of Ueno Bank, the Paraguayan lender that failed this month, through the United States financial system, which could lead to a criminal case in the US. Manuel Doldán, deputy prosecutor for international affairs at the Ministerio Público (Paraguay’s prosecution service), said on Thursday 26 November 2026 that such a case could bring extradition requests, according to Paraguayan press reports of his remarks.

Paraguay’s search for the money behind its failed Ueno Bank now also involves the US financial system. So far that is a possibility, not a US case.

Ueno Bank is a Paraguayan lender that the central bank, the Banco Central del Paraguay, put into a resolution process (a formal rescue or wind-down) on 3 November 2026 after its solvency fell below half the legal minimum. About two dozen people, including bank executives, now face criminal proceedings, and all are presumed innocent until a court rules.

“We have detected the use of the North American financial system,” Doldán said on 26 November, as quoted in Paraguayan press reports. He added that he could not rule out a US case that would “require an extradition”, and that he had received “no kind of report and no kind of request” from Washington.
