“That does not mean that an investigation does not exist,” Doldán said, adding that one may be under way and not yet known to him. The reports also say his office is in contact with the FBI (the US federal police) and the US Treasury Department through the US Department of Justice, and that no formal US request or report has reached Paraguay yet.

Paraguay and the United States signed an extradition treaty in Washington on 9 November 1998, which Paraguay’s Congress approved in Law 1,442 of 25 June 1999. The law replaces a 1973 treaty, and the date the 1998 treaty took effect could not be confirmed.

The dollar link is concrete in one respect: Ueno Bank said it completed a US$350 million international bond sale on 3 March 2026, the largest ever by a Paraguayan bank. The five-year notes pay a 6.70% coupon and are governed by New York law, and the bank said demand was 1.5 times the amount offered.

The bond sale came eight months before the central bank began the resolution process on 3 November 2026, so the failure reaches international investors as well as Paraguayan savers. The reports do not say whether holders of the notes face losses or how they would be treated in the resolution.

The notes were sold under US rules known as Rule 144A and Regulation S, which let a company sell bonds to large institutional investors in the US and to buyers elsewhere. The reports do not say that the transactions Doldán described are tied to these notes, or that any bondholder is part of the inquiry.

Paraguay has sent formal requests for judicial help, known as letters rogatory, to Argentina and Luxembourg to trace assets. Our earlier report on the Luxembourg letters covers the European track of that effort.

For US readers the open question is whether American banks or investors in the New York-law bonds become witnesses or victims in the case. The reports do not say that any US institution is under suspicion.

No US step has been announced. A formal request from Washington, or a Paraguayan request for judicial help sent to the United States, would be the clearest next signal.

The distinction matters for what comes next: a US case would be heard by American prosecutors and courts, while a Paraguayan request would run under the extradition treaty. Neither exists today, and Doldán has named no one who would be the target of either.

Not confirmed. Paraguay’s prosecutors say they have received no request or report from US authorities.

Has anyone been charged in the United States?

No such charge has been reported. The people charged so far were charged in Paraguay and are presumed innocent.

Floods and Infrastructure: Paraguay

Paraguay’s lower house is widening a flood-emergency bill and plans to question the minister in charge of roads and bridges. The Budget Committee of the Chamber of Deputies, chaired by Cristina Villalba of the Colorado Party, said on Thursday 26 November 2026 that it plans to hear Public Works Minister Juan Carlos Baruja on Monday 30 November at 14:00 local time (17:00 GMT, noon in New York).

The hearing follows Villalba’s remark that heavy rain has brought down several bridges in Canindeyú, the eastern department she represents. The committee is also studying whether to extend a 90-day emergency, now proposed only for San Pedro department, to the whole country.

Baruja heads the Ministry of Public Works and Communications, known as MOPC, which builds and repairs the country’s roads and bridges. The Chamber’s press office said on 26 November that the meeting will examine the bill in depth and assess the infrastructure and aid needs of the affected areas.

The bill comes from Leonardo Saiz, a Colorado Party deputy for San Pedro, who says floods are hitting the department. It asks for 90 days of emergency to coordinate national and departmental bodies, channel funds and give timely help to damaged families, and it names priority districts including Puerto Antequera, San Estanislao and General Resquín.

Saiz’s explanatory memorandum, as summarised by the Chamber on 26 November, warns that floods destroy crops and threaten rural incomes. The Chamber’s release reports no committee vote and gives no cost for the emergency or figure for crop losses.

Villalba said the committee is studying a nationwide emergency because bad weather affects several departments, according to the Chamber’s release of 26 November. She gave Canindeyú as an example, saying rebuilding the fallen bridges takes time and money; the release does not name the bridges.

For US readers the bill matters because Saiz’s own text ties San Pedro’s economy to farming and cattle, in a country that sells farm goods abroad. No official estimate of lost crops or delayed shipments has been published.

Paraguay’s weather service, the DMH, forecast scattered storms on 26 November, mainly in the north and east of the Eastern region, where Canindeyú lies, and the Chamber’s release gives no river-level readings. Our earlier reports on the Paraná River flood and the El Niño warning cover the earlier phase of this season.

The next dated step is Monday 30 November at 14:00, when the committee plans to receive Baruja. The Chamber has not said whether he has accepted, whether the committee will vote on a nationwide version, or when the bill would reach the full chamber.

Who is Juan Carlos Baruja and why do deputies want to hear him?

He is the minister of public works, whose ministry rebuilds roads and bridges. Deputies want to hear what repairs the flooded regions need.

Would the emergency cover the whole country?

Not yet. The committee is only studying that option, and the bill as filed covers San Pedro department alone.

World.title: Beijing Says Nicaragua Trade Passed US$1.4B
World.content:
Five years after Nicaragua dropped Taiwan for Beijing, China lists what it has built. Washington, meanwhile, prepares a tariff step on Nicaraguan goods.

File photo, undated. The old cathedral and the National Palace on the Plaza de la Revolución in Managua, Nicaragua. Photo: Martin Thurnherr, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Nicaragua: China Ties

China’s ambassador to Nicaragua, Qu Yuhui, said on Thursday 26 November 2026 that trade between the two countries passed US$1.4 billion in 2025, up almost 13% on 2024. He spoke ahead of the fifth anniversary, on 10 December 2026, of the restoration of diplomatic relations between Beijing and Managua.

The figure is his own, and we could not confirm it independently. On 1 January 2027, five weeks after the speech, the United States raises its tariff on Nicaraguan goods outside the US free trade pact from 0% to 10%.

Key Facts Who. Qu Yuhui, China’s ambassador to Nicaragua, spoke on Thursday 26 November 2026.

What. Ambassador says 2025 trade passed US$1.4 billion; we could not confirm it independently.

When. The US tariff on Nicaraguan goods rises from 0% to 10% on 1 January 2027.

As of. 27 November 2026, 04:30 GMT

Five years after Nicaragua dropped Taiwan for Beijing, China lists what it has built. Washington, meanwhile, prepares a tariff step on Nicaraguan goods.

Nicaragua restored ties with Beijing on 10 December 2021, after cutting ties with Taiwan. The ambassador called that a strategic decision for both countries.

The China-Nicaragua free trade agreement entered into force on 1 January 2024. MIFIC, Nicaragua’s trade ministry, has a page on the agreement.

Qu described China as Nicaragua’s second-largest trading partner and said it still sells Nicaragua more than it buys. He named Nicaraguan coffee, meat, tobacco leaf and cigars as products that are welcome in China, without giving values.

The ambassador said a Chinese company is building an international airport, and that 40% of the works are finished. He also said three solar plants totalling 200 megawatts, about 6% of national electricity demand, are coming, with one delivered and two due in April 2027.

He cited the first phase of Nuevas Victorias, a social housing project, with 920 homes. A Chinese firm is building the second phase, he said.

Passengers load buses at a bus station in Managua, Nicaragua. File photo. photo. Passengers load a bus at a station in Managua. Photo: Ridiculopathy, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Qu said China “nunca imponemos condiciones adicionales para nuestra cooperación” (our translation: we never impose additional conditions on our cooperation). That claim is the ambassador’s own, and Washington reads Nicaragua’s record differently.

On 10 December 2025 the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR), which runs American trade policy, announced an additional tariff on Nicaraguan goods after finding on 20 October 2025 that Nicaragua’s labour-rights, human-rights and rule-of-law practices are “unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce”. The investigation behind the action opened on 10 December 2024.

The tariff applies to goods that do not originate under CAFTA-DR, the US free trade agreement with Central America and the Dominican Republic. It stands at 0% in 2026, rises to 10% on 1 January 2027 and to 15% on 1 January 2028.

USTR said it stacks on other duties, including the 18% reciprocal tariff, a broad US import duty, in force in December 2025. It added that the rates may change if Nicaragua shows a lack of progress.

The two stories meet in one trade ledger: China sells Nicaragua more than it buys, by the ambassador’s own account, while the US is about to make Nicaraguan exports dearer. The ambassador gave no split of his total, and we could not confirm the 13% growth.

Earlier Rio Times reports cover how Nicaragua turned to China amid the US showdown and how it launched its free trade era with China. The next dated steps are the anniversary on 10 December 2026 and the tariff rise on 1 January 2027, and more is on the Nicaragua news page.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can the trade figure be trusted?

It is the ambassador’s own claim, and we could not confirm the total independently. He gave no split between what China sells and what it buys.

Does the US tariff apply to all Nicaraguan exports?

It covers goods that do not originate under the CAFTA-DR trade pact. Washington says the rates could change depending on Nicaragua’s progress.

Why does the anniversary matter?

It marks five years since Nicaragua switched recognition from Taipei to Beijing. The ambassador spoke ahead of that date.

World.title: Fire Near Pemex Pipeline in Nuevo León
World.content:
A fire near a pipeline close to the town of Cadereyta was reported under control without injuries, but the basic questions remain open. Pemex says it is still checking the site and the origin of the incident.

File photo, 2008. A Pemex pipeline on a steel bridge over the Atoyac River in Puebla, Mexico. Photo: Isaacvp, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Mexico: Brief

A fire broke out near a Pemex pipeline in Cadereyta Jiménez, a municipality in Mexico’s northern state of Nuevo León, on Thursday 26 November 2026. The state Civil Protection agency, the emergency-response service, received the report at about 16:40 local time (about 22:40 GMT, Greenwich Mean Time), and says no one was hurt.

Pemex, short for Petróleos Mexicanos, Mexico’s state oil company, has not said what the pipeline carries or what caused the blaze. Early reports called it an explosion, but Pemex did not use that word.

Early accounts spoke of an explosion. Pemex said in a statement on social media that specialised staff were attending an incident at a pipeline in the Las Palomitas ejido, a communal farming community.

The company added that the conditions of the site and the origin of the incident were being verified. Its statement did not say what the pipeline carries or what caused the fire.

Preliminary information from Civil Protection says a pipeline section of about 250 metres (about 820 feet) was affected. That figure comes from preliminary information and may change.

State and municipal Civil Protection units from Cadereyta and from Juárez, a neighbouring municipality in Nuevo León, responded, working with Pemex security staff. State Civil Protection said that nobody was injured.

Authorities said there was no risk to nearby communities, and the fire was reported under control the same evening. The reports do not say when the flames were fully out.

Nuevo León borders Texas and includes Monterrey, Mexico’s industrial city. The photo below was taken in the city’s metropolitan area, not at the incident.

Estadio BBVA, the football stadium of the Monterrey club, in the city’s metropolitan area. Photo: Presidencia de la República (Mexico’s presidency), CC BY 2.0.

Neither Pemex nor the authorities have said what caused the fire. It is also not known whether a toma clandestina, an illegal fuel connection, was involved.

Pemex has not said what the line carries, so it is not known whether fuel supply is affected. Whether this was an explosion at all remains unconfirmed.

The fire follows a Pemex pipeline fire in Tototlán, Jalisco, on the night of 5 November 2026. That blaze hit the Salamanca-Guadalajara pipeline, and Pemex first reported four people injured.

A Pemex worker died the next morning, which shows how an early injury count can change. The no-injury report from Nuevo León is the current account, not the final word.

Pipelines in northern Mexico carry fuel and crude to refineries and cities, so the cause matters for safety and supply. Pemex has not said whether any flow was shut off near Cadereyta.

No date has been given for findings on the cause. More is on our Mexico news page.

Frequently Asked Questions

Was anyone hurt in the Cadereyta fire?

State officials say no one was injured. They also said nearby communities were not at risk.

Was it an explosion?

Early reports said so, but Pemex did not use that word. The cause has not been verified.

World.title: Brazil Court Returns Chilean Pulp Mill Case
World.content:
A federal appeals court sent the fight over a Chilean pulp mill’s licence back to a lower court, leaving the permit in force while a second permit is still missing.

Courts: Brazil

The Third Panel of the TRF4, the Federal Regional Court of the 4th Region, annulled a lower-court ruling on Tuesday 24 November 2026 in a case over a R$27 billion (about US$4.7 billion) pulp mill planned by the Chilean group CMPC. It told the lower court in southern Brazil to reassess the prosecutors’ case, including how prior consultation of Indigenous and other traditional communities should be organised.

The licence stays in force, because the panel did not suspend it. The ruling comes eight days after four groups, including a Guarani association, said they had filed another lawsuit on Monday 16 November 2026.

Key Facts What. The mill’s first permit, issued by state agency Fepam on 22 October 2026, stays in force.

Where. Barra do Ribeiro, Rio Grande do Sul, near Porto Alegre; cost R$27 billion (about US$4.7 billion).

When. Ruling on Tuesday 24 November 2026; no date is known for the lower court’s decision.

Power Index. Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 74.2 points (November 2026 edition).

As of. 27 November 2026, 04:00 GMT.

A federal appeals court sent the fight over a Chilean pulp mill’s licence back to a lower court, leaving the permit in force while a second permit is still missing.

The Federal Public Prosecutor’s Office, known by its initials MPF, filed the civil action on Wednesday 13 May 2026 against CMPC, the state environmental agency Fepam, the federal government, the land agency Incra and the federal Indigenous affairs agency Funai. It says licensing advanced without the free, prior and informed consultation of artisanal fishers and of Indigenous and quilombola communities, descendants of escaped slaves, that the International Labour Organization’s Convention 169 requires (MPF press release, 13 May 2026).

The Rio Grande do Sul government says the Barra do Ribeiro plant is designed for 3 million tonnes a year. CMPC, a Chilean pulp, paper and packaging group, also runs a separate Guaíba pulp mill near Porto Alegre, which we covered in a separate report.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 74.2 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

File photo of eucalyptus pulp, pine fluff and wood chip samples at a pulp unit in Brazil. Not the CMPC site.

Projeto Natureza, or Project Nature, is a R$27 billion plan, and the state government lists an additional R$1.5 billion (about US$259 million) export terminal at the port of Rio Grande. We convert reais at a rounded R$5.80 per US$1.

The site is Barra do Ribeiro, a small town on Lake Guaíba, the lake beside Porto Alegre. The Rio Grande do Sul government projects up to 12,000 workers there at the peak of construction.

The Rio Grande do Sul government called the mill the largest private investment in the state’s history in its release of 23 October 2026. The installation licence, the permit that lets works start, is still to come.

Prosecutors say the plant would discharge 216,000 cubic metres of effluent a day into Lake Guaíba, containing 720 kilograms of toxic chlorine-based pollutants (organochlorines, dioxins and furans), a few kilometres from water intakes of Porto Alegre’s water utility Dmae and of the Corsan water utility in Barra do Ribeiro (MPF, 13 May 2026). They add that the company limited the area of direct impact to a 5 km radius although more than 7,000 artisanal fishers work in the Jacuí Delta and the Patos Lagoon.

The lower court is the 9th Federal Court of Porto Alegre, which in June had refused the prosecutors’ request to halt the licensing. The appeals panel has now told it to look at the consultation case again.

Rio Times membership Read everything we publish for US$1 in the first month. Then US$8.99 a month. Cancel anytime. Start for US$1

Fepam granted the preliminary licence on Thursday 22 October 2026 and handed it to CMPC the next day, after Funai gave a favourable opinion on the company’s studies of eight Mbyá Guarani communities on the site and 18 more nearby. The Mbyá Guarani are an Indigenous people, and Fepam described a technical review, a public hearing and a period for public comments.

Roberto Liebgott of Cimi-Sul, the southern branch of the Catholic Indigenist Missionary Council, answered on 23 October 2026. He called Funai’s opinion “worrying and contradictory, since approving a technical study is not the same as consultation” (translated from Portuguese; the quotation continues).

The text of the 24 November ruling was not available online when we checked. Reports dated 25 and 26 November 2026 say it did not suspend the licence.

The lower court has not said when it will rule, and no start date for works has been announced. It is not known whether CMPC has applied for the installation licence, the permit that allows works to start.

Until that licence is issued, none of the peak construction jobs can begin. The ruling therefore adds a court step without removing a permit, and it hands the consultation question to the lower court.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did the court cancel the CMPC mill’s licence?

No, the licence stays in force while the lower court reassesses the prosecutors’ requests. The ruling annulled an earlier decision but did not suspend or invalidate the permit.

Why do prosecutors oppose the mill?

They argue that fishers and Indigenous and quilombola communities were not consulted as international labour rules require. They also warn about effluent discharged into Lake Guaíba near drinking-water intakes.

Can construction start now?

Not yet, because the project still needs an installation licence. The lower court’s timetable is not known.

World.title: Costa Rica Cuts Interest Rate to 2.75%
World.content:
COSTA RICA · ECONOMY

Costa Rica’s central bank, the Banco Central de Costa Rica (BCCR), cut its main interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point, or 25 basis points, to 2.75% a year on Thursday 26 November 2026. The cut comes as consumer prices are rising again after a long slump, and the new rate takes effect on Friday 27 November 2026.

The monetary policy rate, known as the TPM, is the main reference for loans and deposits in colones, Costa Rica’s currency. The bank’s board of directors voted unanimously for the cut.

Key Facts What The central bank cut its policy rate by 25 basis points to 2.75%, effective 27 November.

Why Inflation expectations near 2% sit below the bank’s 3% target, and risks to its projection lean downward.

Trend Prices rose 0.55% in the year to October, after 16 months of falling prices.

Power Index Costa Rica ranks 9th of 14 in Costa Rica ranks 9th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 35.5 points (November 2026 edition).

As of 27 November 2026, 05:00 GMT

The central bank is easing because it fears that low inflation expectations could hold prices below target, even as prices begin to rise.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Costa Rica economy Email address Follow

Róger Madrigal, the bank’s president, told a press conference on Thursday afternoon that inflation expectations weighed most on the decision. They stand near 2% for the medium and long term, below the 3% target.

“In a flexible inflation-targeting scheme, the formation of expectations is decisive,” Madrigal said, in our translation from Spanish. He added that a policy response consistent with the target “must help realign inflation expectations and thus preserve the credibility of the central bank”.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Costa Rica ranks 9th of 14 with 35.5 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (75); weakest: military means (0). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB). See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Consumer prices rose 0.55% in the year to October 2026, according to INEC, the national statistics institute, after 0.34% in September. September’s reading ended a run of 16 consecutive months of falling prices.

The bank says inflation has stayed below its 3% target for 42 consecutive months. It also sits below the bottom of the bank’s tolerance range, one percentage point either side of the target, and last stood inside that range in April 2023.

The cut is the second of 2026, after the July cut to 3.00%, and takes the rate down by 50 basis points from 3.25%. It was the last of the BCCR’s six policy meetings this year.

The BCCR expects headline inflation to rise in the last quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2027, because of the delayed effect of earlier oil and grain price rises. Core inflation, which strips out the most volatile prices, would also rise, but by less, and the bank sees no general pass-through to other prices so far.

“There will be a little more inflation (with the cut), and this will affect expectations, which could be unanchored,” Madrigal said, in our translation. He said the board still found room to cut, because monetary policy works with a lag and the cut would not affect inflation in those two quarters.

File photo, 2023. The Banco Central de Costa Rica building in San José. Photo: MyCatIsAChonk, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

From the second quarter of 2027 the bank projects inflation to rise gradually to values close to, but below, 3%. Madrigal stressed that the risks to that projection lean to the downside, which the BCCR says justified the cut.

The board also weighed upside risks: El Niño, a recurring weather phenomenon, ample liquidity (cash) in the financial system, and a widening gap between domestic and international interest rates. That gap could change how investors split their portfolios, the bank says.

Since the September meeting, international prices of most basic grains and of hydrocarbons have fallen, the bank said in its statement. Uncertainty has moderated but remains high.

Mauricio Moya, head of market investments at the Costa Rican brokerage Mercado de Valores, said inflation stays low and economic activity keeps slowing, which opened room for a cut. “The effect of this adjustment on economic activity will not be immediate and will depend on its transmission to the interest rates of the financial system,” he added, in our translation.

Changes in the policy rate typically show up in the Tasa Básica Pasiva, the average rate banks pay on deposits, about six months later. The BCCR says it will keep watching inflation, its drivers and the risks, and will adjust the rate in whichever direction conditions require.

For US readers, the BCCR’s reference rates for 26 November 2026 were 440.90 colones to buy and 445.95 to sell one US dollar. The policy rate is the main reference for colón loans and deposits, so the cut matters most to people who borrow or save in colones.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Costa Rica’s central bank cut the rate?

It says inflation expectations near 2% sit below its 3% target and that risks to its projection lean downward. It also weighed upside risks from El Niño and ample liquidity.

Will borrowing get cheaper straight away?

Not immediately. The central bank says changes in the policy rate usually reach deposit rates after about six months.

Will inflation rise after the cut?

The bank expects inflation to rise anyway in the coming quarters, and its president said the cut itself would add a little. It projects inflation to approach, but stay below, the 3% target from the second quarter of 2027.

Sources: Banco Central de Costa Rica (BCCR, the central bank), monetary policy statement and press conference of 26 November 2026 (https://www.bccr.fi.cr); BCCR board decision of 24 July 2026; Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censos (INEC, the statistics institute), consumer price index for October 2026, published 6 November 2026.

World.title: Colombia Charges Two Ex-Congress Presidents
World.content:
COLOMBIA · CORRUPTION

Colombia’s state watchdog has charged two former heads of Congress with taking cash from a disaster-agency fund, in a decision issued on Thursday 26 November 2026. The Procuraduría General de la Nación, the watchdog that disciplines public officials, accuses Iván Name, a former Senate president, and Andrés Calle, a former president of the House of Representatives.

The charges concern the UNGRD, the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management, a government agency, and allege the two men accepted 4 billion pesos (about US$1.12 million) in all. A disciplinary charge is not a finding of guilt, and neither man has been convicted of anything.

Calle, the text says, “in his capacity as Representative and president of that body, accepted the sum of 1,000 million pesos” (about US$281,000) from resources obtained illegally from the UNGRD. It alleges that Sneyder Pinilla Álvarez, then UNGRD sub-director for disaster management, delivered the money.

According to the file, Ortiz visited Name’s apartment in north Bogotá on 12 and 13 October 2023 and made two deliveries. The Fiscalía, Colombia’s prosecutor general’s office, has sent Ortiz to trial in the same web of corruption, where prosecutors call her “the messenger”.

The money allegedly came from the purchase of 40 water tanker trucks, known as carrotanques, meant to bring drinking water to La Guajira department. The case originates in public statements by Pinilla, the former UNGRD sub-director for disaster management.

Investigators say the money was used to win legislative support for the reforms of the government of President Gustavo Petro. Statements by Pinilla and López, who both negotiated with prosecutors, were key to building the file.

The disciplinary case dates from 3 May 2024, and the conduct it examines took place in 2023. The Procuraduría closed its investigation and gave the parties time to file pleadings before issuing this decision.

The Procuraduría said the conduct, if proved, could amount to “cohecho impropio”, meaning a public official accepting money for an act that is part of his duty. That offence is set out in Article 406 of Law 599 of 2000, the criminal code, but the disciplinary case is separate from the criminal one.

In the criminal case, both men have been accused since August 2025, and the trials have not started. On Friday 9 October 2026 the Supreme Court ordered both men freed from La Picota, a prison in Bogotá, because the legal limit for detention without trial had expired, as our earlier report on the Supreme Court releasing both men described.

Name, who became Senate president on 20 July 2023, lost his Senate seat in a “loss of investiture” ruling by the Council of State, Colombia’s top administrative court, in September 2026, as our earlier report on the loss of his Senate seat noted. Calle held a House seat for Córdoba department and was House president when the alleged conduct took place.

No appeal is possible against a statement of charges. When the two men and their lawyers, Fahid Name Gómez for Name and Andrés Ricardo Suárez for Calle, have been notified in person, the file goes to the Procuraduría’s trial chamber for elected officials, which will run the disciplinary trial.

The two men’s response to the charges has not been published, and no hearing date has been set. The order was signed by delegate attorney Patricia Carrillo Blanco under file IUS E-2024-289494.

World.title: Costa Rica Holds 58% of the World’s Quetzals as Northern Forests Vanish
World.content:
Costa Rica is home to nearly six of every ten resplendent quetzals left on Earth, according to a new study that puts the species’ total population at about 334,000 birds, less than half of the most recent published figure. The research, published in the peer-reviewed journal Bird Conservation International, estimates that about 193,900 quetzals live in Costa Rica’s highland forests and another 83,700 across the border in Panama. Together the two countries hold roughly 83% of the global population.

The remaining birds, about 56,500, are spread across southern Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador and Nicaragua, where the study found that the bird’s breeding forests have been cut roughly in half in three decades.

Lead author Edward H. Backus, an independent scholar based in Oregon, worked with four co-authors, among them Sofia Solórzano of the National Autonomous University of Mexico and Knut Eisermann of Bird Studies Guatemala. The team combined satellite forest records for 1990, 2011 and 2021 with elevation data to map cloud forest between 1,500 and 3,000 meters (4,900 and 9,800 feet), the band where quetzals nest.

They found about 864,000 hectares (2.1 million acres) of core breeding habitat still standing across Mesoamerica in 2021. Some 361,000 hectares (892,000 acres), close to 30% of the forest that existed in 1990, had disappeared. The losses were far from even. El Salvador lost 73% of its quetzal breeding habitat over the period, Mexico 65%, Guatemala 53%, Nicaragua 52% and Honduras 37%. Costa Rica lost 8%, or about 32,800 hectares (81,100 acres), and Panama 5%.

The difference comes down largely to one mountain range. The Cordillera de Talamanca, which runs from Costa Rica into Panama and includes La Amistad International Park, holds a single block of breeding forest of about 442,000 hectares (1.09 million acres). The next largest, in Guatemala’s Sierra de las Minas, covers about 50,700 hectares (125,000 acres), less than one-eighth the size.

Protection also sets the south apart. Of the roughly 388,000 hectares (958,000 acres) of core habitat the study mapped in Costa Rica, about 371,000 hectares (917,000 acres) of quetzal habitat lay inside protected areas in 2021. The bird continues to turn up in new corners of that network, including a first record at a Cartago refuge last month.

The quetzal is divided into two subspecies, and the study shows them on very different paths. The northern form, found from Mexico to Nicaragua, lost 51% of its breeding habitat between 1990 and 2021. The southern form, found only in Costa Rica and Panama, lost 7%.

On that basis the authors recommend that the International Union for Conservation of Nature move the species from Near Threatened to Vulnerable on its Red List, and they argue the northern subspecies warrants a higher category still. Habitat for the species as a whole shrank 26% between 2000 and 2021, just under the 30% threshold for a threatened listing but within the study’s margin of error.

The authors identify the conversion of forest to farmland and pasture as the main threat. They also point to climate pressures on cloud forest, including drought, fire and the loss of cloud cover, a concern already documented in the drying of Monteverde.

The population figure carries real uncertainty, the authors caution. It rests on assumptions about how many birds a given area of forest supports, and field counts are sparse and were made with different methods at different times. For Costa Rica and Panama the team assumed 50 birds per 100 hectares (247 acres) after halving the upper field estimates to avoid overcounting.

Even so, the new total is a sharp downward revision. A rough estimate published in 2023 by Alan F. Poole, a co-author of the new paper, had put the population at about 770,000.

The authors single out the Talamanca highlands as a priority for long-term monitoring. The quetzal is also among the main draws of a birdwatching sector that has become a growth area for Costa Rican tourism, which leaves the country holding both the largest share of the species and the largest stake in what happens to it.

World.title: President Puts Illegal Gold Mining Losses at Crucitas Near $2 Billion
World.content:
President Laura Fernández said Wednesday that illegal miners have taken about $2 billion in gold from Crucitas, in northern Costa Rica near the Nicaraguan border. She called the figure preliminary and did not explain how it was calculated. Speaking at her weekly press conference at Casa Presidencial, Fernández described the mining as a blatant violation of national sovereignty and said the problem was getting out of the government’s hands.

She blamed the Legislative Assembly, saying a negotiated solution has been available for nearly three years without becoming law. Fernández said the gold belongs to Costa Rica and that its value could have paid for roads, schools, health services and pensions. She said an ounce was trading at $3,674 this week, which in her view raises the cost of every month without a solution.

The $2 billion estimate is not new. Former ruling-party legislator Pilar Cisneros cited the same figure in June, and no methodology was released with Wednesday’s statement. The president also pointed to a 61.3% rise in Nicaragua’s gold exports, without saying how much of that gold she believes came out of Crucitas.

On enforcement, Fernández said authorities have made 537 apprehensions in Crucitas, 243 of them tied to immigration status and illegal gold extraction. Police seized 2,000 sacks of mining sediment in the most recent operation. Security Minister Gerald Campos said recent operations in Crucitas and nearby Conchudita cost the state more than 30 million colones (about $67,000). Those operations have included US helicopter support for the crackdown on illegal gold mining. Fernández also linked the mining zone to the smuggling of cocaine, crack and marijuana and to human trafficking.

She said the excavations and settling ponds used by the miners threaten aquifers and forest and estimated that restoring the area would cost more than $20 million. She questioned whether restoration would hold while illegal mining continues. Crucitas was the site of a proposed open-pit gold mine that never opened. Costa Rica banned open-pit metal mining in 2010, and the deposit has since drawn illegal miners, whom the government says cross mainly from Nicaragua.

The government’s proposal would allow the gold to be auctioned, with proceeds going to education, health and security. Opposition blocs including the National Liberation Party and the Broad Front have held it up with motions in the Assembly. Fernández also asked lawmakers to advance a separate bill that would toughen penalties for illegal mining, even if the broader Crucitas plan remains stalled.

Presidency and Finance Minister Rodrigo Chaves has said he would recommend that she call a referendum on the proposal. Fernández has said she is considering putting Crucitas gold mining to a national vote but has not decided. The president is scheduled to meet Friday, Nov. 27, with residents of San Carlos, Cutris, Crucitas and nearby communities to discuss new measures.

World.title: Costa Rica Opens 4 Days of Walk-In Driving Tests in San José
World.content:
If you have had trouble landing an appointment for your practical driving test, you get four days next week to skip that step. From Monday, Nov. 30, through Thursday, Dec. 3, you can show up at Ciudad Vial in San José and take the test with no appointment and no login to the online booking system.

The days are split by vehicle, so go on the one that matches yours. Car tests for the B1 license run Monday, Nov. 30, and Tuesday, Dec. 1. Motorcycle tests for the A1, A2 and A3 licenses run Wednesday, Dec. 2, and Thursday, Dec. 3.

Testing runs from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. on all four days, longer than the usual schedule. That includes Tuesday, Dec. 1, a national holiday. Sindy Coto, director of Educación Vial, the road education office of the Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MOPT), said staff will work that day because many people are expected to use the day off to take the test.

Expect company. When the office ran the same walk-in format for motorcycles only in the last week of October, 1,279 people turned up over five days. Arriving early gives you the best chance of getting through. Ciudad Vial is the MOPT testing track beside Parque de la Paz, in southern San José.

You still have to meet the normal requirements. You must have already passed the theory test, and you need a valid ID in good condition. Bring the vehicle you will test in, along with its circulation permit (derecho de circulación) and its technical card (tarjeta técnica vehicular). The examiner needs to confirm the vehicle is legally on the road before you drive it on the track.

Pay the 5,000-colón test fee (about $11) before you go. You can pay at any authorized bank or financial institution, and you need to bring the receipt with you. You also need a medical certificate (dictamen médico) issued within the last 180 days. If yours is older than that, get a new one before you go.

Two groups will be turned away. If you already have a practical test appointment booked, you cannot use the walk-in days. And if you failed the practical test recently, you have to wait out the 20 business days that must pass before a retake. The system blocks both cases automatically, so there is no way around it at the gate.

It is worth practicing before you go, in a year when nearly half of all driving tests have been failed. In the October session, 940 riders passed and 339 failed, a pass rate of 73 percent.

The mistakes that failed people were basic ones. Riders put a foot down or crossed the lines in the parallel-line and zigzag exercises, ignored road signs and pavement markings, knocked over or brushed cones, and forgot to use their turn signals. Educación Vial is asking everyone to arrive well prepared.

Coto said the October session produced very good results, which is why the office is repeating it and adding car tests this time. Educación Vial said the walk-in days are meant for people whose work or study schedules have kept them from finishing the process of getting a license.

World.title: Costa Rica Will End 2026 Short of Its 2019 Visitor Record, Forecast Shows
World.content:
Costa Rica is on course to receive about 3.05 million international visitors in 2026, a gain of 3.6% over last year that would still leave us short of the record 3.14 million who arrived in 2019, according to a projection by the Center for Tourism Studies (CET). The center’s scenarios range from 3.03 million to 3.08 million.

Reaching the central figure would require November and December to roughly match the 594,530 arrivals recorded in the same two months of 2025, according to a Tico Times calculation based on the published figures. The year began at a record pace. The first quarter brought 1,033,777 visitors, 11.3% more than a year earlier and the first time that period had surpassed its 2019 level, the CET reported.

The growth stopped there. From January through October, arrivals by all points of entry totaled 2,454,330, an increase of 4.5%, and all of that gain came in the first three months. April through October brought 1,420,553 visitors, nearly unchanged from the same stretch of 2025.

Shirley Calvo, executive director of the National Chamber of Tourism (Canatur), said the cumulative growth largely reflects the strong first quarter. The most recent months were weaker. October brought 144,010 visitors, 1.1% fewer than a year earlier and the third consecutive monthly decline, after drops of 5.1% in August and 2.4% in September. Across the three months, the country received 14,767 fewer visitors than in the same period of 2025, Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT) figures show.

Flight schedules have thinned along with arrivals. The CET counted 523 weekly flights to Costa Rica in the third week of November, compared with 609 a year earlier, and 82 routes against 90. All 14 routes that were discontinued served Juan Santamaría International Airport near San José, which now has 94 fewer weekly flights, while Liberia gained eight. The capital’s airport has lost arrivals for seven straight months as Guanacaste has grown.

CET director Víctor Umaña said airlines reassign aircraft according to cost and demand, and that routes to San José, which are the most sensitive to price, are the first to be cut. Former Tourism Minister Gustavo Segura attributed the capital’s decline to the exit of the low-cost carrier Spirit, ticket prices, oil prices and the country’s international image.

Analysts also point to the high cost of visiting and operating in Costa Rica, an appreciated exchange rate, weak transport infrastructure, insecurity and growing competition from Mexico, the Dominican Republic, Colombia and the rest of Central America. The high season runs through early April. Arrival figures for November, expected next month, will give the first reading on whether the forecast holds.

World.title: King Tides Peak on Costa Rica’s Pacific Coast and Run Through Saturday
World.content:
If you are on Costa Rica’s Pacific coast this week, expect the sea to come higher up the beach than usual through Saturday. Unusually high tides, often called king tides, peaked before dawn Thursday and will return each early morning and afternoon until Nov. 28. The University of Costa Rica’s oceanographic information unit, MIO-CIMAR, forecast the highest water between 2 a.m. and 4 a.m. Thursday. Golfito, on the southern Pacific, was expected to see the highest tide at 3.48 meters (11.4 feet).

Puntarenas, Bahía Herradura, Uvita and Bahía Culebra were each forecast at 3.08 meters (10.1 feet). The Gulf of Santa Elena, in northern Guanacaste, was forecast at 3.05 meters (10 feet) and Quepos at 2.87 meters (9.4 feet). Two things are stacking up. Tuesday’s full moon lined up the sun, Earth and moon, which produces the strongest tides of the lunar cycle. On top of that, El Niño has warmed the Pacific, and warmer water expands and raises the average sea level.

That extra height is what pushes seawater into streets and homes that normally stay dry, even when there is no rain or storm. MIO-CIMAR oceanographer Rodney Mora said the conditions can cause flooding and coastal erosion. The places to watch are low-lying coastal neighborhoods. During the last episode, from Oct. 26 to 31, high tides flooded homes in Puntarenas, where residents of Barrio El Carmen reported water up to their knees. The National Emergency Commission confirmed damage at Playa Zancudo, in Golfito, and Playa Preciosa, near Puerto Jiménez.

If you live or are staying close to the shoreline in those areas, move vehicles and anything that can be damaged by salt water off low ground before the early-morning and afternoon high tides. The water arrives on a schedule, so you have time to prepare. On the beach, you will have much less sand at high tide. Set up well above the wet line, and do not leave a car parked on the sand or beside an estuary mouth, because those are the first places the water reaches.

Swimming and boating are not ruled out. MIO-CIMAR said the tides by themselves do not create generally adverse conditions for bathers or for navigation. If you have booked a night tour during turtle nesting season in Guanacaste, ask your guide whether the tide changes the timing.

The Caribbean coast is not affected. The difference between low and high tide there is about 60 centimeters (2 feet), which is normal. Pacific tides are expected to return to their usual range on Sunday, Nov. 29. MIO-CIMAR updates its forecast every six hours at miocimar.ucr.ac.cr.

World.title: Costa Rica Doctors Call a February Strike as Surgery Waits Average 449 Days
World.content:
Costa Rica’s largest doctors’ union is calling on general practitioners, specialists and medical residents across the public health system to prepare for a general strike starting in February 2027, a move that could hit hospitals, clinics and the waiting lists millions of patients already depend on.

The National Medical Union (UMN) announced the call on Wednesday at a press conference alongside the nurses’ union ANPE and Siprocimeca, which represents medical professionals at the Costa Rican Social Security Fund (CCSS). The unions said the strike would cover both regular and overtime shifts. No specific start date has been set.

UMN president Randall Cabrera Garita said the union’s central demand is that the CCSS cancel a new set of rules on overtime pay. According to the union, the changes cut pay for work outside regular hours, including the extra shifts and on-call duty that keep many hospital services running, and could push more doctors out of the public system.

Cabrera also warned of what the union described as a creeping privatization of public health care. The unions argue that money meant for hospitals, clinics, local EBAIS health posts and new staff positions could instead flow to private providers, and they object to cuts in payments tied to programs meant to shorten surgery waiting lists.

A report published hours after the announcement brought that concern into focus. Massimo Manzi, executive director of the Costa Rican Health Chamber, which groups private providers, said the CCSS completed a market study last week on contracting private services for outpatient consultations, diagnostic tests and surgeries. Manzi said 24 providers took part. The CCSS had not responded to press questions about the study by this morning.

Manzi said the chamber wants providers outside the Greater Metropolitan Area included, and proposes contracts that would activate only when patients wait longer than the limits set by a Health Ministry decree. Any deal would have to follow Costa Rica’s public procurement law. The idea of paying private doctors to ease the backlog has been under discussion since earlier this year.

The scale of the backlog explains why both sides are pushing. The CCSS reported in late October that the average wait for surgery stood at 449 days, down from 535 days in April 2023. It also reported 816 people who had been waiting since 2021 or earlier, and an average wait of 769 days for a first orthopedic consultation.

The unions listed other grievances, including staff shortages, the departure of specialists, saturated emergency services and lagging infrastructure. They also cited the effects of the Public Finance Strengthening Law and the Public Employment Framework Law on pay. The UMN said the state owes the CCSS more than 4 trillion colones (about $9 billion), and complained that the government has blocked the appointment of a union representative to the CCSS board of directors.

Cabrera said the union has asked for a meeting with CCSS Executive President Mónica Taylor to discuss the demands before any walkout. The union said escalation can still be avoided if authorities open a dialogue, but that the strike call stands until the contested decisions are reviewed. Taylor had previously said the CCSS is reviewing its overtime payment tables. The institution had not issued a public response to the strike call by this morning.

The threat comes after a difficult year of labor conflict in the public health system, from a nurses’ strike at Hospital México in August to a nationwide health workers’ strike threat in September over unpaid salaries. Hospitals have also struggled with capacity, with some patients in Liberia waiting days in a chair for a bed.

The CCSS is the backbone of health care in Costa Rica. Workers, employers and legal residents, including foreign retirees and others with residency, are required to pay into the system, and most of Costa Rica relies on its hospitals and clinics. How the institution answers the unions over the coming weeks will help decide whether patients face a disruption in February, and whether more of their care ends up being delivered by private providers paid with public money.

World.title: Costa Rica Sloth Rope Bridges Reach 410 With 22,000 Crossings
World.content:
Costa Rica’s sloth rope bridges are drawing international attention, with The Associated Press publishing a feature yesterday on the conservationists and caretakers working to keep the sloths in the trees. The story begins behind a beachfront hotel in Puerto Viejo de Talamanca, where a small crew strings rope from one trunk to the next. To a passing tourist it looks like little more than a clothesline. To a sloth it can be the difference between staying safely in the canopy and coming down to the ground, where dogs, cars and power lines are waiting.

The work is led by The Sloth Conservation Foundation, founded by British zoologist Rebecca Cliffe, who has spent close to 20 years studying the animals on Costa Rica’s southern Caribbean coast. Her team has now installed roughly 410 rope bridges, most of them in places where roads, houses and hotels have opened gaps in the forest.

The design is deliberately simple, usually a single line. Cliffe says that for animals built to live in the trees that is enough, giving them a way over a gap they could not otherwise cross. Unlike monkeys, sloths cannot jump. Cliffe has a name for the problem, microfragmentation. A break of just 2 or 3 meters (about 7 to 10 feet) between neighboring treetops can force a sloth to look for another route, and the other route is often the ground or an electrical cable.

Making matters harder, sloths tend to stick to the paths they learned when young, even after the landscape around them has changed. Cliffe began experimenting with bridges nearly two decades ago after working at the Sloth Sanctuary of Costa Rica in Penshurst, where she kept seeing animals brought in after dog attacks, collisions with vehicles and electrocutions. With almost no funding, she started hanging single ropes.

Cameras mounted on some of the bridges have since recorded more than 22,000 wildlife crossings, and sloths are not the only users. Today the team responds to sightings at hotels and private properties, plants trees and works with neighbors to reconnect their lots. The ropes are not permanent. Tropical sun and rain wear them out in four or five years, and they have to be replaced.

The paradox is that Costa Rica is a celebrated reforestation success. A 2023 OECD report put forest cover at 59 percent of the national territory, up from about 21 percent in 1987. But geographer Carlos Morera Beita of the National University points out that much of that regrowth took place on old pastureland, in a countryside still divided up by farming. Sloths have proven more adaptable than scientists once believed, getting around through pastures with scattered trees, living fences and vegetation along rivers.

Those links matter, he says, because an isolated sloth has a hard time finding food, shelter and a mate. In his view bridges fix specific choke points, but lasting protection depends on keeping existing forest standing, restoring biological corridors and stopping further fragmentation. Back at the Sloth Sanctuary, founder Judy Avey-Arroyo cares for the animals that cannot go home.

Her work began when she and her husband took in an orphan named Buttercup, and today the sanctuary houses sloths with severe injuries or disabilities along with babies whose mothers were killed by cars, dogs or power lines. The smallest are raised in incubators and fed milk, while older juveniles move on to leaves, time outdoors and climbing practice. Avey-Arroyo says a mother cannot really be replaced.

A young sloth spends about a year learning which leaves are safe, which plants to avoid, how to move through the forest and even how to deal with parasites, and orphans that miss those lessons can struggle in the wild even when they look healthy. Accepting that some of her animals will never return to the forest, she says, is the hardest part of the job.

Climate change adds another layer. Small patches of forest heat up and dry out faster than continuous forest, and sloths control their body temperature by moving between sun and shade. Cliffe says extreme heat can drain their limited energy reserves while cold can interfere with digestion, so her group is planting shade trees alongside the bridges.

Scientists still lack reliable estimates of how many sloths Costa Rica has or whether their numbers are rising or falling. Cliffe’s team is testing thermal imaging drones, trained detection dogs and field surveys to find out. Two rescue centers in the region take in around three sloths a day, but without historical data no one can say whether that figure is climbing. Costa Rican conservation groups have separately backed a U.S. bill to ban sloth imports.

The idea is spreading beyond the Caribbean. On the southern Pacific coast, Alturas Wildlife Rescue Center and the state utility ICE are installing eight rope crossings along the coastal highway between Dominical and Uvita to cut down on wildlife being hit by traffic or electrocuted. Four were in place by late September.

The best outcome, Cliffe told the AP, would be for the bridges to become unnecessary once the trees grow close enough for sloths to move freely on their own. Until then she believes their future rests on many small acts, a tree planted here and a rope hung there. She calls it “the cumulative power of many individual actions” and says that is what keeps her hopeful.

World.title: Expect Two Weeks of Night Lane Closures on Costa Rica’s Route 1 Near Naranjo
World.content:
If you drive Costa Rica’s Route 1 at night, expect lane closures and a short detour near Naranjo for the next two weeks. Crews are demolishing the former Naranjo toll station on the Bernardo Soto Highway. Work runs from 6 p.m. to 6 a.m. and started today. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MOPT) and the National Road Council (CONAVI) expect it to take about two weeks, with partial lane closures while crews are on site.

If you are heading from San Ramón toward Alajuela, you will be moved onto a temporary lane that runs alongside the old toll station. That is the direction drivers take toward San José and Juan Santamaría International Airport, so it affects night trips in from Guanacaste, San Carlos and the western Central Valley.

The overnight schedule keeps the work out of rush hour, but you should still leave extra time, especially if you have a late-evening or early-morning flight. Slow down as you approach the work zone, follow the temporary signs and do what the crews on site tell you. They will be working next to moving traffic in the dark.

The Naranjo station has not charged a toll since September 1, 2025. Authorities suspended collection that day at Naranjo and at Río Segundo de Alajuela, citing constant backups at Río Segundo and changes tied to the highway project at Naranjo. The booths stayed in place after the toll ended.

In April 2026, then-President Rodrigo Chaves ordered both toll stations removed, calling the unused structures an unnecessary obstacle for drivers. Crews began demolishing the Río Segundo booths in late April. The Naranjo structures stood until this week. Transportation authorities say taking down the Naranjo station is part of the San José to San Ramón highway expansion. Removing the abandoned booths clears an obstacle from the road, improves safety and ends vandalism at the unused site.

World.title: Halo BPO continues recruitment of work from home sales agents in Belize
World.content:
Halo BPO continues recruitment of work from home sales agents in Belize

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Halo BPO is still accepting applications for sales agents in Belize.

The positions are full time, work from home roles in outbound sales.

Agents earn BZ$9.00 per hour during training and BZ$10.00 per hour after training is completed. Commission and bonuses are paid on top of the hourly rate, and agents are paid weekly.

The company requires at least two years of sales experience. Experience in credit repair is a plus.

Applicants must also have a home internet connection with speeds of 85 Mbps download and 45 Mbps upload.

To apply, send a resume to [email protected] with your full name in the subject line.

World.title: Orange Walk student charged with driving without a licence
World.content:
Orange Walk student charged with driving without a licence

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police have charged Martin Jimenez, 19, a student of Orange Walk Town, with driving a motor vehicle while not being the holder of a Belize driver’s licence.

The stop was made around 11:48pm on Sunday, November 22.

According to police, officers on mobile patrol on San Francisco Street in Orange Walk Town pulled over a black F150 pickup truck.

An officer asked the driver for the vehicle’s documents. Police say the vehicle licence was valid through the end of November 2026, and the insurance was valid until February 19, 2027.

When asked for his driver’s licence, the driver reportedly told the officer he did not have one.

He was informed of the offence, cautioned and arrested, then escorted to the Orange Walk Police Station, where he was advised of his rights.

On November 23, Jimenez was formally charged. Police say he chose to remain silent.

He was granted police bail to appear in the Orange Walk Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday, November 24.

World.title: Belize advances Climate Action through Policy and collaboration
World.content:
Belize advances Climate Action through Policy and collaboration

By Zoila Palma: The Government of Belize, through the Climate Change Department (CCD), presented the final Climate Change and Carbon Market Policy Package, marking an important step in strengthening the country’s climate governance framework and advancing climate action.

The presentation brought together key policy priorities, institutional responsibilities, carbon market mechanisms, environmental integrity, and the next steps towards implementation of the Policy, supporting the operationalization of the Climate Change and Carbon Market Initiatives Act, 2026.

This important initiative is implemented by United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), Expertise France, and Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ), in collaboration with NEYEN, under the European Union’s EUROCLIMA Programme.

The Belize Climate Change Department says that through these strategic partnerships, Belize continues to advance its efforts towards effective climate governance, strengthened institutional capacity, and a more sustainable, inclusive, and climate-resilient future.

World.title: Belize reviews Draft Country Gender assessment
World.content:
Belize reviews Draft Country Gender assessment

The Ministry of Human Development, Family Support and Gender Affairs, in collaboration with the Caribbean Development Bank (CDB), is convening a validation workshop today at the Grand Resort Hotel and Residences in Belize City to review the findings and recommendations of Belize’s draft Country Gender Assessment.

Commissioned by CDB and prepared by Shidaa Sustainable Development Solutions Ltd., the 2024/25 assessment builds on Belize’s 2016 Country Gender Assessment. It looks at where Belize has made progress on gender equality and where barriers remain. The draft examines differences in access to education, employment, and leadership opportunities, as well as the impact of unpaid caregiving and gaps in services for survivors of gender-based violence.

The opening programme features a welcome by Starla Bradley, Director of the Family Support and Gender Affairs Department, and remarks from Adele Catzim-Sanchez, Chief Executive Officer in the Ministry, and Elbert Ellis, Portfolio Manager and Social Analyst at CDB. The assessment team will present the draft findings before participants review the report in working groups and discuss their feedback in plenary.

The workshop gives participants an opportunity to identify gaps, assess whether the findings reflect their experience, and consider which recommendations should take priority. Their feedback will inform revisions to the report, which is intended to guide national policy, programme planning, and future CDB support in Belize.

World.title: Belize marks commencement of Domestic and Intimate Partner Violence (Prohibition) Law
World.content:
Belize marks commencement of Domestic and Intimate Partner Violence (Prohibition) Law

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Human Development, Family Support and Gender Affairs is pleased to announce that the Domestic and Intimate Partner Violence (Prohibition) Act, Act No. 22 of 2026, officially came into force on November 25, 2026.

In accordance with Statutory Instrument No. 135 of 2026, gazetted on November 14, 2026, the Hon. Thea Garcia-Ramírez, Minister of Human Development, Family Support and Gender Affairs, appointed November 25 as the date for the commencement of the Act.

The coming into force of this legislation marks a significant milestone in Belize’s efforts to strengthen legal protections, improve access to justice for survivors, and promote greater accountability for acts of domestic and intimate partner violence.

Its commencement on the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women, which also marks the beginning of the annual 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence, is particularly meaningful. It reinforces Belize’s commitment to moving beyond awareness and advocacy towards meaningful action. Under this year’s national theme, “Ensure Justice. Protect Survivors. End Impunity,” the Ministry continues to emphasize the importance of translating legislative reform into effective protection, accessible services, and coordinated institutional responses.

The Ministry reaffirms its commitment to working alongside its national partners, communities, and families to build a Belize where every person can live safely and with dignity, without fear of violence.

Ensure Justice. Protect Survivors. End Impunity. Building Stronger Families, Safer Communities.

World.title: Mexican Ambassador and media discuss strengthening cultural cooperation
World.content:
Mexican Ambassador and media discuss strengthening cultural cooperation

By Zoila Palma: Today, Ambassador of Mexico to Belize, Ana Luisa Vallejo Barba, met with representatives of various media outlets to strengthen engagement and promote cooperation between Mexico and Belize.

The meeting focused on fostering closer dialogue and strengthening the longstanding bonds of friendship between the two countries. Discussions highlighted the importance of communication in promoting mutual understanding and bringing the people of Mexico and Belize closer together.

During the engagement, the role of the media as strategic partners in promoting cultural events, traditions and Mexico’s diverse artistic expressions was emphasized. The discussion also explored opportunities for greater collaboration in sharing cultural initiatives with the Belizean public.

Through the meeting, Mexico reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening friendship, understanding and cooperation with Belize.

World.title: Espat says Cayo South housing funds will go to elderly residents in 13 villages
World.content:
Espat says Cayo South housing funds will go to elderly residents in 13 villages

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Minister of Infrastructure Development and Housing Julius Espat has outlined how he intends to use his constituency’s share of the government’s housing assistance funds.

Espat, the area representative for Cayo South, said he will receive about $19,350 a month for four months.

With 13 villages in the division, he said the plan is to assist two recipients per village each month, or 26 in total.

Recipients are being identified through village leaders, who have been asked to bring forward the neediest cases. Espat said that unlike a previous housing programme that focused on young people and single mothers, this round will focus on the elderly.

He said applicants must follow a set procedure, including providing their information, photographs of the need and a quotation.

“The money is not given to the person. The money is paid to whatever establishment gives the quotation,” Espat said.

He said the process was adapted from the housing programme already run by his ministry, and he recommended that all area representatives follow the same procedure.

Asked why the funds are not being distributed nationally through the ministry, Espat said that approach has advantages, including experience and accountability, but takes longer. He estimated that the ministry’s process takes about a month from application to delivery because of the approvals required.

He said government wanted a system that could deliver results more quickly over a period of four to five months.

Espat put the approximate value of assistance at $1,500 per recipient, saying smaller amounts would not go far.

“Two hundred, five hundred dollars in purchasing of construction material is basically nothing,” he said.

He added that each area representative has the responsibility to make sure the needy receive the assistance.

World.title: International News: All hostages freed after 16-hour supermarket siege in Colombia
World.content:
International News: All hostages freed after 16-hour supermarket siege in Colombia

By Zoila Palma: Colombian security forces have freed all remaining hostages unharmed following a 16-hour siege at an Éxito supermarket in Cartagena.

The operation ended early Wednesday after police and military personnel stormed the building in the La Castellana neighbourhood. One of the hostage-takers was killed, while others were arrested, according to the Defence Ministry.

Authorities said the incident began Tuesday morning when armed men attempted to rob a cash-in-transit vehicle.

After police thwarted the robbery, the suspects reportedly entered the supermarket and took customers and employees hostage. Before the final operation, police had already secured the release of 10 people, while reports indicated that approximately 30 customers and employees were initially being held.

President Abelardo de la Espriella travelled to Cartagena to oversee the security operation, which involved police, navy personnel and special forces, with helicopter support.

World.title: Portmore ministers oppose AI data centres without consultation, impact studies
World.content:
In this Scotland File photo A young demonstrator holds a placard outside the Scottish Parliament Building after a march through Edinburgh on November 14, 2026, against the building of data centres and the growth of AI. (Photo by STEVE WELSH / AFP)

ST CATHERINE, Jamaica — The Portmore Ministers’ Fraternal, a Christian group based in Portmore, St Catherine, has expressed it does not support the proposal to establish artificial intelligence (AI) data centres in the city in the absence of consultation with the citizens and stakeholders of the municipality and thorough, publicly available environmental impact assessments.

The fraternal’s statement on Thursday follows the recommendation by Member of Parliament for St Catherine East Central Alando Terrelonge, that Portmore become home to AI data centres during his contribution to the State of the Constituency Debate in the House of Representatives on November 17.

While acknowledging the importance of technological advancement, youth empowerment, employment creation and economic development, the fraternal said proposals with potentially significant consequences for the environment, public infrastructure and community well-being must be informed by sound evidence, transparency and meaningful public participation.

“Citizens and stakeholders of Portmore have not been consulted on this proposal. The people who live, work, worship and raise families in the municipality must have a meaningful voice in decisions that could affect their quality of life and the resources upon which they depend,” the group said.

Citing international experiences with data centres, the group noted concerns about the demands data centres can place on electricity systems and water resources, alongside their implications for emissions, infrastructure costs and surrounding communities.

“The extent of these impacts depends on the scale, location, technology and operating arrangements of each development. These concerns warrant careful examination before any commitment is made to establish such facilities in Portmore,” the group added.

It is calling for:

– Thorough, independent environmental impact assessments and baseline surveys addressing water availability, energy requirements, cooling systems, noise, emissions, waste management, drainage, flood risk and the cumulative effects of any proposed facilities.

– Meaningful consultation with citizens and stakeholders, including residents’ associations, churches, community organisations, businesses, young people, environmental specialists and the municipal authorities. Consultation must occur early enough to influence decisions.

– Public disclosure of relevant project information, including proposed locations, the scale of development, water and electricity sources, environmental safeguards, anticipated employment opportunities and any costs or obligations to be borne by the public.

– Clear evidence that essential services and community well-being will be protected, with enforceable safeguards, independent monitoring and accountability arrangements.

The group maintained that these assessments and consultations must precede decisions on siting, approval and construction. It added that their findings must help determine whether data centres are appropriate for Portmore and, if so, under what conditions.

The group shared that it believes that the holistic development of Portmore must encompass economic opportunity, environmental stewardship, social well-being and the protection of present and future generations.

“Promised benefits must be carefully weighed against potential costs and risks to the community,” it said adding that The Portmore Ministers’ Fraternal stands ready to engage constructively with the political directorate, relevant public agencies, technical experts, investors, citizens and other stakeholders in shaping a responsible and inclusive development agenda for Portmore.

World.title: Dominica could help ease regional water shortages
World.content:
KINGSTOWN, St Vincent (CMC) — Dominica could help strengthen regional water security by supplying freshwater to neighbouring Caribbean territories as countries prepare for the 2026-2027 dry season, including through the possible transportation of water by barges.

Caribbean Water and Wastewater Association (CWWA) Executive Director Laurayne Lucky said the island’s abundant freshwater resources could position it to help countries facing worsening water shortages in the coming months.

Speaking on the sidelines of the 2026-2027 Dry Season Caribbean Climate Outlook Forum (CariCOF) Stakeholder Forum, Lucky said the region must explore alternative approaches to water supply as climate projections point to potentially challenging conditions during the upcoming dry season.

“Countries like Dominica, if they can spare additional water and they can budget to nearby countries, I think that would be an option,” Lucky stated.

She identified transporting water by barges as one possible non-traditional approach that could be explored.

“I spoke earlier on the panel about looking at non-traditional approaches to water supply, and barging water may be one of them,” she said.

Lucky said water utilities across the region were already facing significant challenges, including high levels of non-revenue water, financial constraints and difficulties securing adequate raw water supplies.

She said Dominica’s freshwater resources could therefore become a greater regional asset, but cautioned that any initiative to supply other territories would need to be properly structured and supported by clear policies and agreements.

Lucky recommended that Dominica establish formal arrangements, including memoranda of understanding (MOUs), with countries seeking to access its water resources.

“Anything we are doing should be policy-driven. We should ensure that it is either supported by some level of agreement, whether it’s an MOU or some sort of agreement between the two countries,” she said.

World.title: ‘I will take it to court!’
World.content:
BUCHANAN... reminded the House that he had advocated in the Privy Council case that led to the renewed focus on jury tampering and the birth of ‘The Vybz Kartel Amendment’.

THE House of Representatives has approved Senate amendments to the Jury Act, allowing judges to discharge juries from criminal trials if satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that jury tampering has occurred, despite Opposition spokesperson on human rights Isat Buchanan warning before the vote that he would take the Government to court if the changes were passed.

The amendments were put to a division and approved by the House on Tuesday, with 27 members voting in favour and 17 against, while 18 members were absent. They replace the requirement for proof beyond a reasonable doubt with the lower standard of a balance of probabilities when a judge is deciding whether jury tampering has occurred before or during a trial.

The change has drawn objections from Opposition members who argue that a lower standard could make it easier to deprive an accused person of a jury trial.

Buchanan, who reminded the House that he had advocated in the Privy Council case that led to the renewed focus on jury tampering and the birth of ‘The Vybz Kartel Amendment’, warned the House that the change could face a legal challenge.

“If this was to pass, I’m going to put it on record, it will be challenged as an incompetent move by this House. I personally will take it to court!” he said.

His warning came before the amendments were put to a vote and approved. The amendment was a central point of contention during the debate, with Opposition Leader Mark Golding questioning why the Senate had moved away from the criminal standard of proof.

He told the House that the change meant a judge could decide to take away an accused person’s right to have a case heard by a jury using a lower standard than the one normally required to convict someone of a crime.

“The issue is that for an accused person to lose his or her right to a jury trial is being decided by a judge, based on certain facts which have to satisfy that judge that it is the right thing to do to deprive that person of that right to a jury trial. And the standard that is being set is a civil standard in the context of a right which exists in a criminal trial — and I think that is something which different people may have different views on,” Golding said.

Buchanan, in his contribution to the debate, argued that it could weaken the protection afforded to an accused person by the right to trial by jury. He said the House appeared to be overlooking the importance of the presumption of innocence and the need to protect people from being deprived of a jury trial on a lower standard of proof.

He also questioned why Jamaica would depart from the criminal standard used in England, arguing that the legal protection afforded to accused people should not be weaker in Jamaica.

“The constitution speaks about the presumption of innocence. The constitution speaks about due process. If somebody is being accused of a crime, they are cloaked in the presumption of innocence. The very legislation that we copied, the English standard, the English standard respectfully says it is the criminal standard,” he said.

“What I’m hearing from members, whether they be in the Senate or here today, is that somehow a man in England breathes a different, much cleaner air than that in Jamaica. Are we saying that the rights of Jamaicans are less important than those in England? I think not,” Buchanan added.

While referring to the Vybz Kartel case, he argued that the ruling did not establish that the accused men were responsible for the alleged attempt to bribe jurors, and warned against making changes that could result in an accused person losing the right to a jury trial because of interference by someone else.

Justice Minister Delroy Chuck defended the change, explaining that the standard used to decide whether jury tampering has occurred should not be confused with the much higher standard required to find an accused person guilty.

He said the Government had initially supported the use of the criminal standard when the Bill was debated in the House, but reconsidered after discussions with senators and other stakeholders.

“The point is that once there is some evidence of jury tampering then a balance of probability is enough, because there’s evidence that there is jury tampering and you don’t have to go to that highest standard which is required at the end of a case when a jury or a judge has to say he’s satisfied, or the jury is satisfied beyond reasonable doubt, which you will appreciate is the highest standard before the person is convicted,” he said.

Chuck maintained that the change would apply to decisions about protecting the trial process, not to the final determination of guilt.

State minister in the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs Marisa Dalrymple Philibert also supported the amendment, arguing that people who interfere with jurors should not expect to retain the benefit of a jury trial.

Opposition Member of Parliament Damion Crawford questioned why the amendments were being approved before the promised joint select committee review of the Jury Act. He argued that the issue deserves further examination because of the serious consequences an accused person could face if convicted without a jury deciding the case.

He also questioned whether the lower standard is appropriate when a person facing a serious criminal charge could lose the opportunity to have a jury hear the case.
