Chuck told the House that a joint select committee would still be established to review the Jury Act but argued that the amendments should proceed without waiting for that review because jury tampering could occur at any time.

World.title: ‘Cowardly leadership!’
World.content:
Scores of People’s National Party (PNP) supporters gather in Cross Roads, St Andrew, on Wednesday to voice their disappointment with the Government’s approach to Hurricane Melissa relief efforts. (Photo: Llwellyn Wynter)

THE People’s National Party (PNP) leadership, flanked by party supporters, took to the streets of Cross Roads, St Andrew, on Wednesday, demanding accountability from the Government over its handling of Hurricane Melissa relief efforts and reiterating their dissatisfaction with the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM).

Led by Opposition Leader Mark Golding, several PNP members of parliament and councillors joined aggrieved citizens in marching and chanting their dissatisfaction with the state of the country’s affairs.

“A year ago Jamaica suffered a terrible hurricane, and since then this Government has dropped the ball. They have received millions of dollars, many containers of items to provide assistance to people who need it, and what we have found, because of the auditor general, is that so much of that money never reached the people. So much of those goods never reached the people who need it. Weevil in rice, crackers spoiled, only 30 of over 200 container homes accounted for, and 15 containers of relief not even open to help the people,” charged Golding as he addressed the disgruntled crowd.

His comments follow last Tuesday’s release of an auditor general’s report which uncovered various discrepancies at disaster management agency ODPEM in relation to its handling of relief supplies meant for victims of the Category 5 Hurricane Melissa, which devastated south- and north-western parishes in October 2025.

According to Auditor General Pamela Monroe-Ellis, only 31 of 200 container houses donated by the Chinese Government had been accounted for; and hundreds of bags of rice, crackers, and other food items became spoiled after they became infested with insects. The audit’s findings also brought to light the use of approximately $45 million from donated funds to facilitate the customs clearance of relief supplies consigned to third parties.

For his part, ODPEM’s Director General Commander Alvin Gayle has challenged findings in the report, insisting that all prefab houses were accounted for — 200 houses were donated to the Government, 169 of those units have been distributed, and 31 remain in ODPEM’s custody.

Gayle also said that all monies channelled through the agency were accounted for.

But Golding called for Gayle’s resignation during a press conference at the Office of the Opposition Leader in St Andrew on Monday. He further argued that Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness must take accountability for relocating ODPEM to the Office of the Prime Minister in November 2025, and failing to ably oversee its operations.

On Wednesday, Golding’s message was much of the same, further highlighting the slow pace of rebuilding efforts and the struggle still facing many Jamaicans affected by Hurricane Melissa.

“…In areas affected by the hurricane, much of western Jamaica, people continue to suffer. People continue to live under tarpaulins, kotching with friends, kotching with neighbours, kotching with relatives. Schools still don’t fix; many small businesses [are] still closed because they lost their liquor shops, they lost their stocks in trade, and the Government has been so slow to help them,” he said.

“And yet this prime minister who brought the whole relief effort under his control, taking ODPEM from Minister of Local Government Desmond McKenzie and putting it in his office, and when we discover all of what has not been done that should have been done, all that has gone wrong, he doesn’t want to take any responsibility for that. That is weak and cowardly leadership! That is not a leader who deserves to be prime minister of this country,” argued Golding.

His criticisms of the Government were echoed by St Andrew South Western Member of Parliament (MP) Angela Brown Burke, who insisted that “enough is enough”. Pointing to the plight of citizens still recovering in western Jamaica, Brown Burke asserted that the situation shows the Government’s neglect of the people it was elected to serve.

“When we listen and hear what has been happening with ODPEM and with the prime minister not even taking responsibility, enough is enough! ‘Weh di money deh?’ is not just a little saying, it is a real concern of Jamaicans about what our Government is doing with the funds that have been entrusted with them on behalf of the Jamaican people and those who need it most,” said Brown Burke, referring to the question which has become popular due to a public squabble between Holness and dancehall artiste Moses “Beenie Man” Davis.

Brown Burke, who was suspended from Parliament after the Government used its House of Representatives majority on November 18 to pass a motion condemning her conduct toward House Speaker Juliet Holness, told the Jamaica Observer that the sanction would not silence her on the matter.

“I say to persons all the time: I’m a member of parliament. There are several things that I do as a member of parliament. It just means that I concentrate on doing some others right now. My voice cannot be silent. I may be suspended, but never silenced,” she said.

Also weighing in on the state of the country’s affairs was Kingston Eastern and Port Royal MP Philip Paulwell. He told the Observer that he supports the people in the west, and condemned the Government’s handling of recovery efforts so far.

“We are here to protest and show solidarity, firstly, to our people in western Jamaica who suffered through the hurricane and are still suffering because of this careless Government. It is really a shame that food that was meant for the people have spoiled, and that monies that were sent from overseas to assist our Jamaicans in the west, that such funds have not yet been made available. In fact, a lot of it has been wasted doing things other than taking care of the needs of our people,” said Paulwell.

Meanwhile, Westmoreland Eastern MP Dayton Campbell described the current recovery efforts as “deplorable”, and charged that someone must be held accountable for the continued suffering of Jamaicans affected by the Category 5 storm.

“This is our protest to register our discontentment with the Government in their handling of the recovery, and especially what has been revealed from the auditor general’s report…I think it is a disgrace and I think someone has to be held to account for it,” charged Campbell.

World.title: Skillibeng keeps his focus on Cya Stop The G
World.content:
Skillibeng.

Dancehall artiste Skillibeng weighs the pressures of success against his determination to get further ahead on his latest single, Cya Stop The G.

The St Thomas-born deejay worked with YGF Records and Crownboss Recordz on the track released through VPAL Music. It was released on November 20.

Financial ambition runs through the song, as does the question of how to stay focused when success brings opposition.

Skillibeng approaches both with the confidence and unconventional melodies that have marked his work since Brik Pan Brik.

The title phrase recurs throughout the track, giving his response to those pressures a refrain.

“Cya Stop The G is about staying focused on your goals regardless of the obstacles or negativity around you. I’ve always believed in trusting my journey, putting in the work, and never allowing anyone or anything to limit what I can achieve,” Skillibeng told the Jamaica Observer.

Since breaking through with Brik Pan Brik, Skillibeng has built a catalogue that includes Mr Universe, Whap Whap, and Torpedo. His distinctive flow and melodic choices have carried those records to listeners in Jamaica and overseas. One of his biggest international breakthroughs came with Crocodile Teeth, which drew further attention through a remix featuring Trinidadian-American rapper Nicki Minaj.

Last year the deejay and Shenseea — with whom he has been making the rounds on social media of late due to dating rumours — were featured on Moliy and Silent Addy’s global monster hit Shake It to the Max (Fly) remix. This track dented multiple major charts globally, including the UK and US Billboard charts, and has been certified gold in Greece and the US, and platinum in New Zealand, the UK, and France.

In September of this year Skillibeng also gave a memorable performance at KOKO in Camden, which was part of the Notting Hill Carnival celebration.

His single General also officially released that month, entered the top 10 of the iTunes Reggae Singles Chart in less than 24 hours.

World.title: ‘Snail’s pace’
World.content:
Former head of Caribbean Maritime University Fritz Pinnock.

AFTER over a year, only approximately 10 to 11 per cent of witnesses in the trial of former education minister Ruel Reid, former head of Caribbean Maritime University Fritz Pinnock, and their co-accused have taken the stand.

“We are not going at a good rate, mathematically,” noted Senior Parish Court Judge Sanchia Burrell, in sharing her calculations with the court on Wednesday, urging the defence and prosecution to pay heed to differentiated case management (DCM) guidelines set out by the nation’s judiciary.

Citing the initial witness list of 90-plus people, now cut down by 13, Burrell said if the trial continues at this pace, the projected end date is 2034, a result that she stressed would not do the case any justice.

“The people in the dock are presumed innocent until proven guilty. Let’s not impose a sentence on them before we even come to that stage…” she said.

Under DCM, which is a system aimed at reducing delay, cases are expected to be completed within certain time frames depending on their complexity, the number of accused, and other factors.

While Burrell noted the timelines are not rigid, a case such as the trial in question is generally expected to be completed within two years.

“We are aiming for matters like this to be in and out of the court in two years and if it can’t be two years, then we are expecting that it not be five years,” she expressed.

Prosecutors, in response, maintained that the case is expected to conclude far before 2034 and, while acknowledging the slow pace initially, pointed to the last few months of the trial, stressing that the case had picked up considerably between September and December.

Acknowledging this, Burrell commended the Crown and noted that she was pleased to hear that the prosecution is also of a mind to complete the matter with swiftness.

While the case has been before the courts for seven years, since the 2019 arrest of the accused, which includes Councillor Kim Brown Lawrence, Reid’s wife Sharen Reid, and daughter Sharelle Reid, the trial began in October 2025.

Since then, it has faced continuous delays caused by adjournments over disclosure, the repeated absences of different defence attorneys, and clashes with other cases in which defence counsel appear.

Burrell had made other case management pronouncements in July, setting an end date for the trial in July 2027.

Decrying the current “snail’s pace”, the judge maintained that, while July may no longer be feasible, dispensing with the matter in 2027 is still the goal and set November as the new mark for completion.

Upon hearing that July 2027 was no longer the end date, Sharen Reid, with a shake of her head, expressed to the judge that she did think July was possible, appearing frustrated with the timeline.

Burrell acknowledged the cost to retain lawyers for an extended period is also a consideration.

“To pay a lawyer to go to a trial for nine years, that’s expensive; that may even be prohibitive,” she said.

Turning her attention to the defence attorneys, none of whom were physically present in the room but were represented by a single attorney holding in limited capacity, she maintained that members of the private bar must take DCM into consideration when planning their diaries to assist them in assessing whether they truly had the time and resources to take on certain cases.

She noted that the DCM system is supposed to be beneficial for everyone — the Crown, the defence, and the accused.

Burrell has at length shared concerns about the protracted absences of certain attorneys in the case. Calling each accused by name, she added sternly that they would have to present themselves and do their own cross-examination of witnesses if their attorneys did not make arrangements for them to be ably represented.

Burrell maintained that enough is on the record to show that she did all she could to impress upon all affected parties to make alternative arrangements to complete the matter.

“If we can use the dates better, I see where we can be close to the finish line next year,” she said.

World.title: WOMAN POWER
World.content:
Arnett Gardens FC’s Shikira Douglas (left) dribbles under pressure from Los Perfectos FC’s Rhonda Rhooms during the Jamaica Women’s Premier League second-round match at Brooks Park on June 21, 2025. The league is set to resume on December 5, 2026. (Photo: JWPL Media)

THE Christine Hudson-led Professional Women’s Football Jamaica Limited (PWFJL) has shown its commitment to the Jamaica Women’s Premier League (JWPC) by handing over $400,000 each to the 12 clubs for mobilisation when the season kicks off on Saturday, December 5.

At the launch on Thursday at the GWM showroom on South Camp Road, Kingston, Hudson announced that they have accumulated $77 million in sponsorship investment in cash and kind, the largest in history, and of which 70 per cent, or $53 million, will go directly to the clubs.

“Our clubs are the heartbeat of this league, and our responsibility is to give them the resources and support they need to succeed,” Hudson said.

The JWPL, in its third season, is preparing for its most ambitious season yet, with the more than $77 million in investment, the introduction of a second-tier competition featuring promotion and relegation, and weekly global exposure through

FIFA+ TV — marking a major step in the professionalisation of women’s football in Jamaica.

“For the first time ever, Jamaica’s Women’s Premier League matches will be streamed globally on FIFA+, with a featured match every week of the season, complementing coverage on the league’s YouTube channel and the Public Broadcasting Corporation of Jamaica (PBCJ),” said Hudson.

She continued: “That means our players, our clubs, and the talents we are developing right here in Jamaica will now have the opportunity to be seen by audiences around the world.

“It’s another big step towards raising the profile of women’s football at home and positioning our league on the international stage,” she reiterated.

Hudson noted that growing interest in the league has led the Jamaica Football Federation to introduce a tier-two competition with promotion and relegation for the first time.

Currently, there are 12 clubs in champions Fraziers Whip, Arnett Gardens, Cavalier, Federal United, Los Perfectos, Mile Gully, Proven Girls, Real Mobay, Real Mona, Springers, UWI Women’s and WiFi United.

Further progress towards professionalisation includes 11 clubs attaining regional club licences, which Hudson explained made them eligible to compete in the Concacaf Women’s Champions League.

Then there are new partnerships with the Jamaica Urban Transit Company (JUTC), which will provide transportation support, as well as with Xpress Sports and Soccer Xpress for kits, equipment and additional resources for clubs.

“Through JUTC’s support we’re lifting much of that burden, allowing clubs to redirect those funds towards their players, training programmes, and long-term development. This is a game changer,” said Hudson.

“Our second new partnership is with Xpress Sports, who will be outfitting all 12 clubs. In addition to the usual home-and-away kits, footballs, and training equipment, this season we’re going a step further. Our players will now receive sports bras, sports bottles, and team backpacks; while our coaches, managers, and administrators will also receive team shirts,” she added.

In a video message, FIFA expert Shannon MacMillan commended Jamaica’s continued investment in women’s football, encouraging stakeholders to “continue to lean in and support the women and show up for them”.

The Kind Hearts Foundation returns as title sponsor, alongside FIFA’s continued support through its Women’s League Development Programme.

Other sponsors and strategic partners include WATA, KFC, Supreme Ventures, MPOWA, YO Foundation, Pure National Limited, TruShake, Powerade, Express Fitness, , SORA Media, Acroscopic, PBCJ, ISSA Construction and Mailpac.

The Jamaica Observer returns as the official media partner of the league, with support amounting to over $7.5 million in value.

Meanwhile, Government support is provided by the Ministry of Culture, Gender, Entertainment ,and Sport through the Sports Development Foundation (SDF), and by the Ministry of Energy, Transport and Telecommunications through JUTC.

World.title: Kyle Butler, Vauxhall High part ways
World.content:
Vauxhall High School Head Coach Kyle Butler

Kyle Butler says his stint as head coach of Vauxhall High School’s football programme has come to an end after two seasons.

Butler made the announcement on social media, saying he was proud of what he had accomplished at the school, highlighting the team’s consistency in the Inter-Secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) competitions and his role in helping players secure professional contracts and college opportunities.

“Thank you, Vauxhall, for two seasons I’ll always be proud of. Together, we reached three quarter-finals and made one round-of-16 appearance,” Butler posted.

The development follows Vauxhall’s exit from the under-16 schoolboy football competition after their 3-2 win against Kingston College (KC) was reversed, handing KC a 3-0 victory, due to what ISSA said in a release were “irregularities”.

ISSA is yet to rule on the matter as the punishment could be severe seeing that allegations are that the school used two ineligible players in other players’ names.

Butler, in his announcement, identified player development and creating opportunities beyond schoolboy football as his biggest achievement.

“My biggest achievement was helping eight players sign professional contracts and opening doors to college for even more,” he said, while thanking the players for trusting him as their coach.

Butler explained that he had agreed to remain at Vauxhall for another season at the end of the previous campaign, but believes the time has now come to pursue a new challenge.

“At the end of last season, I agreed to stay at Vauxhall for one more year. My time at Vauxhall has now come to an end, and I’m proud of what we achieved together. Now I look forward to finding a new home,” he said.

The ambitious coach is now looking to take his experience in Jamaica to Europe, where he hopes to learn from some of the continent’s leading coaches and further his professional qualifications.

“I’m excited to take what I’ve learned in Jamaica overseas and learn from some of the best coaches in Europe. My ambition is to earn my UEFA Pro Licence, coach some of the biggest clubs in the world and one day lead Jamaica’s national team,” Butler said.

Despite his overseas ambitions, Butler made it clear that he has not closed the door on local schoolboy football, indicating that he would be willing to return to the competition when the right opportunity presents itself.

He also outlined the importance of loyalty, unity and mutual commitment in any future coaching appointment, insisting that success requires the backing of everyone involved in a programme.

“When I take on another programme, I want the board, the coaching staff and the players to know we can count on each other. That means celebrating the wins together and standing side by side when things get difficult, on and off the pitch,” he said.

— Howard Walker

World.title: How Costa’s budget talks sparked a new crisis
World.content:
Thursday’s European Council summit ended in disarray after frugal countries pushing for a smaller EU long-term budget walked out of planned negotiations led by European Council President António Costa. Some are even pushing for him to give up his role trying to broker a deal.

While no one expected a final deal on the MFF at this summit, talks have been acrimonious. What went so wrong? Will Costa be pushed out as a negotiator? And why are EU diplomats booking extra hotel room nights for December’s Council meeting?

Kathryn Carlson, covering Sarah Wheaton’s maternity leave, asks what’s next for the budget talks after the disastrous summit. She also discusses the EU’s newfound boldness in picking fights with the U.S. over a digital tax and European preference for defense procurement. And she digs into the challenges the next European Central Bank president, Pablo Hernández de Cos, will face when he succeeds Christine Lagarde.

She’s joined by Chief Foreign Affairs Correspondent Nick Vinocur, finance reporter Gregorio Sorgi and Deputy Finance Editor Bjarke Smith-Meyer.

(António Costa clip courtesy of European Broadcasting Service.)

**A message from Fusion for Energy: Fusion for Energy is an EU organisation delivering the energy of the future. Fusion will make Europe more sovereign, competitive and resilient. Fusion for Energy is working with more than 3000 companies to help Europe lead in fusion technologies. Learn more on fusionforenergy.europa.eu.**

World.title: Bank of England boss warns AI must benefit humans
World.content:
“It’s a bit like rearing children. You have to give them the chance to do things, but you also have to set some sort of boundaries as it were,” he said in an interview from his office in the Bank of England.

With the G20 presidency fast approaching, Burnham has said he wants to use the U.K. to establish “a single set” of global standards for AI.

U.S. President Donald Trump shot down any global oversight of the giant American companies dominating the development of the technology, which he has rebranded as "super intelligence."

Against that backdrop, Bailey called for more international testing and access to AI giants’ frontier models, which he said are “critical questions” as the U.K. takes on the G20 presidency.

The U.K. central banking chief will make that push internationally in his role as chair of the Financial Stability Board, a global watchdog for the financial system.

With the number of cyber incidents already rising, Bailey said AI models are being built on “the good, the bad, and the ugly” of human behavior, and are now training themselves.

World.title: Ukraine cajoles allies to keep Putin’s athletes out
World.content:
Ukraine has near-unanimous EU backing for keeping Russian athletes out of European sport, and wants the bloc’s new visa ban on Moscow’s combatants also applied to soldiers who compete on national teams, Bidnyi added.

With the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics on the horizon, the dispute is becoming a test of who’ll shape Russia’s return to world sport: governments, or federations and courts. Kyiv is desperate for Europe to coordinate its response before more restrictions are lifted.

Bidnyi said he presented three demands to EU sports ministers on Nov. 20: a ban on Russian symbols; verified neutral status for athletes; and funding cuts for federations that let Russians compete. He added that the proposals found “wide support.”

“I have heard no voice against it,” Bidnyi said. Asked whether all 27 EU countries are on board, he said that “almost all of them” had expressed willingness to make it a common position.

No propaganda in sport

On Monday, the European Commission proposed barring Russian teams and athletes from competing in the EU, which would also restrict financial flows from Russian sponsors to European sports and cultural associations. The sanctions package needs the approval of all 27 member countries.

In addition, seven EU countries had written to European Council President António Costa and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen before the sanctions package was presented asking for tougher visa rules on Russian nationals.

World.title: Spain’s looming right-wing pivot on climate is already playing out in Valencia
World.content:
The two parties’ dismantling of climate policy can already be seen in Spain’s Valencia region, where the PP has governed with Vox’s backing since 2023, coinciding with a rollback of environmental protections and the deadly floods of October 2024.

“The dangerous climate skepticism that will define a PP-Vox government at the national level has been on display here in Valencia from the moment they took power,” warned Raül Camacho Segarra, a spokesperson for the Valencian grassroots movement working to rebuild flood-damaged areas responsibly.

The floods put the government’s approach to land use, environmental regulation and climate adaptation under intense scrutiny. Yet shortly after, PP politician Juanfran Pérez Llorca was sworn in as the region’s new president and reaffirmed his opposition to parts of the climate agenda, describing the center-right European People’s Party’s Green Deal as a “threat” to Valencia’s farmers.

Local critics like Camacho accuse the right-wing government of failing to learn the lessons of the disaster and endangering the region’s communities.

“The policies they instituted ahead of the floods made us more vulnerable, and instead of recalibrating after the tragedy, they’ve actually doubled down since 2024,” he said, pointing to the allocation of public funds to bullfighting events instead of emergency response and promoting construction in areas needed for flood prevention.

Ana Camarasa, a physical geographer and regional flood risk expert at the University of Valencia, questioned politicians’ ability to pursue effective long-term resilience strategies while casting doubt on the threat posed by climate change.

World.title: Welfare wars: review, rinse, repeat
World.content:
MPs in Westminster have spent the week chewing over yet another review of how to reform the U.K.’s welfare system.

But with questions over whether the Milburn or Timms reviews will ever lead to meaningful change, Westminster Insider went on a mission to find out why so many government reviews end up kicked into the long grass or, worse still, completely ignored.

Carol Black, who has chaired four separate reviews, spills her secrets on how to actually get politicians to act on your recommendations. But she admits it’s “pretty awful when … nothing happens.”

Sascha also speaks to Jill Rutter, senior fellow at the Institute for Government, who explains how to avoid the dreaded “graveyard of landmark reviews.”

Labour MP Rachael Maskell, who lost the whip in July 2025 after taking part in a rebellion against Keir Starmer’s welfare proposals, says she is “Team Timms” and warns of the potential tensions between the two welfare reviews that could be coming down the track.

World.title: Swingin’ on the flippity-flop with chicken nuggets: The perils of young people’s slang
World.content:
Three months after I stood in a field listening to “Smells Like Teen Spirit,” a journalist from The New York Times called up Sub Pop, the record label that released Nirvana’s first album and did more than any other to give the world grunge, and fell victim to a prank.

Megan Jasper, a one-time receptionist at the label who went on to become its CEO, proceeded to make up a list of fake slang terms being used by the kids of the day. The NYT published the list in full*.

When it comes to politics, it’s hard to know what’s worse: pretending to be down with the kids when you’re old enough to know better or being clearly out-of-touch and missing out on what the youth really care about.

This week, Andy “have I mentioned I like The Smiths” Burnham was stung after getting too close to the TikTok generation (a bit like Icarus flying too close to the sun, if Icarus was the British prime minister and the sun was people doing shitty dances).

Burnham invited a bunch of creators to an event earlier this month (what’s the collective noun for influencers? A virus?) but footage only emerged this week of one miming the words “bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets” outside the famous black door of No. 10 Downing Street.

Bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets is a) an unwieldy name for a pet, b) a good name for a punk band, and c) offensive if you understand what young people are talking about (‘bomboclaat’ is a Jamaican profanity referring to a menstrual cloth, ‘pussy’ is a slang term for female genitals, and some accounts reckon ‘chicken nuggets’ refers to women being ‘cheap white meat’ — although it could also just mean chicken assholes and eyelashes mashed up, breadcrumbed and deep-fried).

World.title: Spain’s right turn: What a PP-Vox government would mean for Madrid — and Brussels
World.content:
Since the last election in 2023, migration has risen to second on Spaniards' list of top concerns, behind housing. The Ceuta crisis — where tens of thousands of mainly young men from Morocco poured into Spain — has hardened the rhetoric of both Vox and the PP, which have embraced the term “invasion."

Vox’s flagship policy on migration is known as "national priority," essentially a Spaniards-first approach that gives preferential access to public services, from housing to schools and benefits. Feijóo’s party manifesto includes “priority criteria for access to certain benefits, services and public resources,” but the PP doesn’t limit the criteria to nationality, saying it should also cover long-term legal residents in Spain.

Vox has also made remigration — a term imported from far-right circles in Germany and Austria — one of its core election campaign proposals. But the European Commission has already found that remigration proposals cannot be squared with EU law and the PP distances itself from the idea.

Workers clear debris from a dismantled migrant settlement at the entrance to the Tarajal warehouses, in Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta on Oct. 18, 2026. | Antonio Sempere/AFP via Getty Images

On almost all other migration-related issues, the PP and Vox would align with the new mainstream in an EU that takes a much tougher line, including the idea of return hubs.

Agriculture: Vox's turf

The far right frames rural Spain as the true heart of the nation. Abascal’s party has always tried to secure the agriculture departments in regional governments where it rules jointly with the PP — and the agriculture ministry would likely be one of its top targets in a coalition government.

A significant proportion of immigration in Spain is linked to the agricultural sector, which relies on a vast pool of cheap migrant labor. Vox has spoken of extending the national priority principle to this sector as well, calling for pay rises to make these jobs attractive to Spaniards, although it has avoided making it a central issue of its immigration policy. The PP proposes temporary visas and hiring in the workers’ home countries.

World.title: Budget summit walkout leaves EU one month to salvage deal
World.content:
Costa hadn't organized Thursday's summit to get a deal. Rather, his goal was to bang heads together and try to bridge splits between the two main rival camps: those like Spain and Italy, that want a bigger budget and to protect "traditional" EU spending in areas such as farming and poorer regions, and those like Germany and Sweden demanding the bloc scales down its ambitions and refocuses investment toward defense and security.

But after hours of meetings among small groups of leaders, several countries pushing for budget cuts — Denmark, Sweden, Belgium and Austria — walked out, claiming this negotiating method was aimed at pitching them against each other.

“It was obvious this was a move to divide us, to buy each of us seven off with a gift,” a diplomat from a country that wants a smaller budget said. “It just went really badly. It was not a real discussion.” They were granted anonymity, like others in this article, to speak candidly about the dramatic unfolding.

European Parliament’s trade committee chair Bernd Lange, who said there was "absolutely nothing to show for it" after all the buildup. | Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images

Costa abandoned plans to return for a second day and cut his concluding 1 a.m. press conference with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to just 11 minutes.

'Strategic mistake'

The EU’s 27 leaders will now make a push to secure a deal at December's summit, which multiple diplomats and officials said will probably last several days and nights.

While technically the bloc has an entire year to reach agreement on what's called the Multiannual Financial Framework for 2028-2034, the current leadership are determined to get it settled before April's election in France, where the far-right leader Marine Le Pen is the favorite to become president.

World.title: 'A lot of political theatre': EU summit ends in disarray as leaders cling to red lines
World.content:
A summit specifically convened to find a breakthrough on the European Union's next budget ended in disarray after leaders, split in opposing camps, refused to abandon their red lines and openly questioned whether a deal could be reached by December.

 

The meeting was plagued by tensions, reproaches and even boycotts, raising serious questions on the leadership of European Council President António Costa, whose credibility now rests on whether these negotiations succeed or fail.

Costa's compromise proposalworth €1.78 trillion in current prices across seven years – a 10% cut from the original draft – was met with fierce pushback from all sides, taking the Council presidency aback.

"This meeting was a necessary step in the process. This is a negotiation process. It is normal that the different parties are starting to underline and mark their starting points. Everybody knows that we cannot fail Europe, and we need to have a new budget from the 1st of January 2028," Costa said at the press conference at the end of the summit.

The summit appeared doomed from the outset.

Leaders showed virtually no willingness to compromise as they made their way into Thursday's gathering and huddled with their respective groups.

On one side, the seven "Frugals", bent on slashing the budget. On the other side, the 17 "Friends of Cohesion", determined to push back against further cuts.

The tone was set by Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who told reporters upon arrival that a deal on the seven-year budget was "light years away".

Meloni questioned Costa's much-repeated objective of reaching a deal by the end of the year to prevent the process from spilling over into the 2027 electoral cycle.

"I don't have a time limit. I have specific conditions," she said. "When the agreement is one that I consider valid and fair for Italy, then I'll sign it."

Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, a staunch "frugal", was equally dismissive.

"There's no need to hurry," he said. "For me, there's no deadline."

The budget negotiations began around midday after leaders settled the matter of Christine Lagarde's succession as European Central Bank president. They first met all together in the main room, where they shared their well-known positions.

Nobody caved in during this session, waiting for others to move first, diplomats said.

Then, Costa split the summit into small groups of leaders. First, the "frugals", then the "cohesion friends", and then the six largest member states. After that, he began breakout sessions with geographically mixed leaders.

The proceedings increasingly frustrated the "frugals", who saw it as an attempt to pile pressure on them in favour of the "cohesion friends".

Feeling unfairly targeted, the "frugals" closed ranks and decided to boycott the small-group format, which Costa continued without their participation.

Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron raised the stakes, calling a press conference to deliver a stark ultimatum: reach a deal by December or walk away empty-handed.

Macron warned that protracted negotiations risked becoming dangerously entangled in the French presidential campaign. Far-right firebrand Marine Le Pen, who is leading opinion polls, has vowed to slash France's contribution to the EU budget.

"I intend to make it very clear to our colleagues that, for political and democratic reasons, it will not be possible to reopen or conclude negotiations on the budget after 31st December," Macron said, decrying Costa's proposed cuts as a "strategic mistake".

"We are not prepared to reach a deal at any cost. We can conclude by 31st December, but that is the absolute limit."

Other member states consider Macron's threat of a future Le Pen presidency a tactic to extract concessions and eventually get his way, despite Costa's compromise widely seen as being overly French-friendly.

"That's quite rich," a diplomat quipped about the French reaction.

Macron's mid-summit appearance, a rare occurrence, wiped out chances of a breakthrough and precipitated the collapse of the talks.

In his own press conference, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz adopted a hardline "frugal" stance and vowed to slash the budget even further.

The deep political divide between Paris and Berlin, the EU’s two main powerhouses, has cast a shadow over the negotiations.

"Are we any further ahead? Yes and no. We are trying to define which direction it is going. I think I may say that," Merz told reporters.

The cuts to the budget, he said, will not stop at the €204 billion proposed by Costa. "It will become less," he added. "How much it will be then is open."

The fact that Costa announced early in the summit that the talks would not continue on Friday as originally planned dampened the energy among national delegations and immediately lowered expectations for a breakthrough, a diplomat said.

A second diplomat was more positive on the outcome of the summit, despite the messy proceedings. "You need to have a bad European Council to have a good one," they said. "It was a lot of political theatre. We did not have detailed negotiations."

Forgotten in the talks was Ukraine.

The summit was supposed to discuss a €45 billion support loan for the country, which faces a ballooning wartime deficit amid Russia's relentless attacks. But the budget fight sucked in all the energy and left Ukraine relegated to an afterthought.

World.title: Germany: Christmas markets open across the country amid tight security
World.content:
Germany's Christmas markets are drawing crowds as the country's roughly 3,000 festive venues prepare for an estimated 170 million visits this season. In Berlin, skaters glide beneath the television tower beside a brightly lit Ferris wheel, while Munich and Cologne welcome visitors against some of Germany's most recognisable architectural backdrops.

 

Munich's Christkindlmarkt, a tradition dating back to the 14th century, features 138 stalls selling gingerbread, wooden carvings and festive decorations. A dedicated nativity market and the traditional Krampus run complement the celebrations, which continue until Christmas Eve.

At the foot of Cologne Cathedral, more than 140 red-roofed stalls surround a 25-metre fir tree decorated with some 50,000 lights. The market offers traditional crafts, mulled wine and more than 100 free performances until 23 December.

Despite heightened security following the deadly attacks in Berlin in 2016 and Magdeburg in 2024, the German capital continues to embrace its festive traditions. Berlin alone hosts more than 80 Christmas markets, ranging from torchlit medieval fairs with fire shows to Alt-Rixdorf’s charity market, which opens for just one weekend each December.

World.title: Thanksgiving storms flood US coasts and disrupt holiday travel
World.content:
Storms brought flooding and strong winds to parts of the United States on Thanksgiving, complicating holiday travel.

 

Streets were inundated in New Jersey's Sea Isle City and Ocean City, while water spread across parts of Avalon. Borough of Avalon business administrator Scott J. Wahl said the town was seeing some of the worst flooding in its history. A few drivers had to be rescued after driving around barricades and into floodwaters, but no injuries were reported, Wahl said.

At Philadelphia International Airport, aircraft were seen stranded on the tarmac amid the bad weather. The National Weather Service warned of disruption at eastern US airports through Friday morning, citing poor visibility, turbulence, strong winds and ice forming on aircraft.

Wind gusts of 80 km/h or higher were expected along the Interstate 95 corridor. All of New Jersey was under a state of emergency declared by Governor Mikie Sherrill, and parts of New York were under one declared by Governor Kathy Hochul. More than 600,000 homes and businesses were without electricity on Thursday afternoon, mostly in East Coast states, according to the outage tracking website poweroutage.us.

Rain kept falling on Norfolk, Virginia, on Thanksgiving morning, stranding drivers on Hampton Boulevard. 25 November, 2026. AP Photo

Macy's postponed its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade in Manhattan until Saturday. It said it acted in an abundance of caution after consulting city officials, amid worries about how the parade's giant balloons would fare in the wind.

Rain and snow also affected the St. Louis area in Missouri, where up to 33 cm of snow was expected. In Wentzville, Missouri, heavy snow partly collapsed the roof of the Wentzville Ice Arena.

On the West Coast, coastal flood warnings were issued from Southern California to the Oregon and Washington coasts because of king tides. These occur when the gravitational pulls of the moon and sun align to raise water levels. A wave tore down part of a pier in Pacifica, California, on Wednesday.

Although both coasts of the US were affected, travel is usually busier in the days leading up to Thanksgiving than on the holiday itself.

World.title: France's presidential hopefuls speak to Euronews as they court local politicians for endorsements
World.content:
Five months ahead of France’s presidential elections, the country’s annual mayoral congress transformed into a political hunting ground as candidates sought to win over local officials and get their endorsements this week.

 

Although around forty figures have so far declared their intent to run in the presidential election — or are seen as potential candidates — not all will go the full way. To qualify, they must secure at least 500 endorsements from elected officials, with mayors representing the largest pool of potential sponsors.

After nearly a decade of Emmanuel Macron's presidency, France's government has been criticised for concentrating power and decision-making at the national level. Against this backdrop, candidates have been seeking to demonstrate their local roots and build support among rural communities.

David Lisnard: 'rules are like cholesterol'

David Lisnard, the mayor of Cannes, was re-elected on Wednesday as head of the Association of Mayors of France (AMF), while pursuing his presidential ambitions with his conservative Nouvelle Énergie party.

Speaking to Euronews, he warned that democracy was under attack from both external and internal threats, calling for a stronger role for local government and praising grassroots politics.

France's mayoral association brings together the mayors of some 34,000 French municipalities, most of whom are elected without a partisan party label.

"We must regain the ability to act and let the local level show the way," said Lisnard, while criticising excessive bureaucracy, red tape and contradictory regulations.

He added that "rules and standards are necessary, but like cholesterol or technocrats, too much is harmful."

Meanwhile, on foreign policy, he warned against "illiberal empires" with expansionist ambitions, naming Russia and China, while also calling out radical Islamism.

A fragmented political race

Lisnard's standing in the polls has risen in recent weeks, amid divisions within the centre-right bloc.

Certain polling scenarios have placed him ahead of former Prime Minister Édouard Philippe, who was previously viewed as a potential challenger to the far-right National Rally party's Marine Le Pen in a second round.

Polls indicate that Le Pen is currently heading the presidential race, followed by the left's Jean-Luc Mélenchon with his France Unbowed party on the left.

Lisnard is campaigning on a programme centred on cutting public spending and taxes, easing business regulations and sharply reducing immigration — leading Le Pen to accuse him of seeking to "grind down" workers' rights with his labour and social policies.

He has also cited Argentine President Javier Milei as an example of radical economic reform and pledged to “turn off the tap” on immigration.

Lisnard has also faced criticism over allegations that he is using his position at the head of the AMF, which he has led since 2021, to advance his presidential ambitions and secure the endorsements needed to qualify for the race.

'All eyes in Europe are on our country'

Former French Prime Minister Dominique de Villepin, who failed to secure the 500 endorsements required to stand in the 2012 presidential election, has called for a "strong France", which can restore its credibility.

He told Euronews that it was vital for France to address its "triple" debt,calling for a strong country that "regains its credibility and regains its health".

"We have a significant financial debt to settle", he stressed, while also pointing to an ecological debt and social debt in "a country where inequalities are increasing".

Meanwhile, centre-left presidential hopeful Raphaël Glucksmann, leader of the Place Publique party, told Euronews that "the eyes of Europe are on France" ahead of its elections.

Referring to the 18 November summit involving Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, he described the three leaders as "masters of the world who intend to share it."

He argued that "the only obstacle" to this division of the world was "a powerful, independent and free Europe". France, he said, would be "the cornerstone of this Europe", adding that this was "the most important issue at stake in the election."

World.title: UK: London's Gingerbread City returns with 50 edible architectural creations
World.content:
Unveiled on 26 November 2026, the tenth edition of The Gingerbread City brings together 50 architectural creations, from intricately crafted replicas of famous landmarks to futuristic skyscrapers. Among the highlights is a miniature Royal Albert Hall, painstakingly recreated by architect Zak Wharton using computer-aided design to capture the building's distinctive symmetry. Gingerbread bridges cross rivers of blue sugar, marshmallow monsters roam snowy landscapes and Father Christmas stretches between towering buildings.

 

Organised by the Museum of Architecture, this year's exhibition takes "Future Forward" as its theme, challenging architects to imagine how buildings might adapt to climate change and improve people's wellbeing. A futuristic skyscraper named SpireHive explores innovations such as living algae and self-healing concrete. The exhibition also features a partnership with homelessness charity St Mungo's, for which former Great British Bake Off contestant Carol Pui Man Li has created five structures inspired by the experiences of people who have faced homelessness. Celebrating its tenth anniversary, The Gingerbread City opens to the public at Space House in Holborn on 28 November and runs until 3 January 2027.

World.title: Belgium: Farmers and tractors descend on Brussels to defend EU subsidies
World.content:
Rolling into Brussels’ European quarter alongside a convoy of tractors, protesters marched past the European Parliament with banners demanding that agricultural funding be protected, one machine bearing a stark placard reading "Agriculture for sale, €0". Chanting slogans against looming cuts, demonstrators echoed warnings from farming unions that subsidies could drop by 20% under the EU’s next long-term budget, tightening the squeeze on already strained rural incomes — a plight underscored by Lucas Bierlaire of the Walloon Farmers Federation, who warned that many growers were already struggling to make a decent living.

 

The rally coincided with a two-day summit in which EU leaders are locked in fractious talks over the bloc’s 2028-2034 budget, divided over the European Commission’s proposed €2 trillion spending plan that would substantially erode agricultural support in real terms. Arnaud Rousseau, head of France’s largest farming union, the FNSEA, urged Brussels to show greater ambition for European agriculture despite fiscal pressures, ahead of a follow-up summit in mid-December aimed at sealing a deal before the year’s end.

World.title: UK-EU food deal carries exit penalty, legal text shows
World.content:
Britain and the European Union would each have to pay to rebuild border checks if they walked away from their new food and drink deal within the first 10 years, according to the legal text published on Thursday.

 

The termination clause requires whichever side quits early to cover "reasonable and proportionate costs" of restoring the infrastructure the deal removes. Any dispute over the bill would go to an international tribunal, UK officials said.

"That termination clause is a standard practice in international treaties, and this one applies equally to both sides, including the EU," Prime Minister Andy Burnham's deputy spokesperson told reporters.

The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) agreement was one of three deals Burnham signed with EU leaders in Brussels, Belgium, on 20 November. The other two link the two sides' carbon markets and allow young people to study and work across borders.

The government says the SPS deal, due to take effect in 2028, could add £5.1 billion to the UK economy by cutting red tape on food and drink exports.

The clause was published days after Reform UK leader Nigel Farage vowed to "repeal" the reset. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said on Thursday she "does not support" it.

Charles Grant, director of the Centre for European Reform think tank, told AFP the provision was "an insurance policy" for the EU, given Britain's continuing debate over its relationship with the bloc.

Legislation to put the deals into effect was introduced in parliament on Thursday, and MPs are due to debate it on 7 December. It would align the UK with EU rules in the sectors covered. British experts would be consulted on new laws but would have no vote, which critics say makes Britain a "rule taker".

Burnham, who replaced Keir Starmer in July, has said the agreements are probably the most that can be achieved in this parliament. He plans a year of informal brainstorming with EU leaders before setting out options for the long-term relationship. These range from keeping things as they are to rejoining the bloc, which he has said would be "unthinkable" without a referendum.

World.title: Son of Myanmar's Suu Kyi 'relieved' by first call in five years, questions military's motives
World.content:
Aung San Suu Kyi's son says he was relieved to hear his mother's voice for the first time in five years but remains concerned about her condition after Myanmar's military moved the 81-year-old to house arrest at an undisclosed location, questioning whether the gesture was genuine.

 

Kim Aris, who has campaigned for his mother's release since the military seized power in 2021, speaking at universities and meeting with governments to press for action, spoke to Euronews' The World Conversation after the call — the first contact the family had had with her in five years.

"Obviously I was very happy to hear her voice and it was a huge relief to actually know that she's alive and well after all this time," Aris said, adding that for two or three years the family had not even known whether she was alive.

Aris, who holds British citizenship through his late father, academic Michael Aris, said he had run a proof-of-life campaign last year, and that the Red Cross visited her earlier this year and confirmed she was alive.

The call was arranged after the Myanmar embassy in London contacted the British Foreign Office the week before it took place, Aris said. It was recorded and monitored, and the two kept to family matters. His mother's first question was whether he had been looking after himself.

"They call this house arrest, but I do not call this a house arrest. She's not in her own home. She's allowed no access to any sort of media, as far as I'm aware," Aris said.

He said she had been held in solitary confinement in a prison in the capital Naypyidaw, with access only to military doctors and no contact with anyone outside military or police personnel.

He said the military was using the transfer to project an image of moderation and urged the international community to maintain pressure rather than re-engage.

"The military have been able to circumnavigate these sanctions for all of this time, and they're still receiving the money and the weaponry that they need to suppress their people," he told Euronews.

No return to civilian rule yet, Aris says

Suu Kyi led the National League for Democracy to a landslide election victory in 2020 and served as Myanmar's de facto head of government. The military refused to recognise the result, seized power in February 2021 and has held her ever since.

The coup triggered a civil war in which pro-democracy forces and ethnic armed groups have taken control of large parts of the country.

More than 4 million people are internally displaced and a further 2 million have fled abroad, Aris said, in part due to conscription laws introduced by the military.

Min Aung Hlaing, who led the coup, was elected president in April by the military-dominated parliament. Aris dismissed suggestions that the country was returning to civilian rule.

"The so-called elections that they held at the end of last year or the beginning of this year were so far from being free and fair," he said.

Asked why young people had taken up arms despite Suu Kyi's commitment to non-violence, Aris said the military had left them no alternative.

"When they came out in peaceful protests at the start of the coup, they were shot in the streets," he said.

He called on the military to stop bombing civilians and release all political prisoners as conditions for peace. "Without those steps, I can't see peace coming back to Burma soon," he said.

'Trying to hold together a very fragile democracy'

Last Thursday, the International Court of Justice ruled for the first time that Myanmar had committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority during a military crackdown in 2017.

The court ordered Myanmar to pay reparations, ensure the safe return of displaced Rohingya and prosecute those responsible.

On Monday, the UK formally recognised the genocide, sanctioned five senior Myanmar military officers and announced plans to restrict aviation fuel supplies to the country.

Min Aung Hlaing has since said his government would reject some of the court's demands, describing the case as a "one-sided accusation".

Suu Kyi appeared before the ICJ in December 2019 to defend Myanmar against the genocide allegations.

Aris defended the decision, saying his mother established the Kofi Annan Commission on the Rakhine State on the second day of her term in office, before the issue drew wider international attention.

"They say that she went to The Hague to defend the military. That's just not the case," he said. "She was trying to hold together a very fragile democracy, which the military could have dismantled at any point, which they have done now."

Five years after the coup, Aris said he believed his mother could still play a role in rebuilding Myanmar.

"It's very hard to know what the situation in Burma will be like in 10 years. I hope that the civil war will have finished and democracy will have been re-established," Aris said.

"And whilst I know my mother will always be involved one way or another, I hope she's able to take a step back and look after herself a bit more."

World.title: New Zealand election ends in hung parliament
World.content:
A final vote count showed that neither the center-right bloc nor the opposition left bloc was able to secure a majority.

The final vote in New Zealand's election showed on Friday that neither the ruling conservatives nor the opposition bloc has enough seats to form a majority government.

The incumbent three-way coalition government is led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon of the center-right National Party.

He governed with two other smaller right parties. The incumbent coalition government won 65 seats, two down from election night, final results show.

The left-wing opposition bloc, led by the Labour Party's Chris Hipkins, won 58 seats, up by one from election night.

In terms of vote share of each of the main parties, Luxon's center-right National Party secured 40 seats, while Hipkins main center-left Labour Party won 36 seats.

The official vote count was released after election authorities counted 400,000 so-called special votes.

Those include ballots cast by New Zealanders living abroad.

Voters delivered a stinging rebuke with the result to the two parties, National and Labour, that have dominated elections in the country [Photo: November 7, 2026] Image: Hollie Adams/REUTERS

Opportunity Party to play kingmaker role in formation of next government

Preliminary results from the November 7 election showed that the ruling coalition held a slim, two-seat majority — that's now been adjusted to the coalition falling short of a majority by a single seat.

The figures leave a new entrant to parliament, the Opportunity Party, as having a preeminent position because it will decide the shape of the next government.

The leader of the centrist party, Qiulae Wong, a 38-year-old former business consultant and a political newcomer , has said earlier this month that she was willing to speak with either party to form a government.

Luxon says negotiations with Opportunity Party will take time

Luxon will have to negotiate with the Opportunity Party if he wants to form the next government.

He said those negotiations will be "challenging" and will take time.

"I want to be upfront with New Zealanders. These negotiations may be challenging, and they could take some time," he told journalists.

"But getting it right matters far more than getting it done quickly. New Zealanders need a government that is stable, that works together, and will last for the full term," he added.

Experts say that if Luxon is not able to form a government with Opportunity, then New Zealanders will have to return to the polls for a new election, according to Australia's public broadcaster.

World.title: At odds over the EU budget, European leaders cut summit short
World.content:
Skip next section Antonia Costa wraps up EU summit that fails to close gaps in budget disputes

Antonio Costa has a tough job to get EU members to agree on a common budget Image: Marius Burgelman/AP Photo/picture alliance

European Council President Antonio Costa said that 24 out of 27 members of the EU supported a proposal for a €45 billion loan for Ukraine .

That loan is split into two sections, with €20 billion to help finance for civil services and the other €25 billion going to arms and ammunition.

Euro News reported earlier in the day that Bulgaria reversed course and was ready to join the loan, so long as it was only paying into the part that wasn't covering Ukraine's military needs.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said there was considerable work to be done before a deal could be in place.

EU leaders cut short a second day of talks that was due to take place tomorrow and pushed discussions to another summit in December.

The disagreements over a shared EU budget for the years between 2028 and 2034 stem from different priorities among EU members.

Some countries prefer greater funding for defense and enhancing competitiveness, while others seek to keep in place funding for agriculture, among other issues.

EU leaders ultimately weren't able to reach an agreement at the end of Thursday.

World.title: Albania's youth are protesting in Flamingo Revolution, not leaving the country anymore
World.content:
Youth protests against a rigid political system and corruption have shaken the government of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama. They also show that fewer young people are willing to emigrate in search of a better future.

In mid-October, students in the Albanian capital Tirana set a suitcase on fire and threw it into the courtyard of the Education Ministry. Everyone in the country understood the symbolism: According to the 2023 census, the population of this Western Balkan country shrunk by about 420,000 between 2011 and 2023 — by nearly 15% — primarily because of emigration.

For a generation of young Albanians, this was the response to a system that gave them little voice. But now young people want to stay, and the protesters are saying that the system has to change.

Known as the "Flamingo Revolution," the social movement began in May with demonstrations against a luxury resort in a coastal reserve that US President Donald Trump's daughter Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner were involved in.

It quickly evolved into broader criticism against corruption, Prime Minister Edi Rama's government and his ruling Socialist Party and the country's entire political class.

Thousands marched almost every evening for four months in protests that were largely peaceful. But on October 13, a student protest escalated and there were clashes with police. Since then, the unrest has continued, with police using tear gas, water cannons and rubber bullets against demonstrators. There have been hundreds of arrests and many injuries, amid damage to public and private property.

'Flamingo revolution' has broad support

The protesters have called for Rama's resignation, a transitional government, electoral reform and fresh elections. The movement, which has no leader, has support from people across the political spectrum. And while the prime minister has blamed "foreign hands" for the movement, there seems to be little evidence that external actors are orchestrating the protests, though they may have attempted to exploit the unrest online.

The protesters, who do not feel represented by Albania's democracy, are driven by domestic issues: corruption, the high cost of living and low wages. This is nothing new, but many factors have converged recently: a series of high-level corruption charges, including against ministers and two of Rama's former deputies, rising prices and the fact that Albania is being measured against EU standards by a new generation.

In certain areas, Rama has transformed Albania since taking office in 2013: the economy has grown significantly, as the government likes to point out, and tourism is booming. But the prosperity remains unevenly distributed. Critics accuse the government of channeling too much taxpayer money into a small number of well-connected companies through prestigious projects and public-private partnerships, and in some cases through corrupt business deals, at the expense of healthcare, education and better economic prospects for the wider population.

Rama has rejected the calls for his resignation and has invited protesters to engage in dialogue, which they have so far refused.

Clashes with police erupted in mid-October like here in Tirana Image: Adnan Beci/AFP

Alternating between Socialist and Democratic Party

In 2008, Rama and Sali Berisha, the long-time chairman of the opposition Democratic Party, worked on a reform to Albania's constitution and electoral law, which was approved by parliament. Since then, it is party leaders who have determined who enters Parliament, which weakens ties between lawmakers and their constituents.

In addition, it has become significantly more difficult for new parties to win seats. In 2025, a new party received about 64,000 votes, but only one seat. The Socialists, by contrast, won about one seat for every 10,000 votes.

Rama has been the leader of the Socialists since 2005, while Berisha first became the chairman of the Democratic Party in 1991. For 21 years, Albania's prime minister has either been Rama or Berisha. Freedom House, a US nongovernmental organization that promotes democracy worldwide, classifies Albania as "partly free" and describes the country's political parties as being "often organized around leading personalities."

Protesters on the streets have said that they want both men to be jailed. Rama has argued that governments should be replaced at the ballot box, not on the streets.

Though the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) acknowledged that parliamentary elections in 2025 were "competitive and professionally managed" it said that they had taken place "in a highly polarized environment and contestants did not enjoy a level playing field."

It added that there were "reports of intimidation, misuse of public resources and pressure on public employees, which undermined equal opportunities."

The Democratic Party also spoke of election fraud and intimidation. Turnout was below 45%.

Protesters call out corruption, face high cost of living

Many protesters also allege that when it comes to business, what matters is the proximity to people in power. They criticize the public procurement, public auctions and concessions system, which has led to state-owned land, including coastal and protected areas, being sold to private investors.

Ordinary Albanians are feeling the financial brunt. According to the Albanian Institute of Statistics (INSTAT), half of all employees earn less than 60,000 lek (roughly €620 or $680) per month after taxes. But according to Eurostat, food prices are slightly above the EU average and real estate prices in Tirana have nearly doubled since 2018, with rents rising just as quickly.

For many years, young Albanians who were dissatisfied with the system opted to leave the country. The number of Albanian citizens in Germany more than doubled between 2018 and 2024, reaching almost 120,000.

Though it is still too early to say whether there are fewer Albanians leaving today, for many protesters staying has become a political statement.

Albanians continue to call for the prime minister's resignation Image: Florion Goga/REUTERS

Albanians largely pro-EU

Rama has argued that his resignation would jeopardize Albania's bid to join the European Union by 2030, but the vast majority of Albanians are pro-European, including those on the streets and in the opposition. From the protesters' perspective, it is the government headed by Rama that is the real obstacle on the path to the EU.

Though there is currently a wave of protests across Europe, the only obvious comparison is with Serbia, where a student-led movement recently forced a long-time ruler from office. Whether Albania will follow this example depends on whether young people, who have traditionally not been deeply engaged in politics, can turn their protests into votes.

What is certain is that for three decades, Albania's leaders have relied on their citizens' suitcases. Now, the country's students have burned that very luggage.

Andi Balla is a doctoral candidate at the Leibniz Institute for East and Southeast European Studies (IOS) in Regensburg, where he is conducting research on demographic debates in Albania. He has written numerous articles on Albania for an international audience.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Gerard Depardieu to stand trial in France for rape and sexual assault
World.content:
The Paris Court of Appeal upheld the order for the 77-year-old French actor to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting an actress in 2018.

French actor Gerard Depardieu failed in his attempt to overturn an order for him to stand trial on rape charges.

On Thursday, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that Depardieu should face trial for the alleged rape and sexual assault that occurred on August 7, 2018. However, the court dismissed the allegations relating to a second incident that occurred six days later.

Depardieu still has the option of appealing to a higher court. His lawyer, Delphine Meillet, told the Associated Press that she disputes Thursday's ruling, though she did not specify whether she will challenge it in France's highest civil and criminal court.

This decision comes just two weeks after the 77-year-old Depardieu dropped his appeal against a sexual assault conviction in a separate case. He accepted an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issued a public apology.

What are the charges against Depardieu?

An actress, who was 22 years old at the time, accused Depardieu of raping and sexually assaulting her at his Paris apartment on August 7 and 13, 2018. Depardieu was 69 at the time of the alleged incident.

She reported the allegations to the police a few days later. Depardieu denies the allegations, claiming that the encounter was consensual.

Last year, a trial was ordered regarding the allegations. If the trial goes ahead, Depardieu could face up to 20 years in prison.

Carine Durrieu Diebolt, the victim's lawyer, said that the Thursday decision was a genuine relief and a victory for her client.

In France, Gerard Depardieu has become a very controversial figure because of the many allegations and obscene remarks he has made [FILE: March 2025] Image: Julien De Rosa/AFP

Accusations overshadow Depardieu's legacy

Depardieu was born in 1948 into a working-class family in Chateauroux, a city in central France. He overcame a speech impediment to become one of France's most prolific actors.

The film star was a dominant figure in French cinema for half a century, becoming a renowned cultural export. He earned an Oscar nomination for "Cyrano de Bergerac" and a Golden Globe for "Green Card."

Accusations of sexual misconduct and his subsequent conviction, however, have increasingly overshadowed his cinematic legacy.

The international media has also been paying attention to Depardieu's off-screen antics. One of the most notable instances was when he accepted a Russian passport from President Vladimir Putin in 2013 amid a dispute over French taxes.

World.title: Guinea-Bissau junta delays presidential vote for 2 years
World.content:
The decision came exactly one year after the military took power on November 26, 2025. The junta said the conditions were insufficient to hold presidential elections for now.

The ruling junta in the West African nation of Guinea-Bissau announced Thursday that it is postponing elections by two years until November 26, 2028.

What do we know so far?

The decision came on the 1-year anniversary of the military takeover in Guinea-Bissau on November 26, 2025. The country is currently led by military general Horta Inta-a, who serves as transitional president.

Inta-a said in a statement that there was "an insufficiency of the technical, material and financial conditions" to hold the election.

"It is essential to guarantee effective conditions for preparing and holding elections in accordance with the principles of legality, democratic participation, equal opportunity, transparency and electoral integrity," he said.

The military coup in Guinea-Bissau came three days after a general election last year, with the military deposing incumbent President Umaro Sissoco Embalo. Both Embalo and opposition candidate Fernando Dias da Costa claimed victory in the election, with the military arresting Embalo one day prior to the results being released.

Guinea-Bissau army names general as new leader To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What's the political and human rights situation in Guinea-Bissau?

West African bloc ECOWAS has urged Guinea-Bissau to transition back to civilian rule.

Guinea-Bissau is a small tropical Portuguese-speaking nation on the West African coast which has seen multiple coups in its history. The country faces a high level of corruption and is also a key point for cocaine trafficking to Europe.

According to Washington DC-based think tank Freedom House , Guinea-Bissau is only "partly free" due to military interference in elections.

Reporters without Borders ranks Guinea-Bissau 100 out of 180 countries on its press freedom index, saying the "sharp deterioration of security for media professionals, combined with political and economic pressure, has severely tested the practice of journalism in recent years."

World.title: Trial of Berlin woman accused of spying for Russia begins after delay
World.content:
Despite delays due to health issues, the trial of the Berlin woman accused of spying for Russia has begun. Prosecutors say the defendant used her military contacts to provide information on German defense and Ukraine.

The trial of a German-Ukrainian woman on charges of spying for Russia started Thursday.

The start of the proceedings was delayed in the morning after the accused developed health problems that required treatment by emergency medical workers, a spokeswoman for a Berlin court said.

Later, however, she was brought into the courtroom in a wheelchair, wearing dark sunglasses. Her lawyers caused further delay when they said she would not confirm her personal information.

Several times throughout the afternoon, the defense attorneys said their client was feeling nauseous, and a bucket was brought in. A doctor was present in the courtroom.

Espionage process with diplomatic fallout

The arrest of the 57-year-old Berlin businesswoman triggered a diplomatic clash between Berlin and Moscow.

The Russian ambassador was summoned regarding the incident, and Andrei Mayerov, the deputy military attache at the embassy, was expelled from Germany.

Ilona W., who holds German and Ukrainian citizenship, is accused of working for the intelligence service of a foreign power.

Her full name has not been released due to German privacy laws. She was arrested on January 21 and put in pretrial detention.

The trial is expected to last until May 2027.

What is Ilona W. accused of?

She is accused of having contacts with current and former German Defense Ministry officials to provide information about defense industry locations, drone tests and planned drone deliveries to Ukraine.

She was also said to have been in contact with a man, her alleged handler, working for Russian intelligence at the Russian Embassy in Berlin since at least November 2023, prosecutors say.

On several occasions, she allegedly helped her contact at the embassy attend political events in Berlin under a false identity in order to establish contacts there. She is also suspected of having compiled background information on participants in high-level political events.

German spy chief warns of rising Russia threat To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Berlin summoned the alleged handler, who was identified by Der Spiegel magazine as the embassy's deputy military attache, over the incident and expelled him from Germany.

Ilona W. led an advocacy group for years that called for international cooperation, focusing particularly on German, Russian, Ukrainian relations.

In addition to her advocacy work, she also ran a small marketing agency.

Both positions allowed her to be active in Berlin's political circles and provided her with connections within the military.

Russia rejects the allegations

The Russian ambassador to Berlin, Sergei Nechayev, denied the allegations this week.

"The Russian Embassy has no connection whatsoever to this woman, and even if she happened to cross paths with one of our representatives, perhaps at some reception, that means absolutely nothing," Nechayev told news agency AFP.

Why Berlin remains an espionage hot spot To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He also said "he may have seen her himself at an event."

"But she is not a Russian citizen and, as far as we are aware, has no ties to Russia. She is a German and Ukrainian citizen, and, frankly, we do not associate with such individuals here," he said.

World.title: Saudi pop music is thriving — but for the right reasons?
World.content:
As part of Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia's music scene has evolved hugely thanks to state funding and support. Local musicians and DJs are optimistic. But are they actually just helping prop up an authoritarian state?

Today, rapper Asayel Bishi is one of Saudi Arabia's rising hip-hop stars, signed to the country's biggest record label for new music, MDLBEAST. But not so long ago, she was making international headlines for a totally different reason.

In 2020, after Bishi released a music video for a song, "Bint Mecca," or "girl from Mecca," featuring people dancing in a local cafe, Mecca's governor called for the arrest of Bishi's whole production team. He said the video violated the holy city's local customs and traditions. In the end, the situation was resolved with a discussion about filming permits.

And by early 2023, Bishi was signed to MDLBEAST and has since racked up hundreds of thousands of streams on music platforms like Spotify.

In the past, other Saudi rappers have ended up in prison for similar, alleged transgressions. The fact that Bishi's story went a different way is probably partially because the 31-year-old's career path is on a similar trajectory to the Saudi pop music industry as a whole.

Music part of Vision 2030

As part of Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman's Vision 2030 plan, announced in 2016 and which aims to move the country away from economic dependence on oil, the country has poured billions into the local music industry.

The pace of development increased in 2019 after the country held its first major festival, Soundstorm, an annual event that now draws major international acts and over 400,000 guests. MDLBEAST was created then, primarily as the festival organizer. Since then, it has also become a record label, radio station, distributor, promoter and talent incubator.

After decades of bans on concerts, the first officially sanctioned music gigs began to be held in 2017. Here, visitors arrive at the Soundstorm music festival in Banban in December 2025 Image: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

A recent report for the Saudi Music Commission suggests the music sector could be worth $500 million (€455 million) by 2034. But it's difficult to figure out how well Saudi pop is really doing now because independent monitoring of the sector only began relatively recently.

Streaming platform Spotify reports that people listening to Saudi-made music inside Saudi Arabia increased by 195% between 2020 and 2024. However, the most-streamed artists inside the country are still international.

'Tied to the destiny of crown prince'

Although there was a mostly-hidden Saudi music scene before this recent boom, observers say the growth of the Saudi music sector is not organic.
