The mayor of Warsaw has refused permission for opposition protests outside the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which was taken over last month by a group of government-backed judges, to continue. City hall, which is under the control of Poland’s main ruling party, the centrist Civic Coalition (KO), says that the demonstration threatens public safety. However, opposition figures have condemned the decision as “authoritarian” and one of the organisers of the protest has pledged to challenge it in court. Bum. Jest zakaz organizacji kolejnej manifestacji przed Trybunałem Konstytucyjnym.https://t.co/Ol8gQxC3A1 pic.twitter.com/bUqAkdojxe — Tomasz Skory (@TomaszSkory) November 25, 2026 On 30 October, a group of eight judges chosen this year by the government’s parliamentary majority – but five of whom opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has refused to swear in – effectively took control of the TK. They declared that the tribunal’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, was suspended. Meanwhile, riot police surrounded the court and held back protesters, including Święczkowski himself. Since then, the demonstrators have maintained a constant presence outside the court, while Święczkowski has also periodically appeared. He and Nawrocki argue that the actions of the eight “usurper” judges are illegal and that Święczkowski remains chief justice. Given the ongoing demonstration in front of the court, the judges currently controlling the TK have used a separate entrance that leads in from the next-door chancellery of Prime Minister Donald Tusk. On Monday this week, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, the judge who has declared herself acting head of the court, arranged a meeting with Warsaw’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, and the commander of Warsaw police, Krzysztof Ogroński, to discuss the protest. She argued that, by preventing access to the tribunal, the demonstrators were “violating the constitutional and European standard of the right to a court”. On Wednesday morning, Warsaw city hall announced that Trzaskowski, who is a deputy leader of Tusk’s centrist KO party, had rejected a request for permission to continue the public assembly outside the TK from the end of November until January. ‼️ Rafał Trzaskowski zakazał zgromadzenia pod Trybunałem Konstytucyjnym! Protest trwa tam od września i dotyczy sporu o to, kto ma w TK zasiadać. W poniedziałek osoba podająca się za „Zastępującą Prezesa TK” zaprosiła ratusz i Policję, by „przywrócić” wstęp do Trybunału. Dwa… pic.twitter.com/a0EzqVzRDn — Magdalena Majkowska (@MagdaMajkowska) November 25, 2026 “While the freedom to organise and participate in peaceful assemblies constitutes a fundamental constitutional freedom, it is not unconditional,” wrote the municipal authorities. They noted that the current gathering outside the TK has been ongoing since 17 September (as protesters anticipated an attempted takeover of the court) and that the organisers had given assurances that they would not obstruct the roadway. In fact, tents, a television stage and other structures have blocked the road, wrote city hall. This “causes significant disruption for local residents” and “undoubtedly hinders emergency service vehicles, thereby threatening the life and health of residents”. The authorities also noted that, while the protests were initially peaceful, there had later been a number of “dangerous incidents”, including attempts to block vehicles from entering the TK and scuffles with police, which included throwing objects at officers, physical confrontations, verbal abuse and spitting. Such developments “have caused the gathering to lose its peaceful character”, wrote city hall. There are also “grounds to assume that the intention is, in effect, a long-term blockade of the entrance to the Constitutional Tribunal and the street itself”. One of the organisers of the protest, Adam Borowski, told Polsat News that it is a “lie” that they are preventing the TK from functioning properly. It is the judges “illegally occupying” the tribunal who are responsible, he said. Borowski announced that they would appeal against the city’s decision in court. They have 24 hours from the issuing of the decision in which to do so. PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, meanwhile, declared that the decision to ban the protest was “authoritarianism in its purest form…trampling citizens’ constitutional rights”. Russia has “categorically denied” that the three missiles which struck Poland last week were Russian and has accused Warsaw of seeking to “stoke anti-Russian sentiment” around the incident. Its remarks came after Poland’s foreign ministry on Tuesday summoned Russia’s ambassador, Georgy Mikhno, to present him with a protest over the missiles. Today, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski said that expelling the ambassador is “one of the options” Poland could take, though it remains unlikely. ⚡️Komentarz Ambasady Rosji w Polsce 24 listopada 2026 r. JE Pan Gieorgij Michno, Ambasador Federacji Rosyjskiej w Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej, został zaproszony do MSZ kraju przyjmującego, gdzie przekazano mu protest w ramach rzekomego „powiązania” naszego kraju z incydentami… pic.twitter.com/GUJB0RWZgt — Russian Embassy, PL (@rusemb_pl) November 24, 2026 On Friday morning last week, three objects struck at different locations in southeastern Poland, not far from the Ukrainian border, amid large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine. On Sunday, Poland confirmed that all three were Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles. Subsequently, on Monday night this week, a Russian drone entered Polish airspace from Ukraine and spent a few minutes above Poland before turning back into Ukraine. On Tuesday, Mikhno was summoned to the Polish foreign ministry, which said it had presented him with “a very strong diplomatic note” regarding the missile strikes. Afterwards, Mikhno read a statement to the media saying that “Russia categorically rejects the accusations of involvement in the incidents”, which were being made based on “political judgements and unsubstantiated assumptions”. He also condemned what he said was “openly Russophobic rhetoric around the incident”, which suggests “a desire to exploit the situation to further stoke anti-Russian sentiment”. The ambassador claimed that “no convincing and verifiable evidence has been presented” to establish the origin of the missiles. He then refused to answer journalists’ questions before leaving. Russia has installed an exhibition titled “Ten Centuries of Polish Russophobia” outside a cemetery for thousands of Poles murdered by the Soviets in the 1940 Katyn massacre. It opened just before Poland marked its annual day of remembrances for victims https://t.co/HcfmeNrerB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 16, 2026 Mikhno’s claims were immediately rejected by the Polish foreign ministry’s spokesman, Maciej Wewiór, who said that it was “beyond dispute” that the missiles were Russian and that Moscow “knows [this] perfectly well”. On Sunday, Polish prosecutors said that the remains of the missiles leave no doubt they are Russian, and added that preliminary findings even indicate which specific factory they were manufactured in and when. A number of Poland’s NATO allies, as well as the alliance’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, have also condemned Russia over the missile incident and expressed solidarity with Warsaw. NATO has approved the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System to Poland in response to three Russian missiles striking Polish territory last week. Hours after the decision was announced, Poland’s airspace was again violated by a Russian drone https://t.co/gudQJsPlQ5 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 24, 2026 On Wednesday morning, Sikorski was asked during an interview with Polskie Radio whether a “strong diplomatic note” was a strong enough response, given Russia’s repeated and continued hostile actions towards Poland. When it was put to the foreign minister that Poland should expel the Russian ambassador, Sikorski said that “this is one option” and “of course, it can be done”. However, he added that “we won’t pursue it yet” and noted that any such action would be met with an equivalent response from Moscow. In 2024 and 2025, Sikorski successively ordered Russia to close all of its consulates in Poland in response to Russian acts of sabotage. Moscow responded by shutting down all Polish consulates on its territory. 🗣️ "Czy jest sens rozmawiania z ambasadorem Rosji? To symboliczny gest pokazania dezaprobaty. Liczą się sankcje i naciski gospodarcze. (…) Nie ma decyzji, by zerwać stosunki dyplomatyczne, ale one wiszą na cienkim włosku" Rzecznik rządu @adamSzlapka w rozmowie z @Piekarski_M… pic.twitter.com/JU9up9cm5N — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) November 25, 2026 On Monday morning, Polish government spokesman Adam Szłapka told broadcaster TVP that “relations [with Russia] are hanging by a thread”. He added that, while presenting a protest note to the Russian ambassador had been “a symbolic gesture of disapproval”, most important are “the sanctions and the pressure on Russia”. “I think [this pressure] is strong from the entire European Union…[but] we’ve had doubts from the United States regarding these sanctions in recent months,” said Szłapka. “Poland believes [the pressure] should be consistent and stronger…I hope the entire Western world will be very clear on this.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland and the United States have signed an agreement on defence research, development, testing and evaluation, concluding 17 years of negotiations and opening the way for deeper technological cooperation. The agreement establishes a framework for joint defence projects, as well as the exchange of technical data and expertise, giving Poland – which is already a major importer of US arms – a formal role in the development of American defence technologies for the first time. Under Secretary Emil Michael (@USWREMichael) and Mr. Cezary Tomczyk, Poland’s Secretary of State at the Ministry of National Defence, signed the Agreement Between the Government of the United States of America and the Government of the Republic of Poland for Defense Research,… pic.twitter.com/7EAgK3nD2i — Department of War CTO (@DoWCTO) November 23, 2026 The agreement was signed at the Pentagon by Poland’s deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk and US under secretary of war for research and engineering Emil Michael. According to the Department of War, the deal will help “turn research and development into validated military capabilities to jointly support US and Polish warfighters”. Tomczyk said the agreement would allow Polish universities, research institutes and companies to participate in joint research and development work on defence technology with US partners and would enable such technologies to be tailored more closely to the requirements of the Polish armed forces. During a briefing in Washington, Tomczyk admitted that the agreement had been negotiated for what he described as a “probably record-breaking” 17 years, but he noted a “significant acceleration in relations” between the US and Poland over the last six months. General Marcin Górka, who oversees innovation in the Polish armed forces and accompanied Tomczyk to the United States, likewise welcomed the agreement, which he said would “open the doors to American military laboratories for our scientists and engineers”. Górka also said the agreement would enable Poland and the United States to jointly develop anti-drone systems and advanced drones, with testing taking place in both countries. Poland is a major importer of US military hardware. Between 2021 and 2025, it was the biggest overall importer of arms in NATO, with around 44% of that equipment coming from the US, including F-35 fighter jets, Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence systems and HIMARS rocket launchers. But Poland has recently sought to move from being a client of the US defence industry to more of a partner. Earlier this month, Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth signed a declaration on expanding bilateral defence-industrial cooperation. Poland and the US have signed a statement of intent on strengthening defence industry cooperation. Polish defence minister @KosiniakKamysz said his country would be "the US ambassador in the EU", including seeking EU funds for jointly produced equipment https://t.co/SKHrxTEKIW — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 11, 2026 Last month, Poland was chosen as the location for a planned Patriot missile maintenance and servicing facility, the first of its kind outside the United States. In May, an agreement was signed to establish a centre in Poland for servicing the engines of Abrams tanks. This year, Polish state defence group PGZ was chosen as the first European producer of American Barracuda-500M cruise missiles, while US defence giant Northrop Grumman and Polish arms manufacturer Niewiadów-PGM announced plans to jointly produce artillery shells in Poland. Poland is also seeking to host a new permanent US military base, with Tomczyk reiterating during his Washington visit that a decision is expected from the Trump administration in early December. NATO has approved the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System to Poland in response to three Russian missiles striking Polish territory last week. Hours after the decision was announced, Poland’s airspace was again violated by a Russian drone https://t.co/gudQJsPlQ5 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 24, 2026 The new agreement on defence technology was signed amid heightened tensions with Russia. On Friday, three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles struck separate locations in southeastern Poland, near the Ukrainian border. Tomczyk said the Polish delegation had briefed Pentagon officials on the missile strikes, which he described as a “provocation” by Russia. The Polish minister was also asked about US President Donald Trump last week calling Russia’s Vladimir Putin his “friend”. “One thing is certain: Vladimir Putin is not our friend; he is a threat to us,” replied Tomczyk. “This is the most important message that should come from Poland and resonate with the people of the United States.” Subsequently, on Monday night, a Russian drone entered Polish airspace from Ukraine for a few minutes before turning back. World.title: Poland, Lithuania and Latvia violated rights of migrants sent back to Belarus, finds European court
World.content: Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland, Lithuania and Latvia violated the human rights of migrants from Afghanistan, Iraq and Cuba who entered their countries illegally from Belarus in 2021 and 2022, the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has ruled. However, the ECHR did also recognise that states have the right to prevent the entry of migrants who have been “instrumentalised” by Belarus in order to create a crisis on the European Union’s eastern borders. That latter finding prompted Poland’s deputy interior minister with oversight of migration policy to hail today’s rulings as a victory and endorsement of the government’s tough border policies. It was also described as a groundbreaking moment by a leading human rights organisation. 📽️ Watch a video explainer on the Grand Chamber cases concerning instrumentalisation of migration. 📽️ Regardez la vidéo explicative sur les affaires de Grande Chambre sur l'instrumentalisation de la migration. pic.twitter.com/ZhXqZ6lIur — ECHR CEDH (@ECHR_CEDH) November 24, 2026 In 2021, Belarus began encouraging, assisting and, in some cases, forcing tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to irregularly cross into the neighbouring EU states of Poland, Lithuania and Latvia. Belarus engineered the migration crisis as part of the various “hybrid actions” undertaken alongside its ally Russia with the intention of destabilising countries they regard as hostile. In response, Poland, Lithuania and Latvia took a variety of measures intended to prevent the entry of irregular migrants from Belarus. In many cases, they carried out so-called “pushbacks”, sending migrants who had crossed the border back into Belarus. On Tuesday, the ECHR announced three sets of rulings on cases brought against Poland, Lithuania and Latvia in relation to actions they had taken against specific migrants who had entered from Belarus. The European court noted that the migrants had “entered unlawfully” as part of Belarus’s “instrumentalisation of migration”, which it described as a “hostile action” that had “the intention of destabilising the respondent states or the wider region”. This “represented a deliberate threat to the state” and “was liable to put at risk its essential functions, including the maintenance of law and order and the safeguarding of its national security”. Poland wants the European Union to deny the right to asylum for migrants who cross EU borders in organised, aggressive groups, just as Poland has itself done on its border with Belarus https://t.co/7Gbsvs6I1e — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026 The court found that states do have the right to control entry, and even fully close their borders, as well as to “remove a foreign national to the instrumentalising state”, without it automatically being a violation of the human rights convention. However, the ECHR also deemed that, “before removing an individual in such circumstances, national authorities had an obligation to detect those individuals who would be particularly at risk of suffering or enduring ill-treatment”. That included those who had personal vulnerabilities (such as old age, ill health or a disability) or who would face a threat to their life or serious risk of mistreatment by being returned to Belarus. In the cases of Poland and Latvia, the ECHR found that they had breached the obligation to undertake such an assessment before returning certain migrants. A court has found that Poland's border guard violated the law when sending two Afghan and Ethiopian men back to Belarus after they injured themselves crossing the anti-migrant border fence. One of them had made clear his wish to claim asylum in Poland https://t.co/42yOuGEgns — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2024 For Poland, the case concerned an unnamed Afghan national who had been part of a group that had crossed back and forth over the Polish-Belarusian border multiple times, as often happened in the early stages of the crisis. The ECHR noted that it had, at the time, issued an interim measure requiring that the Afghan man not be returned to Belarus. However, the Polish authorities did not take this into account, and sent him back to Belarus on 20 October 2021, thereby demonstrating they had not complied with their obligation to properly assess his need for protection, found the ECHR. The court also ruled that, in the case of that applicant as well as a fellow Afghan national, Poland had violated their rights by preventing lawyers from having access to them. It ordered Poland to pay the two men €20,000 (89,000 zloty) and €5,000 respectively as compensation. Two Afghan asylum seekers who crossed from Belarus into Poland have been awarded compensation for their mistreatment by Polish border guards. They were detained and driven back towards the border by officers, who did not accept their asylum applications https://t.co/M9bSHakS5j — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2025 In Latvia’s case, the ECHR ruled that the country had violated its obligations by sending Iraqi Kurdish children, some of whom were infants, back into Belarus, “disregarding the[ir] evident vulnerability”. At the same time, the European court dismissed further complaints by adult migrants against Latvia and Lithuania, finding that they had not demonstrated any vulnerability or risk. However, it did find that Lithuania had violated some Cuban migrants’ rights by failing to properly inform them of the reasons they were being held in a detention camp and thereby also of their right to legally challenge their detention. It also ruled that Latvia had violated the rights of migrants on its territory due to the poor conditions they found themselves in when camped out on Latvian territory, with no access to sanitary facilities and insufficient protection from rain and cold nighttime temperatures. ⚖️ Grand Chamber cases ➡️ Responding to realities of instrumentalisation of migration at Belarus border, European Court safeguards essential rights and reiterates limits of Convention protections. 🔗 Press release: https://t.co/nflEyCWKb1 — ECHR CEDH (@ECHR_CEDH) November 24, 2026 In response to today’s ruling on Poland, the deputy interior minister with oversight of migration policy, Maciej Duszczyk, hailed it as “very important and favourable for us”. He said that the ECHR’s findings regarding states’ rights to defend their borders from instrumentalised migration effectively endorsed Poland’s policies. The Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights (HFPC), a Warsaw-based NGO, also noted that the ECHR’s Grand Chamber had, for the first time, defined the scope of states’ obligations when another state has instrumentalised migration. “In the ECHR’s view, when migration is instrumentalised, states are not obliged to assess whether people being returned to the state instrumentalising migration will have access to an adequate asylum procedure there,” noted HFPC. Bardzo ważny i dobry dla nas wyrok Europejskiego Trybunału Praw Człowieka. Niezakwestionowano naszego modelu walki z nielegalną migracją. Trybunał odniósł się do instrumentalizacji jako sprzecznej z Konwencją i podkreślił prawo państ do obrony i ochrony swoich granic. — Maciek Duszczyk (@MaciekDuszczyk) November 24, 2026 A number of Polish courts have also found that the authorities violated the rights of migrants on the Belarus border. Last year, two Afghan asylum seekers were awarded 5,000 zloty compensation for their mistreatment by Polish border guards. In 2024, another court found that the border guard violated the law when sending Afghan and Ethiopian migrants back to Belarus after they had injured themselves while crossing the border. Last year, Poland’s government effectively formalised pushbacks by introducing a ban on asylum claims by people crossing the border irregularly from Belarus, who are now sent back without their applications being accepted. The measure has been criticised by human rights groups – including the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and Poland’s own human rights commissioner – as a violation of international law and Poland’s constitution. The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98% Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 Poland has also implemented a number of other tough policies, including easing rules for the use of firearms by uniformed officers protecting the border from illegal migration. This year has seen the migration crisis abate significantly, with Poland reporting a 98% decline in attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, as well as a 100% success rate in apprehending those who do cross. NATO has approved the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) to Poland in response to last week’s incident in which three Russian missiles struck Polish territory. Shortly after the decision was announced, Poland’s airspace was again violated by a Russian drone that entered from Ukraine. However, although the military was given authorisation to shoot the object down, they did not do so after the drone began to move back into Ukraine. Today, NATO Ambassadors met in the North Atlantic Council to discuss last week’s violations of Polish airspace. This was a dangerous incident and Russia bears full responsibility. NATO and Allied assets reacted quickly to the airspace violations, and the Supreme Allied Commander… — NATO Spokesperson (@NATOpress) November 23, 2026 On Friday morning last week, three objects struck at different locations in southeast Poland, not far from the Ukrainian border. The incidents took place amid large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine, and on Sunday Poland confirmed that all three were Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles. The missiles were in Polish airspace for around three minutes before striking the ground. Two Swedish Gripen fighter jets, which were patrolling Polish skies as part of a NATO air policing mission, received authorisation from NATO’s Combined Air Operations Centre to fire upon the objects if certain conditions were met. However, the pilots were unable to confirm their identity in time due to poor weather conditions. On Monday, an extraordinary meeting of the North Atlantic Council, NATO’s main decision-making body, took place to discuss the incident. Afterwards, deputy defence minister Paweł Zalewski, who represented Poland at the meeting, announced that NATO had agreed to place an AWACS “at Poland’s disposal”. Later, NATO’s spokeswoman, Allison Hart, confirmed that “the Supreme Allied Commander Europe has authorised the forward deployment of a NATO AWACS aircraft” and is also “examining the deployment of additional assets as he continues to assess our deterrence and defence posture in Poland and elsewhere”. Poland has confirmed that the three objects which struck its territory last Friday were all Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles. Preliminary findings indicate the missiles were recently manufactured at a plant in Dubna, Russia https://t.co/4N6k3eBUGN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 23, 2026 “This is a very serious capability that gives us enhanced situational awareness,” said Zalewski, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. “This is an immediate NATO response, and we are very happy about it.” “What I heard today is a great demonstration of the alliance’s unity with Poland in the face of Russian attacks,” he added. “It’s safe to say that the Russians have moved up the escalation ladder in their relations with NATO.This means…the need for an appropriate response.” Zalewski emphasised that “we’re not talking about offensive actions in any way, but about the ability to defend against all the attacks Russia is launching against NATO countries”. The aim is “not to escalate, but to…discourage Russia from attacks”. Wiceminister @ZalewskiPawel w Kwaterze Głównej #NATO: Do dyspozycji Polski będzie jeden samolot szybkiego ostrzegania #AWACS. The operational command of Poland’s armed forces announced shortly before midnight that it had continuously tracked the object and granted authorisation to shoot it down. However, after the drone changed course and began to head east, back towards the border, a decision was made to refrain from engaging it, “taking into account the potential threat to civilians and the possible consequences of shooting down the object”, said operational command. Russia has so far not commented on either its missiles hitting Poland last Friday nor the latest drone incursion. They are the latest in a series of airspace violations. World.title: Filmasia to Bring 16 Asian Films to Prague, Brno and České Budějovice
World.content:
The 22nd edition of the Filmasia Asian Film Festival will take place in Prague from December 3 to 13, bringing 16 films from Hong Kong, South Korea, Japan, Taiwan and Vietnam.

The festival will also welcome filmmakers from Hong Kong and South Korea before travelling to Brno and České Budějovice in January and February.

This year’s theme is “the thread of fate,” connecting established filmmakers with emerging artists.



The programme is divided into five sections, alongside a special retrospective dedicated to director Wong Kar Wai.

The festival will open on Friday, December 4, at 7 p.m. at Bio Oko with Good Trip, a Hong Kong comedy about a seriously ill father and his daughter embarking on a road trip. Directors Norris Wong and Wong Hoi will attend the screening.

The festival will also revisit four films by Wong Kar Wai in the In the Mood for Wong Kar Wai section. Audiences can see Chungking Express and Fallen Angels on Saturday, December 12, followed by Happy Together and In the Mood for Love on Sunday, December 13.

“We are delighted to welcome several prominent figures from Asian cinema to this year’s Filmasia. Meeting filmmakers in person is extremely important to us, as it allows our audiences to discover not only the films themselves but also the stories, experiences, and countries behind their creation,” said festival director Karla Stojáková.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Filmasia (@filmasiafestival)

The festival will take place at Bio Oko in Prague from December 3 to 13, 2026.

Selected films will then be screened at Kino Art in Brno from January 6 to 23, 2027, and at Biograf Kotva in České Budějovice from January 27 to February 1, 2027.

All films will be screened in their original languages with Czech and English subtitles.

World.title: Prague Christmas Markets Reveal Prices for Mulled Wine, Sausages and More
World.content:
Prague’s main Christmas markets will open on Saturday, November 28, with mulled wine priced at 100 CZK and sausages costing 180 CZK.

Organizers say prices for several popular refreshments have remained unchanged, while the sausage is the main item to have become more expensive.



The markets on Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square will run until January 6, 2027, with stalls open daily from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

The company Taiko, which organizes the markets, says Prague remains among the most affordable Christmas market destinations in Europe for food and drinks.

The price of mulled wine has remained at 100 CZK since 2024. A hot apple drink will cost 70 CZK, the same as last year.

The price of sausages has increased, however. The item rose from 160 CZK to 180 CZK during the Easter markets and will remain at that level for the Christmas season.

The company also points to the ingredients used at its stalls. The sausages are made exclusively for the markets and contain up to 97 percent meat, while the mulled wine is produced from grapes supplied by the Moravian winery Chateau Valtice.

Prices at Prague’s main Christmas markets:

Mulled wine: 100 CZK

Hot apple drink: 70 CZK

Sausage: 180 CZK

Hot dog: 90 CZK

Sausage in a baguette: 180 CZK

Langoš with garlic, cheese and ketchup: 200 CZK

Draft Pilsner, 0.4 litre: 80 CZK

Hot chocolate: 130 CZK

Spiral potato: 100 CZK

French fries: 185 CZK

Record number of performers expected

The 2026 programme will feature a record 5,329 performers. Activities will include weekend workshops for children, a St. Nicholas Day event and the traditional Christmas Eve celebrations.

On December 24, festive soup will be served on Old Town Square from 11 a.m. A performance of the Czech Christmas Mass is scheduled for 9 p.m.

For safety reasons, the organizers have not announced the exact time of Saturday’s tree-lighting ceremony. They are also encouraging visitors to spread their first visits across the weekend and avoid bringing bulky luggage to the markets.

World.title: Expedia to Acquire Czech Flight Booking Company Kiwi.com
World.content:
American travel company Expedia Group has agreed to acquire Czech flight booking platform Kiwi.com, bringing a change of ownership to the Brno-based business.

The transaction is expected to be completed by the middle of 2027, although the companies have not disclosed its value.

The acquisition will see the departure of Kiwi.com’s current majority shareholder, US investment fund General Atlantic, which has controlled the company since 2019. Co-founder Oliver Dlouhý, who holds a minority stake, is also expected to exit.



Expedia said the deal would strengthen its technology and expand its position in the European air travel market. Kiwi.com generated approximately €227 million in revenue last year, equivalent to around CZK 5.6 billion.

Expedia said the acquisition would give travelers access to a wider selection of flights and provide new opportunities for growth across its brands, including Expedia, Hotels.com and Vrbo.

Kiwi.com was founded in Brno in 2012 by Dlouhý and his business partners. The company became known internationally for its search technology, which allowed it to combine flights from airlines that did not necessarily have direct partnerships with the platform.

The company has since developed into an international flight retailer, focusing on technology, automation and artificial intelligence to improve its operations.

The acquisition comes after several years of restructuring at Kiwi.com, which faced financial difficulties following the decline in air travel during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The company reduced its workforce by more than 200 employees in 2024. Earlier this year, it announced plans to cut approximately 250 jobs from a workforce of around 700.

Expedia Group was founded in 1996 as a division of Microsoft. It operates an online travel platform offering bookings for flights, accommodation, car rentals and activities, as well as technology services for corporate partners.

World.title: Christmas Trees You Can Replant After the Holidays Are Available in Prague
World.content:
Residents of Prague and Brno can choose a living Christmas tree this year and give it a chance to grow in the forest after the holidays.

Both cities are offering small potted firs that can be planted in spring with the help of foresters.

In Prague, the Forests of the Capital City of Prague are running their Christmas fir project for the tenth consecutive year. The initiative, known as A Christmas Fir with a Future, allows people to buy a young silver fir for 150 CZK.

The trees, approximately 50 centimeters tall, have been grown in a forest nursery in Čimický háj. Unlike cut Christmas trees, they retain their roots and can continue growing after Christmas.



The organizers acknowledge that the firs may not look like traditional Christmas trees. Their branches are often irregular, and each tree has its own shape.

The project also aims to support the return of silver fir to Czech forests. The native species (Abies alba) became scarce during the 20th century, partly because of air pollution, forestry practices and excessive numbers of wild animals.

Where to buy a living Christmas tree in Prague

The potted firs are available at several locations, including the Ďáblice Garden Center, the Prales eco-center and forest lodges in Hostivař, Chuchle, Šárka, Běchovice, Kunratice and Čimice.

How to care for a potted Christmas tree

A living Christmas tree needs more attention than a cut one. It should remain outdoors in a cool place, such as a balcony or garden, for as long as possible before being brought inside.

The tree should be gradually acclimatized to the warmer indoor temperature. The room should ideally stay below 20 degrees Celsius, and the soil needs regular watering. Spraying the needles with water can also help.

After Christmas, the tree should be moved back to a cooler environment gradually.

Even with careful handling, survival is not guaranteed. According to the Masaryk Forest Křtiny School Forest Enterprise, around 60 percent of the Christmas firs planted in previous years have successfully taken root.

World.title: Higher Prices, Fuller Hotels: Prague Is Becoming a Luxury City Break
World.content:
Prague is strengthening its position as a high-end tourist destination, attracting visitors willing to spend more on accommodation and services.

The Czech capital has ranked ahead of Vienna and Berlin in an international tourism index, while demand for luxury hotels continues to rise.

More than 2.3 million tourists visited Prague between July and September 2026, representing a three percent increase compared with the same period last year.



The city received a score of 92.7 out of 100 in the Global Tourist Perception Index, compiled by Data Appeal and Mabrian Intelligence. Vienna scored 85.6, while Berlin received 78.4.

The ranking assessed several aspects of the visitor experience, including satisfaction with accommodation, safety and the variety of tourist attractions.

According to František Cipro, chairman of the board of Prague City Tourism, the results reflect a shift in the city’s tourism profile.

“Prague clearly demonstrates that it is no longer a budget tourist destination, nor does it wish to be one,” he said.

The trend is also reflected in visitor spending. During the first half of 2026, Prague welcomed more than 3.8 million tourists, a one percent increase year-on-year. However, Mastercard payment data showed that spending by visitors from selected foreign markets rose by 18 percent.

Tourists from China and South Korea recorded the most significant increases in spending.

Accommodation figures point in the same direction. Almost two-thirds of guests staying in Prague hotels choose four- or five-star properties.

In 2025, the average price of a hotel room in the capital stood at around CZK 3,000 per night. In central Prague, the average rose to approximately CZK 4,100, while luxury hotels charged around CZK 5,800.

Demand for higher-end accommodation has remained strong despite rising prices. In September 2026, luxury hotels recorded an occupancy rate of 83 percent, their highest September result in seven years.

Germany Remains the Largest Source Market

Tourism continued to grow during the first nine months of 2026, with Prague recording more than 6.1 million visitors, a two percent increase compared with the same period in 2025.

Germany remained the largest source market for international visitors during the third quarter.

Some other markets also recorded notable growth. Visitor numbers from Taiwan increased by 27 percent, followed by Israel at 26 percent and Ireland at 23 percent.

World.title: How to Choose a High School in the Czech Republic: Open Days and School Fairs
World.content:
Choosing a high school is an important decision for students and their families.

School websites and brochures can provide useful information, but visiting schools in person offers a much better idea of what studying there is actually like.

Open days and high school fairs are two ways to explore the available options, meet teachers and students, and find out which school might be the right fit.



This is the first article in our series on choosing a high school in the Czech Republic.

Visit Schools During Open Days

Open days give prospective students and their parents the opportunity to look around a school before applying.

High schools open their doors to visitors, allowing them to explore classrooms, workshops and laboratories, meet teachers and current students, and ask questions about studying there.

An open day can help families find out more about:

Study programmes: What courses and specialisations does the school offer?

Admission requirements: What are the conditions for applying, and how does the entrance examination work?

Future opportunities: What options are available after graduation, including further education and employment?

School environment: What is the atmosphere like, and would the school be a good fit for the student?

Open days take place throughout the school year, with many schools organising them ahead of the application period.

Dates vary from one institution to another, so check individual school websites or use the online overview of high school open days to find upcoming events.

Compare Schools at High School Fairs

High school fairs offer another opportunity to explore different institutions without having to visit each one separately.

In Prague, one of the main events is SCHOLA PRAGENSIS, where visitors can meet representatives of secondary schools from different regions.

You can visit META stand at Schola Pragensis, Prague’s high school fair, taking place from 26 to 28 November at the Prague Congress Centre

– stand number 245 on the 2nd floor.

The META team of professionals will help you explore the options and answer all your questions.

Students and parents can compare study programmes, ask questions about admission procedures and learn more about individual schools directly from their representatives.

These events are particularly useful for students who have not yet decided what they want to study or are still considering several different options. Meeting representatives from multiple schools in one place can help narrow down the choices.

If you live outside Prague, you can also find a high school fair in your region.

Use Worksheets to Help Make Your Decision

Comparing schools, admission requirements and study programmes can quickly become confusing, especially when several institutions are under consideration.

Free worksheets are available to help students organise information, compare their options and think about what they want from their future school.

You can download the worksheets here.

World.title: EF English Proficiency Index: Brno Speaks Better English Than Prague
World.content:
Prague has improved its English proficiency score, but it still trails Brno, according to the latest EF English Proficiency Index (EF EPI).

The Czech capital gained nine points over the past year, while Brno recorded a slight decline. Despite the contrasting trends, the South Moravian city remains ahead.



The Czech Republic ranked 24th out of 117 countries and regions in this year’s global index, published by education company EF Education First. Its score of 569 points represents a drop of 13 points and one place compared with the previous year.

The country remains in the high-proficiency category, although several neighboring states performed better. Austria ranked second worldwide with 613 points, followed by Germany in fourth place with 611. Slovakia came 11th with 594 points, while Poland ranked 15th with 587.

Slovakia’s performance is particularly notable. The country has gained 49 points since 2016, making it one of Europe’s most improved performers over the past decade. Although its score fell slightly compared with last year, it still leads the Czech Republic by 25 points.

Brno Maintains Its Lead Over Prague

Brno scored 613 points in this year’s assessment, placing it 28 points ahead of Prague, which recorded 585.

The gap between the two cities has narrowed, however. Prague improved from 576 points last year, while Brno fell from 620.

Brno’s result is particularly strong in an international comparison. Its score matches Austria’s, which ranked second among the countries included in the global index.

The regional figures also support Brno’s position. The South Moravian Region recorded 606 points, the highest score among Czech regions.

Sweden Takes First Place in Global Rankings

The Netherlands has lost its position at the top of the global English proficiency rankings, with Sweden taking first place this year with 615 points.

The Dutch finished fifth with 609 points. Austria, Denmark and Germany occupied the places between them, scoring 613, 612 and 611 points, respectively.

The survey was conducted through the Ipsos Instant Research application and focused on respondents’ self-assessments of their language abilities.

World.title: Massive Attack to Headline Colours of Ostrava in 2027
World.content:
British trip-hop pioneers Massive Attack will perform at Colours of Ostrava on July 22, 2027, organisers have confirmed.

The band will take the main stage at the four-day festival, which runs from July 21 to 24 at the former Dolní Vítkovice industrial complex in Ostrava.

The announcement marks Massive Attack’s return to the Czech Republic after a nine-year absence.

The Bristol-born group, formed in 1988, is regarded as one of the most influential acts in the development of trip-hop.

The band is best known for songs including Teardrop, Angel and Unfinished Sympathy. Its music combines electronic sounds with elements of hip-hop, soul and dub, creating a distinctive style that helped shape British music in the 1990s.

Massive Attack’s live performances also feature large-scale visual projections, often incorporating political and social commentary.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Colours of Ostrava official 💛 (@colours_cz)

They join an already announced line-up for Colours of Ostrava 2027 that includes Robbie Williams, Ellie Goulding, Martin Garrix, 5 Seconds of Summer and David Kushner.

World.title: FM Anita Orbán: dozens of Hungarian companies willing to help rebuild Ukraine
World.content:
More than 40 Hungarian companies have told the government they are willing to take part in Ukraine’s reconstruction once the war ends, Foreign Minister Anita Orbán has announced, following high-level talks between the two countries.

Hungary to help rebuilding Ukraine after the war

Speaking on Kossuth Radio on Thursday, Anita Orbán said post-war rebuilding had been among the subjects discussed during Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s visit to Transcarpathia on Tuesday. The talks also covered railway and road infrastructure developments and the possible opening of a new border crossing.

She said many Ukrainian industrial facilities had relocated to Transcarpathia, making the region an increasingly prosperous part of the country’s economy. Hungarian businesses, particularly those based in eastern Hungary, could benefit from participating in reconstruction projects, she added.

The minister did not identify the companies involved or specify which sectors they represent. The figure therefore reflects expressions of interest communicated to the Hungarian government, rather than confirmed contracts or reconstruction commitments.

Bilateral talks to continue in 2027

Orbán described Tuesday’s meeting between Magyar and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as an opportunity to establish the main directions for renewed cooperation. The next step is expected to be a meeting of the bilateral intergovernmental committee in the first quarter of 2027. The two countries’ agriculture and economy ministers are also due to hold talks.

Energy cooperation was another topic. Orbán said Hungary already imports crude oil from Ukraine, and companies believe the volume could be doubled. Hungary, meanwhile, supplies diesel to Ukraine, generating revenue for Hungarian oil and gas company MOL.

The minister also discussed the gradual improvement in bilateral relations over the past six months. She said Ukraine had begun addressing the rights of the ethnic Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia, after which Hungary took steps towards opening one of the clusters in Ukraine’s EU accession negotiations.

Budapest has asked Kyiv to accelerate the implementation of language legislation adopted by the Ukrainian parliament. According to Orbán, Ukraine has promised to do so. She stressed that enforcement of the law had been included as a condition in the EU accession process, and said Ukraine could not make further progress if it failed to protect the rights of its Hungarian minority.

In case you missed it: Magyar and Zelensky discuss energy, trade and EU membership as Hungary and Ukraine seek closer ties

Hungary wants to stay outside Ukraine loan

Orbán also reiterated that Hungary would prefer not to participate in a proposed €45 billion loan programme for Ukraine. However, she confirmed that Budapest would not block the process.

Asked about Russia’s response to the Hungarian-Ukrainian meeting, she said the Kremlin had made no official or unofficial comment. Diplomatic relations between Budapest and Moscow remain in place, she added, describing Russia’s reciprocal response to the expulsion of ten Russian diplomats as normal diplomatic practice.

Separately, Orbán announced that Hungary would join the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children, which aims to support the safe return of children taken during the war and reunite families.
