World.title: Viktor Orbán establishes new international foundation with one goal
World.content:
Former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán has established a new international foundation intended to bring together organisations and intellectuals committed to national sovereignty and traditional values, while also supporting political resistance to Hungary’s current government.

Viktor Orbán created a new institution

The Pro Patria International Foundation was announced on Thursday by Balázs Orbán, a Fidesz politician and member of the European Parliament, who serves as a curator of the new organisation. Its creation was first reported by Politico, which Balázs Orbán subsequently confirmed.

According to the foundation’s stated mission, it aims to develop an international research institute focused on strengthening cooperation between what it describes as national forces. It will seek to connect like-minded thinkers and organisations around the world, draw on the experience of Hungarian state leadership and help young talents establish themselves internationally.

Former campaign chief confirmed the leaks

Balázs Orbán told Politico that the institute created by Viktor Orbán also intends to stimulate debate about reforming the European Union’s institutions. Fundraising has now begun, with the organisation seeking donations from both Hungarian and foreign supporters.

The foundation has not yet decided whether it will apply for funding from the United States. The Trump administration has made several million euros available to support conservative research organisations in Europe. The new institute plans to maintain a presence in Brussels, although it does not intend to open an office there.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Political ambitions extend beyond international research

The organisation’s plans also include a domestic political dimension. In his Facebook announcement, Balázs Orbán said that one of its important tasks during its first years would be to organise and support resistance against what he called the ‘liberal authoritarian system’ in Hungary.

He also criticised the current government’s treatment of research institutions, claiming that internationally recognised institutes had been nationalised and closed at Brussels’ request. He did not identify the organisations he was referring to.

The remarks appear to refer, at least in part, to changes affecting institutions previously supported by the Mathias Corvinus Collegium (MCC). Its Brussels-based research centre closed in September after losing its funding, following the new government’s decision to dissolve the foundation maintaining MCC and reclaim its assets. The previous government had provided the foundation with substantial state assets.

Read also: How business interests close to Orbán and Vučić became intertwined in Hungary and Serbia

The new foundation will stand in line among the rest

Other conservative organisations, including the Centre for Fundamental Rights and the Danube Institute, remain operational. However, the Batthyány Lajos Foundation, which has provided state support for them, is also set to lose government funding.

The Centre for Fundamental Rights has faced additional scrutiny: its background company was searched in September as part of an investigation into suspected mismanagement of funds. Meanwhile, Századvég’s economic research company has undergone substantial staff reductions and continues under the name Hungarian Economic Research.

The Pro Patria foundation’s funding arrangements and future activities remain to be established. Its stated ambitions, however, combine international conservative networking and research with an explicitly political role in Hungary.

World.title: PM Magyar says EU summit talks are entering their final stretch, but agreement remains elusive
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar warned that the “real fight” was only just beginning as EU leaders gathered in Brussels on Thursday for talks on the bloc’s next long-term budget and support for Ukraine.

In a Facebook video, Magyar said the leaders were approaching the “last but one round” of negotiations. Given the sharply differing positions in the room, he said the chances of an agreement on Thursday were “roughly zero”, adding that a deal by Christmas also looked unlikely.

Hungary rejects cuts to its funding

The main issue at the summit is the EU’s 2028–2034 budget, which requires unanimous approval from all 27 member states, as well as the European Parliament’s consent.

Magyar said Hungary would not accept a proposal that reduced the funds allocated to the country or required it to pay more into the EU budget. Budapest wants continued support for traditional cohesion and agricultural policies, rather than shifting funding away from them towards newer priorities.

Hungary is coordinating with the “Friends of Cohesion” group, which brings together 17 member states, and is also in contact with the Visegrád Four, Magyar said. He added that the countries were reinforcing one another’s positions and jointly defending cohesion policy and Central European interests.

If you missed it: Ukraine pledges to accelerate minority rights progress for ethnic Hungarians

Budapest opposes linking the budget to Ukraine funding

Magyar also said Hungary, alongside several other member states, could not accept linking the long-term budget negotiations to a proposed €45 billion loan for Ukraine.

Several countries, led by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, want all member states to share responsibility for the loan, rather than allowing Hungary, Slovakia and Czechia to remain exempt. Bulgaria has also sought an exemption.

However, a possible compromise is emerging. According to Index’s report, Bulgaria is open to contributing to the €20 billion portion intended to support Ukraine’s general budget, while refusing to take part in the military assistance component. Hungary and Bulgaria were reported by Politico to be more open to a compromise than Slovakia and Czechia.

European Council President António Costa hopes to make enough progress at Thursday’s summit to reach an agreement on the EU budget at a further meeting in December. But leaders remain divided over the budget’s overall size, how funding should be distributed and whether Ukraine’s financing should be tied to the negotiations.

World.title: Women leaders meet in Budapest to discuss tackling violence against women
World.content:
A Budapest luncheon organised by the EIB Group and UNHCR brought together women from diplomacy, business, public institutions and civil society to discuss prevention, protection and women’s economic independence.

On the occasion of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, the European Investment Bank (EIB) Group’s Budapest Office and the UNHCR Representation for Central and South-East Europe jointly hosted a luncheon bringing together senior women leaders and professionals from across Hungary and the international community.

The event opened with remarks by Stefania Ciraolo, Head of the EIB Office in Budapest, who highlighted the role of financial institutions in supporting women’s empowerment. She said economic empowerment was about more than income, describing it as a source of choice, independence and opportunity.

Ciraolo also stressed that the EIB Group has zero tolerance for gender-based violence and harassment, and seeks to identify and address gender-related risks in the projects it supports. “Behind every investment are people,” she said, adding that investment should help create conditions in which women can thrive and reach their full potential.

Refugee women face heightened risks

Noémi Ambrus-Kiry, operations manager of Hegyvidéki Ízlelő restaurant, shared her experience of building a social enterprise that promotes inclusion by providing meaningful employment opportunities for people with disabilities.

The discussion brought together international, European and Hungarian perspectives. Nicole Epting, UNHCR Representative for Central and South-East Europe, highlighted the risks faced by forcibly displaced women and girls, including trafficking, exploitation and gender-based violence.

Epting said more than 60 million women and girls are forcibly displaced worldwide. In 2025, UNHCR and its partners reached approximately 1.6 million people through specialised gender-based violence programmes in 77 countries, but funding shortages continue to leave many without essential protection services.

She called for access to medical care, legal assistance, psychosocial support and safe accommodation, alongside opportunities for economic independence. “Escaping conflict does not always mean escaping violence,” she said.

Barbara Kovacs, Fundamental Rights Portfolio Holder at the European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Training (CEPOL), addressed the role of law enforcement training and capacity-building. Dorottya Szalay, representing the NANE Women’s Rights Association, discussed challenges faced by survivors in Hungary.

Photo: UNCHR

Turning awareness into action

Participants, including diplomatic representatives, business leaders and civil society professionals, shared experiences from their countries and sectors and discussed how their institutions and networks could contribute to addressing violence against women.

Those contributing to the open discussion included Yvette Szepesi, Deputy Head of Mission at the Embassy of the Netherlands; Gülsun Erkul, Ambassador of Türkiye to Hungary; Anita Simon, Deputy CEO of ALTEO; German diplomat Sibylle Pfaff; Andrea Istenes Solti, President of the Hungarian Business Leaders Forum; and Judit Kuszkó, Managing Director of the Hungarian Private Equity and Venture Capital Association.

The discussion highlighted the need to turn awareness into practical measures, including better access to protection and specialised support, greater economic independence for women, safer and more inclusive workplaces, and sustained investment in prevention and response.

The organisers said the exchange underscored that tackling violence against women requires a whole-of-society approach, with businesses, public institutions, international organisations and civil society all playing a role. The informal format also offered participants an opportunity to build connections and explore potential future collaboration.

World.title: Subway plans 300 new restaurants in Central Europe, with Hungary a key target
World.content:
Subway is preparing a major expansion across Central Europe, with Hungary identified as one of the fast-food chain’s priority markets. Its regional master franchise partner, Vienna-based Emerging Bites Holding GmbH, plans to open 300 new restaurants in five countries over the next decade.

Subway to expand across Europe

The expansion programme covers Austria, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Slovenia. Emerging Bites has been responsible for developing and supporting the Subway brand across these five markets since September 2026.

Hungary will be among the central targets of the strategy, with the company choosing Budapest for its first new opening in the country. A restaurant at the WestEnd City Centre shopping mall is scheduled to welcome customers on 27 November.

The new outlet is expected to employ 12 people. According to the company, a typical Subway restaurant creates between 10 and 12 jobs, meaning further openings could also bring additional employment opportunities across the region.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Local franchise partner to operate Budapest outlet

“Hungary is one of our priority growth markets, and we are beginning our expansion in the country in Budapest,” said Emerging Bites chief executive Farshad Abbaszadeh. He said the choice of the WestEnd location, one of the capital’s busiest shopping and transport hubs, reflected the potential the company sees in the Hungarian market.

The new restaurant will be operated by Sub Premier, a local franchise partner owned by Dániel Varga and Katalin Sampers. Emerging Bites said its approach was to combine the international brand’s recognition and central operational support with the knowledge and experience of local partners. The company believes this model will help it respond to market conditions and customer preferences in each country.

Read also: Three Hungarian restaurants named among the world’s Top 100

Long-term regional ambitions

Varga said the partnership would allow the local operator to create new jobs while offering Hungarian customers the Subway experience. The WestEnd restaurant is due to open at 11 AM on 27 November. The launch is expected to be attended by Abbaszadeh, Varga and James MacIsaac, Subway’s executive responsible for master franchise markets in Europe.

The planned 300 openings represent a substantial expansion of Subway’s presence across the five markets, although the company has not provided a country-by-country breakdown or a detailed schedule for the new restaurants. For Hungary, the Budapest opening marks the first step in a wider development plan that places the country among the brand’s most important regional growth opportunities.

World.title: Hungary braces for freezing rain, heavy snowfall and huge temperature drops
World.content:
Hungary is facing a spell of hazardous winter weather, with heavy snowfall and freezing rain expected in several regions before temperatures plunge to as low as -10°C next week. Authorities have urged people to avoid unnecessary travel in areas covered by severe weather warnings.

Yellow and orange warnings for issued for several counties

HungaroMet issued a second-level, orange alert on Thursday for parts of Veszprém County, warning that persistent freezing rain could last for several hours and produce more than 1mm of ice. A first-level warning for lighter freezing rain was also in force in Fejér, Heves, Komárom-Esztergom, Nógrád, Pest, Vas and Zala counties.

The greatest snowfall is expected in the north-western border region. According to HungaroMet, areas around Sopron, Kőszeg, Lake Fertő and Mosonmagyaróvár could receive 10–20cm of fresh snow, with even higher totals possible in the Sopron and Kőszeg Mountains. Elsewhere in western Transdanubia, a thinner covering of up to 5cm is forecast.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Negaive temperatures and freezing rain will make life much harder

Snow is also expected initially in the Northern Hungarian Mountains, where higher elevations could see 5–10cm. At lower levels, however, snowfall may turn into mixed precipitation or rain, depending on its intensity.

The Bakony region is particularly vulnerable to freezing rain, with HungaroMet warning that 1–3mm could fall there before midday on Thursday, potentially creating a substantial layer of ice. Lighter freezing rain is also possible in the Alpokalja region and the Northern Hungarian Mountains. Further showers may bring additional light snow to parts of Transdanubia and northern Hungary on Friday.

Authorities warn against unnecessary journeys

Hungary’s National Directorate General for Disaster Management has advised people in affected areas not to travel on foot or by car unless absolutely necessary. Anyone who must drive should check current warnings and road conditions, use a properly equipped vehicle and allow extra time.

Motorists are advised to keep their fuel tanks fuller than usual and carry a charged mobile phone, food, drinks, warm clothing and blankets in case they become stranded. Drivers should also clear snow and ice from their vehicle roofs before setting off, as falling snow can cause accidents. Ice-laden branches and power lines may break, so cars should not be parked underneath them.

Read also: Hungary to spend an extra EUR 325 million on public roads in 2027

Severe frost expected from Sunday

After the unsettled weather, daytime temperatures are expected to remain between 0°C and 7°C for the rest of the week. Conditions should gradually become drier, with sunny and cloudy spells replacing widespread precipitation.

A significant cold spell is forecast to begin on Sunday. Although daytime temperatures may still reach 0–5°C, overnight lows in northern Hungary could fall to -10°C. By Monday, western parts of the country may experience temperatures remaining below freezing even during the warmest hours of the day.

World.title: Hungary joins international coalition working to bring abducted Ukrainian children home
World.content:
Hungary has joined the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children, an initiative aimed at helping children taken from Ukraine during Russia’s war return safely to their families.

Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced the decision on Thursday, thanking Hungary and his Hungarian counterpart, Anita Orbán, for joining the coalition.

“I thank Hungary and my colleague Anita Orbán for the important decision to join the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children,” Sybiha wrote on X.

Orbán also confirmed the decision in a Facebook post, saying Hungary would support the safe return of Ukrainian children abducted during the war and the reunification of families.

I thank Hungary and my colleague @_OrbanAnita for the important decision to join the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children. All 27 EU Member States are now members of the Coalition. This sends a clear signal of European unity and shared responsibility for the return of Ukrainian children illegally deported and forcibly transferred by Russia. Russia has no right to decide the fate of our children, alter their identity or sever their ties with their families and homeland. Every day of delay in their return is another day of childhood stolen by Russia. International efforts must focus on bringing every Ukrainian child home and ensuring that those responsible for these crimes do not escape justice. — Andrii Sybiha 🇺🇦 (@andrii_sybiha) November 26, 2026

All 27 EU member states now part of the coalition

Sybiha noted that all 27 European Union member states have now joined the initiative. He described this as a clear sign of European unity and shared responsibility for bringing back Ukrainian children whom Russia has illegally deported or forcibly transferred.

He also stressed that Russia has no right to determine the children’s future, change their identities or sever their ties with their families and homeland. International efforts, he said, must focus on bringing every child home and ensuring that those responsible face justice.

Orbán said that few things were as devastating as children being separated from their families because of war. According to estimates cited by the minister, as many as 25,000 children have been taken from Ukraine, while around 3,000 have returned so far.

If you missed it: Hungary approves extra EUR 2.7 million in support for ethnic Hungarians in Transcarpathia

Previous political disagreements over the issue

Hungary’s decision comes after a previous disagreement within the European Parliament over the issue. In May 2025, Fidesz MEPs did not support a resolution condemning the forced removal of Ukrainian children. The text was adopted with 516 votes in favour, two against and 35 abstentions.

Tisza Party MEPs supported the resolution, while Zsuzsanna Borvendég of Mi Hazánk abstained. Fidesz representatives did not take part in the vote, according to HVG.

Russia has acknowledged transferring large numbers of people, including children, from occupied Ukrainian territories to Russia, describing the transfers as evacuations. In August 2022, the Russian Defence Ministry said around 3.5 million people, including half a million children, had been “evacuated” from the conflict zone.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) issued arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova, Russia’s presidential commissioner for children’s rights, in March 2023. The court cited the alleged war crimes of unlawful deportation and transfer of children from occupied areas of Ukraine to Russia.

World.title: Former UN chief Ban Ki-moon attends 1956 anniversary conference in Budapest Parliament
World.content:
Former United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon is attending an international conference at the Hungarian Parliament on 26 November, marking the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution. The event examines the relationship between Hungary’s historic uprising and the United Nations, including the organisation’s response to the Soviet intervention and the fate of Hungarian refugees.

The conference, titled The 1956 Revolution and the United Nations, is being held under the patronage of Ágnes Forsthoffer, Speaker of the National Assembly. Opening speeches are being delivered by Anita Orbán, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, and Zoltán Tarr, Minister for Social Relations and Culture.

Initiated and organised by former Hungarian UN Ambassador Katalin Bogyay, the event brings together international diplomats, historians and researchers. Ban Ki-moon, who led the United Nations between 2007 and 2016, is the guest of honour.

Former UN chief Ban Ki-moon delivers a speech in the Hungarian parliament. Photo: Daily News Hungary

The opening speeches

In their opening speeches, the three Hungarian officials highlighted the continuing relevance of the 1956 Revolution and the principles underpinning the United Nations. Parliament Speaker Ágnes Forsthoffer recalled that around 180,000 Hungarian refugees were welcomed by 37 countries following the crushing of the uprising, with 100,000 resettled in less than ten weeks. She also paid tribute to Danish diplomat Povl Bang-Jensen, who insisted on keeping the identities of witnesses to the Soviet intervention confidential, a decision that cost him both his career and, ultimately, his life.

Foreign Minister Anita Orbán stressed that the strength of the UN today, as in 1956, depends on how faithfully its member states uphold the principles of its Charter. She reaffirmed Hungary’s support for reforming the organisation and called for a Security Council that better represents its members and can respond more effectively to threats to peace.

Meanwhile, Minister for Social Relations and Culture Zoltán Tarr said the courage and solidarity of university students in 1956 had helped revive civil society. He argued that lasting peace requires autonomous universities, a freely operating civil society and organisations capable of holding those in power to account, adding that Hungary plans to adopt a national civil society strategy based on broad dialogue.

Previously restricted UN documents on 1956 opened in 2016

One of the most significant aspects of the conference is its connection to the release of previously restricted United Nations documents concerning the 1956 Hungarian Revolution.

Following the Soviet military intervention in Hungary, the UN Security Council discussed the situation and attempted to secure the withdrawal of Soviet troops. On 4 November 1956, however, the Soviet Union vetoed a US-backed draft resolution calling for their withdrawal. The Security Council subsequently adopted Resolution 120, calling an emergency special session of the General Assembly to address the crisis. The General Assembly also called for Soviet troops to leave Hungary and addressed the humanitarian situation facing Hungarian refugees.

In December 1956, the General Assembly established a special committee to investigate the events in Hungary. Its members collected testimonies from Hungarian refugees and other witnesses abroad, as the committee was not granted access to the country.

A particularly controversial chapter involved Danish diplomat Povl Bang-Jensen, the committee’s second secretary. He refused to hand over the names of Hungarian witnesses who had given confidential testimony, fearing that their relatives remaining in Hungary could face reprisals. The UN subsequently initiated disciplinary proceedings against him. He was found dead in New York in November 1959.

Some documents concerning the committee’s work and the Bang-Jensen case remained restricted for decades.

Photo: Daily News Hungary

If you missed it: Why 4 November is a day of mourning in Hungary: 70 years since Soviet tanks crushed the 1956 revolution

How Hungarian diplomacy helped unlock the archives

The efforts to make these historical records accessible began with research initiated by Hungarian historian András Nagy. In 2016, Katalin Bogyay, then Hungary’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, launched and led diplomatic negotiations involving the United States, Russia and UN officials.

The discussions included the countries’ then UN ambassadors, Samantha Power and Vitaly Churkin, as well as the leadership of the United Nations and Bang-Jensen’s son.

The diplomatic process resulted in approximately 1,500 pages of previously restricted documents becoming available for research in 2016. Around 400 pages of highly confidential material were held in the UN archives, while the remaining documents were kept in Columbia University’s Cordier collection.

The records include material relating to the UN special committee, witness testimonies and the Bang-Jensen case. Historian András Nagy was the first researcher granted access to the material and has since published his findings in both Hungarian and English.

Ban Ki-moon also has a personal connection to the events of 1956. As a school student in South Korea, he was chosen to read aloud a letter addressed to then UN Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld, appealing for international assistance for Hungarians fighting for freedom and democracy.

Later, as UN Secretary-General, Ban supported the release of the historical documents and the international commemoration of the revolution’s 60th anniversary in New York in 2016.

Zoltán Tarr. Photo: Daily News Hungary Anita Orbán. Photo: Daily News Hungary Ágnes Forsthoffer. Photo: Daily News Hungary

International experts examine the lessons of 1956

The Budapest conference also looks at the international significance of the revolution and the lessons it offers for the United Nations today.

In the historical section, András Nagy is presenting the findings of his research into the newly accessible UN documents. Mark Kramer, a Cold War historian from Harvard University, is examining the international context of the revolution, while historian Gusztáv D. Kecskés is discussing the UN’s role in assisting Hungarian refugees.

A separate session focuses on the organisation’s present-day crisis management challenges. Speakers include Vuk Jeremić, former President of the UN General Assembly, and Ambassador György Busztin, former Deputy Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General for Iraq.

The conference is organised by the United Nations Association of Hungary in cooperation with the National Assembly, Ludovika University of Public Service, Széchenyi István University, the Hungarian National Commission for UNESCO, the World Federation of United Nations Associations and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Institute for Cultural Diplomacy, based in Berlin and New York, is supporting the event.

The 70th anniversary conference brings the discussion back to the Hungarian Parliament, the historic location from which messages and appeals for international support were sent during the 1956 Revolution.

World.title: European Parliament Backs Vukovar Anniversary Resolution Criticising Serbia
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

The European Parliament on Thursday adopted a resolution on the 35th anniversary of the fall of Vukovar in eastern Croatia, urging Serbia to grant access to documents in wartime archives and cooperate to help find the remaining missing persons from the Yugoslav wars.

The resolution called for “the cooperation of the competent authorities to establish the fate and whereabouts of those still missing”.

It urged the Serbian authorities to “grant access to relevant wartime archives, disclose all available information on the locations of individual and mass graves, fight against impunity for wartime crimes, and facilitate the recovery, identification and dignified return of victims’ remains to their families”.

The Croatian border town fell to the combined forces of the Yugoslav Army and Serbian paramilitaries on November 18, 1991, who went on to commit numerous atrocities. By then, the town was largely destroyed.

The resolution also strongly condemned “all forms of denial, minimisation or glorification of war crimes”, noting the public honours paid to the convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic at his funeral in Belgrade in July this year.

It further called for educational, cultural and commemorative programmes that promote a “fact-based understanding of the Croatian Homeland War and the 1990s”, while encouraging reconciliation and respect for all victims.

The legacy of the 1990s war has long been a key issue of disagreement between Croatia and Serbia, and the resolution has sparked renewed controversy.

Ahead of the European Parliament vote, the resolution was criticised by Serbia’s student movement, which under the name Student List won Serbia’s recent parliamentary elections.

The student movement argued that there should also be recognition of war crimes committed against Serb civilians during the Croatian conflict. It said the resolution did not contribute to an “objective understanding of historical events” or to reconciliation.

It further argued that the draft resolution overlooks killings, persecution and mass displacement of Serbs, particularly during the Croatian military operations Flash and Storm in 1995.

“Responsibility for war crimes must be individual and established on the basis of evidence and final court judgments, rather than attributed to entire nations,” the student movement said.

Austrian MEP Helmut Brandstatter, from the Renew Europe liberal political group, had proposed an alternative resolution, centred on regional scope of responsibility. His proposal was supported by the RECOM Reconciliation Network, the Humanitarian Law Centre, the Humanitarian Law Center Kosovo, Documenta – Centre for Dealing with the Past, the Centre for Civic Education, Human Rights Action and the Association for Social Research and Communications.

But the media outlet N1 reported that Renew Europe gave up on its proposal after a few minor changes were made.

Among the material added to resolution was a line saying that “families of missing persons of all nationalities also continue to wait for answers”. It was also added that in 2010, Serbia’s then President Boris Tadic “paid tribute to the victims, apologised for the crimes committed there and stressed the importance of reconciliation and of establishing the fate of those still missing”.

The resolution instructs the European Parliament’s President to forward the resolution to the governments and parliaments of EU member countries, and those of the Western Balkan countries. However, there is no obligation for them to adopt the resolution themselves.

World.title: Romanian Far-Right Leader Charged With Inciting Violence
World.content:
Romanian prosecutors on Thursday charged hard-line right-winger George Simion with public incitement over remarks calling for members of the Central Electoral Bureau, BEC, to be “skinned in a public square”.

The investigation concerns a video Simion posted on Facebook in March 2025, after the BEC rejected Calin Georgescu’s presidential candidacy on the grounds that it did not meet the legal requirements.

Prosecutors say Simion’s remarks encouraged people to commit crimes.

“Through the video, the defendant urged the public to commit acts constituting serious criminal offences, namely extreme physical assaults, torture or murder,” said a statement issued by the General Prosecutor’s Office.

“The message posted on social media was delivered against the backdrop of a protest taking place outside the BEC headquarters on the same day. The demonstration escalated into violence, with property being set on fire and vandalised and gendarmes injured,” it added.

Public incitement is punishable in Romania with prison terms of three months to three years, or a fine. But if committed by a public official, the penalty increases from one to five years.

Simion dismissed the case as a “farce” and a “politically motivated dossier”. He denied wrongdoing.

Hundreds of his supporters gathered outside the General Prosecutor’s Office, where they chanted his name and accused the justice system of being politically manipulated. No incidents were reported.

Simion’s indictment comes as Romania cracks down on far-right rhetoric and incitement to violence.

Last month, prosecutors sent AUR vice-president and lawmaker Dan Tanasa to trial on charges of inciting hatred and discrimination against foreign workers after he urged people to “refuse orders which are not delivered by a Romanian” and “not to encourage the import of unqualified labourers from Asia and Africa”.

Prosecutors said his statements encouraged discrimination and could damage relations between citizens by undermining mutual respect. Although Romanian lawmakers enjoy parliamentary immunity for statements made in the exercise of their mandate, prosecutors said the immunity did not apply in this case.

Far-right former presidential candidate Calin Georgescu is also facing charges in three cases related to the promotion of fascist and other extremist ideas, as well as alleged complicity in undermining the constitutional order. Georgescu is also under house arrest in a separate case in which he is accused of defrauding a businessman of more than one million euros.

Georgescu, who emerged as the frontrunner in the first round of the November 2024 presidential election before the result was annulled, has denied any wrongdoing.

World.title: Serbia’s New Speaker Sets December Presidential Election, Vucic Signals Boycott
World.content:
New Speaker of Parliament Aleksandar Cupic on Thursday signed the decision calling a presidential election for December 27.

The election will follow the resignation in September of former President Aleksandar Vucic and the defeat in October 25 parliamentary elections of his long-ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS.

“Building democratic institutions is a task for all of us, particularly political actors and the media. Good laws are the walls of our society, while informed citizens are the true masters of the political community,” Cupic said on Thursday.

“I hope we will face a difficult choice between excellent candidates and their programmes. May public debates and a democratic electoral process encourage high voter turnout,” he added.

Vucic, who now heads the SNS-led parliamentary group, has called for a boycott of presidential elections, although his party has yet to announce its final decision. On Wednesday, Vucic described the upcoming election as “the most pointless election in history”, according to news agency Tanjug.

“There are different views within the party. Some want us to support an independent candidate, some want us to field our own candidate, while others, like me, want us to simply ignore the election and let them boast about having taken over everything and won 94 per cent of the vote,” Vucic said, adding that he would await the party’s decision.

Earlier, on Monday, Vucic also said he favoured boycotting a presidential election, but his party would make its final decision at its assembly on December 13. He said he personally leaned towards “not granting them that kind of legitimacy”.

Vucic claimed taking part in an election was pointless under conditions of “absolute terror”.

The Student List, which secured 140 of parliament’s 250 seats in October’s elections, has said it will unveil its presidential candidate shortly after the election is called.

The SNS’s 14 years of rule were marked by allegations of corruption, nepotism, electoral irregularities, a lack of the rule of law and restrictions on media freedom, among others. These issues were also highlighted in the European Union’s regular reports.

Following its defeat, it has accused the Student List of using “revolutionary terror” and seeking to arrest SNS officials and supporters, even though the SNS still officially controls the government, as the Student List has yet to form a new government.

So far, the Student List has only constituted the new parliament, where SNS representatives have also accused it of not providing the party with sufficient space and of denying it any leadership positions within parliamentary bodies.

World.title: EU Could Unlock Additional €338 Million for Albania, Montenegro, North Macedonia
World.content:
The European Union could unlock another 338 million euros with the Growth Plan for the Western Balkans funds in the coming weeks for membership hopefuls Albania, Montenegro and North Macedonia, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Wednesday.

Speaking at a press conference after the EU-Western Balkans Summit in Brussels, von der Leyen said that this year implementation of the Growth Plan reforms “has shifted into high gear”.

“A year ago, partners had delivered 38 per cent of the reform steps due. Today, we have already reached 63 per cent. And these are reforms that make a difference. They could unlock another 338 million euros for Albania, Montenegro and North Macedonia in the coming weeks,” she said.

At the press conference following the summit, Council President Antonio Costa highlighted the progress towards membership made by Montenegro and Albania, saying that “enlargement is a realistic possibility, and it should be seized”.

Serbia did not attend the summit. Costa said he had spoken with Serbia’s acting President, Parliament Speaker Aleksandar Cupic, who had explained that he could not attend because of urgent parliamentary business in Belgrade.

“Of course, we understand, and we will have further opportunities to continue our engagement with the Serbian authorities to continue the accession process into the European Union,” Costa said.

Cupic declined the invitation to Brussels citing his parliamentary obligations amid the institutional transition following the October 25 parliamentary elections, which saw the opposition Student List defeat the long-ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS.

Serbia also skipped last December’s EU-Western Balkans summit in Brussels after its then-President, Aleksandar Vucic, decided not to send a representative following the EU’s failure to agree on opening Cluster 3 in Serbia’s accession negotiations.

World.title: Protesters Across Balkans Demand Action to Curb Violence Against Women
World.content:
Seven women have been killed by partners or relatives in Kosovo this year. Protests were also held followed the killing of Arlinda Zekaj, who was killed in Peja/Pec minutes after police escorted her home after she had reported her former husband for domestic violence.

Zekaj had repeatedly warned the authorities that she was in danger. Kosovo’s Police director resigned after the protests, and 11 police officials and two prosecutors were suspended.

In September, after two women in Kosovo were murdered by their partners within days, BIRN reported on the institutional failures in Kosovo to protect victims who had asked for help.

World.title: Croatia’s War Victims, Mass Graves Documented by New Independent Research
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Nejra Mulaomerovic, Nikola Mokrovic, Tena Banjeglav and Vuk Tesija at the event in Zagreb. Photo: Documenta.

Civil society groups are carrying out the task of documenting wartime crimes and compiling lists of victims – a role that should fall to state institutions, an event at the Cultural and Information Centre in Zagreb on Wednesday was told.

The event showcased the new Croatia research conducted for BIRN’s mass graves database Bitter Land, and the online platform Croatian Book of Remembrance (Hrvatska knjiga pamcenja), newly published by the NGO Documenta – Centre for Dealing with the Past.

Establishing the facts about war crimes and their victims is important for their families, but also for society as a whole and for future generations, as it is the only way to counter nationalist manipulation, Tena Banjeglav from Documenta told the event, which was titled ‘Civil Society, Mass Graves and the Documentation of War Victims in the Former Yugoslavia’.

“We hope that the scope for distorting facts will diminish, allowing for the construction of a society based on trust, solidarity, respect for human dignity and peace,” Banjeglav said, adding that systematic work on such issues is impossible without cross-border cooperation.

The impetus for Documenta’s research was the fact that, when the organisation began work in 2009, no comprehensive list of war victims existed – and none exists to this day.

“Out of approximately 21,000 victims in Croatia, we have already published findings on 12,000, but data on only just over 1,000 victims has so far been made available on the platform,” explained Nikola Mokrovic, Documenta’s coordinator of research into human losses.

“Once all the data has been published on the platform, it will constitute the first comprehensive list of victims in Croatia from 1991 to 1995. For now, the amount of available data is limited, and the process will continue for some time,” Mokrovic said.

The platform includes victims’ names, basic biographical information and details about the research and methodology. In addition to individual data, such as full name, status, ethnicity, citizenship, place of birth, place of residence and location of death, the database also includes narrative accounts providing more detailed descriptions of the suffering endured by victims.

BIRN’s Bitter Land database is a complementary project, focusing on mapping wartime mass graves across the former Yugoslavia.

“The goal of the research is to show the extent of the crimes, make the archive and information available to the public, and bring the data together in one place to facilitate research,” said BIRN’s transitional justice project manager Nejra Mulaomerovic.

Research into mass graves in Bosnia and Herzegovina began in 2020, and the Bitter Land online database became publicly accessible in 2021, initially mapping more than 30 locations in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia, including some of the largest mass graves discovered in the former Yugoslavia.

To date, 95 locations have been mapped in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo and Serbia – and most recently in Croatia.

The platform features contemporary photographs of the sites, archival photographs and footage of exhumations, as well as geographical coordinates, the number of identified persons, court judgments related to the crimes, brief descriptions of the crimes, survivor testimonies and links to sources.

Explore the Bitter Land database here.

World.title: Kosovo Privatisation Process Leaves Many Ex-Workers Out of Pocket
World.content:
Faridin Berisha waited more than a quarter of a century for the privatisation of the Union of Cooperatives of Kosovo, expecting to receive his part of the 20 per cent share of the sale price guaranteed by law to former employees.

The enterprise, which managed cooperatives and their credit operations but had been inactive since 1998, was sold in March last year for 800,000 euros.

Berisha, however, was informed last week by Kosovo’s Privatisation Agency that he was no longer eligible for a share of the proceeds because he had already reached retirement age at the point the enterprise was put up for sale. Indeed, none of the enterprise’s former employees were eligible, according to officials at Kosovo’s Privatisation Agency, PAK.

“The building was usurped by a political party and some warlords, and nobody dared to sell it,” said Berisha, 67. A court took years to rule on the status of the enterprise’s property, and by the time it could eventually be sold, the former employees had either died or entered retirement.

World.title: Letter from Washington: ‘Blue Tsunami’ Puts Trump’s Balkan Relationships in Disarray
World.content:
Greetings from Washington, where Congressional Republicans and President Donald Trump have entered a lame-duck period after being swept away by a “blue tsunami”. Democrats won convincing majorities in both chambers of Congress, including in states that have voted Republican for decades, such as Texas, Kansas, and Mississippi. Voters turned to the Democrats out of frustration with high fuel and food prices caused by the war in Iran, while watching the President and those close to him grow richer.

The midterms were a referendum on the President, but Trump does not see himself as responsible for the Republicans’ rout and remains combative. A confrontation with Democrats is all but guaranteed; once they officially take control of Congress in January, gridlock in Washington’s domestic politics is virtually certain. On foreign policy, Congress could pull in one direction while the White House pulls in another. This could have implications for the Balkans, too.

World.title: BNB: Loans to households in Bulgaria in October 2026 up 20.5% on annual basis
World.content:
Loans to households and NPISHs (non-profit institutions serving households) in Bulgaria added up to 33.635 billion euro at the end of October 2026, an increase of 20.5 per cent compared with October 2025, Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) said in a regular report on monetary statistics on November 26.

This followed 20.7 per cent annual growth in these loans in September 2026, BNB said.

At the end of October 2026, loans for house purchases added up to 20 billion euro, an annual increase of 24.1 per cent, following 24.8 per cent annual growth in September 2026.

Consumer loans amounted to 12.589 billion euro. Compared with October 2025, this was an increase of 16.3 per cent (16 per cent annual growth in September 2026).

Deposits of Households and NPISHs were 57.799 billion euro at the end of October 2026.

This was an increase of 15.4 per cent compared with October 2025 (16.2 per cent annual growth in September 2026), BNB said.

World.title: PM Radev says EC’s proposal that Bulgaria be fined over excessive deficit is unfair
World.content:
Prime Minister Roumen Radev said on November 26 that European Commission’s proposal that Bulgaria be fined for its excessive budget deficit is unfair, given the country’s efforts to improve public finances and that other EU countries are also in an excessive deficit procedure but are failing to reduce it.

Radev, speaking to reporters on arrival for a special two-day meeting of the European Council said that Bulgaria was the first for which such a fine is proposed under the new European rules, and he described the reasons as procedural, not political.

“I see purely procedural reasons, because for the first time there is a change in the rules for sanctioning, and for the first time this is happening precisely with the arrival of the Bulgarian budget,” Radev said.

“Don’t forget that this is not a standard budget, it came in August. That’s how we found ourselves – the change in the political situation, the elections in April, a new government in May, a budget only at the end of July,” he said.

“So for the first time our budget encountered a change in the rules. And they are that the fines were much larger. Over 10 times larger and many countries before us had excessive deficits and they were sanctioned under this old procedure,” Radev said.

“But because it has a large ceiling on fines, it has never come to actual fining. Now the ceiling is very low, you know, 0.02 per cent. But we are the first country to come with an excessive deficit under these new rules.”

This fine is “symbolic” in financial terms, Radev said.

“But it is of course reputational and is used with great enthusiasm by the opposition in Sofia, which is actually the reason we got here.”

Under no circumstances will we fulfill the opposition’s nihilistic dreams of having European funds and payments under the Recovery and Resilience Plan stopped, he said.

“There is no question of this at all and it will definitely not happen. Because Bulgaria is very clearly implementing a strict financial policy in our face and this is appreciated. There can be no question of any suspension of EU funds. This is a standard procedure that was necessary due to an excessive deficit and exactly at the moment when our budget was released. So things are clear there.”

According to Radev, the European Commission gave a positive assessment of the government’s measures for the 2027 Budget.

“That is, the assessment of our Budget, which we are making for 2027, is positive and encouraging, that Bulgaria, with the measures taken in this budget, is already starting to significantly reduce its deficit,” Radev said.

“Otherwise, it is unfair, it is unfair, because we have the largest gradient of deficit reduction from 2026 to 2027. And I expect that there will still be reason here, because we should be encouraged for reducing the deficit with such a gradient, while there are other countries that simultaneously have an excessive deficit and fail to reduce it at all. The procedure will be activated for them next year as well.”

The European Commission must analyse its abilities to realistically assess the financial situation in the member states, Radev said.

“Why did the European Commission suddenly find that Bulgaria has such an excessive deficit?” he said.

“How did it suddenly find that we have macroeconomic imbalances? But excuse me, these macroeconomic imbalances do not happen in three months, nor in six months. They accumulate over years.

“How did the Commission now find out that budget funds are being spent indiscriminately in Bulgaria, without the necessary control? How did Bulgaria suddenly, in April and May of last year, lower its inflation enough for the convergence report to be published,” he said.

“And in August, inflation again went beyond any criteria. There are things here that the European Commission must analyse in terms of its ability to realistically assess the financial situation in the member states. If it does not do so, it means that there are political motives, not economic ones, behind our admission to the euro zone.”

Radev commented on what Bulgaria’s position will be in discussing the EU budget.

“There are three important pillars of our demands,” he said.

“First of all, we must not back down from cohesion, we know that this is the main instrument for the unity of the union, for the economic development of the union.

“Second, we insist on clear financial support for the Black Sea region, and not just mentioning it. We all know how much countries like Bulgaria and Romania are involved in the actions in the Black Sea, especially with the attacks on merchant ships,” he said.

“These are significant costs for us and they must be taken into account. Next, this is the refusal of own resources based on the European emissions trading system and tobacco excise duties. For us, this approach is unacceptable because it harms Bulgaria disproportionately. These are our lines of action under this budget.”

“What we are negotiating with President Antonio Costa is a plus for Bulgaria. At least as far as our income in the European budget is concerned. And the amount is not small at all, so I really hope we can find a good balance that will benefit our country.”

He was skeptical that an understanding will be reached on November 26.

“There are many contradictions that we need to iron out. But I rely on the will and responsibility of all member states so that we can reach a consensus. Our view is that the budget must be achieved within this year. So that from 2028 we can already work on this new financial framework.”

Bulgaria wants to implement a new approach to the Ukrainian loan, as Bulgaria is ready to be included in the budget for non-military support, Radev said.

“I want there to be a very clear difference between Bulgaria and Czechia, Slovakia and Hungary. Czechia, Slovakia and Hungary have refused from the very beginning and are not part of the countries that guarantee this loan. From the very beginning. Both 2025 and 2026. They said ‘no’ from the very beginning and are not.”

“While the government of Zhelyazkov and then confirmed by the government of Gyurov, we have so far been guarantors of two loans – 45 billion from last year, 45 billion from this year,” he said.

“That is, Bulgaria has already undertaken to be a guarantor for a loan of 90 billion and we pay the interest within the framework of the general European budget on these loans,” Radev said.

“The question is from now on for next year, the request for another 45 billion for a loan. At our explicit insistence, and I am glad that this is already being accepted by the European institutions and by Antonio Costa, we will also talk today with Mrs. Von der Leyen, but she has already expressed support for our position that this loan is divided into two components.

Twenty-five billion euro goes to military support and 20 billion for budgetary non-military support, he said.

“We are ready to join in non-military support and with a clear request that our support as guarantors go specifically targeted to the areas with a compact Bulgarian population from our historical community,” he said.

“We have over 300 000 Bulgarians in Ukraine. They need healthcare, they need heating, electricity, transport, so I hope the European Commission will accept our approach, which we will insist on, because we, on the other hand, cannot abdicate from our obligations as a state and as a society to our historical diaspora, to our compatriots in Ukraine.”

Radev also commented on the EC’s request to ban Russian athletes from participating in competitions in Europe, as part of the proposed 22nd package of sanctions against Moscow.

“Not just about athletes. We’re also talking about tourism related to sports events and activities, even cultural events. And I think we’re going too far to politicise sports and cultural events in this way. So we have our reservations there,” Radev said.

World.title: Bulgarian Parliament approves draft 2027 Budget package at first reading
World.content:
Bulgaria’s National Assembly passed the 2027 Budget Act at first reading late on November 25, with 126 MPs from Prime Minister Roumen Radev’s ruling Progressive Bulgaria group in favour and 81 opposed.

Earlier in the day, MPs also approved at first reading the health care and pensions budgets, which are separate from state budget and part of the Budget package.

Given Progressive Bulgaria’s majority of 131 MPs in the 240-seat National Assembly, the Budget is expected to pass without much difficulty well before the end of the calendar year 2026.

If that is indeed the case, it would be a rather rare occurrence in Bulgaria’s most recent parliamentary history, where political instability resulted in eight elections in five years, producing short-lived parliaments that often adopted budgets very late. Of the last five Budget packages, only the 2024 Budget Act was passed before the end of the previous calendar year.

The 2027 Budget package tabled by the Cabinet envisions a consolidated fiscal programme with revenues of 51.07 billion euro and 55.97 billion euro in spending, with a target deficit estimated of 4.91 billion euro in real terms, or 3.5 per cent of gross domestic product (on a cash basis, rising to 4.2 per cent with additional defence spending).

The economic growth target set in the Budget is 2.5 per cent and sets the debt ceiling at 44.4 billion euro, with the government allowed to issue 8.6 billion euro in new debt in 2027.

World.title: PM Radev, Finance Ministry, try to shift blame as Bulgaria faces possible fine over excessive deficit
World.content:
Prime Minister Roumen Radev and his Finance Ministry have tried to shift blame on to previous governments as Bulgaria faces a possible fine because of its inaction to address the excessive deficit.

Radev’s comments at a November 25 regular meeting of the Cabinet came nine days after he told his ministers to stop blaming previous governments.

The Bulgarian government information service quoted Radev as telling the November 25 meeting: “Yesterday, the European Commission slapped a resounding slap on everyone who over the years spent recklessly without attracting investments, who borrowed without developing the economy, lied about the real deficit to get us into the euro zone, and led the finances to an excessive deficit and catastrophe”.

According to Radev, the European Commission’s good forecast for next year “is a clear confirmation that the course taken by the government to restore state finances is correct”.

“So we will not fulfill the nihilistic dreams of the opposition to stop our European funding and payments under the RRP (Recovery and Resilience Plan),” Radev said.

Radev said that the government “will continue with the reforms and the elimination of inherited inefficient and corrupt practices in public enterprises”.

“Since the beginning of the year, foreign direct investment has increased by more than 100 per cent, and this percentage is increasing even more,” he said (In fact, going by Bulgarian National Bank data, as reported by The Sofia Globe, the increase in FDI in January – September 2026 is about 66 per cent on an annual basis).

A statement by the Finance Ministry on November 24, when the European Commission announced its recommendation that Bulgaria should be fined, offered similar arguments.

“Today’s assessment by the European Commission (EC)—part of the European Semester’s Autumn Package—points to a significant deviation from the recommended trajectory for net expenditure for 2026, as well as the risk of sanctions for failing to comply with the Council’s recommendation of July 10 2026,” the Finance Ministry said.

“This situation is a direct consequence of accumulated systemic problems and the political crisis of recent years—issues for which all political forces bear shared responsibility,” the ministry said.



According to the Finance Ministry “it is important to clarify that such a sanction has no bearing on the fifth payment under the Recovery and Resilience Plan, nor is it expected to block funds from European sources”.

“The government will continue to restore the state’s financial stability, while strictly safeguarding key social commitments, support for vulnerable groups, and predictability for citizens and public services,” the ministry said.

“The responsibility now lies with the National Assembly—we expect all political parties to demonstrate statesmanship during the adoption and implementation of the 2027 Budget, so that the flawed practices leading to EU sanctions may be consigned to the past once and for all,” it said.

Of the eight governments that Bulgaria had between January 2017 and January 2026, while Radev was president, he appointed four as interim administrations. Of those four, one was in office for 308 days, from 2022 to 2023. It was headed by Gulub Donev, who currently is Radev’s Finance Minister.

Assen Vassilev, leader of opposition party We Continue the Change and a former finance minister, alleged that Radev was lying, saying that the evidence was in the reports of the European Commission on the economy and finances of Bulgaria in the years before 2026.

Vassilev said that the European Commission report clearly states that the 2026 Budget is the one with a problematic deficit.

This budget was written by the Radev Cabinet and adopted by the Progressive Bulgaria MPs – even though the opposition in the form of We Continue the Change and Democratic Bulgaria had warned that it could lead to European sanctions for refusing to optimise spending.

“If there weren’t 1.5 billion euro more for expenses to support the administration, we could easily have a 4.1 per cent deficit, which with the derogation for military spending would have allowed us not to enter an excessive deficit procedure,” Vassilev said.

The derogation to which he was referring is an EU decision that allows a deficit above the three per cent ceiling in the euro zone if the expenditure that leads to it is in the field of defence. The exception is due to the threat to European security from Russia and the war it is waging in Ukraine.

The European Commission said that it also has concerns about the draft Budget for 2027 and will monitor Bulgarian finances closely in the first six months after January 1 due to the risks facing the economy.

Vassilev said that the European Commission’s reports on Bulgaria for each year are public and none of them have mentioned an excessive deficit or a problem with the financial framework.

So far, Bulgaria has not been sanctioned for unbalanced finances, as the Commission is now threatening.

Vassilev said that next year’s Budget, currently at first-reading stage in Parliament, is “even worse” than the criticised Budget 2026, because “it hits the foundation of the economy, investments and consumption and will bring us a recession”.

He again called for the draft Budget to be withdrawn by the Finance Ministry and revised. And for a new version to be submitted “by different Finance Minister”.

(Photo: government.bg)

World.title: European Parliament approves 2027 EU budget
World.content:
In a vote on November 25, the European Parliament gave its final greenlight to the last annual budget of the 2021-2027 EU long-term budget framework.

In the 720-member European Parliament, the 2027 budget was adopted by 406 votes to 184, with 69 abstentions.

In a deal reached on November 11, the European Parliament and member state governments agreed to set the overall level of commitment appropriations (legal promises to pay in the same year or later) at 199.7 billion euro, and payment appropriations (actual payments made to beneficiaries) at 211.5 billion euro.

In commitment appropriations, this sets the 2027 budget at 0.99 per cent of the EU’s gross national income (GNI).

The European Parliament secured an additional 300 million euro for its priorities compared to the European Commission’s proposal, boosting investment in research, transport and energy networks, Erasmus+, civil protection, border management, military mobility, the EU’s neighbourhood, and humanitarian aid. The deal also includes stronger cybersecurity and security capabilities for the EU institutions and delegations.

Key increases compared with the European Commission’s proposal include 39 million euro for the EU’s Southern and Eastern Neighbourhood, 30 million euro for humanitarian aid and 30 million euro for border management and migration.

MEPs secured more research funding through Horizon Europe with 21.5 million euro extra, and for transport and energy networks an additional 22.5 million euro.

For education, the Erasmus+ programme receives an additional 14 million euro and the civil protection mechanism is reinforced by 13.5 million euro.

Further increases support military mobility (10 million euro), and climate and environmental action (10 million euro).

The 4.9 billion euro NextGenerationEU over-run costs are to be dealt with as agreed previously through a “cascade mechanism”, designed to manage the borrowing costs and protect flagship programmes.

The amount allocated to servicing the Ukraine Support Loan debt is set at 650 million euro, in line with the European Commission’s proposal.

The European Parliament, Council and Commission have also acknowledged in a joint statement the possibility of covering the loan’s debt service costs by mobilising the Ukraine Support Loan special instrument in 2027.

As The Sofia Globe reported previously, the Council of the European Union formally adopted on November 23 the EU’s budget for 2027.

World.title: Bulgaria’s capital creates special Christmas in Sofia events website, with version in English
World.content:
Sofia municipality said on November 24 that it has created a special Christmas in Sofia website, where everyone can easily and conveniently find information about holiday events and experiences in Sofia in one place.

After doubling its Christmas decorations last year, Sofia municipality continues to upgrade the city’s festive look, the statement said. This Christmas, Sofia will shine with even more lights, with new and updated decorations along some of the capital’s most iconic streets and boulevards, it said.

For the first time, there will be Christmas decorations on Tsar Osvoboditel Blvd, and Knyaz Alexander Dondukov and Cherni Vruh boulevards will welcome the holidays with renewed decorations.

Sofia municipality will also complete the decoration of Georgi S. Rakovski St., which began last year, by doubling the scope of the holiday decorations.

Additional Christmas lights will also be in front of St. Nedelya Church, and the German Christmas Market will also contribute to the festive look of the city with additional decorations.

On December 1, Sofia mayor Vassil Terziev will light the lights of Sofia’s large Christmas tree in front of the St. Alexander Nevsky cathedral. Festively decorated trees will delight Sofia residents on St. Nedelya Square, Macedonia Square and in front of the National Palace of Culture, the municipality said.

The Christmas train will be among the special experiences for the little ones and will await its passengers at St. Alexander Nevsky Square from December 2 to January 3.

The English-language version of the Christmas in Sofia website is to be found at this link.

World.title: Opposition lashes Radev’s government over EC recommendation to fine Bulgaria over excessive deficit
World.content:
Opposition parties lashed Prime Minister Roumen Radev and his government on November 24 after the European Commission said that it was recommending that Bulgaria be fined for non-compliance with EU fiscal rules through its excessive deficit.

The Commission is proposing to EU finance ministers, who will meet on December 11, that Bulgaria be fined, as well as steps taken to freeze EU payments to Bulgaria.

This is an extremely serious and bad sign that the Bulgarian government received today, opposition GERB-UDF MP and former finance minister Temenuzhka Petkova said.

“When the European Commission says that Bulgaria’s case is particularly serious in terms of non-implementation of measures related to the excessive deficit procedure, this means nothing other than a lack of trust, a loss of confidence by the European Commission in the Bulgarian government,” Petkova said.

Radev’s Progressive Bulgaria has managed to make the worst-case scenario for the country’s public finances come true, she said.

“Such a thing has never happened before. Bulgaria is facing a sanction that could reach 0.02 percentage points of the country’s GDP and this will happen very soon – on December 11. Then the European Commission will submit a proposal to Ecofin, which the Council will vote on for a sanction against Bulgaria. This is a very bad scenario,” Petkova said.

Democratic Bulgaria MP Ivailo Mirchev said: “This fine signals a lack of confidence in the government”.

“We had been warning for weeks that this would happen. Yet, when we issued these warnings, government ministers claimed it was impossible. To prevent the fine from being imposed, two-thirds of the EU finance ministers would have to vote against it. In practical terms, that is impossible,” Mirchev said.



“While the amount of the fine itself is not particularly large, it carries a symbolic message: Bulgaria is an unreliable partner within the euro zone—it fails to honor its commitments, neglects fiscal discipline, and is taking no steps to get its budget in order,” he said.

Mirchev said that Democratic Bulgaria had put forward concrete proposals to bring the deficit below three per cent as early as the 2027 Budget, but these were rejected by Progressive Bulgaria.

Assen Vassilev, leader of We Continue the Change and a former finance minister, said that the government had received a “sound slap” from the European Commission regarding the 2027 Budget.

“Due to its incompetence, Bulgaria will have to pay a 25 million euro fine. The same 25 million that was not found for the doctors’ salaries,” Vassilev said.

“Unfortunately, the fine is the smallest problem. This Budget is leading the economy into recession, and the price will be paid by Bulgarian citizens,” he said.

“Withdraw the three budget laws. Reconsider them from scratch and introduce a competent budget that does not lead the economy to collapse,” Vassilev said.

On the Bulgarian Parliament’s website, the draft Order Paper – yet to be voted on – showed the first reading of the Budget in the National Assembly pencilled in for November 25.

World.title: EC is recommending Bulgaria be fined for non-compliance with recommendations against excessive deficit
World.content:
The European Commission is recommending to the Council of the EU that Bulgaria has taken no effective action to implement recommendations against its excessive deficit and should face a fine, European Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis told the European Parliament on November 24.

Speaking at the start of a debate on the European Semester autumn package, Dombrovskis said that two member states, Bulgaria and Hungary, are at risk of material non-compliance with EU fiscal rules already this year.

“For these two member states, we find that the responses to the EDP (excessive deficit procedure) recommendation have been insufficient and constitute particularly serious cases of non-compliance,” Dombrovskis said.

This warrants a stepping up of the procedure, he said.

“The Commission is therefore recommending the Council to adopt the decision under Article 126.8 of the Treaty that establishes that no effective action has been taken,” Dombrovskis said.

“This would also lead to the first steps in the process of macroeconomic conditionality. And for Bulgaria, as a euro area member state, will trigger a fine of up to 0.02 per cent of GDP,” he said.

Dombrovskis briefed the sitting on the alert mechanism report, “our screening device to identify countries where an in-depth review is needed to assess potential macroeconomic imbalances”.

The Alert Mechanism Report (AMR) is a screening exercise to detect potential macroeconomic imbalances that could affect individual member states, the euro area or the EU as a whole. It marks the start of the annual Macroeconomic Imbalance Procedure cycle, identifying member states requiring in-depth reviews

to assess whether they are affected by macroeconomic imbalances that call for policy action.

This year’s alert mechanism report calls for in-depth reviews for five member states, for Hungary, Italy, Slovakia, and Romania, which are already identified in the previous cycles as experiencing imbalances or excessive imbalances, and as well for the first time, Bulgaria, he said.

In a statement on November 24 on the European Semester autumn package, the European Commission concludes that an in-depth review should be undertaken for Bulgaria “based on concerns regarding a widening current account deficit, fast-deteriorating cost competitiveness, and high house price growth combined with significant household borrowing”.

World.title: €100 Million Investment for New Jadrolinija Fleet Launched
World.content:
November the 27th, 2026 – A €100 euro investment for a new Jadrolinija fleet has now been launched, with 10 brand new vessels planned.

Part of the tenders for the construction of new ships has already been published and is in the implementation phase. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that the Minister of Maritime Affaits, Transport and Infrastructure Oleg Butković stated this week that the recapitalisation of Jadrolinija is now ready. He added that the accompanying contracts will soon be signed for the implementation of the shore power supply system for ships at the Brajdica and Zagrebačka obala container terminals in Rijeka.

fleet modernisation

“Jadrolinija is going into recapitalisation, that is ready. We are going in two directions – with the recapitalisation of Jadrolinija and with the World Bank. Part of the tenders for the construction of new ships has already been published and is in the implementation phase, so Jadrolinija expects to sign contracts for the construction of new ships next year,” Butković revealed. Unofficially, it has been learn edthat the recapitalisation of Jadrolinija should be worth up to €100 million. It is closely linked to modernisation and should secure Jadrolinija’s financial position until 2043. It is a combination of different sources. Jadrolinija Management Board President Robert Blažinović revealed to us that the tenders should be published by the end of November.

“I think that within the next ten days or so we will also proceed to contracting the construction of the first ship,” Blažinović told us. This was preceded by a competitive procedure with negotiations for construction and design. Jadrolinija’s strategy of building ships with alternative propulsion and electric propulsion is well known, and the locations where they will sail have been determined in advance – the Šibenik, Zadar and Dubrovnik areas. The ships with alternative and electric propulsion will sail in the waters around Šibenik, Zadar and Dubrovnik.

alternative fuel vessels

Blažinović revealed that the Ministry of Transport has established very active cooperation with the World Bank and the International Finance Corporation (IFC). It has been known for some time that the company has a mandate letter with the IFC, which is working with Jadrolinija on preparing a sustainable financing model for the fleet renewal programme, as well as on assessing projects from the financial, technical, environmental and organisational aspects. We’re talking about a programme that can cover up to ten new ships and represents one of the largest investment phases in the recent history of this state-owned company. At the same time, the possibility of co-financing from EU funds in the segment of green technologies is also opening up, where maximum co-financing can be secured.

“The new ships should bring greater energy efficiency, reliability and comfort, with capacities adapted to the needs of individual lines. At the same time, we must continue investing in the existing fleet, digitalisation and the knowledge of our employees in order to maintain a leading position in maritime passenger transport and continue building the trust of passengers that we have been gaining for eight decades. The greatest challenge will be to align the scope of the necessary investments with the financial sustainability of operations. The green transition requires significant capital, but its implementation also depends on the availability of alternative fuels and the development of appropriate infrastructure. Jadrolinija must be business-efficient and competitive while at the same time ensuring the connectivity on which the daily life of islanders, the local economy and tourism depend. Our transformation is therefore part of a broader development strategy,” Robert Blažinović concluded.

World.title: New Pension Increases Announced for Croatian Retirees in 2027
World.content:
November the 27th, 2026 – Further pension increases have been announced for Croatian retirees in 2027, commenting on their previous growth and on the economy.

Prime Minister Andrej Plenković commented on the growth of pensions and the societal position of pensioners, emphasising that both wages and pensions have risen in the recent period, and announced additional changes that come into force from 2027. Poslovni reports that Croatia will apparently achieve economic growth of around 2.4 percent this year. During the terms of the current Government, absolute GDP has increased from €47 billion to €101 billion. Today, 1.76 million people are employed in Croatia, while the number of unemployed is around 70,000.

Plenković emphasised that as of the 1st of January 2027, the payment of income tax by pensioners is being abolished, which will further increase pensions for more than 540,000 pensioners. In November, 571,945 pensioners paid almost €20 million in tax into the budgets of cities and municipalities, or an average of €34.62 per pensioner. The opposition has warned that by tax relief for some pensioners the Croatian Government will shift the cost onto local budgets.

The state budget for 2027, presented in the Croatian Parliament, according to the Prime Minister’s words also has an important role in preserving social cohesion. The Government plans to allocate around €11 billion for pensions, which is €875 million more than this year.

wage growth will be reflected in pension growth

Plenković recalled that in recent years, Croatia has faced major external shocks and crises, as well as the devastating earthquakes in Zagreb and Banovina. €5.3 billion has so far been allocated for reconstruction. Croatia has recorded 22 consecutive quarters of economic growth, and projections for next year envisage growth of 2.1 percent. A budget deficit of 2.9 percent and a slowdown in inflation to 2.7 percent on an annual basis are also expected. Such trends should enable further growth in the wages of employees in public services, agreed with the trade unions. The wage base will increase by three percent as of the 1st of January 2027, and as of the 1st of April a meal allowance of €30 is being introduced. This will be followed by an additional one-percent increase in the base from 1 August and an increase in the meal allowance by a further €20 as of the 1st of October. Wage growth in the public sector will also be reflected in pensions through their regular adjustment.
