Beyond developing software, Aju has conducted AI workshops and sessions for students, educators and professionals, with a focus on making the technology accessible to people without technical backgrounds.

"I build things with AI. I talk about them. Sometimes I break them. Then I build them again," he writes in his LinkedIn introduction.

His profile also states that he has delivered eight TEDx talks and conducted sessions at IITs, universities, schools and other institutions. He has built an online following of more than 500,000 people, sharing content related to artificial intelligence and emerging technologies.

World.title: Whatever is scarce wins
World.content:
Two young Indians raised around Antwerp now teach big companies how to sound human on the internet. Their families learned the same lesson over a century: what you are really selling is trust.

In 2020, an 18-year-old in Antwerp was listening to a podcast in which one brother kept giving the other the same advice. The host was Ali Abdaal, a doctor turned YouTuber. His brother Taimur, a start-up founder, told him over several episodes that Twitter was where the founders were, and where the real conversation about technology and business was happening. Ali kept putting it off, though he came round in the end and now has some 350,000 followers there.



The listener, Aadit Sheth, took the advice more seriously than the man it was meant for. On Twitter (I refuse to call it X), the feed was full of it. He found it freeing. Within six months he was boiling down two-hour interviews by Tim Ferriss and Joe Rogan into threads. There was no grand plan. Mostly, he told me, he wanted to make good use of his time.

Six years on, Aadit has more than half a million followers on X and a company built on what he learned there.





He and his co-founder, Arnav Kothari, run The Narrative Company, which helps large technology firms find their voice on X. They call it an AI-native social media agency. It is a curious label for a business whose best idea is that in a feed filling up with machine-made content, a human being is about to become the rarest thing on offer.

Arnav grew up inside the diamond trade around Antwerp. His family's diamond and jewellery business, KGK, is about 120 years old and one of the largest in the world.

He left a software strategy job in Boston and moved to Indore to hire an engineering team for it. The aim was to move buying that happened over calls and WhatsApp onto a platform. Six months in, the beta users did not love it, so the team reworked the design and relaunched three months later.

Within three years the channel grew from nothing to $60m in annual sales, and getting there meant travelling between offices in India, Dubai, Antwerp, and New York to make it work for the teams using it.

He has done sales for both businesses, and the contrast taught him what a brand is worth. In the family firm, a new account goes roughly like this: Someone already knows the head of procurement, there is an introduction, a dinner, and then, a contract. That ease is earned. Behind each introduction sit generations of trust and years of care in keeping it, and working inside the firm taught him to respect both. Flying between offices, he also noticed how much of that care now happens online, between visits.

That gap is the whole subject of their work: how to make narratives clearer. I think it is also one of the most useful things to focus on.

Every business wants a moat, something a rival cannot easily cross. When there is no moat, Arnav says, the moat is what people are already comfortable with. AI is making software, copy and advertising cheaper to produce. Efficiency is becoming the price of entry. What stays scarce is the feeling that a customer knows you and would choose you again.

Aadit gets there through stories. He has been reading Satya Nadella's Hit Refresh, and was struck by the chapter on the birth of Nadella's son Zain, born with severe disabilities, and how fatherhood taught Nadella an empathy he had not had before. Aadit's own brother has special needs. And so, two paragraphs of a father's feelings moved him in a way nothing else could. People find their own lives inside someone else's story, and that is as true of a company as of a person.

When Ivan Zhao tells how Notion nearly ran out of money, let go of almost everyone and moved to Kyoto to rebuild the product from scratch, people warm to the company and to what it stands for.

Narrative began with that feeling. The founders admired how young firms such as Notion, Ramp and Anthropic talk to their users online, with humour and a sense that someone real is on the other side. Then they looked at the world's largest companies and found accounts that sounded like press releases.

The idea was to carry the start-ups' community playbook into those older giants. Their answer is a hybrid: software in the back, people in front.

Their tool, Nia, works like a "For You" feed for engagement: it uses AI to find conversations a company could usefully join, such as a developer describing an AI deployment problem a client could help with. The team then decides whether and how to take part, and Arnav, who leads Nia's development, works with clients on how it fits their needs.

People stay in front because large companies still want a human to talk to, and because selling is still a human game: for now, it is people, not agents, who have to be persuaded to buy. The part no software can copy is taste: Aadit has spent six years learning, as a creator, what makes an audience trust an account.

"Whatever is scarce wins," Aadit told me. If everyone else is selling five hundred AI-generated ads, the winning move is to go the other way.

His favourite example is Hector Serrano, who ran paid ads for the start-up Wispr Flow. By the account of the tech writer Lenny Rachitsky, Serrano made every ad himself for a year and a half. A few videos about how he did it travelled so far that Austin Rief, a co-founder of Morning Brew, publicly asked for a podcast on how Serrano had built a personal brand so fast.

The rÃ©sumÃ©, in Aadit's view, used to record what you have done.

Increasingly it shows how you think, in public. His advice to friends is blunt: open-source your thinking on X.

Indians find this advice hard to take, and I don't think it is because we are shy. An American teenager applying to college writes an essay about who they are. Most Indian students never have to make that case until much later. We grow up inside a meritocracy whose promise is simple: do the work and you will win. It leaves out that someone has to know the work exists.

Aadit points to Kunal Shah, the founder of CRED, who has spent the better part of a decade thinking out loud on X.

A philosophy graduate from NMIMS, he built CRED and was then hired by Mark Zuckerberg to run WhatsApp worldwide. Aadit does not think that leap happens without a decade of public thinking behind it.

Arnav's advice is also surprising. Don't rush it, he says. Build real knowledge first, because posting pays off far more when you have something to say.

It is like going to the gym without a trainer: you will build a habit, but maybe with the wrong form. He does not post much himself. For three years at KGK he took roughly a hundred flights a year and had no settled base. The firm was making it easier to do business across distance while he went without a community of his own.

He is clear now that he wants to spend his life helping people connect, and the new company is where he is starting: working out how companies can build real relationships with their audiences.

That is what he wants to write about first. Maybe you haven't found what you want to say yet, he tells anxious friends, and that is fine.

Which leaves the question hanging over his business: where does a good story end and a convenient fiction begin? And what makes a company's voice genuine when a team and software are helping it show up? Arnav has no formula, only a reasonable test. At 16, he co-founded a non-profit, Khilti Pari.

When he pitched it to his school as an elective, the principal laughed and asked whether they were even incorporated. They were.

It became the school's first student-created elective, drawing 10 to 15 students a year, and its exhibitions of paintings sourced from artists on Instagram raised crores of rupees over the years, enough to fund two vocational centres for girls in Rajasthan.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

On visits to the villages he spoke with the girls' families.

Some fathers had been drinking and did not understand what the charity was trying to do. It made him doubt how much education alone could change while the girls stayed financially dependent, so the work moved towards jobs and independence, including training for government posts. One story is about bringing people together, the other about changing his mind after listening to the people he meant to help.

Both still shape the problems he chooses, building communities among them. So before he tells a story about what he is building, he asks whether it still feels true. Can he sleep at night with it?

The internet offers something fast and strange: You can now be known by people you will never meet, years before you need anything from them. And sometimes you do meet them. That is how the two founders met. Arnav messaged Aadit on LinkedIn to suggest coffee, and they spent most of it showing each other AI tools on their laptops. They became close friends, and then built the company together. Because who would have thought that when Arnav messaged Aadit on LinkedIn for a coffee and they spent most of the time showing each other little optimisations on their laptops, that eventually, they would build the Narrative Company together.

World.title: Centre turns up heat on Zakir Naik: States, UTs get sweeping powers under UAPA to act against banned IRF
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Centre has expanded its crackdown on

's

(

), empowering state governments and Union Territory administrations to freeze funds and restrict access to properties linked to the organisation. The move comes days after the home ministry extended a five-year ban on the IRF

According to a notification issued on Thursday, the Centre has delegated these powers to states and UTs under Section 42 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA).

"The Central Government hereby directs that all powers exercisable by it under sections 7 and 8 of the UAPA shall also be exercised by the state governments and the Union territory administrations in relation to the above said unlawful association,â the notification said.

The notification also refers to the Centre's November 13 declaration of the IRF as an unlawful association under the UAPA. "In exercise of the powers conferred by sub-sections (1) and (3) of section 3 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 (37 of 1967), the Central Government has declared the Islamic Research Foundation (IRF), as an unlawful association vide notification number, S.O. 6182(E), dated the 13th November"

Section 7 of the UAPA empowers the government to prohibit the use of funds belonging to an association declared unlawful.



It allows authorities to issue a written order barring anyone holding money, securities or credits being used, or intended to be used, for the association from paying, transferring or otherwise dealing with them without the government's written permission.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

A government-appointed gazetted officer can also be authorised to inspect the person's premises, examine records and investigate financial transactions suspected to be linked to the unlawful association.





Section 8, meanwhile, empowers the government to notify any place, including a house, building or part of it, a tent or a vessel, that it believes is being used for the purposes of an unlawful association.

Following such a notification, the district magistrate can prepare an inventory of movable property at the premises and prohibit the use of articles suspected to be connected with the association. The magistrate can also restrict entry into the notified premises by people who were not residents there when the notification was issued. Police officers of at least the rank of sub-inspector can search people entering or found at the premises.

World.title: ‘Today one Deepam, tomorrow temples?’ Vaishnaw slams TVK govt over Thiruparankundram Deepam row
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Railway minister

on Thursday launched a sharp attack on the Tamil Nadu government over the Thiruparankundram

row, accusing it of hurting the religious sentiments of millions.

He also cautioned the state government against attempts to restrict temple traditions and religious practices.

Addressing a Constitution Day event organised by the BJP in Chennai, Vaishnaw further targeted the Congress, accusing it of placing family interests above constitutional values.

Referring to the dispute over lighting the ceremonial lamp at the Deepathoon stone pillar, Vaishnaw questioned the Vijay government's position and warned that restrictions on religious practices could have wider implications.



"Tamil Nadu is intact. Stopping one deepam, you have stopped, you have hurt, you have destroyed and disturbed the emotions of millions of people. What will happen? Today you have stopped one deepam, tomorrow you will say that nobody can go to a temple? They'll shut down the temples. Is that what they want?" he said, according to news agency PTI.

Vaishnaw also said, "True respect for the Constitution means safeguarding religious freedom and taking pride in our culture, Lord Muruga, and our ancient heritage."





The remarks came amid continuing tensions over the annual Karthigai Deepam ceremony. Maha Deepam was lit above the Uchi Pillayar temple at Thiruparankundram Hills amid heavy security, but no lamp was lit at the disputed Deepathoon pillar. A team of priests associated with the Subramaniaswamy temple performed the ceremony at the usual location.

The dispute escalated after a scuffle broke out between members of Hindu organisations and police.

Several people, including BJP leaders and members of Hindu outfits, were detained amid restrictions imposed by authorities over law-and-order concerns.

The matter is also before the Supreme Court. On Thursday, a bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi said contempt petitions and other applications concerning the non-lighting of the lamp at Deepathoon would be listed on November 27.

"Everything will be listed tomorrow," the bench said. The Tamil Nadu government had apologised to the court on Wednesday over the incident, blaming the temple authorities.

The apex court had earlier declined to initiate suo motu contempt proceedings.

Vaishnaw also criticised the Congress over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and electronic voting machines (EVMs), alleging that the party questioned electoral processes selectively.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

"Congress wants to just blame SIR for their own failures. And they will keep failing like this. Because for them, it is not the Constitution, it is the family," he said.

Turning to railway development, the minister claimed that Tamil Nadu had acquired only 1,253 hectares, or 24 per cent, of the approximately 4,800 hectares required for railway projects.

He urged the state government to expedite land acquisition, assuring that the Centre would provide the necessary funds. Vaishnaw also highlighted the redevelopment of 77 railway stations in Tamil Nadu and discussed proposed high-speed rail connectivity between Chennai, Bengaluru and Hyderabad.

The Supreme Court's scheduled hearing on Saturday is expected to bring further clarity to the contempt petitions and applications.

World.title: 'We love Yogi very much': Sanjay Raut's praise puts spotlight on BJP's biggest UP question
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Shiv Sena (UBT) MP

on Thursday backed Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister

, describing him as the highest face of Hindutva and expressing confidence that he would continue to lead the state after the 2027 Assembly elections.

"If Yogi ji has declared himself (as CM face), it is commendable. He is a capable man, and we too love Yogi ji. Yogi ji is a face of Hindutva that stands at the very top, and if there is no Yogi, there is no UP. If Yogi ji has said this, then he has full confidence that his party will win a majority in Uttar Pradesh and that the majority of MLAs elected will support him," Raut said.

Raut's remarks come amid growing political activity in Uttar Pradesh ahead of the 2027 Assembly elections, with the ruling

(BJP) and opposition parties stepping up their preparations and political exchanges over the state's leadership.



On Wednesday, Uttar Pradesh Deputy Chief Minister Keshav Prasad Maurya said the BJP's chief ministerial candidate would be decided by the party's elected MLAs after the Assembly elections, indicating that the party had not yet settled on a face for the next polls.

"BJP's face at the time of elections is the lotus flower, and elections are contested based on the lotus flower. After the elections, when MLAs are elected, their meeting is held, and central observers arrive," Maurya said, according to ANI.





Asked whether he could be a contender for the post, Maurya said, "No individual decides this. SP, BSP, and Congress are private limited companies."

"We have a system here. Whenever the leader of the legislative party is chosen, central observers come after the election. Whatever happens, you will find out in 2027," he added.

Meanwhile, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Thursday targeted the BJP over its performance in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, crediting voters in Uttar Pradesh with checking the party's electoral ambitions and forcing Prime Minister Narendra Modi to abandon his '400 paar' slogan.

Addressing a 'Samvidhan Raksha Sammelan' at the Congress office in Lucknow on Constitution Day, Kharge said the BJP had fallen short of its target despite Modi repeatedly invoking the slogan during the election campaign.

"I thank the people of Uttar Pradesh. Prime Minister Narendra Modi used to say in all his speeches, wherever he went, 'Abki Baar, 400 Paar' (this time, more than 400 seats). But did the BJP cross 400 seats? The people sent you (BJP) packing.

The people of Uttar Pradesh brought you to your knees. It is because of Uttar Pradesh that Modi is sitting quietly today," Kharge said.

The BJP-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA) won 36 of Uttar Pradesh's 80 Lok Sabha seats in the 2024 general elections.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Kharge also accused the BJP of allowing its funds to grow while people continued to face inflation, unemployment and rising prices of cooking gas and essential food items.

He further claimed that Union Home Minister Amit Shah had reduced his public statements, adding, "I do not know whether the two (Modi and Shah) are getting along or not."

In an apparent reference to Adityanath, the Congress president also said that another leader in Lucknow had his eyes on the prime minister's chair.

The political exchanges come as the

Samajwadi Party

(SP) and Congress continue discussions over a possible alliance for the 2027 Assembly elections. The SP has offered 26 seats to the Congress in the initial round of negotiations, while the Congress has sought 120 seats and is unwilling to accept a lower number, according to sources.

The SP is seeking to return to power after losing the 2017 and 2022 Assembly elections. It won 111 seats in the 2022 polls.
