World.title: Nobel Committee chair emphasizes human accountability for AI’s potential harms
World.content:
The Nobel Committee chair says human accountability and the rule of law must keep pace with AI’s growing power

MANILA, Philippines – Nobel Committee chair Jørgen Watne Frydnes at Rappler’s Social Good Summit 2026, Saturday, November 21, emphasized that, ultimately, people behind AI technologies as well as governments that utilize them must be held accountable if these systems inflict harm.

Already, these artificial intelligence systems are developing and moving faster than institutions and laws can respond, the chair said. These technologies are reshaping how people work, how wars are fought, and how societies form opinions.

Algorithms determine what people see while advanced surveillance technologies are giving governments more oppressive ways to monitor journalists, citizens, and activists.

This is a technology that is unique in that it is capable of making a decision for itself. “An atomic bomb could not decide who to bomb. AI can,” Frydnes said.

Who’s responsible?

Frydnes’ attempt to answer the question of how the technology can be shaped for good is rooted in two principles that have routinely surfaced throughout the prize’s history.

First, responsibility should always belong to people. Citing the Nuremberg trials after World War II, he recalled how those established that the responsibility for crimes should always fall on specific individuals and not abstract entities.

“A machine cannot stand before a court, cannot feel remorse, and cannot answer to their victims. But those who design it, own it, deploy it, and profit from their existence, they can, and they should. And so can the states that use them. If we allow technology to become a new abstract entity behind which power hides, we will have undone one of the most important achievements of the last century,” he said.

The second principle is that no one is above the law.

This, he said, “must now also apply to the companies and individuals who hold power over information on a scale that rivals that of many states. A legal order enforced only when it’s politically convenient is no legal order at all.”

Looking back at Nobel’s history

Further expounding his point, Frydnes looked to previous laureates, what they represent, and what they mean in the age of AI.

He said the prize’s past offers lessons for understanding the challenges of the present.

Cited were René Cassin, who helped draft the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and received the 1968 Nobel Peace Prize, and Carl von Ossietzky, the German journalist imprisoned in the 1930s by the Nazi regime for exposing its secret rearmament, and more recent laureates such as Maria Ressa and Dmitry Muratov.

He also cited the people behind the Pugwash Conferences who challenged the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction; the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons, which was recognized in 2017; and 2024 awardee Nihon Hidankyo, the Japanese organization of atomic bomb survivors from Hiroshima and Nagasaki, whose members have spent decades sharing their experiences to prevent the world from forgetting the consequences of nuclear warfare.

These specific awardees are a reminder that artificial intelligence too, is something that society can challenge if it runs counter to the good of humanity.

While Frydnes acknowledged that the Nobel Peace Prize cannot regulate artificial intelligence or independently protect journalists from threats and intimidation, what it can do, he said, is to direct the world’s attention toward people who demonstrate that humanity can confront forces that appear greater than itself.

Frydnes offered a promise of his own, on behalf of those who continue to defend these principles: “We will not duck.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Duterte’s ICC trial: How to watch and follow the proceedings
World.content:
DUTERTE. Families of victims of the war on drugs under former president Rodrigo Duterte, along with human rights advocates, gather at the National Council of Churches in the Philippines in Quezon City on September 16, 2026, to watch the live stream of the International Criminal Court’s third status conference.

Former president Rodrigo Duterte's trial at the International Criminal Court begins on November 30, 2026. Here's how you can follow Rappler's coverage.

MANILA, Philippines – Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte will finally face trial before the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, Netherlands after years of calls for accountability over his violent war on drugs.

The proceedings that will start on Monday, November 30, will put Duterte’s bloody anti-drug campaign under scrutiny. The charges cover alleged killings carried out by the Davao Death Squad when he was mayor of Davao City and those linked to his national drug war during his presidency.

Duterte has been detained at the ICC detention center since his arrest in Manila in March 2025.

Hearings for 2026 are scheduled to run until December 17 before the court’s winter recess. Proceedings will resume on January 11, 2027.

Rappler justice reporter Jairo Bolledo and correspondent Michelle Abad will be in The Hague to cover the trial. They will bring updates from the courtroom and report on activities outside the court and detention center.

Here are the ways to follow Rappler’s coverage and stay on top of the latest developments:

1. Join the Justice and Crime chat room

The trial will raise questions about accountability and justice that deserve careful discussion. Join Rappler’s Justice and Crime community to follow the latest developments and exchange views with other readers.

Through the Rappler app you can get notifications and real-time updates. You can also join conversations with Rappler reporters and members of the community. The app is free to download from the Apple App Store and Google Play Store.

Watch Rappler’s livestream of the trial and follow the proceedings as they happen. Our team in The Hague will also share video reports from the court and its surroundings.

Subscribe to the channel and turn on notifications so you don’t miss our live coverage.

For Filipinos following the case from home, the time difference will mean evening viewing. The opening sessions are scheduled to start at 10 am in The Hague or 5 pm in the Philippines.

It is important to remember, though, that the ICC livestream has a 30-minute delay. This means online viewers will see the proceedings begin at 5:30 pm Philippine time.

Check this page to find out more about the key dates and schedules related to the trial.

3. Bookmark the Duterte at the ICC topic page

The trial will involve legal proceedings and decisions that may be difficult to follow. We’ll help make sense of them through our reports and explainers.

Bookmark this page so you can easily find all of Rappler’s coverage in one place. We’ll post breaking news and reports from our team in The Hague, along with explainers and analyses on the charges and the trial process. We’ll keep updating this page as the case moves forward.

Can’t follow every hearing or check the news throughout the day? Get Rappler’s coverage straight to your inbox.

Register for a free Rappler account and subscribe to our newsletters. You’ll receive updates on the trial and other important developments covered by our newsroom.

Covering a trial of this scale takes time and resources. It also requires journalists on the ground and a team working behind the scenes to verify information and explain complex legal proceedings.

You can help sustain this work by contributing to Rappler’s investigative fund or becoming a Rappler+ member. Your support helps us continue reporting on issues of public interest and holding the powerful to account. – Rappler.com

World.title: Dutch groups ask court to halt Meta smart glasses sales over privacy concerns
World.content:
META SMART GLASSES. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg presents the new line of smart glasses during the Meta Connect event at the company's headquarters in Menlo Park, California, USA, September 23, 2026.

Dutch rights groups argue the glasses developed by Meta and EssilorLuxottica both violate privacy laws and force people to constantly worry in public places, with a chilling effect on society

AMSTERDAM, The Netherlands – Dutch consumer and digital rights groups asked a court on Thursday, November 26, to halt sales of Meta AI-powered smart glasses in the Netherlands, arguing they violate European privacy laws by allowing wearers to film people without their knowledge.

While limited in scope to the Netherlands, a summary ruling in the civil suit against Meta at the Amsterdam District Court could set a precedent amid growing public backlash, venue bans and regulatory warnings across the world.

A decision is expected by December 24 at the latest.

The rights groups, which include the Netherlands’ main consumer association Consumentenbond and Offlimits, which campaigns against online sex abuse, argued that the glasses developed by Meta and Ray-Ban owner EssilorLuxottica both violate privacy laws and force people to constantly worry in public places, with a chilling effect on society.

The plaintiffs want Meta to prevent its glasses from being used to record people without their knowledge, stop using recordings to train AI models and halt sales until Meta complies. They sought penalties of €100,000 ($109,600) per day per defendant for non-compliance, capped at €100 million.

Offlimits’ lawyer Karlijn Han said the glasses were used for what she described in court as “creep shots.” “Covert recordings are undoubtedly also being made during exams, in changing rooms, at swimming pools, in hotel rooms and hospitals, but also in playgrounds and on beaches,” she said in opening remarks. “Each invasion of privacy is worse than the last.”

Meta denies images are used to train AI

Meta’s lawyer Bastiaan Kemp said the court should reject the suit. He said the measures demanded would harm legitimate users, damage Meta’s competitive position and amount to a product recall without resolving concerns about similar devices.

“Providers of products cannot be held responsible for every instance of deliberate misuse,” he told the court. He said that a recording light on the frame makes it obvious when they are being used for recording.

And he denied allegations made by Consumentenbond’s lawyer in court that Meta processes images recorded by the smart glasses in Europe or uses them to train AI models in violation of European law. Meta and manufacturing partner EssilorLuxottica sold more than 7 million smart glasses in 2025, around 80% of the global market.

A lawyer for EssilorLuxottica argued that it neither processes nor has access to footage and that a sales ban would be disproportionate and ineffective given the availability of similar products from other manufacturers.

Backlash extends worldwide

From proposed restrictions in Australia and Norway to bans in courts across England, Wales, and New York state, governments and judicial authorities are increasingly seeking to prevent covert recording and protect sensitive information. Cinema operators in the UK are also introducing restrictions over privacy and film piracy concerns.

On Tuesday, Germany’s national consumer federation announced legal action against Meta and Ray-Ban over alleged privacy violations, arguing that the glasses make it nearly impossible for consumers to comply with European data protection rules when using them in public.

The European Data Protection Board warned in October that smart glasses raised serious privacy concerns and called for stronger safeguards.

Dutch privacy regulator AP this month advised consumers to not buy smart glasses, saying they are unsafe for both users and bystanders. In October, Dutch retail chain Hans Anders suspended sales of Meta’s ​Ray-Ban smart glasses in the Netherlands and Belgium.

Meta also faces proposed class-action lawsuits in the United States over alleged improper sharing of private images gathered by the glasses. – Rappler.com

World.title: For a mother who lost 2 sons, Duterte’s ICC trial is a birthday gift
World.content:
Llore Pasco holds a banner during a send-off as she prepares to depart for The Hague, Netherlands, to attend former President Rodrigo Duterte's International Criminal Court (ICC) trial, at the National Council of Churches in the Philippines (NCCP) in Quezon City, Philippines, November 26, 2026.

'My only wish is not just justice for my children, but for all those killed during the time of Rodrigo Duterte. I hope the killings stop for the next generation,' says Llore Pasco who lost her two sons to the bloody drug war

Llore Pasco, a mother who lost her two sons, is traveling to The Hague to attend the trial of ex-president Rodrigo Duterte that will open on her 73rd birthday. She said she had never imagined she would see Duterte in the dock.

“This is the greatest and most beautiful gift you could give me,” she said hours before boarding a plane to the Netherlands.

“My only wish is not just justice for my children, but for all those killed during the time of Rodrigo Duterte. I hope the killings stop for the next generation.”

The former Philippine leader goes on trial at the International Criminal Court on Monday, November 30, for alleged crimes against humanity during a six-year anti-drug campaign in which thousands of people were killed.

“For those who have suffered the most egregious abuses during the war on drugs, this will be a welcome moment in their quest for justice,” said Priya Pillai, an international lawyer who runs the Asia Justice Coalition. It “is a significant moment in Philippine history.”

Duterte, 81, faces allegations relating to 85 murders and two attempted murders from 2011 to 2018, including when he served as the mayor of Davao City and the early years of his presidency. The court’s prosecutors say the victims are only a sample of as many as 30,000 people killed by death squads targeting users and sellers of illegal drugs.

It is one of the highest-profile cases to come before the court in its more than two decades of existence, and the biggest since US President Donald Trump’s administration imposed sanctions that could imperil the court’s ability to function.

If convicted of any of three counts of crimes against humanity, Duterte could face life in prison.

Duterte’s supporters have called for his release. His daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte said on Wednesday that “no foreign court or nation should ever stand above the sovereignty of our country.”

Test of embattled ICC

The proceedings will test the court’s ability to conduct a high-profile trial amid an ongoing campaign by the United States to force its closure. Washington has imposed crippling financial sanctions and called on member states to withdraw from the ICC and isolate it.

The ICC is the world’s sole permanent war crimes tribunal, set up to prosecute individuals accused of war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide when national jurisdictions fail to do so.

Duterte is only the second former national leader to appear before it for crimes allegedly committed while in power, after Laurent Gbagbo of Ivory Coast, who was acquitted in 2019.

Four serving national leaders face ICC arrest warrants: Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Russia’s President Vladimir Putin, Afghanistan’s Taliban leader Hibatullah Akhundzada and Myanmar military leader Min Aung Hlaing.

Duterte will be asked on Monday to enter a plea. Prosecutors will then present opening arguments. His lawyers have told judges he denies the charges.

“There was no state or organizational policy to murder,” they argued in a pre-trial brief. “This is not a crimes against humanity case and, as such, does not belong before this court.”

Death squads

Despite his lawyers arguing that Duterte was unfit to stand trial because of cognitive decline, judges ordered him to stand trial and attend hearings. Court sessions will be shortened to accommodate his age.

During the trial, which is expected to run well into 2027, more than 500 alleged victims will be represented in court.

Prosecutors have said Duterte created, funded and armed death squads responsible for thousands of extrajudicial killings between 2011 and 2019. Philippine law enforcement agencies acknowledged 6,248 deaths.

In language his lawyers dismissed as mere rhetoric, Duterte told supporters during his 2016 election campaign: “I will do just what I did as mayor. You drug pushers, hold-up men and do-nothings, you better go out. Because I’d kill you.”

In March 2025 Duterte was arrested and taken to The Hague, where he is being held in a detention unit for war crimes suspects within a Dutch prison. – Rappler.com

World.title: [DECODED] How Facebook pages used Kitty’s image to amplify Dutertismo
World.content:
Rappler’s analysis shows how digital creators and pages masquerading as news sites are using the former president’s youngest daughter as a vehicle to keep Dutertismo alive

Veronica “Kitty” Duterte has become a prominent voice in her family’s public defense of former president Rodrigo Duterte, now detained in The Hague for alleged crimes against humanity. Supporters celebrate her as a devoted daughter, ready to stand by her “Papa Rody.”

Circulating on Facebook is an image that captures this: the 81-year-old Duterte showing concern that he had “embarrassed” his family and Kitty holding his hand, reassuring him that his children remained “proud to be his flesh and blood.” This storyline has spread, feeding into a broader appeal for Duterte loyalty ahead of the 2028 presidential elections.

Rappler analyzed 260 public Facebook posts containing mentions of Kitty, published between January and October 2026, and found at least three clusters of narratives in which accounts shared nearly identical captions. Some accounts spread content across narratives, while others published posts appearing within short intervals of each other. The largest cluster, gaining almost five million views, centered on Kitty’s support for her detained father.

These posts foreground Duterte’s separation from his family, shifting attention away from the allegations of crimes against humanity he faces at the International Criminal Court (ICC). Duterte was arrested in March 2025 in connection with the ICC proceedings concerning killings during his administration’s anti-drug war campaign.

In his absence, Duterte’s children – Paolo, Sara, Sebastian, and Kitty – have taken up the mantle of speaking on his behalf.

The 22-year-old Kitty, Duterte’s youngest daughter with his common-law wife Honeylet Avanceña, especially finds herself at the frontlines. Her interviews and heartfelt posts on social media have supplied material for online accounts aiming to rally sympathy and support for the Dutertes.

Unlike her siblings, Kitty is a fresh face with no political track record to be judged on, which could make her appeal to supporters stronger, Arjan Aguirre, assistant professor of political science at Ateneo de Manila University, told Rappler.

“With Kitty, they’re trying to project the idea to the general public that even if you are not a supporter of the Duterte bloc, you have to sympathize with us because I am the youngest, I’m the bunso, and I feel sad about what’s happening,” according to Aguirre, who is also pursuing his PhD in political science at the University of Pittsburgh.

Kitty was only 14 when her father was elected president in 2016, while her siblings already held local seats in Davao. That distance from politics, Aguirre said, is what makes her the obvious choice to convey these seemingly innocent narratives.

He highlighted that Kitty’s image projects a gentler tone than her siblings. “Nag-bo-border pa rin siya doon sa pagiging naive. May mga persecution pa rin siyang nababanggit pero hindi gano’n katapang.” (She still borders on being naive. She does mention persecution, but not as boldly.)

Behind the Duterte pride narratives

More than half of the 260 posts analyzed pulled emotionally-charged quotes from Kitty’s interview with blogger Alvin & Tourism on April 20. Posting peaked the following day, April 21, just days before news broke out of the ICC’s confirmation of Duterte’s charges.

The same quotes then resurfaced in September, when Duterte made his first in-person appearance at the ICC courtroom since his arrest.

By October, the posts about the “flesh and blood” narrative had accumulated about 4.76 million views on Facebook, based on Rappler’s monitoring.

Behind those views were 78 pages and profiles that circulated the narrative. Rappler identified 17 pages linked to Pilipinas Today, a network of news and media pages operating across the country. An earlier investigation found that the group is run by Sartine IT Solutions, a political consulting firm previously linked to foreign interference in elections.

Alongside the Pilipinas Today network, some news-branded pages that had previously used partisan names contributed to the narrative’s amplification. For instance, the page News Ngayon – which accounted for 21.67% of the total post views in this cluster – changed its name six times. It was originally Duterte Latest News, when it was created on January 17, 2018.

Another profile, Venielyn Rahman, which categorizes itself as a news and media website, racked up a total of 110,075 views for the same quotes from Kitty on April 21. A closer look at its Profile Transparency information indicated that the primary location of the profile owner is listed in Bangladesh. The account, however, largely published Filipino celebrity content and political news.

It is among the four pages whose administrators are located outside the Philippines, including one based in Macau, one in Canada, and a second one in Bangladesh.

OUTSIDE THE PHILIPPINES. Four pages had administrators located in other countries. Rappler screenshots

Other pages in this cluster hid their political purpose behind misleading names. The page Words of Wisdom: Inspirational Quotes to Live By, which has about 141,000 followers, claims to be “dedicated to providing you with daily inspiration, motivation, and positivity,” but in fact carries political content about the Dutertes.

In a second cluster of posts, Facebook pages cast Kitty as the messenger of her father’s supposed political support for protests back home, and appeared to cash in on this narrative.

At least 19 Facebook fan pages shared identical captions attributing the message to Kitty, accompanied by carousels that steered users toward the same affiliate marketing link. These pages accumulated more than 21,000 post views as of October.

REPETITIVE POSTS. Facebook pages analyzed showed identical posts containing affiliate marketing links. Rappler screenshots

Posts spiked a few days after Iglesia ni Cristo’s three-day demonstration from June 30 to July 2 in support of long-time Duterte ally Senator Rodante Marcoleta.

AFFILIATE LINKS. Facebook pages cast Kitty as the messenger of her father’s supposed political support for protests back home, then added links to an online marketplace. Rappler screenshots

Further inspection of 12 of these pages found similar blue checkmark edits on their profile images, mimicking the verification badges Facebook awards to premium accounts. Some of them also posted the same manipulated photos within minutes of each other.

FAKE CHECKMARKS. Facebook pages found in Rappler’s dataset showed blue checkmarks edited on their profile photos. Rappler screenshots

The 2028 elections

For Aguirre, all these narratives position Kitty as a political force – even a potential successor – within the Duterte dynasty.

“If ever Rodrigo Roa Duterte is gone, who would emerge [a]s the central figure in the Duterte bloc? I’m sure Kitty will put up a fight for that,” he added.

The third cluster of posts echoed this push to keep the Duterte legacy alive through his children. Rappler’s analysis found copypasta messages across 29 pages and profiles in January, claiming that only the Dutertes could put an end to crime and corruption.

“Hindi sila basta anak ni Tatay Digong. Sila ang legasiya ng tapang, disiplina, malasakit, at paninindigang walang atrasan—kahit malalakas pa ang kalaban,” the captions read. (They’re not just children of Tatay Digong. They are the legacy of courage, discipline, compassion, and an unwavering resolve—even when facing formidable opponents.)

One post carrying this message, published by the page Parang May Mali, garnered 1.75 million views. The profile Boss Lee Vlog distributed it across seven Facebook groups, including communities of local buying and selling, hog raising, and religious discussion.

By July, the accounts in this cluster began to explicitly push for #Duterte2028. The Facebook page Kitty Duterte: Unofficial wrote, “Kung sunod-sunod na tatakbong pangulo ang mga Duterte, susuportahan mo ba sila?” (If the Dutertes run for president one after another, will you support them?) In the same caption, it answered its own question, “YES NA YES.”

According to Aguirre, 2028 could be the Dutertes’ year. If the vice president gets impeached, he predicted, whoever they field in the polls could win by saying the family had been persecuted and wronged.

These accounts suggest that the campaign has already begun. With Sara’s presidential bid in the works, these accounts have a clear pitch to the Filipino people beyond sympathy for her father: back the next Duterte. – with reports from Alex Culla/Rappler.com

Nica is a freelance journalist and OSINT researcher reporting on online information manipulation campaigns and tech platform accountability. Her work has centered on information integrity, previously fact-checking mis/disinformation and building news products at VERA Files. She is now pursuing a joint master’s degree in Journalism, Media, and Globalization in Europe. You may reach her at ndhanopol@gmail.com.

World.title: [Market Rider] PSE’s 2027 rebalancing: Will it unlock broader market activity?
World.content:
The message is clear: Size alone is no longer enough for a sure spot of a company’s stock in the PSEi.

In the search for new catalysts that could lead to unlocking broader market activity and growth, the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE) is implementing its biggest index management overhaul since 2011 starting with the February 2027 rebalancing, using the whole-year trading data of 2026.

The revised framework applies to the PSEi, PSE MidCap, PSE Dividend Yield, and sector indices. (READ: What is the PSEi, and why does it matter?)

Unveiled last July, the new rebalancing framework radically departs from the pure market cap methodology by introducing three core changes in the rules for eligibility and liquidity for inclusion in the bourse’s index as it shifts toward free-float trading velocity.

As evaluated, many of our large conglomerates have a high total valuation, but a huge portion of their shares are locked up with founding families or strategic insiders. Under the old rules, a large company could enter or stay in the PSEi simply because of its sheer size and overall peso trading volume, even if its actual public float rarely changed hands.

Three pivotal rule changes

The first of the three pivotal changes made in the rule is that the PSE instituted a 98% cumulative market capitalization screen. Before even undergoing liquidity evaluations, companies must fall within the top 98% of cumulative total market capitalization among eligible securities. This also effectively filters out the exchange’s smallest listed names from the outset.

Second, the exchange replaced its legacy single liquidity metric with a rigorous dual liquidity test combining the Median Trading Activity Ratio (MTAR) and Monthly Average Daily Value Turnover (MADV). MTAR measures how fast a stock’s publicly available shares are being bought and sold relative to its size, rather than just looking at the raw amounts of pesos traded, while MADV is a liquidity metric that measures the average monetary value of a stock traded per day over a given month.

For the PSEi, MidCap, and Dividend Yield indices, prospective entrants must achieve an MTAR of at least 15%, whereas existing constituents need 10% to retain their spots, a buffer designed to prevent excessive index turnover while sector indices require 7%. Simultaneously, both new and current members of the primary indices must rank in the top 25% of all listed stocks by MADV for at least nine of the 12 months in 2026. For sector indices, the bar is looser. A stock only needs to rank in the top half by daily traded value in at least eight of the 12 months.

Third, the PSE introduced a P250-billion mega-cap float carve-out. While the standard minimum public float remains 20%, corporate giants valued at P250 billion or more can now qualify with a 15% float, provided they satisfy all liquidity tests.

Despite these sweeping updates, several foundational eligibility rules remain intact for the 30-member PSEi. Companies must still maintain a PSE Main Board listing tenure of at least 12 months, or six months for early inclusion if they rank among the top 25 firms by market value.

Once candidates clear the market cap screen, public float minimum, and dual liquidity filters, the top 30 eligible companies ranked by full market capitalization secure their places in the index. Furthermore, the exchange retains its semi-annual rebalancing cadence every February and August.

Ultimately, these revisions carry profound implications for market participants. Under the 2011 framework, tightly held conglomerates could qualify through size and sporadic block trades, creating liquidity bottlenecks for institutional funds trying to execute large orders without distorting prices.

Rule recap

The message is clear: Size alone is no longer enough for a sure spot of a company’s stock in the PSEi. A company can be worth hundreds of billions of pesos, but if its public shares sit idle without regular trading turnover, it risks being dropped from the benchmark index. Shares need to trade under the new rules.

For domestic institutional investors, including Unit Investment Trust Funds (UITFs), mutual funds, pension systems, and exchange-traded funds (ETFs), enforcing MTAR reduces execution friction and tracking error. Because trading large institutional blocks in large-cap stocks with tightly held floats or thin turnover can push prices sharply against a fund, requiring active trading relative to free float ensures deeper tradable liquidity during rebalances. This allows funds to buy newly added and sell deleted index stocks cleanly at or near benchmark prices and weights, preventing their returns from diverging from the benchmark index. (READ: EXPLAINER: How mutual funds and UITFs make investing beginner-friendly)

Additionally, the P250-billion carve-out creates an immediate pathway into the PSEi for tightly held utility giants. Conversely, the strict nine-month MADV requirement mathematically delays late-2026 mega-IPOs like Mynt (GCash) from immediate entry, ensuring that new additions prove sustained trading depth before attracting passive institutional capital.

By transitioning from static size metrics toward dynamic free-float trading velocity, the PSE is aligning domestic index construction with international institutional standards and mitigate structural illiquidity — standards that is followed by major global stock indexes like the Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) index and the Financial Times Stock Exchange Russell (FTSE Russell) index. – Rappler.com

A veteran stock market analyst, Den Somera has long years of professional experience in investment banking and stockbroking and founder-convenor of The Monday Circle. You may reach the writer at kapitaltek@gmail.com

World.title: Cardinal David urges SC to review rulings on small-scale fishers
World.content:
Cardinal Pablo Virgilio David on Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, urged the Supreme Court (SC) to reconsider rulings affecting the livelihood of small-scale fisherfolk, noting that their rights must be protected.

MANILA, Philippines — Cardinal Pablo Virgilio David on Friday urged the Supreme Court (SC) to reconsider rulings affecting the livelihood of small-scale fisherfolk, noting that their rights must be protected.

David made the call in line with the observance of World Fisheries Day last November 21, noting that his diocese, as bishop of Kalookan, includes the coastal communities of Malabon and Navotas.

READ: Explainer: How a quiet court case threatens small-scale fishers

Article continues after this 

David cited the plight of fisherfolk, including rising fuel prices that make it difficult for them to venture out to sea, as well as the limited fishing grounds available to them. He cited Republic Act (RA) 8550, or the Philippine Fisheries Code of 1998, which states that municipal waters extend 15 kilometers from the shoreline, primarily for small-scale fisherfolk’s use.

“Yet two judicial rulings have placed these protections in serious jeopardy. The first threatens to open municipal waters to large-scale commercial fishing. The second has invalidated an existing regulation requiring the electronic monitoring of commercial fishing vessels,” he said in a pastoral statement.

In December 2023, the Malabon City Regional Trial Court (RTC) granted the petition filed by Mercidar Fishing Corporation to declare as unconstitutional Section 4(66), Section 16, Section 1 and Section 18, Rule 181 of the Department of Agriculture (DA) Order No. 10 issued in 2015 and Section 5(58), Section 16 and Section 18 of RA 8550.

In its ruling, the lower court said that the control over natural resources belongs to the national government, and not local governments. The court’s decision went unchallenged as the Office of the Solicitor General, representing the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources and the DA, failed to file its response on time.

Meanwhile, the high court, in its decision promulgated last January 21, upheld a ruling of the Malabon RTC that declared the tracking of commercial fishing boats “unconstitutional.” The SC affirmed that Fisheries Administrative Order (FAO) No. 266, signed by the DAA in 2020, was null and void.

Article continues after this 

READ: SC voids vessel tracking rule: What the decision means

The FAO mandates the implementation of the Vessel Monitoring System and installation of the Electronic Reporting System in commercial fishing vessels in the country to detect illegal fishing.

Article continues after this 

“Our fisherfolk are not asking for clarity. They are asking for justice. They are asking the guardians of our Constitution to uphold the rights that the Constitution itself guarantees them, in keeping with the principle that those who have less in life should have more in law,” David stressed.

“And so I humbly appeal to our Supreme Court justices to reconsider, in their wisdom, these rulings. I appeal to Congress to strengthen the protection of our 15-kilometer municipal waters and ensure the effective monitoring of commercial fishing vessels,” he added.

David also said that fisherfolk, Church communities, young people, and concerned citizens will troop to the Supreme Court on December 3, Thursday, to appeal for the reconsideration of the rulings.

He said that the gathering “will be a peaceful but determined assembly, because to appeal to the Court is not to defy it.”

Meanwhile, Catholic Bishops’ Conference of the Philippines President Archbishop Gilbert Garcera expressed his support for David’s call, emphasizing that it is a Christian responsibility to stand in solidarity with small-scale fisherfolk whose livelihoods are threatened by the said rulings.

“In keeping with the social teachings of the Church, particularly the preferential option for the poor, the dignity of human labor, the pursuit of the common good, and the stewardship of creation, we reaffirm our commitment to defending the rights and livelihood of our small-scale fisherfolk whose preferential access to our communal marine and fishing resources is guaranteed by our Constitution,” Garcera said in a separate statement.

World.title: Comedian: Playground post ‘part of dark humor,’ not ‘sexualize’ children
World.content:
Comedian Mr. JP Aguilera of Pencilbox Comedy appears before the National Bureau of Investigation’s VAWC Division on Friday, November 26, 2026, to comply with the subpoena issued to him over his controversial “sexual” playground post involving children. (Photo: Mary Joy Salcedo/INQUIRER)

MANILA, Philippines — “I am confident that I did nothing wrong.”

This was the statement of comedian Mr. JP Aguilera of Pencilbox Comedy, explaining his controversial playground post was only “part of dark humor” and “does not intend to sexualize” children.”

Aguilera appeared before the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI)’s Violence Against Women and Their Children (VAWC) Division on Friday to comply with the subpoena issued to him following his post.

Article continues after this 

READ: NBI subpoenas comedian over ‘sexual’ playground post

‘I AM CONFIDENT NA WALA AKONG GINAWANG MALI’LOOK: Comedian Mr. JP Aguilera of Pencilbox Comedy appears before the NBI’s VAWC Division to comply with the subpoena issued to him over his controversial “sexual” playground post involving children. pic.twitter.com/FgMdZmvayQ — MJ Salcedo (@MJSalcedoINQ) November 27, 2026

His now-deleted Facebook post read, “Sabi ng doktor ko watch what you eat, kaso kumokonti na yung mga playground.”

(My doctor said to watch what you eat, but playgrounds are getting smaller.)

In an interview at the NBI, Aguilera said it was never his intention to sexualize children when he wrote the post on social media.

“Kung sexualize yung intent? Ako yung author eh. I know for myself na wala akong ganoong intent,” Aguilera said.

Article continues after this 

(The intent was to sexualize? I’m the author, after all. I know for a fact that I didn’t have any such intent.)

Aguilera said he was shocked when many interpretations of his post circulated on social media.

Article continues after this 

“Part siya ng humor jokes. Sometimes ginagamit natin yung comedy to bring awareness to certain topics na hindi tayo comfortable na i-discuss,” Aguilera explained.

(It’s part of the humor—the jokes. Sometimes, we use comedy to bring awareness to certain topics that we aren’t comfortable discussing.)

“I can say for myself, I am confident that I did nothing wrong,” he said.

READ: NBI subpoenas comedian over ‘sexual’ playground post

The NBI’s looked into the comedian’s post after receiving complaints Tuesday from the Council for the Welfare of Children (CWC) Executive Director Angelo Tapales, and House Committee on the Welfare of Children Vice Chairperson Ann Matibag

Tapales earlier said messages similar to the comedian’s post “should not be allowed, even if they’re just jokes.”

World.content:

MANILA, Philippines — The resumption of the budget deliberations on Friday began with a lighthearted exchange, with Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian mentioning the #WinRi trend.

“Dahil uso ang WinRi ngayon, ang magbubukas si Win at si Ri,” Gatchalian said.

(Because WinRi is such a trend now, Win and Ri will open today’s session.)

World.title: 3 hurt as ‘rido’ settlement erupts into violence in Maguindanao
World.content:
Police gather information from relatives of one of the victims of a gun attack during a family feud settlement in Sultan Kudarat, Maguindanao del Norte on Wednesday afternoon, Nov. 26, 2026. (Photo courtesy of PRO-BAR)

COTABATO CITY—Three members of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) were wounded in a bomb explosion as a family feud settlement was ongoing in Maguindanao del Norte on Thursday afternoon, police said.Capt. Steffi Salanguit, spokesperson for the Police Regional Office-Bangsamoro Autonomous Region (PRO-BAR), identified the injured as Pahamudin Mundas, 37, Salman Mundas, 39, both residents of Barangay Limbo, Sultan Kudarat, Maguindanao del Norte, and Saipudin Usman, a resident of Barangay Macaguiling, Sultan Kudarat, Maguindanao del Norte.Salanguit said all the wounded were members of MILF’s Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces (BIAF) Inner Guard 19th Brigade.

READ: 1 hurt as rido erupts in Lanao del SurIt transpired in Sitio Pokling, Barangay Sambolawan, Sultan Kudarat, Maguindanao del Norte, at about 6 p.m.According to Salanguit, the victims went to Barangay Sambolawan for an amicable settlement to resolve a family feud involving them and the group of Commander Jun Barang of MILF.During the settlement, the two parties failed to reach an understanding, leading to a heated altercation that escalated into a fistfight.“Several minutes later, an explosion occurred followed by successive gunshots,” Salanguit said.When the gun firing ended, three men were seen lying on the ground, bloodied. Relatives rushed them to Cotabato Sanitarium and General Hospital in Sultan Kudarat town.Salanguit said police have launched a manhunt for Commander Jun Barang and his men./coa

World.title: NGCP: Visayas Grid under yellow alert again on Nov. 27
World.content:
The NGCP compound on Araneta Avenue in Quezon City. (File photo by LYN RILLON / Philippine Daily Inquirer)

MANILA, Philippines — The Visayas Grid will be once again placed under a yellow alert on Friday, Nov. 27, according to the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP).

In an advisory, the NGCP said the alert status will take effect from 5:00 p.m. to 6:00 p.m.

As of Friday morning, the grid has an available capacity of 2,500 megawatts (MW), while its peak demand could reach 2,428 MW.

Article continues after this 

READ: NGCP places Visayas Grid under yellow alert due to plant outages

The agency said that the unavailability of TVI 2 due to an unplanned outage and the derated capacity of TVI 1 caused the yellow alert status.

It added that the unavailability of PCPC and KSPC Unit 2 due to a planned outage, as well as the limited power import from the Mindanao grid, may have also influenced the alert declaration.

“A yellow alert is issued when the operating margin is insufficient to meet the transmission grid’s contingency requirement,” the NGCP said.

Since November 2026, 10 plants have been on forced outage, while one plant has been on forced outage since October, two plants since September, two plants since August, and one plant since June.

Article continues after this 

Three plants were also on forced outage in 2025, while one plant has been on forced outage since 2024, two plants since 203, and one plant since 2021.

At least 20 plants were operating at derated capacity, leaving a total of 599.2 MW unavailable to the grid. /cdv

World.title: Baguio Museum rehab set but sparks ‘takeover,’ ‘mummy’ concerns
World.content:
The summer capital’s public museum is undergoing a P30-million facelift as a dispute over ownership has erupted between the Baguio government and some residents, including half of the Baguio Museum Inc. board of trustees.

BAGUIO CITY — The summer capital’s public museum is undergoing a P30-million facelift as a dispute over ownership has erupted between the Baguio government and some residents, including half of the Baguio Museum Inc. board of trustees.

The Baguio City Council was briefed last week on the city’s plans to renovate the interiors of the former Baguio-Mountain Provinces Museum, built in 1975 and opened in 1977.

Architect Johnny Degay, the city building officer, told the council during its November 16 session that the museum’s modernization would infuse “stories about Baguio” at every level of the four-story structure that would be redesigned and completely overhauled using a government grant.

Article continues after this 

READ: Baguio Museum unveils images of Kidlat Tahimik

But the council was not provided with any architectural and engineering plans.

None of these plans have also been transmitted officially, “or even informally,” to museum administrators, said its executive director, Stella De Guia, on Monday, November 23.

A group of female teachers, artists, and published scholars, who described themselves as Friends of the Baguio Museum, met with de Guia on Monday to discuss their legal options and to demand more transparency regarding the government’s modernization plan. “We are not against improving the museum,” they stressed.

One of their concerns included the museum’s artifacts, including an authentic Ibaloy mummy entombed in a casket and protected by a glass case.

Article continues after this 

In a November 19 letter, Mayor Benjamin Magalong asked Baguio Museum Inc. President Peter Ng to provide the city government with an inventory of the museum’s artifacts and other items to prepare for their storage once work on the building starts.

Given the spiritual and cultural nature of its artifacts, City Hall must first consult indigenous elders, de Guia said.

Article continues after this 

Moving the mummy will require its “permission” through a series of rituals, so indigenous Ibaloy clans must first be consulted about its possible transfer, she said.

READ: Origins of Benguet mummification

The museum sheltered the mummy because no one could determine which clan it belonged to after it was returned to the Philippines, said de Guia, sister of National Artist for Film Kidlat Tahimik, a trustee.

The Friends of the Museum also said the Baguio government must first acknowledge the museum’s autonomy once it shares details about its artifacts.

Since October, de Guia has feared a “takeover” since learning that the museum’s tax declaration now reflected the owner of the lot and building as the City of Baguio.

City Assessor Normita Ramon informed the museum in a September 18 letter that there were “no documents or deeds conferring ownership of the Baguio Museum building to the Baguio Museum Inc.”

De Guia formally objected when Ramon revealed that she had revised the tax declaration entry in favor of Baguio, first in an October 12 letter and again on October 26.

She had asked for a full disclosure of “records supporting, written clarification, and review of the reported change of the tax declaration for the building (which the museum) occupies.

“The Baguio Museum was in continuous possession of the building from 1975 until the July 1999 earthquake,” initially based on a July 11, 1975 memorandum of agreement between the city and the Philippine Tourism Authority, which reserved a 1,599-square-meter lot for the museum that PTA built and opened in 1977, according to documents acquired by the Inquirer.

The Baguio Museum Inc’s predecessor, the Baguio-Mountain Province Museum, secured a 25-year lease that would have expired in 2003 with a one-peso annual rent.

The museum, which was destroyed in the 1990 earthquake, housed its artifacts at Camp John Hay until 1997. The museum was gradually rebuilt through grants from the National Commission on Culture and the Arts and congressional allocations and was completed in 2003. It continues to receive donations, most recently from the United States Embassy.

READ: Memorial to 1990 quake soon to rise in Baguio

De Guia, a former Cordillera director of the Department of Tourism, said one of her successors, who was recovering and consolidating PTA properties within Baguio in 2015, almost wrested back the museum.

That DOT attempt was made even though the building and lot were ceded to the museum in 2003 by Baguio Rep. Mauricio Domogan, a former mayor, in turnover ceremonies witnessed by OIC Tourism Secretary Evelyn Pantig. De Guia said this justifies the museum’s continuing possession of the area.

She said the city must reconcile “inconsistent record entries,” citing the museum’s tax declaration reflected as PTA property in 2025.

The museum today exhibits both the history of Baguio as designed and constructed by the American colonial government in 1908, and the Cordillera with artifacts curated by indigenous scholars to represent highland provinces.

It also features a living showroom for woodcarver Ernesto Dul-ang, who recently sculpted a wooden relief of a painting depicting the formal surrender of Imperial Japanese Army General Tomoyuki Yamashita, which ended World War II in the Philippines.

World.title: Imee Marcos, Padilla seek Duterte’s return, halt dela Rosa arrest
World.content:
File photo

MANILA, Philippines — Senators Imee Marcos and Robinhood Padilla have filed a resolution urging the government to secure the release and repatriation of former President Rodrigo Duterte from the International Criminal Court (ICC) and halt enforcement of the arrest warrant against Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa.

Duterte is detained in The Hague, Netherlands, over charges of crimes against humanity before the ICC, while dela Rosa remains in hiding amid reports of an ICC arrest warrant against him for his alleged role in Duterte’s bloody drug war.

Proposed Senate Resolution No. 797, filed by the two senators on Wednesday, calls on the Executive Department to immediately cease all cooperation with the ICC, exhaust available legal and diplomatic means to bring Duterte back to the Philippines, and discontinue efforts to enforce the arrest warrant against dela Rosa.

Article continues after this 

READ: ICC outlines Duterte’s trial schedule

In a statement on Thursday, Marcos questioned the government’s continued cooperation with the ICC despite the Philippines’ withdrawal from the Rome Statute in 2019.

“Bakit sunud-sunuran pa rin tayo? Kung may kaso, dito sa sarili nating mga korte!” Marcos said.

(Why are we still blindly following them? If there is a case, it should be filed in our own courts!)

“We are not a province of The Hague. A former President was handed over, and now a sitting senator is being hunted for a court we already left. That is not justice. That is surrender,” she added.

Article continues after this 

The resolution cited the Nov. 19 Heads of State Declaration toward Peace issued by United States President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

According to the resolution, the declaration recognized the importance of state consent and respect for the immunities of state officials, while cautioning against abuses of jurisdiction by the ICC and similar bodies.

Article continues after this 

READ: Bato dela Rosa manhunt: PNP says it receives at least 500 tips

“Washington, Moscow, and Beijing rarely agree on anything but they agree that the ICC cannot overreach. If the three most powerful nations on earth can say it, why can’t Manila?” Marcos said.

The Philippines’ withdrawal from the Rome Statute took effect on March 17, 2019.

However, the ICC maintains jurisdiction over alleged crimes committed in Philippine territory while the country was still a state party to the treaty.

Duterte was arrested on March 11, 2025, and subsequently turned over to ICC custody in The Hague, Netherlands where he remains detained.

His trial is scheduled to begin on Monday, Nov. 30, with the prosecution set to present its evidence against Duterte.

Meanwhile, the resolution likewise cited the reported ICC arrest warrant against Dela Rosa, which was issued on Nov. 6, 2025, and unsealed on May 11, 2026.

World.title: Pagasa: Fair weather to prevail over most of PH on Friday
World.content:
Satellite image from Pagasa

MANILA, Philippines — Most parts of the country may experience generally fair weather on Friday, Nov. 27, the state weather bureau reported.

Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) weather specialist Obet Badrina said during a 5 a.m. weather advisory that large parts of the country may see fair weather with a chance of localized thunderstorms by the afternoon until evening.

READ: Most of PH to have fair weather; expect rain in parts of Luzon, Mindanao

Article continues after this 

“Inaasahan natin generally fair weather sa malaking bahagi ng ating bansa ngayong araw. Posible pa rin yung mga localized rain showers and thunderstorms, kadalasan nangyayari po yan sa hapon hanggang sa gabi,” Badrina reported.

(“We expect generally fair weather across a large part of the country today. Localized rain showers and thunderstorms are still possible—typically occurring from the afternoon into the evening,”)

According to Pagasa, the isolated rain showers are associated with the easterlies.

Meanwhile, Batanes is forecast to experience cloudy skies and isolated rain showers due to the shear line.

Badrina said that the northeast monsoon, or the amihan, may strengthen over the weekend, affecting the northern portion of Luzon on Saturday, Nov. 28.

Article continues after this 

“Inaasahan natin ngayong long weekend po na ito, posible po na muling lumakas yung amihan bukas, araw ng Sabado, makakaapekto dito sa may Northern Luzon,” he stated.

(“For this long weekend, we anticipate that the amihan may strengthen again tomorrow, Saturday, and affect Northern Luzon,”)

Article continues after this 

On the other hand, the easterlies and the shear line are expected to affect the eastern section of Luzon and Visayas from Sunday to Monday.

“Habang pagdating po ng Linggo at Lunes, inaasahan naman natin na magiging maulap ang kalangitan sa may silangang bahagi ng Luzon at Visayas dahil po muling natin inaasahan yung epekto ng shearline at easterlies,” he reported.

(“Meanwhile, by Sunday and Monday, we expect cloudy skies over the eastern part of Luzon and Visayas as we again anticipate the effects of the shear line and easterlies,”)

Moreover, Badrina said that the low pressure area outside the Philippine area of responsibility remains unlikely to develop into a tropical depression or enter the country.

As of 3 a.m., the weather disturbance was located 510 kilometers west southwest of Pag-asa Island, Kalayaan, Palawan.

“Wala itong direkta epekto sa ating bansa at inaasahan nating patuloy na kikilos palayo ng Philippine area of responsibility at hindi na po natin ito inaasahan na papasok pa ng PAR. At maliit din ang posibilidad na ito ay maging bagyo,” he said.

World.title: Myanmar’s Putschist President Shrugs at ICJ Genocide Verdict
World.content:
Myanmar’s putschist president, Min Aung Hlaing, hit back at the International Court of Justice (ICJ)’s genocide ruling on Wednesday, telling his cabinet that the regime will not implement “unacceptable” measures.

“As a responsible country, we will carry out measures we consider necessary but will not comply with those that should not be followed,” he said.

The World Court ordered Myanmar to implement several measures after ruling on Nov. 19 that it committed genocide against the Rohingya during military operations in Rakhine in 2016-17: Prosecute the perpetrators, provide reparations, ensure safe repatriation, guarantee non-repetition, and pass laws criminalizing genocide.

The junta chief claimed the ruling had damaged Myanmar’s national dignity, dismissing the case brought by the Gambia as a one-sided accusation.

“I will not accept anything that harms the country,” said the self-appointed president, who as military chief oversaw the 2016-17 Rakhine “clearance operations” now ruled as genocide. He also stands accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity following the coup he staged in 2021.

Legal experts noted that the ICJ ruling is legally binding, meaning the losing party cannot selectively choose which parts of the judgment to accept or reject.

“It was a final judgement from the international court — not a statement, recommendation or instruction,” human rights lawyer Zar Li Aye told The Irrawaddy.

“As per UN charter 94 (1), every member state is legally obliged to comply with orders from the International Court of Justice,” she stressed.

She added that Myanmar risked being found guilty of violating additional international laws if it failed to comply with the ICJ’s decision.

The ruling has drawn widespread international backing from Western and regional governments, the EU, UN officials, and major human rights organizations, which welcomed the landmark decision as a decisive step toward accountability for the Rohingya community.

Permanent members France and the UK requested a closed-door UN Security Council meeting on Wednesday to press members on Myanmar’s compliance with the ruling. The outcome of the meeting remains unknown.

Meanwhile, the judgement has triggered a chorus of denial from the regime and its allies. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs rejected it as “a great disappointment delivered with dissenting opinions” and “not decided unanimously by judges,” referring to the 9-6 ruling.

However, it remains unclear what effect the judgement will have on the regime’s international standing.

“We may see no direct impact from the ICJ’s decision in the short term,” Myanmar political researcher Sai Kyi Zin Soe told The Irrawaddy.

“We expect to see different responses from different countries, depending on how Myanmar responds and to what extent it complies with the court’s decision,” he said.

World.title: Myanmar’s Economy Reeling as Kyat Nosedives
World.content:
The rapid depreciation of the kyat is tearing across Myanmar’s economy, disrupting imports, driving up production costs and raising fears of further economic shocks.

The kyat market rate steadily weakened since last month before nosediving to reach over 5,400 kyats to the dollar on Thursday.

Exporters as well as importers say their businesses are increasingly unprofitable, exacerbated by regime restrictions.

One exporter told The Irrawaddy that although businesses are officially allowed to exchange 85 percent of their export earnings at market rates, banks are often unable to offer them, plus the regime requires the remaining 15 percent to be converted at the fixed rate of 2,100 kyats per dollar, resulting in significant losses.

Rising operating costs and volatile exchange rates are forcing some exporters to scale back overseas shipments. Traders are also struggling to determine how to price imported goods as foreign-currency costs fluctuate sharply.

“Importers are finding it difficult to set prices because the dollar rate is so unstable. This problem needs to be resolved immediately or domestic consumption will also be affected,” said a trader.

The latest decline is due to several factors, not least that the regime has announced it will borrow over 2 trillion kyats from the Central Bank to pay plug the hole in its budget—essentially telling the bank to print money. The rubberstamp Parliament has already approved an additional budget for the Central Bank to churn out fresh banknotes.

At the same time, the regime recently issued new import licenses, driving up demand for dollars. Another factor at play is planned salary increases for civil servants in the next fiscal year.

The regime also relaxed the fixed exchange rate for remittances from overseas workers from 3,600 kyats per dollar to 4,600 kyats in a bid to encourage them to go through official banking channels—but that backfired and was read as a sign of weakness by the market.

Other currencies have soared apace, with 100,000 kyats falling from 700 Thai baht earlier this month to around 600 baht.

That is bound to make Thai consumer goods and clothing forbiddingly expensive, to say nothing of imported medicines, cooking oil and industrial raw materials.

As usual when the situation runs away from it, the regime is targeting currency traders to try and frighten the market into submission. Yangon money traders say officers from the Bureau of Special Investigation are roaming the markets in search of anyone to fine and arrest.

World.title: Myanmar’s Democratic Opposition Urges ASEAN to Shun ‘Genocidal’ Junta Leaders
World.content:
Myanmar’s democratic opposition has urged ASEAN not to reintegrate regime leaders accused of war crimes and responsible for genocide, following an ASEAN-backed stakeholders’ dialogue in the Philippines.

The two-day meeting, hosted by the ASEAN chair in Tagaytay on Nov. 22-23, brought together representatives from the National League for Democracy (NLD), the Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw (CRPH), the Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF), resistance organizations and civil society groups.

CRPH spokesperson Sithu Maung said participants warned against any ASEAN move to recognize Myanmar’s de facto military regime.

“We reiterated that ASEAN should no longer provide space for military leaders who have committed war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide,” he said, referring to recent remarks by Min Aung Hlaing that his administration is reconsidering ‌the country’s relationship with the regional bloc. The putschist president spoke out after ASEAN leaders at last week’s Manila summit reaffirmed the ban on regime leaders attending high-level regional meetings.

Singapore, which will assume the ASEAN chair next year, attended the stakeholders’ dialogue as an observer. Delegations from both the Philippines and Singapore received the SCEF’s policy paper on Myanmar during the meeting.

Also in attendance were representatives from Chin resistance forces, the All Burma Students’ Democratic Front (ABSDF), elected lawmakers and other stakeholders. Discussions focused on the military situation, obstacles to delivery of humanitarian aid, implications of the Rohingya genocide ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), and the regime’s escalating airstrikes against civilians.

SCEF said last week’s genocide ruling should spur stronger efforts to enforce accountability for the regime’s past atrocities and ongoing crimes in Myanmar. It urged the international community not to shield military leaders from responsibility or enable further violence.

Then-military chief Min Aung Hlaing oversaw the 2017 “clearance operations” against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine that the World Court said amounted to genocide.

The regime rejected the ICJ ruling as “unfair” and stated its repatriation of Rohingya refugees would continue on its own terms, ignoring UN calls to grant them citizenship rights.

The democratic opposition’s appeal comes amid growing debate over ASEAN’s approach to Myanmar. While the bloc continues to exclude Min Aung Hlaing and his leadership from top-level meetings, members including Thailand, Malaysia, the Philippines, Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia have expanded bilateral engagement with the regime in recent months.

World.title: Myanmar Records Worst Landmine Casualties in the World for 3rd Year
World.content:
Myanmar recorded the highest number of casualties from landmines and unexploded ordnance in the world last year with nearly 1,900, according to the Landmine Monitor report released Tuesday.

The group’s research shows that Myanmar was the country worst affected by deaths from landmines and so-called “explosive remnants of war” for the third year running.

Worldwide, some 6,929 casualties were recorded in 2025, counting both civilians and military personnel. Myanmar accounted for a massive proportion of over 27 percent or nearly one-third with 1,891.

The military has regularly used antipersonnel mines since 1999 and increased their use notably after the coup in February 2021, the report pointed out.

Casualties soared as a result, from just 368 in 2021 to 1,003 in 2023 before doubling to 2,029 the following year.

They are regularly planted around military bases and outposts as well as mobile phone towers, mining operations and fuel pipelines.

One regime combat engineer reported that he was ordered to plant mines in Kachin and Rakhine states near populated areas, marked only by “Danger Do Not Enter” signs without mentioning mines.

“Often there are no signs,” said Thet Oo of the resistance Yinmabin–Salingyi Strike Committee in heavily mined Sagaing Region.

He said the regime frequently plants landmines when launching offensives or raiding villages, placing them at the entrance of houses.

They are designed to sever legs.

He admitted that the heartland resistance People’s Defense Forces (PDF) also used remote-controlled handmade landmines across the country after the coup. But when resistance governing bodies were formed, they banned mines near settled areas except for military purposes that require their authorization.

“The mines are meant to injure or delay the enemy,” he added. But he claimed they are always cleared before residents return.

The report says ethnic armed organizations reported seizing regime landmines almost every month between January 2022 and this September 2026, showing how prevalent their use is.

Regime-aligned ethnic Border Guard Forces (BGF) and the militias under the regime’s command also use landmines, it says.

“We urge all states to reject the production and use of antipersonnel mines, by any actor, under any circumstances,” Tamar Gabelnick, director of the International Campaign to Ban Landmines (ICBL) told AFP.

Syria was the second-most affected country with an equally massive 1,602 casualties, trailed at a substantial distance by Afghanistan with 497.

World.title: Myanmar’s China Dilemma: Turning Beijing’s Need Into Leverage Requires Legitimate Leaders
World.content:
Anyone seeking clarity on China-Myanmar relations must first ask one crucial question: does China need Myanmar, or does Myanmar need China?

Some argue that Beijing’s often-cited desire for access to the Indian Ocean through Myanmar is overstated. Others contend that China barely needs Myanmar at all, and that the relationship matters far more to Naypyitaw than to Beijing.

The reality is more complicated.

The Malacca Dilemma

Some analysts state that China needs Myanmar to secure overland access to the Indian Ocean, bypassing the Malacca Strait chokepoint. Others dismiss this view, saying the chokepoint is no longer a problem for a country which now boasts the world’s largest navy.

Chinese leaders began wrestling with the “Malacca Dilemma” in the early 2000s under President Hu Jintao. Around the same time, Beijing and Myanmar’s previous junta began talks on pipelines to transport oil and gas from the Bay of Bengal to Yunnan Province. Agreements were reached in 2007-2008, and construction began in June 2010.

At that point, China had yet to commission a single aircraft carrier. Its first carrier — a Soviet-made ship bought from Ukraine in 1998 and modified — did not enter service until 2012. Today, China operates three aircraft carriers and is reportedly building a fourth, which is expected to be nuclear-powered.

In other words, the strategic calculations underpinning the China-Myanmar energy corridor were made before Beijing emerged as a major naval power.

More than one energy corridor

In reality, China has never relied on a single route to meet its vast energy needs. Myanmar’s gas and oil pipelines provide a direct energy corridor from the Indian Ocean, but are only one piece of a much larger network. Beijing also imports oil through the Kazakhstan-China pipeline and receives oil and gas from Russia via overland routes. Meanwhile, the Central Asia-China pipeline network pumps natural gas from Turkmenistan and other Central Asian states into western China. Additional pipelines from Central Asia and Russia are planned or under construction.

For a country the size of China, a single pipeline or supply source is never enough. Beijing’s strategy is diversification.

Why Myanmar matters

Those who argue that China does not need Myanmar often point to Beijing’s expanding network of rail, road and pipeline connections across Eurasia.

China has rail links with Laos, Vietnam, Russia, Mongolia and Central Asia. It has energy corridors stretching north into Russia and west into Central Asia. On paper, Myanmar is only one route among many.

Yet, China is not an economic monolith; its interests vary sharply from province to province. Here is where geography gives Myanmar a unique advantage.

For inland provinces such as Yunnan, Sichuan and Guizhou, Myanmar provides the most direct route to the Indian Ocean. It is also the closest overland entry for energy imports arriving from the Middle East and Africa.

A railway or trade corridor through Myanmar would offer southwestern China a global shipping link that is shorter, cheaper and likely more efficient than ports to the east.

It would also help bridge the yawning gap between the country’s wealthy coastal provinces and its underdeveloped inland regions. Coastal provinces like Guangdong have prospered through direct access to ports, global shipping networks and export markets, outpacing inland neighbors facing higher logistics costs and weaker international connectivity.

For Beijing, plugging southwestern China into international markets is not simply a foreign-policy objective, but part of a broader strategy to reduce economic inequality inside China itself.

This is where Myanmar enters the picture.

The China-Myanmar Economic Corridor, Kyaukphyu projects, road links, railways and pipelines are not intended for China as a whole. They are aimed at accelerating development in China’s southwest including Yunnan, Sichuan and other inland regions seeking easier access to the Indian Ocean and global markets.

A relationship of mutual interests

When it comes to foreign investment, countries only inject capital where they see strategic or economic returns.

During the so-called reform period between 2011 and 2020, Myanmar failed to attract large-scale investment from Western countries despite their stated commitment to the country’s democratization. They were reluctant to invest because the prospects of economic returns were low.

Beijing invests because it sees a tangible benefit — access to the Indian Ocean that will integrate China’s landlocked southwest into global trade networks.

In return, Myanmar gains infrastructure, jobs, technology transfer and improved connectivity. The ousted National League for Democracy government recognized the benefits in 2020 when it signed agreements for the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor.

A well-governed Myanmar could turn China’s need for access into an opportunity, negotiating terms that serve its national interests, and ensuring a win-win situation for both. The question is whether military-ruled Myanmar is in a position to do so today.

The real question

The argument over whether China needs Myanmar or Myanmar needs China misses the point. Both need each other.

China needs Myanmar as an Indian Ocean gateway, a trade partner and a critical link in the development of its southwestern provinces. Myanmar needs investment, infrastructure and access to the world’s second-largest economy. The ingredients for a mutually beneficial relationship are in place.

The real question is whether Myanmar has leaders capable of translating that potential into national gains rather than debt, dependency and unequal agreements.

A military regime lacking a public mandate, mired in corruption, and facing war crime accusations cannot negotiate from a position of strength — or ensure that Chinese investment serves Myanmar’s national interests.

China’s need for Myanmar is real. The challenge for Myanmar is ensuring that need works in its favor.

World.title: Arakan’s Next Battle Is for Legitimacy, Not Territory
World.content:
The International Court of Justice’s (ICJ) November 19 ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during its 2017 military operations marks a historic moment for international justice. But its implications extend beyond Myanmar’s military and the courtroom in The Hague.

For the United League of Arakan/Arakan Army (ULA/AA), which now controls most of Arakan (Rakhine State) in western Myanmar, the judgment raises a fundamental question: Can a movement that has achieved remarkable military victories build a political system that protects the rights of all communities, including the Rohingya?

The ICJ judgment is legally binding on Myanmar, not directly on the ULA/AA, which was not a party to the case. Nevertheless, the organization now controls much of the territory from which hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fled to Bangladesh. Its policies will influence the prospects for reconciliation, refugee repatriation and Arakan’s international engagement.

The ULA/AA’s next challenge is therefore not simply territorial control, but establishing political legitimacy through responsible governance.

The politics of identity

One of the most sensitive issues facing the ULA/AA concerns the terms “Rohingya,” “Bengali” and “Muslim.”

For Rohingya communities, their name represents ethnic identity, historical belonging and the right to recognition. Arakan political actors and the people of Arakan, however, reject the term “Rohingya,” preferring “Bengali” because of competing interpretations of the region’s history and migration.

The ULA/AA has sometimes encouraged the use of “Muslim” as a less politically contentious term in efforts to improve relations between communities.

Such an approach may help reduce tensions, but it cannot resolve the underlying disagreement. “Muslim” describes religious affiliation, while “Rohingya” represents ethnic self-identification. The terms are not interchangeable, and not all Muslims in Arakan identify as Rohingya.

The ICJ’s treatment of the Rohingya as a protected group under the Genocide Convention underscores the significance of their collective identity.

Yet peaceful coexistence does not require every community to agree on a single historical narrative. It requires accepting that disagreements over identity cannot justify discrimination or the denial of fundamental rights.

For the ULA/AA, respecting ethnic self-identification while ensuring equal treatment would demonstrate political maturity rather than weakness.

Social harmony requires more than symbolic gestures

Decades of discrimination, communal violence and displacement have created deep mistrust between Arakanese (Rakhine) and Rohingya/Muslim communities.

Some local initiatives under ULA/AA administration, including intercommunal meetings, sporting activities and limited Muslim participation in local governance, suggest efforts to rebuild relations.

These developments may be constructive, but genuine social harmony requires more than symbolic gestures.

It depends on freedom of movement, access to education and healthcare, protection of property, fair administration and meaningful participation in decisions affecting communities.

The ULA/AA also faces serious human rights scrutiny. United Nations reporting has raised allegations of abuses against Rohingya civilians in areas under Arakan Army control, including arbitrary detention, forced labor, forced recruitment and restrictions on movement.

The organization has disputed allegations of wrongdoing, while citing security threats from armed groups operating near the Bangladesh border.

Such threats require legitimate security responses, but they cannot justify collective punishment or discrimination against civilians. The actions of Rohingya/Muslim armed organizations must be distinguished from the rights of Rohingya/Muslim communities.

Credible investigations, accountability and transparent administration would do more to build trust than political assurances alone.

International engagement is not recognition

The ULA/AA’s territorial advances have transformed the political landscape along the Myanmar-Bangladesh border.

Bangladesh, which hosts more than a million Rohingya refugees, has publicly acknowledged communicating with the AA as part of efforts to address the refugee crisis.

This creates opportunities for practical engagement with regional governments, the United Nations and international humanitarian organizations.

China and India also have strategic interests in Arakan, particularly concerning regional stability, trade and infrastructure development.

However, practical engagement and formal diplomatic recognition are fundamentally different.

Governments and international organizations may cooperate with authorities exercising effective territorial control without recognizing them as sovereign governments.

The ICJ judgment does not confer international recognition or political legitimacy upon the ULA/AA. Nor does it guarantee that regional governments or the United Nations will recognize the organization.

Nevertheless, the ULA/AA could strengthen its international standing by demonstrating respect for human rights, facilitating humanitarian assistance and establishing credible policies for all communities.

The opportunity is significant, but international credibility must be earned through conduct rather than military victories alone.

Preparing for the Rohingya challenge

The Rohingya issue remains one of the most complex long-term challenges facing the ULA/AA.

Refugees in Bangladesh continue to face uncertainty over citizenship, security, freedom of movement, destroyed homes and the possibility of renewed persecution.

Although the ULA/AA cannot independently resolve Myanmar’s citizenship framework or confer internationally recognized Myanmar citizenship, it exercises considerable influence over local security, administration and conditions affecting eventual refugee returns.

Rather than waiting for formal international recognition or a nationwide political settlement, the ULA/AA should develop a comprehensive and transparent policy addressing the Rohingya issue.

Such a framework should prioritize equal protection, respect for ethnic self-identification, intercommunal dialogue and safeguards against discrimination.

It should also establish credible mechanisms to investigate alleged abuses, protect housing and land rights, preserve residency records and consult Rohingya representatives, including refugees in Bangladesh.

Cooperation with Bangladesh, relevant UN agencies and humanitarian organizations could help prepare the groundwork for future repatriation.

Any return process must be voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable. Premature repatriation without adequate security and rights protections would risk repeating past failures.

These steps would not immediately resolve historical grievances or guarantee international recognition. But they would demonstrate that the ULA/AA is preparing to govern a diverse society rather than merely administer territory captured through war.

The real test of Arakan’s future

The ICJ judgment concerns Myanmar’s legal responsibility for genocide. It does not determine Arakan’s constitutional future or confer recognition upon the ULA/AA.

Yet it presents the organization with an important political opportunity.

For decades, Arakanese communities have pursued greater autonomy, political rights and self-determination. Those aspirations remain central to Arakan’s political struggle.

But self-determination becomes more credible when it respects the rights and identities of other communities sharing the same territory.

The ULA/AA has demonstrated its military capabilities. Its next challenge is to establish institutions capable of protecting people regardless of ethnicity, religion or political affiliation.

International engagement may expand as the organization becomes increasingly relevant to regional security, humanitarian operations and the Rohingya refugee crisis.

However, lasting legitimacy will depend on whether it can translate territorial control into inclusive governance, accountability and peaceful coexistence.

The ULA/AA has won control of territory. Its next battle is to earn the trust of all the people who live there.
