According to TI, in 2026 the Special Penitentiary Service was the largest public procurer using non-competitive tenders. Through this mechanism, the agency awarded contracts worth a total of 203.7 million lari (approximately $78.6 million).

Almost the entire amount – 201.4 million lari – went towards two contracts for providing meals to prisoners.

In May 2026, the Special Penitentiary Service awarded contracts worth 152.4 million lari to Giorgi 2020 and 49 million lari to Delfood.

Both companies were the sole bidders in their respective tenders. Moreover, their bids exactly matched the estimated values set in advance.

The contracts were awarded amid a scandal over the quality of food served in Georgian prisons. Earlier, in March, the Special Penitentiary Service terminated its contract with Ili Group, which had been responsible for providing meals to prisoners.

According to TI, Giorgi 2020 had never previously won a public procurement tender.

On 3 April 2026 – the day the tender was announced – the company’s owners transferred 33% of its shares to Irakli Letodiani free of charge.

According to the TV Pirveli television channel, Letodiani is a former employee of the State Security Service.

Which sectors have the least competition?

According to the study, several sectors have particularly high proportions of tenders with only one bidder:

Transport services – 85%;

Software and information systems – 81%;

Repair and maintenance – 78%;

Medical equipment and medicines – 59%.

The proportion of construction tenders attracting only one bidder was relatively low, at 29%. However, construction ranked first in terms of the total value of contracts awarded.

Non-competitive construction contracts were worth a total of 517.9 million lari (approximately $199.8 million).

Tbilisi and Batumi account for the largest sums in non-competitive procurement

According to TI, 43% of tenders organised by municipalities – including those run by mayors and bodies established by them – attracted no competition. The figure for central government agencies and other state institutions was 48%.

Municipalities awarded contracts worth a total of 625 million lari (approximately $241.1 million) without any competition.

In monetary terms, Tbilisi ranked first, with 277 million lari, accounting for 38% of the capital’s procurement spending. Batumi came second, with 63 million lari, or 30% of its procurement spending.

In terms of the proportion of non-competitive tenders, the highest figures were recorded in Ambrolauri (61%), Terjola (59%) and Khulo (55%).

The risk of tailoring tender requirements to specific companies

TI notes that one possible reason for the high proportion of tenders with only one bidder is that authorities tailor procurement requirements to suit specific suppliers. The organisation cites several examples of this practice.

In June 2026, TI reported on five road repair tenders announced by Batumi’s Department of Infrastructure and Improvement.

Under the terms of the tender, bidders had to either own an asphalt plant within a 30km radius of the work site or provide a contract with such a facility. This requirement applied to a tender worth 29.2 million lari (approximately $11.3 million), in which Gza was the sole bidder.

Another example is a security services tender announced by Georgian Railway in 2023. To qualify for the contract, worth 7.8 million lari (approximately $3 million), bidders had to demonstrate at least 20 years of uninterrupted experience.

According to Transparency International (TI), only two companies in the entire country met this requirement. The sole bidder was Intersecurity Georgia LLC, owned by Ioseb Alavidze, a former head of the Tbilisi police. The company’s bid exactly matched the estimated contract value.

The organisation also cites a tender for the provision of social canteen services announced by Rustavi City Hall in 2022.

In that case, the company offering the lowest price was excluded from the tender because its revised price schedule listed figures to four decimal places instead of two. The contract was ultimately awarded to a company whose bid was 155,000 lari (approximately $59,800) higher.

The problem extends beyond large-scale tenders

TI says that a lack of competition in public procurement is not a new problem. The organisation refers to a 2024 study which found that half of the large tenders – those worth more than five million lari – announced between January and July 2024 attracted no competition.

Figures for 2026 show that the problem is not limited to large-scale procurement: only one bidder took part in half of all tenders worth up to 100,000 lari.

The organisation also criticises reports prepared by the State Procurement Agency. TI notes that although the agency’s reports point to an increase in competition, none of its annual reports published since 2019 has mentioned that almost half of all public tenders attract only one bidder.

Non-competitive public procurement in Georgia

World.title: Broader Eurasian trade network: How Turkmenistan could expand Minsk’s transport options
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 27. On November 25, at the international conference "International Transport and Transit Corridors: Interconnection and Development - 2026" (ITTC 2026) in Ashgabat, Belarusian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Terekhov said Minsk is interested in making greater use of the eastern route of the North-South international transport corridor, which passes through Turkmenistan.

Speaking at the conference, Terekhov noted that the development of international transport corridors is among Belarus' key economic priorities. According to him, the country has well-developed terminal infrastructure and is ready to ensure stable cargo transit along the North-South and West-East routes.

During the visit, the Belarusian deputy prime minister also met with Deputy Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers of Turkmenistan Mammet Akmammedov. The sides discussed the modernization of railway infrastructure, the management of transit cargo flows and the further development of transport and logistics cooperation between Minsk and Ashgabat.

The transport agenda is part of a broader rapprochement between the two countries, marked in 2026 by intensified contacts at the highest and governmental levels. On May 22, Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov received Belarusian Prime Minister Alexander Turchin in Ashgabat. The sides discussed the development of trade and economic cooperation, industrial cooperation and the implementation of joint projects.

A new stage of political dialogue began in October. On October 7 in Awaza, Foreign Ministers Rashid Meredov and Maxim Ryzhenkov discussed prospects for bilateral relations and signed a cooperation program between the foreign ministries for 2027-2028. Two days later, as part of events related to Turkmenistan's CIS chairmanship, Serdar Berdimuhamedov met with Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko. Both leaders expressed interest in achieving mutually beneficial results in the implementation of joint projects.

Against this backdrop, mutual trade has also grown. In 2025, trade turnover between Belarus and Turkmenistan more than doubled, reaching about $268.5 million. This dynamic strengthens the economic foundation of bilateral relations and increases the practical importance of transport links between the two countries.

Through Turkmenistan to Iranian ports and Asian markets

Practical development of the eastern branch of the North-South corridor began back in February 2025, when Turkmenistan's Transport and Logistics Center (TULM) organized the first test shipments of potash fertilizers from the Belarusian company Belaruskali. Two container trains, each consisting of 62 forty-foot containers, traveled through Russia, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan to Iran. The cargo was then shipped by sea from the port of Bandar Abbas to eastern ports in China. TULM also announced its intention to expand the geography of shipments in the future and send Belarusian potash fertilizers to Indian ports.

In December 2025, the Belarusian operator Beltamozhservice announced the launch of an express route for container shipments along the Belarus–Russia–Kazakhstan–Turkmenistan–Iran corridor. The stated delivery time was about two weeks. The route offers Belarusian exporters an additional overland access to the Iranian market and makes it possible to use Iran's port infrastructure for further maritime shipments.

Belarus' interest in the southern direction may also be linked to efforts by regional players to strengthen transport links between Central and South Asia. Pakistan has consistently promoted the idea of turning its ports of Karachi, Port Qasim and Gwadar into maritime gateways for landlocked Central Asian countries. This agenda received additional momentum within the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO), where Islamabad named the development of road, rail and multimodal corridors among the priorities of its 2026-2027 chairmanship.

As Trend noted earlier in its analytical article "Pakistan's southern gateway: How ECO could bring Central Asia closer to the Indian Ocean," three possible routes can be seen in this transport configuration: through China and Kyrgyzstan, and through Turkmenistan with further transit via Afghanistan or Iran. For Minsk, connecting to such a system could open additional opportunities for access to South Asian markets and the use of Indian Ocean port infrastructure.

Exports as the backbone of Belarus' industrial model

Exports play a significant role in Belarus' economic model. According to the World Bank, in 2025 exports of goods and services amounted to about 55.1% of the country's GDP, reaching nearly $40 billion. Industrial exports are mainly formed by large enterprises in the chemical and machine-building industries.

One of the best-known examples is Belaruskali. According to the US Geological Survey, in 2024 Belarus ranked fourth in the world in potash production, accounting for 10.7% of global output. Over the year, the country exported 6.43 million tons of potash products in terms of potassium oxide content, while production at the enterprise rose by 7.2% to 7.1 million tons.

The machine-building segment is represented by manufacturers such as MAZ, MTZ and BelAZ, which produce trucks and buses, tractors and heavy-duty mining dump trucks. The regional scale of this sector is also telling: in 2025, more than 21,000 people worked in machine building in the Mogilev Region, and the sector comprised over 100 organizations. The region's largest enterprises include Mogilevliftmash, the Mogilev Railcar Building Plant and Bobruiskagromash. They produce elevator equipment, freight cars, agricultural machinery and components.

Another major production group is the agro-industrial complex, primarily the dairy, meat and food industries. In 2025, Belarusian food exports reached $8.1 billion, up 17.5%.

At the same time, the export model of Belarusian industry faces a growing foreign trade imbalance. According to Belstat, the share of exports in industrial output fell from 57.3% in 2021 to 50.9% in 2025. Over the same period, exports of industrial products rose by only 2.6%, to $37.9 billion, while imports grew by 17.8%, to $45.3 billion. As a result, the foreign trade deficit in industrial products reached $7.4 billion, having increased almost fivefold in five years. This dynamic heightens Belarusian manufacturers' interest in expanding sales geography and finding additional buyers.

State policy is also aimed at supporting exporters and reducing costs when entering foreign markets. "It's no secret that Belarus is an export-oriented country. Most of our goods are exported," Gennady Klyga, Deputy Chairman of the Belarusian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, said in September 2026. According to him, in the first half of the year, with the chamber's assistance, enterprises signed export contracts worth more than $270 million. Among the support measures, he singled out the recently introduced mechanism for compensating transport costs.

Under these conditions, the search for new markets and logistics routes takes on particular importance for Minsk. The southern direction, including Iran and potential access through it to South Asian markets, could become one such option. The activity of the Belarusian delegation at the transport conference in Ashgabat and the talks on developing transit cooperation with Turkmenistan fit into this strategy.

West and South of the CIS: the geography of shared transport connectivity

Belarus and Turkmenistan occupy different geographic positions in the former Soviet space: the former lies in its west, the latter in the south, on the Caspian Sea and at the crossroads of routes between Central Asia and the Middle East. The development of transport links between them could strengthen interaction between two distant parts of the CIS, creating additional opportunities for the movement of goods between European markets and southern destinations. In this sense, Belarus' interest in Turkmen infrastructure is consistent with the goal of closer integration of the transport systems of the Commonwealth states.

Notably, strengthening such connectivity became one of the central priorities of Turkmenistan's CIS chairmanship in 2026. In the chairmanship concept, Ashgabat named the development of the North-South and East-West corridors as key areas of economic cooperation. At the October summit in Awaza, President Serdar Berdimuhamedov proposed declaring 2029 the CIS Year of Transport Connectivity. The initiative received the support of the Commonwealth heads of state. It is a long-term task of building a more integrated transport system in which each country's infrastructure helps expand interregional links.

Thus, the development of transport connectivity between Belarus and Turkmenistan serves the mutual economic interests of the two countries. Further alignment of their transport strategies could open additional opportunities for Minsk and Ashgabat to make use of each other's geographic advantages and infrastructure potential.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan’s trade deficit reaches about $11B on 12-month basis - ING
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 27. Kyrgyzstan's merchandise trade deficit has reached around $11 billion on a 12-month rolling basis, while remittance inflows remain an important source of support for household incomes, domestic demand and the foreign exchange market, ING said.

According to the bank’s Caucasus and Central Asia (CCA) macro and credit report, in which Kyrgyzstan was added to its regular coverage for the first time, the trade deficit is increasingly driven by machinery and other imports from China and economies outside the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). Some of these imports reflect the domestic investment boom, while part of the exceptional expansion in trade has been related to regional re-exports.

ING said the latter appears to have peaked in 2024–2025 and has since normalised. Meanwhile, trade ties with Russia remain deep, with bilateral trade exceeding $4 billion annually. The bank said this supports near-term economic activity but also reinforces Kyrgyzstan's exposure to Russia-related external risks.

Gross remittance inflows remain close to $3 billion per year and continue to be dominated by Russia, which accounts for around 90% of total inflows. Net remittances amount to approximately 11% of GDP, supporting consumer spending, household earnings and currency stability.

The report also cautioned that official balance-of-payments figures should be interpreted with particular care. Citing International Monetary Fund estimates, ING said unrecorded re-exports materially distort the measured current account deficit.

Annual structural current account deficits of $5 billion–$7 billion require continued external financing, while large unrecorded trade and financial flows make headline current account figures unusually difficult to interpret.

According to Trend's calculations based on official data from the Ministry of Economy and Commerce of the Kyrgyz Republic, Kyrgyzstan recorded a merchandise trade deficit of $8.7 billion in January–September 2026 as imports of $11.4 billion exceeded exports of $2.7 billion by more than fourfold, while trade with non-EAEU countries reached $8.9 billion, or 63.1% of total foreign trade turnover.

World.title: Polish PKP eyes stronger rail freight links between Uzbekistan and Europe (Exclusive)
World.content:
Photo: The Ministry of Transport of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 27. Polish State Railways (PKP) sees opportunities to expand freight transportation between Uzbekistan and European markets through the development of multimodal services, logistics infrastructure and potential cooperation between PKP CARGO and Uzbekistan Railways, Michał Stilger, a PKP spokesman, told Trend in an exclusive interview.

A memorandum of cooperation signed by PKP and Uzbekistan Railways in Tashkent on November 9 marks an initial step toward planning joint activities, focusing on freight and multimodal transportation, logistics infrastructure and the exchange of expertise.

"The memorandum signed in Uzbekistan marks the first step toward planning cooperation in areas of key importance to both the PKP Group and Uzbekistan Railways, with a particular focus on freight and multimodal transport, logistics infrastructure, and the exchange of experience," Stilger said.

A major factor underpinning the potential partnership is growing trade between Uzbekistan and the European Union. According to European Commission data cited by PKP, bilateral trade exceeded 5.5 billion euros in 2025, up nearly 16% from the previous year.

The EU's main exports to Uzbekistan include machinery and equipment, chemical products and agri-food goods, while imports from Uzbekistan consist primarily of chemical products and textiles.

PKP noted that the predominantly containerized nature of these goods creates opportunities to expand rail freight transportation between the two markets.

"Rising trade volumes create potential for the development of intermodal services for our PKP CARGO Group – the second-largest freight carrier in Central Europe," Stilger said.

Polish logistics hubs could support regional cargo flows

PKP is exploring opportunities to use its terminal infrastructure as logistics hubs supporting trade between Central Asia and Europe.

One facility whose potential could be assessed is the multimodal terminal in Zduńska Wola-Karsznice, located in central Poland.

The company's ambitions extend beyond launching new freight connections to establishing a broader logistics partnership linking China, Central Asia, Poland and the European Union.

"From the PKP Group perspective, establishing a lasting logistics partnership, strengthening trade between China, Central Asia, Poland, and the European Union market, will create a stable 'bridge' between these regions," Stilger said.

PKP CARGO S.A. and Uzbekistan Railways already cooperate through the relevant commissions of the Organization for Cooperation of Railways (OSJD).

According to Stilger, PKP CARGO is also participating in initiatives aimed at strengthening Poland's position as a transit country for cargo flows from Central Asia to Western Europe.

PKP CARGO outlines cross-border transport capabilities

PKP CARGO S.A. independently provides rail freight services in Poland and across the railway networks of Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Slovenia, Austria, Hungary, the Netherlands and Lithuania, using 1,435-millimeter standard-gauge tracks.

The company's operations are supported by the necessary licenses and certificates, while its subsidiaries provide cross-border services at the interface between the 1,520-millimeter and 1,435-millimeter railway systems.

These services are supported by terminals and logistics centers in Małaszewicze and Medyka-Żurawica, as well as a transshipment terminal in Braniewo.

PKP CARGO also sees potential in using the logistics infrastructure at Zduńska Wola-Karsznice to support future cooperation with Uzbekistan.

The potential partnership could focus on expanding freight transportation and developing multimodal logistics solutions to connect Central Asian cargo with distribution networks across Poland and other European markets.

World.title: Trump says US military presence in Europe discussed in detail with Mark Rutte
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 27. US President Donald Trump has said that the issue of maintaining an American military presence in Europe was discussed in detail during his meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.

Trump made the remarks in response to a journalist's question about whether the issue had been raised during their meeting at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida.

“We discussed this in detail,” the US president said.

Commenting on the possibility of reducing the US military presence in Europe, Trump noted that NATO allies “did not provide much help to Washington” during the conflict with Iran.

He then added: “But we have Greenland. It’s three times the size of Texas. Honestly, that’s changed my thinking a bit.”

It should be recalled that in September, Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen signed an agreement transferring responsibility for the security of the Arctic island to Washington. Greenland is an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark.

Meanwhile, the US administration has postponed until next year the release of the findings of its review of the American military presence in Europe, which had originally been scheduled for December.

World.title: Former IDPs return home to Azerbaijan's Aghdere, Khojaly, and Khojavend
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 27. As part of Azerbaijan’s “Great Return” program, another group of former internally displaced persons (IDPs) has been resettled in the Aghdere, Khojaly, and Khojavend districts.

The resettlement is being carried out in line with the directives of President Ilham Aliyev as part of the return of citizens to territories liberated from occupation.

Previously, the families had been temporarily accommodated in various parts of the country, mainly in dormitories, sanatoriums, and administrative buildings.

At this stage, a total of 73 families, comprising 271 people, are returning to their homeland.

In the Aghdere district, 10 families (42 people) have been resettled in Vanli village, 15 families (49 people) in Childiran village, two families (six people) in Kolatag village, and one family (one person) in Heyvali village.

In the Khojaly district, four families (seven people) have moved to Badara village, nine families (32 people) to Khanyurdu village, and eight families (33 people) to Khanabad village.

Meanwhile, seven families (30 people) have been resettled in the town of Khojavend, while another 17 families (71 people) have moved to Guzeykhirman village in the same district.

World.title: Kazakhstan's telecom investment expected to reach $1.09 billion in 2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 27. Investment in Kazakhstan's telecommunications sector is projected to reach 500 billion tenge ($1.09 billion) in 2026, up from 482 billion tenge ($1.06 billion) in 2025, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev reported.

According to the press service of the Kazakh government, the announcement was made during a government meeting chaired by Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov, where officials discussed the development of telecommunications infrastructure.

According to Trend's calculations, investment in the sector increased by 35% in 2025 compared to 2024. The projected figure for 2026 represents a further 3.7% increase year-on-year.

Bektenov emphasized its importance for the country's digital transformation.

"In his State of the Union Address, the head of state set out a number of goals for building a people-centered digital economy. Telecommunications infrastructure is the foundation for its development," he said, referring to President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev's address to the nation.

Notably, Kazakhstan has been expanding its telecommunications infrastructure to support growing demand for mobile and fixed internet services. At the end of 2025, the country had 27.4 million cellular subscribers, including 19.1 million mobile internet users, while the number of fixed internet subscribers reached 3.3 million, according to the Bureau of National Statistics.

Alongside subscriber growth, the country has been upgrading its network capacity through fibre-optic expansion and the rollout of 5G technology. By the end of 2025, Kazakhstan's telecommunications infrastructure included more than 96,000 kilometres of fibre-optic lines and 8,983 mobile base stations. A further 1,154 5G base stations were commissioned during the year. In January-October 2026, the physical volume index of telecommunications services increased by 4.9% year-on-year, according to the Bureau of National Statistics.

World.title: Сontainer ship ran aground off coast of Cuba
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 27. At least one person has died, 12 have been rescued, and three others remain missing after a Panama-flagged container ship capsized off the coast of Artemisa Province in western Cuba.

The Cuban Maritime Administration announced this on November 26.

According to the agency, 13 crew members have been located, including one who was found dead. The search for the three remaining crew members is ongoing.

The survivors are receiving medical attention and all necessary assistance in accordance with established protocols.

An interagency government commission has also been established to investigate the causes of the incident and coordinate search and rescue operations with the vessel's owners.

World.title: Uzbekistan-China freight via Kyrgyzstan surges 53-fold in five years - EDB
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 27. Uzbekistan's trade turnover with China reached $17.5 billion in 2025, while freight transportation between the two countries through Kyrgyzstan increased more than 50-fold from 2020, highlighting the growing importance of regional transport corridors, according to a report by the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB).

The report, titled Central Asia’s Transport Links with China, said cargo transportation along the multimodal China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan route reached 1.8 million metric tons in 2025, compared with 33,700 metric tons in 2020.

According to Trend's calculations based on the EDB's figures, freight volumes along this route rose approximately 53.4-fold over five years, representing an increase of around 1.77 million metric tons, or approximately 5,240%.

Under the existing arrangement, cargo is transported by rail across China before being transferred to trucks in Kyrgyzstan for onward delivery to Uzbekistan. The EDB noted that this multimodal route has become an increasingly important channel for trade between China and Uzbekistan.

The growth comes amid a broader expansion in regional trade. Trade between China and the five Central Asian countries nearly tripled between 2020 and 2025, rising from $23.5 billion to almost $70 billion. China's share of the region's total merchandise trade increased from 17–18% in 2020–2021 to nearly 30% in 2025, making it Central Asia's leading foreign trade partner.

Uzbekistan accounted for approximately one-quarter of the region's trade with China in 2025, based on its $17.5 billion turnover and the regional total of nearly $70 billion. Kazakhstan remained China's largest trading partner in Central Asia, accounting for approximately half of the region's trade with the country.

The EDB also highlighted the scale of freight movement across the region. A total of 51 million metric tons of cargo was transported between Central Asia and China by rail and road in 2025. Rail accounted for 35.6 million metric tons, while road transport handled 15.4 million metric tons.

Rail accounted for approximately 69.8% of total freight volumes, compared with 30.2% for road transport. Kazakhstan handled around 84% of the overall freight flows, reflecting its central position in regional rail and road connectivity with China.

For Uzbekistan, one of the key projects expected to reshape transport links is the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway. The planned 523-kilometer line will connect Kashgar in China with Andijan in Uzbekistan through Kyrgyzstan. Around 50 kilometers of the route will pass through Uzbek territory.

According to the EDB, the railway's estimated freight capacity will reach 7 million metric tons annually under the initial single-track configuration and could increase to 20 million metric tons following the construction of a second track. The project is intended to establish a more direct transport connection between the three countries and provide additional opportunities for freight movement toward other regional markets.

The EDB also identified the development of modern warehouses, border-crossing infrastructure and more efficient logistics services as important conditions for sustaining growth in road freight transportation. A shortage of modern Class A warehouses across Central Asia could constrain the further expansion of international road transport.

The EDB attributed the expansion of road freight transportation to the growth of small and medium-sized businesses, which increasingly require transport services for smaller consignments. The liberalization of international road transport agreements, China's accession to international transport conventions and the digitalization of cross-border procedures have also facilitated cargo movement.

The report further noted that freight flows between Central Asia and China continued to increase in 2026, with rail transportation rising 8% year over year to 31.8 million metric tons in January-October.

World.title: The four 'workhorse' appliances you need to deep clean at home
World.content:
When it comes to keeping our homes clean and running efficiently, there are a few appliances doing the heavy lifting.

Washing machines, dryers, fridges and vacuum cleaners also come with big price tags, so looking after them is important for their longevity.

Experts say if we're not regularly cleaning these appliance "workhorses", our homes and clothes may not be as clean as we think.

Here's how to give them a deep clean and how often to do it.

Vacuum cleaner

Cleaning the things that clean our home, especially vacuum cleaners, is an "annoying" but important job, according to Leanne Neiland, a cleaning content creator based in Brisbane/Meajin.

"If your vacuum cleaner is not clean, it'll have less suction, therefore decreasing the air quality in your house because you're not vacuuming up as much dust," she says.

" What is most important is visually looking at your appliance to see if it needs cleaning. "

Matthew Steen, the director of Reviews and Testing at CHOICE, says checking the manufacturer's instructions is the first step for cleaning any appliance.

"These will show how to access and replace the filters, [and] which parts are safe to wash," he says.

"If you have a problem and [the manufacturers] turn around and say, 'we can tell that you didn't clean it [as recommended]', then basically you're killing your warranty."

Deep cleaning bagless vacuums should be done once a year. (Supplied)

Choice recommends cleaning once a month by brushing off any accumulated dust on washable filters and rinsing them under a tap or in a sink of warm water.

Deep cleaning bagless vacuums should be done once a year:

Remove and clean the dust bin/canister and wash in warm water (if recommended)

You may be able to remove and wash the hose, wand and accessory heads too

Use a second vacuum cleaner, if possible, to help remove built up dust

Wipe the exterior with a soft cloth

Replace the filters if needed

Make sure all parts are completely dry before you put the vacuum cleaner back together

You should replace any worn out parts such as the hose, roller drive belt and accessories

Fridge

When it comes to cleaning the fridge, Choice recommends doing this more regularly to make sure it's running at its best.

"It actually is costing you money not cleaning your fridge out because mould and bacteria cause your food to break down quicker," Ms Neiland says.

" I actually do it every time I get my groceries … all you need is a wet microfiber cloth and wipe out the shelves. "

Choice recommends once a month pulling out the shelves and crisper and giving them a clean with warm soapy water, and at the same time checking for anything that's expired.

Mould and bacteria in your fridge can cause your food to spoil more quickly. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

For deep cleaning seasonally or annually:

Roll your fridge out and clean behind and under it

Check internal temperatures with a thermometer and adjust to compensate for changes in ambient temperature

Clean and dust the external condensers at the back of older models

Check and clear the drainage or evaporation pans

For manual defrost fridges and chest freezers, defrost and clean the freezer compartment

Check and replace your water filter if necessary

Check the door seals for wear and replace if necessary

Washing machine

Mr Steen says washing detergents and fabric softeners can adhere to the drum of your washing machine and can "create stains on your clothes".

Ms Neiland recommends keeping the machine's door open in between uses to allow moisture to dry out and avoid mould build-up, which will make deep cleans easier.

How to deep clean a washing machine:

Check manufacturer's cleaning instructions

Run the machine empty on its hottest cycle with a bit of detergent (or run a cleaning cycle if it has one)

Wipe away mould on door seals and other surfaces using hot soapy water and a soft cloth

In top loaders, clean the lint filter out

In front loaders, check the coin trap or lint trap

Remove any scud with hot soapy water and a sponge or toothbrush (including detergent dispenser)

Check if the machine in properly levelled and adjust the feet if needed

Check the hoses for damage and replace them if necessary

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

Dryers

The methods for deep cleaning your dryer will depend on the model you have.

It is one of the most important jobs to stay on top of according to our experts, because excess or clogged lint in filters can cause fires.

Queensland Fire Department recommends cleaning your lint filter before or after each load.

Deep clean vented dryers every three to six months:

Turn off and unplug the dryer

Remove the lint filter and pick off dry lint, wash in soapy water and let it dry

Use a toothbrush or small paintbrush to remove any lint from tight corners in the filter slot, then vacuum it out with a narrow nozzle attachment

Vacuum and wipe slats on the front vent grille

Wipe down the drum and rubber door seal with a damp cloth

A dirty lint filter on a clothes dryer. (Adobe Stock)

Choice says heat pump dryers are becoming more popular because of their energy efficiency.

For these, "it's really the electric ventage that you need to worry about," Mr Steen says.

" They don't have as much lint as you would in a vented dryer, but keep an eye on lint build-up. "

Clean a heat pump dryer every six months to a year:

World.title: Wildlife carer warns invasive fire ant could be 'devastating' to native species
World.content:
Australia's native animals could suffer if an infestation of red imported fire ants in Sydney affects the availability of insects and other food sources, a wildlife carer has warned.

A biosecurity control order is in place for the next six months across a 2-kilometre area in Auburn in the city's inner west, where the invasive insect has been discovered.

Under the order, materials such as soil, mulch and plants must be treated before they can be moved outside the area.

The area covers about 2,400 residents and 4,800 businesses, a number of which regularly import products from overseas.

Another detection of fire ants occurred at the Enfield Intermodal Logistics Centre in September, with imported goods believed to be the source of both infestations.

The ants can become aggressive and sting if disturbed, with illness and death possible in severe cases.

Other insects and plant life could also be affected, which could in turn reduce the food supply for koalas, spotted quolls, bats and other vulnerable native species.

Koalas like Elvis could be at risk if Sydney's fire ant infestation continues to spread. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

WIRES volunteer carer Morgan Philpott said the consequences of an out-of-control infestation could be "quite devastating".

"When you understand that other animals, other native animals need those insects to survive … then the impact from having serious red ant infestation is quite high," he said.

"It's a very complex ecology in our bush, and it doesn't take much to start to cause disruption to that.

"I think most people are aware that Australian wildlife [species] are under growing pressures and threats to their existence here, and adding another threat like this invasive species could be just enough to tip the scale beyond repair.”

Mr Philpott says it does not take much to disrupt food supply chains in the bush. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

Eradication efforts continue

NSW Agriculture Minister Tara Moriarty said state and Commonwealth authorities were "throwing everything at eradicating these ants".

"We're not accepting that they're here to stay," she said.

"We're putting resources into eradicating them, that's what the biosecurity order is for.

"Our tracing operations will be able to trace back the [contaminated] products from where they've come from so that we can then do more to stop any more coming through."

Ms Moriarty conceded it was possible the ants had already spread across the city.

"There's certainly a risk that that's the case, and that's why I am very strongly calling on the federal government to do more, to put more resources into stopping these things from coming through our borders," she said.

Ms Moriarty says authorities were working hard to eradicate the invasive pest. (ABC News: Floss Adams)

As part of the biosecurity response, additional staff are being sourced from the Commonwealth, Queensland and other states to increase surveillance and baiting capacity.

Experts believe the infestation at the Auburn site could be up to 12 months old.

NSW Premier Chris Minns said education for the public and local councils would be key to ensuring the ants were reported and eradicated quickly.

"I accept that maybe local councils don't have the expertise as it relates to fire ants, but we're going to have to rapidly educate the public and council officials as well," he said.

Anyone who spots a suspicious ant or earth mound should take a photo of the site and contact the NSW Biosecurity Helpline on 1800 680 244.

World.title: Affected families in despair after $24m in unit deposits goes missing
World.content:
Like hundreds of other impacted home buyers, Aziz Namazov and his family were excited to move into their newly built Landmark apartment in Sydney before their deposit vanished.

About three years ago, Mr Namazov and his wife bought an off-the-plan apartment in the Casa Delmar development in Dee Why.

"To do so, we had to sell our only property that we had," he said.

"We were meant to settle today [on the Dee Why unit]. A few days ago we received an email that settlement would not proceed, with no explanations.

" Then it became obvious that pretty much our deposits are now gone, and we don't know where. "

More than $24 million in deposits from prospective apartment buyers have gone missing, with Landmark launching legal action against Branston Neville Lawyers and solicitor Ken Neville to recoup the missing funds.

More than $24 million in deposits from prospective apartment buyers has gone missing. (ABC News: Quentin Theron)

The developer alleges only part of the deposits held in trust were transferred to Hendrix Legal as directed after the company changed firms.

The matter is due to return to the Supreme Court on November 30.

The ABC has contacted Branston Neville Lawyers and Mr Neville for comment.

Almost 300 home buyers were due to get the keys to their newly built apartments between this week and early next year but have been left in limbo.

The situation affects about 140 purchasers at the Dee Why development and about 145 purchasers at the Second Avenue development at Blacktown.

The situation affects about 140 purchasers at the Casa Delmar development in Dee Why. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht )

The Landmark development in Blacktown remains under construction. (ABC News: Quentin Theron)

Landmark founder Arash Tavakoli told the ABC: "Our purchasers are angry and frustrated, and they have every right to be.

" We are actively pursuing every avenue to get purchasers into their homes, including looking at whether they can move in before settlement. "

The Law Society of NSW confirmed it had suspended the practising certificate of Mr Neville and appointed a manager to Branston Neville Lawyers to "take control of the practice with immediate effect".

Landmark projects missing unit deposits Almost 300 home buyers were waiting to get the keys to their newly built apartments in Sydney's Dee Why and Blacktown.

The Supreme Court of NSW made freezing orders, and subpoenas were issued to financial institutions to help establish where the funds were.

Mr Namazov and his family had been planning to move into their Dee Why apartment on December 2 and, in preparation, had terminated their lease on their current rental property.

They had also transferred their electricity, gas and internet plans over to the new property, with their belongings packed before they received the terrible news.

"We are facing a real, real chance that close to Christmas our family with two kids will be just out there on the streets with nowhere to go," he said.

Landmark says they are working to address the situation promptly. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

'Never thought this would happen'

Mr Namazov said the past few days had been "extremely stressful".

"My wife had a breakdown when she got the news … what we put in [our deposit] is two generations of hard work," he said.

'It's everything we have, that's our home."

Home buyers were due to get the keys to their units between this week and early next year. (ABC News)

Daniel Uzun de Oliveira is in the same predicament.

"We gave a deposit two years ago, that deposit was taken into a trust account … we have all the receipts and as far as we are aware, that money is gone," he said.

He and his family were supposed to settle last Wednesday, and move into their Dee Why unit on December 1.

Daniel Uzun de Oliveira is also impacted. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht )

Mr Uzun de Oliveira had given his current rental property a termination notice in preparation for moving, and said he was thankful the landlord had since given them the all-clear to stay for now.

"Our solicitors are working and keeping us updated as much as they can," he said.

"It's stressful, it's frustrating. I came to Australia 11 years ago and never thought this would happen in a first world country."

'Why can't we settle?' says solicitor

Despite the Dee Why apartment complex being ready for buyers to move in, the legal action has left purchasers in limbo.

"The building is ready … we as buyers fulfilled our obligations in full, so we don't understand why we can't just settle in," Mr Namazov said.

Clare Wainwright is representing a number of buyers. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht )

Wainwright Legal principal solicitor Clare Wainwright, who represents 42 affected Dee Why purchasers, said it was a distressing situation.

"It's honestly been some of the hardest news that we've had to communicate with them. In my entire career I've never had phone calls like this," she said.

"At the end of the day we've got purchasers without homes, there's already proceedings afoot that we're aware of in relation to those deposits … so why can't we settle? They [the buyers] have done all of the right things."

NSW Premier Chris Minns said the situation was "a concern".

"They [the deposits] should be held in trust accounts; if that hasn't been the case then there needs to be a full investigation," he said.

Chris Minns reacted to the missing deposits situation. (ABC News)

There were calls for the Law Society of NSW to lift the cap on the compensation available through its Fidelity Fund.

The fund is administered by the Law Society to compensate people who lose money due to law firms acting improperly in relation to trust funds or property.

It is capped at $1 million for claims relating to a single law practice, unless the Law Society authorises a greater payment.

For now, the hundreds of buyers wait with bated breath.

"We are hoping for the best," Mr Namazov said.

World.title: Veggie workers allegedly underpaid and illegally hired in Gippsland
World.content:
Three vegetable farms around Bairnsdale in Victoria's east have been caught allegedly underpaying workers and using unlicensed labour hire companies.

Inspectors from the Victorian Labour Hire Authority (LHA) discovered the activity during unannounced visits in the region in recent weeks.

More than 20 workers on three farms were found to be employed through unlicensed labour hire providers.

They were picking and packing vegetables, including broccoli, green beans and lettuce.

During the inspections, LHA officers found records showing the workers were paid up to 35 per cent below the minimum horticulture rate.

Labour Hire Licensing Commissioner Wayne Gatt said it was a "significant concern".

"We know that workers at those locations are most vulnerable to exploitation," he said.

Wayne Gatt says farmers are responsible for checking if labour providers are registered. (Supplied: Labour Hire Authority)

Mr Gatt said the use of workers hired through unlicensed labour companies was illegal in Victoria.

"It's serious, to be quite honest," he said.

"People breaking the law face significant penalties in Victoria, up to $660,000 for a corporation.

"If you're an individual that's responsible for a company or responsible for the activity, up to $160,000."

Horticulture is a high-risk industry for worker exploitation due to the seasonal and transitory nature of the work and the high number of migrant workers.

More labour hire inspections are planned for other horticulture regions in Victoria. (ABC Rural: Warwick Long)

The LHA has stepped up inspections during the busy harvest period, with further visits planned in the Mildura, Yarra Valley and Shepparton areas.

"It's too late when inspectors are at your front gate to check if you're doing the right thing," Mr Gatt said.

At a time when 85 per cent of Australian vegetable growers are considering leaving the industry in the next 12 months because of high costs, according to peak body Aus Veg, Mr Gatt said compliance was even more important.

"If they're competing against people who aren't even paying their workers correct wages, that makes it even harder," he said.

"We know that growers are doing it tough, we know that the margins are tight, but the industry is not supported by people undercutting and acting unlawfully."

World.title: 'Appalling' vandals chainsaw 500yo tree in southern WA
World.content:
Conservationists fear a 500-year-old king jarrah tree in southern Western Australia may not survive after vandals used a chainsaw to cut near its base.

At 36 metres tall, the beloved jarrah is one of the tallest trees at the Wellington National Park, about 193 kilometres south of Perth.

Police are appealing for public assistance as they investigate the incident, which they said occurred sometime between Saturday and Sunday.

Officers said occupants of a silver Jeep, seen in the area in the days following the incident, may be able to assist with inquiries.

The king jarrah tree is thought to be up to 500 years old. (Supplied: DBCA)

A Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA) spokesperson said an arborist had assessed the tree and all options to save it were being considered.

The spokesperson said a chainsaw had been used around the base of the tree, which also has an existing large hollow butt.

"Formal technical advice from the consultant arborist around whether the king jarrah tree can be saved is expected next week," the spokesperson said.

Preston Environment Group convenor Peter Murphy said he was shocked by the incident.

"It made my heart sink," he said.

Police are investigating the incident, which they say occurred sometime on the weekend. (Supplied)

" What a terrible loss to the community and to our heritage. "

Mr Murphy believed the tree may need to be felled due to safety risks.

"Looking at the damage on scene photographs … I fear it may have to actually come down," he said.

Vandalism of this kind can attract penalties of up to $10,000 and one year in prison.

Tree a tourism icon

Mr Murphy said it was not the first time trees in the Wellington district had been targeted in this fashion.

He believed the vandals knew exactly what they were doing.

"It was done by a very experienced tree feller and we can see by the damage that they knew basically how much of the tree to vandalise, knowing quite well that now it constitutes a safety [risk]," he said.

Environmental groups believe vandals targeted the tree to force its removal. (Supplied)

In 2024, an 800-year-old peppermint tree was mistakenly cut down to a stump by state government contractors.

Mr Murphy said the king jarrah was a drawcard for the region.

"The sad part about it is this particular tree was such a huge tourism icon that actually had international significance," he said.

'Senseless and heartbreaking', minister says

WA Environment Minister Matthew Swinbourn said it was hard to fathom why someone had vandalised the tree.

"In an act that I can only describe as appalling, senseless and heartbreaking, some absolute jerk has seen fit to vandalise the Wellington National Park's iconic king jarrah tree with a chainsaw," he said on social media.

"Whoever did this has damaged something precious to all of us."

DBCA has closed the site to the public and is urging anyone with information to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or DBCA's Collie or Bunbury offices on 9735 1988 or 9725 4300.

World.title: Data centre proposed for NT station amid water licence dispute
World.content:
A Central Australian cattle station at the centre of controversy over one of the nation's largest water licences has become the site of the latest proposal to establish a data centre in the Northern Territory.

Environmentalists have labelled the plan for Singleton Station, 130 kilometres south of Tennant Creek, "tone-deaf" and one they will fight "tooth and nail" due to a long-running dispute over a licence granted to owner Fortune Agribusiness to establish a 3,500 hectare irrigated fruit and vegetable farm at the site.

The Northern Territory government granted the company in 2021 the licence to extract 40 billion litres of water annually for 30 years, but native title holders fought the matter all the way to the High Court, which quashed the licence in August.

The decision to grant Singleton Station a water licence to extract 40 billion litres of water annually for 30 years was quashed in the High Court. (ABC News: Samantha Jonscher)

As the NT government reassesses Fortune Agribusiness's licence to irrigate the Singleton horticulture project, it has been revealed that the company has invested in Central Australia AI (CAAI) and a proposal to establish a hyperscale data centre on the station.

The Victorian-based CAAI did not respond to the ABC's request for an interview, but a LinkedIn post from its chair Russell Board says it is "developing a 1GW+ renewable-led AI and high-performance computing campus".

"The campus will have an integrated power supply comprising 3.3 GWp solar, 10GWh solar storage, 450 MW gas-backed reliability, a private HV grid, water-enabled cooling and strategic fibre in one master-planned platform," the post reads.

CAAI says it is developing a "AI and high-performance computing campus" at Singleton Station. (ABC Alice Springs: Samantha Jonscher)

An Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) extract shows Fortune Agribusiness holds 25 per cent of CAAI's shares. while a company that shares the same address and a similar name, Fortune AI, owns 37.5 per cent.

One of CAAI's four directors is well-known NT identity Vivian Oldfield, who bought Murranji cattle station, north of Elliott, in September last year.

Murranji Station is the planned home of Project Ares, another hyperscale data centre, which is currently undergoing an NT Environment Protection Authority environmental impact assessment.

In a statement, Fortune Agribusiness said the Singleton proposal was being discussed with the NT government and the Central Land Council (CLC), which represents Indigenous custodians across the Red Centre.

CLC general manager Josie Douglas said the land council was "notified very recently that there was a proposal for a data centre".

Josie Douglas says water use at the proposed data centre will likely be a concern for traditional owners. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald)

"It's in the very early stages of development and we expect to receive a full proposal from the company early next year," she said.

She said the CLC's role was "to represent the interests of native title holders and traditional owners, and we will be doing that once we receive a full proposal from the company".

She said she expected water for a data centre would be a concern for those "who have said from the very start water is precious", adding "we need water for the environment and water for country and water for people".

Protesters to fight 'tooth and nail' against proposal

Environmentalists have rejected the data centre plan, with a group of about 30 concerned citizens rallying outside NT Environment Minister Joshua Burgoyne's electorate office in Alice Springs on Thursday morning.

The protesters decorated an office window with droplet-shaped cards featuring messages including "water is life" and "back off NT groundwater".

A group of protesters outside Joshua Burgoyne's office yesterday. (ABC News: Will Green)

The Arid Lands Environment Centre's Alex Vaughan labelled the data centre proposal as "shocking, outrageous, and tone-deaf".

"Communities across the NT and across this country are resisting AI data centres, but also we want to protect and conserve our groundwater, which is critical to our local economies, environments, cultures and communities," he said.

"It makes one of the largest groundwater grabs in the country even bigger and sees even more free water and more clearing of habitat.

" A super-campus AI data centre at Singleton Station will be resisted and we'll be fighting tooth and nail to make sure this proposal does not get up. "

Parliament passes new water laws

Mr Vaughan was also critical of the NT government's new water laws, which passed parliament on Thursday.

"The Northern Territory already has some of the weakest water laws in the country and these reforms are further gutting the Northern Territory's water laws," he said.

Alex Vaughan says the proposed data centre at Singleton Station is "outrageous". (ABC Alice Springs: Samantha Jonscher)

Ms Douglas agreed, saying the CLC was concerned that the government was assessing Fortune Agribusiness's water licence after the company had withdrawn its farm proposal from an environmental impact statement (EIS) evaluation.

"In terms of water planning in the NT, it's going backwards, and we have urged Mr Burgoyne not to make a decision on the water licence until he has had full consideration of the environmental impact assessment," she said.

"We would expect he would make a decision based on robust, sound evidence."

Protesters have criticised the CLP government's new water laws, which passed parliament this week. (ABC News: Will Green)

Fortune Agribusiness said in a statement it had withdrawn because it "considers it appropriate to await the minister's decision before progressing aspects of the EIS that may be affected by that decision".

"Our intention is to ensure the new EIS process can take account of the minister's decision and relevant new and updated scientific information," the statement said.

Mr Burgoyne said the current Fortune Agribusiness water licence under consideration was for the farm, and a data centre project would need separate approval.

World.title: Breaking: Former RAAF pilot Robert Crawford found guilty of wife's murder
World.content:
A jury has found former Queensland RAAF pilot Robert Crawford guilty of the murder of his wife.

49-year-old Frances Crawford died at her Upper Lockyer property in July 2024.

She was discovered fatally injured at the base of a rock retaining wall, near a toppled over ride-on lawnmower in the early hours of the morning.

More than two months later, her husband Robert Crawford was charged with her murder, which he pleaded not guilty to.

He maintained he discovered Ms Crawford trapped underneath the 200-kilogram machine, before pulling her from beneath it and trying to revive her.

The 49-year-old believed Ms Crawford must have died while attempting to move it away from automated sprinklers while he was asleep.

It was alleged by prosecutors he strangled his wife, manipulated her body and the scene, before calling emergency services and providing a false story.

Psychologist Frances Crawford died at her Upper Lockyer home in July 2024. (Supplied: Queensland Police Service)

His lawyers argued their client had nothing to do with Ms Crawford's death, and it was a tragic accident.

After hearing from more than 40 witnesses, including three defence experts, the jury deliberated for more than three days before returning its verdict.

When the verdict was delivered, Crawford did not react.

Ms Crawford's family, who have been in proceedings every day, celebrated and cried.

Crawford, who had previously been on bail, was taken into custody.

He will be handed a mandatory life sentence and will face a sentencing hearing this afternoon.

The house where Frances Crawford was found dead. (Queensland Police Service)

Jury accepted Crawford killed wife and 'has been lying ever since'

Intimate details about the couple's life were aired in the Supreme Court throughout the course of the four-week trial.

Much of the crown evidence centred on the period just before Ms Crawford's death, when they had been attempting to repair their relationship, after separating the year prior.

The split came after Ms Crawford discovered more serious occasions of infidelity, but she had decided to take her husband back on a 3-month trial-basis.

In this time, they began counselling, and Ms Crawford had a list of strict rules Crawford was to abide by or else she would leave him.

This included not speaking with women unnecessarily, watching pornography or masturbating, and spend more than $30 without her approval.

He was also required to take regular polygraph tests.

Frances Crawford died in a suspicious incident on her Upper Lockyer property. (Supplied)

Messages between the pair and digital notes penned by Ms Crawford showed she constantly went back and forth about whether she wanted to stay married.

She often became upset and angry with Crawford about his past infidelity and told friends and family she was unhappy and did not feel safe.

Crawford also told colleagues and former lovers, he felt trapped, and he was still trying to romantically pursue other women.

During his closing arguments, crown prosecutor Chris Cook said it was obvious they were in a "crumbling marriage" and both Crawford and his wife were trying to leave.

"He wasn't enjoying being around Frances … he felt controlled, he felt worthless," he said.

Mr Cook said in addition to Crawford being a "love rat" he also had a financial motivation to kill his wife, as "he stood to lose out" in a divorce settlement.

He said Crawford was "never going to leave his house" he built and "loved his superannuation more than his family".

"He did not want his wife to take half of the estate," he said.

Mr Cook said it was a "pressure cooker" situation, and Crawford was "ready to snap".

"He strangled his wife, he caused her to hit her head … he staged the scene and he's been lying ever since," he said.

World.title: Sam Walker signs with PNG Chiefs for 2028 NRL season
World.content:
Premiership-winning halfback Sam Walker has signed with the Papua New Guinea Chiefs for the 2028 season.

Walker, whose relationship with the Sydney Roosters fell apart after the club's grand final victory, will head to Port Moresby on a two-year deal.

The Queenslander is coming off the best year of his career, making State of Origin and Australian Test debuts.

"Sam is undoubtedly a gifted footballer who has already shown that he has tremendous vision, an outstanding kicking game and an ability to create something out of nothing," PNG Chiefs coach Willie Peters said.

"He is also a very smart footballer who understands how to influence and control a game and has shown that he can perform on the biggest of stages across club, state and now international level.

"We're really excited about what he can bring to the team and his partnership alongside Jarome Luai allows us to have one of the game's most creative and influential halves combinations — something which I'm excited to see develop as we take to the field."

Walker made his Test and Origin debuts this season. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

The 24-year old was the 2021 Dally M Rookie of the Year and has been the Tricolours starter ever since.

He also attracted interest from South Sydney and Canterbury.

PNG Chiefs General Manager of Football Michael Chammas said the team believed Walker's best football was still yet to come.

"Sam was someone we identified as a player who we believe could have a transformational impact on our team — both in how we play on the field but also on the way we build our side and the way other players excel around him," Chammas said.

"He is a premiership winner, an Origin star and a World Cup winner and he has shown that he can perform under pressure in the biggest moments of our game.

Walker is the latest star signing for the PNG Chiefs. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"He is also still young and we believe that his best years are ahead of him.

"We're thrilled that Sam has committed to what we are building and we look forward to seeing him play a key role in the bright future of the PNG Chiefs."

Walker is the latest star signing for the Chiefs, who have created shockwaves in the player market with their ability to offer tax-free contracts.

In the past week, they have signed Canberra and New South Wales backrower Hudson Young and North Queensland star Jeremiah Nanai.

Luai, Brian To'o, Zac Lomax and Joseph Manu will also line up for the Chiefs in their inaugural season.

Walker is the ninth player they have signed with either Test or Origin experience.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Labor’s gas reservation laws pass, parliament concludes for the year; Houthis strike Saudi oil refineries
World.content:
Telstra has switched on emergency roaming for the first time in Australia, opening its network to customers of rival telcos on bushfire-hit Flinders Island.

Telstra is the only mobile provider on the Bass Strait island, so visitors and emergency crews on other networks would normally have no coverage.

About 150 people are now using Temporary Disaster Roaming to make calls, send texts and access basic data at no extra cost.

The telco said the capability is available in only three other countries globally.

The phones need to support VoLTE roaming - so must be newer models - and medical alarms and Eftpos terminals are not covered.

World.title: Erin Patterson launches High Court appeal in last-ditch bid for freedom
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts Erin Patterson launches High Court appeal in last-ditch bid for freedom Erin Pearson Updated November 27, 2026 — 4:00pm ,first published 12:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Mushroom cook killer Erin Patterson has launched an eleventh-hour High Court bid for freedom over her convictions for murdering three family members and attempting to kill a third. Last month, the 52-year-old mother of two had her appeal thrown out by the Court of Appeal and her sentence was instead increased, with her prospects of parole scrapped. Three Court of Appeal judges – Stephen McLeish, Lesley Taylor and Peter Kidd – found Patterson’s crimes so cold, calculated and shocking that they ruled she should die in jail. Erin Patterson outside court in April 2025. AAP That ruling meant Patterson became the first Victorian woman, and only the second in the country’s history, to be sentenced to life without parole, after she served beef Wellington laced with death cap mushrooms to four lunch guests at her Leongatha home in July 2023.



On Friday afternoon, Patterson’s legal team filed paperwork with the High Court in the hope of securing a second appeal hearing in the county’s highest court. The appeal is against both conviction and Patterson’s life sentence, according to legal sources. In 2025, Patterson was found guilty by a jury of the poisoning murders of her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail’s sister, Heather Wilkinson. She was also convicted of attempting to murder Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, who survived the lunch. From left: Don Patterson, Gail Patterson, Heather Wilkinson and Ian Wilkinson were poisoned. The Court of Appeal found Patterson’s persistent murderous intent had protracted the suffering of her victims.



The appeal court judges found Patterson had coldly planned and carried out the murders over nearly three weeks. This, they said, included extending the invitation to lunch, false denials of having foraged for mushrooms, false assertions she had cancer, and hiding the truth for nearly a week as her victims lay dying. This, the judges found, represented a cruel breach of trust. Following their dismissal of Patterson’s appeal, the killer’s legal team had 28 days to file an appeal application with the High Court before the 5pm deadline on Friday. Defence barrister Richard Edney outside the Court of Appeal in August. Joe Armao In fighting for a fresh trial, Patterson’s appeal barrister, Richard Edney, earlier argued there were a number of potential irregularities in his client’s case, including during the jury’s seven-day sequestration at a Gippsland hotel while they were deciding Patterson’s fate. The jurors stayed in the same Traralgon hotel as the prosecution and police involved in the case. Edney claimed this amounted to a catastrophic and fundamental failure to comply with the trial rules.



Patterson was found guilty on all charges following an 11-week trial in Morwell, in Victoria’s east, in mid-2025. The trial heard from more than 50 witnesses. During Patterson’s recent appeal, Director of Public Prosecutions Brendan Kissane, KC, dismissed Edney’s concerns as baseless and not warranting the granting of an appeal. Heather Wilkinson and Gail Patterson died on August 4, 2023, from multiple organ failure, with a diagnosis of amanita mushroom poisoning. Don Patterson died the following night. Ian Wilkinson, a pastor in the area, survived after spending several weeks in an induced coma. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Manhattan scores $30M Canadian gold farm-in
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Manhattan scores $30M Canadian gold farm-in Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward November 27, 2026 — 3:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Manhattan Gold Corporation has struck a massive deal worth more than A$30 million to fast-track exploration at its Hook Lake gold and base metals project in Nunavut, Canada, signing on US-based USFM Corporation as its new farm-in partner. USM is a private US exploration company based in Colorado that has just agreed to agreed to reverse merge with Nasdaq listed Twin Vee Powercats Co. The agreement will see USFM pump A$28 million into exploration over three years to earn an 85 per cent stake in the project. In addition, USFM will pay the company US$1.5 million (A$2.27M) in cash within 90 days, US$1M (A$1.513M) on signing of the transfer agreement for a 7.5 per cent interest and a further US$500,000 (A$757,000), for a total of 12.5 per cent. Once the A$28M is spent, Manhattan will retain a 15 per cent interest that will be free-carried all the way through to a bankable feasibility study. Manhattan Gold’s Hook Lake project in Nunavut, Canada has attracted a significant farm-in partner on the back of impressive maiden drilling results. The deal is structured in stages, with USFM earning its interest as it meets cash payment and expenditure milestones. It can earn a 51 per cent majority stake by spending A$8 million on exploration within 12 months. Its interest can grow to 75 per cent with an additional A$10 million spend in the second year, and finally to 85 per cent with a further A$10 million in the third year. The agreement also includes a provision for USFM to sell a 1 per cent net smelter royalty, with Manhattan receiving 50 per cent of the proceeds from any sale. Importantly, the company has confirmed with the ASX that shareholder approval is not required for the transaction, removing a key hurdle for deal completion. The sale of the initial 12.5 per cent project interest and the earn-in is subject to any necessary regulatory or third-party approvals as well as signing of the formal agreements, which is expected to happen within the next 30 days.



‘USFM’s significant commitment of over $30m over 3 years enables development of Hook Lake at pace and scale.’ Manhattan Gold Corporation general manager Bayard Rezos The deal lands on the back of a stellar maiden 25-hole, 4592-metre reverse circulation drilling campaign, at Hook Lake by Manhattan in 2026, the first at the project since 1988 which delivered a suite of high-grade gold and polymetallic hits. Drilling at its Jaws prospect returned a cracking 41.15-metre intersection grading 4.66 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 83.82m which included a richer 7.62-metre core of 18.67g/t gold. Other significant intercepts at Jaws featured hits of 74.67m assaying 1.61g/t gold from a shallow 21.34m and 51.82m grading 1.88g/t gold from 47.24m. The drilling doubled the known mineralised strike at Jaws to more than 1.8 kilometres, with a tantalising 1km gap between two of the drill holes remaining untested. Additionally, maiden drilling at the nearby Spectre prospect confirmed a high-grade volcanogenic massive sulphide (VMS) system. One hole hit a stunning 19.81m at 1.77 per cent copper, 84.3g/t silver and 0.8g/t gold from just 42.67m. That hit included a sweet 6.1-metre section going 3.18 per cent copper, 147.9g/t silver and 1.37g/t gold. Adding to the intrigue, a separate near-surface zinc zone in the same hole yielded 19.82m running at 5.55 per cent zinc, with a remarkable 3.05-metre section landing an eye-watering 29.5 per cent zinc. Adding further flavour, assays are also pending for a further three drillholes and over 550 till samples from the company’s Omega prospect along with continuing metallurgical test work and the interpretation of final airborne magnetic data from both Jaws and Spectre.



Manhattan Gold Corporation general manager Bayard Rezos said: “Bringing USFM in as funder and operator at Hook Lake is a strong endorsement of the results of our 2026 maiden program. USFM’s significant commitment of over $30m over 3 years enables development of Hook Lake at pace and scale without Manhattan relying on capital markets. With Manhattan retaining 15% of Hook Lake, free-carried all the way to a Bankable Feasibility Study, our shareholders will be able to benefit from USFM’s efforts in defining both a gold resource and a polymetallic copper, zinc, gold and silver resource at Hook Lake across this district-scale project.” The new partnership will see an aggressive exploration program kick off early next year, with USFM planning an initial 10,000m diamond drilling campaign as part of its first A$8 million commitment. The program will target extensions to the Jaws gold system, follow up the high-grade VMS zones at Spectre and test new targets generated from recent geophysical and sampling work. The A$2.27M cash injection will allow Manhattan to turn its attention to its 100 per cent-owned Tibooburra South licences in New South Wales which cover an 80-kilometre strike of deep-seated faults that have not yet been tested by modern drilling. The cash will fund geophysics, mapping and a maiden drill campaign. The 2195-square-kilometre exploration package at the Tibooburra gold project in New South Wales covers a significant portion of the emerging Koonenberry gold district, which shares structural characteristics with the rich Stawell goldfields zone in Victoria. To keep costs down, the northern section of the project is managed under a strategic farm-in agreement with Novo Resources. Novo is actively funding and executing exploration on this ground, allowing the company to retain exposure to any discovery upside without incurring direct capital expenditure.



With a well-funded partner now set to unleash the drill rigs on its Canadian ground and cash in the bank to get the rods spinning in NSW, Manhattan has effectively added two fully-funded exploration plays. For a company with a market cap of just over A$30 million, securing a free ride on a A$28 million exploration spend while retaining a meaningful stake in a project with this much potential could be a game-changer. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: ‘Alarmed’ UN experts call out Vietnam over alleged kidnapping of Australian
World.content:
WorldAsiaAustralians abroad ‘Alarmed’ UN experts call out Vietnam over alleged kidnapping of Australian Zach Hope November 27, 2026 — 3:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Singapore: United Nations experts have called out Vietnam for the alleged transnational kidnapping of Australian pro-democracy campaigner Tran Hiep alongside two of his colleagues while they were travelling in neighbouring Cambodia. It is the first time the UN has weighed in publicly on the highly sensitive case since the men disappeared on September 18 and turned up in Vietnamese detention on alleged terrorism offences. Australian human rights activist Tran Hiep. “We are alarmed by these alleged transboundary abductions, which violate international human rights law, including the prohibitions on arbitrary detention, enforced disappearance and torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment,” the panel of 11 independent experts said in a statement published by the UN on Thursday (Geneva time). The panel also said Cambodia had an international obligation to investigate, including “whether Cambodian officials knew of, facilitated, or tolerated their alleged arbitrary detention and transfer”.



View post on X Hiep and Norwegian citizen Nguyen Duc Thuan, along with Vietnamese man Thai Cong Truong Son, are members of Viet Tan (VT), a diaspora political party championing human rights and a transition to democracy from one-party, communist rule. The Vietnamese government brands it a terrorist organisation. Related Article Cambodia Australian activist charged in Vietnam as pro-democracy group accuses Hanoi of kidnapping VT said the men were in Cambodia to meet with other members when they were snatched and driven across the border, labelling it a “brazen act of transnational repression”. The group said the Australian and Norwegian men were booked to fly to Bangkok on September 19, the day after they went missing, before flying home to their respective countries. The trio’s fate was a mystery for 10 days until Vietnamese authorities announced they were arrested while allegedly trying to enter Vietnam, which holds that VT is responsible for “recruiting, training and directing its members to infiltrate into Vietnam to provoke protests and riots, undermine security, conduct assassination [sic] and kidnapping”.



Hiep told Australian officials on an October 15 consular visit he “never entered or crossed the Vietnam border on his own” and that he “remained terrified and traumatised from being attacked and kidnapped in Cambodia”, according to VT. The UN panel agreed witness accounts were “inconsistent” with the Vietnamese government’s explanation of events. “We urge Vietnam to disclose the circumstances and legal basis of the arrests, investigate any involvement of its officials in the alleged abductions, transfers and enforced disappearances, and co-operate fully with Cambodia’s investigation,” the experts said. “We are concerned by the growth of transnational repression in the region and prevailing impunity surrounding it. We call on states to combat it, including through the Association of South-East Asian Nations (ASEAN).”
