World.title: Backed by Helen Haines, this rural doctor is putting a safe Liberal seat in play
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Backed by Helen Haines, this rural doctor is putting a safe Liberal seat in play Annika Smethurst November 27, 2026 — 3:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A rural doctor who made the switch to politics at the urging of federal independent MP Helen Haines is turning one of the safest Liberal electorates in the state into a contest. Independent Lachie McKeeman is riding of wave of support in Benambra fuelled by anti-major party sentiment, the retirement of veteran Liberal MP Bill Tilley, and the community’s ongoing shock at the attack on Haines. Helen Haines with Lachie McKeeman. Instagram His feel-good strategy has even extended to his rivals – photographed arm-in-arm with the local One Nation candidate, saying it had been a pleasure to campaign alongside her. Three Liberal sources, speaking to The Age on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal party polling, said the party had become increasingly convinced it would lose the once-safe electorate despite the Coalition being on track to form government after Saturday’s poll.



“We are worried about Benambra and Prahran,” one senior Liberal source said. “But Benambra has always been ours.” Held by conservative parties at a state level since 1877, the electorate is based around Wodonga and takes in the towns of Beechworth and Chiltern. McKeeman’s campaign has sought to capitalise on longstanding frustrations with the major parties and underinvestment in regional healthcare, prompting the Liberal Party to pledge $100 million towards the Albury Hospital redevelopment if elected. “As a doctor, you’re inherently a very political person because you engage with people in a very close, caring way ... and you see the impacts of political neglect on their everyday life,” McKeeman told The Age.



The father of three’s candidacy is backed by Haines, who represents the overlapping federal seat of Indi. The 65-year-old MP lost both legs as a result of an allegedly targeted attack outside her Wangaratta office on October 19. Floral tributes fill the pavement outside Helen Haines’ electorate office. Jason South Four sources, linked to both Haines and the Liberal Party and speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss the campaign, said McKeeman was benefiting from an outpouring of community support for her. McKeeman, who worked alongside the Indi MP while advocating for better hospital infrastructure, said it was Haines who first encouraged him to run for politics. “Helen’s the one who probably lit the fire and asked would I ever entertain it,” he said.



“She’s an excellent role model for what community independent representation can deliver. “But if you live in an area with such a scale of political neglect ... eventually you can either get angry at the system from outside or you can try and contribute and affect meaningful change.” The contest comes just months after voters across the border in Sussan Ley’s former federal seat of Farrer abandoned the Liberals in favour of One Nation. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election ‘A shocker for working people’: Bracks pleads with Labor voters to reject One Nation While One Nation how-to-vote cards for the state election put McKeeman in last position, local candidate Kellie Sheappard told voters at a recent forum to put McKeeman or Libertarian candidate Tim Quilty second.



“I am sitting in this seat today because I am incredibly passionate about youth mental health and our hospital,” Sheappard said at the Better Border Health forum. “My how-to-vote card has obviously come out today ... I have to be honest it doesn’t necessarily reflect what I would have chosen. “I would personally have gone with the other candidates who most closely aligned with my values which would be Tim or Lachie.” Related Article Queensland votes Katter party considers running candidates in Brisbane amid One Nation’s rise The retirement of Liberal veteran Tilley, after two decades in parliament, has further opened up the race for Benambra where the margin, now sitting at less than 1 per cent, has repeatedly narrowed after strong challenges by community independents at the 2018 and 2022 state elections.

World.title: ‘Non-royal royals’: How Harry and Meghan are finding their feet back in Britain
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeRoyal family ‘Non-royal royals’: How Harry and Meghan are finding their feet back in Britain Karla Adam November 27, 2026 — 3:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

London: When Prince Harry and Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, visited a food bank last month in Nottingham, England, they had a request. No formal etiquette. No need for the bows or curtsies that are traditional for members of the royal family. They could be greeted simply as “Harry and Meghan”. Prince Harry and Meghan’s return to the UK has resurfaced questions about their status. AP The co-founder of the charity, Sajid Mohammed, obliged with an ordinary handshake. But around him, people curtsied, some volunteers wept with emotion, and six parents tried to bring their babies forward. Even royals who have stepped back from official duties still inspire reflexive ceremony in some parts of the British public, it turns out.



“It’s very much like Harry’s mother, the late Princess Diana,” Mohammed said in an interview afterwards. “There’s an aura around the couple. It’s beyond normal celebrity.” The rapturous response they received in Nottingham underlines the challenge, and potential benefit, that the newly repatriated Sussexes offer to Britain’s monarchy, six years after they left the country and their royal duties. Loading Queen Elizabeth II reluctantly blessed their self-imposed exile in 2020 but said they must give up state funding and could no longer be considered full working royals. Their return to Britain, which Harry said in a recent GQ interview was to pursue “opportunities for the family” and to school their children, has resurfaced questions about their status. They appear intent on carving out a specific profile, managing public appearances on their own terms and tightly controlling what they share, including where in England they have chosen to live, a fact that remains undisclosed.



Their careful image management partly reflects the couple’s fraught relationship with the British media and its often hostile coverage in the past, which they previously said had contributed to their departure from Britain. Related Article Analysis

Royal family Why King Charles felt he had to clarify Prince Harry’s status For now, their popularity in opinion polls remains low, particularly compared with Harry’s older brother, Prince William, and his wife Catherine, Princess of Wales. But can a pair armed with Hollywood glamour and global celebrity operate on their own terms without eclipsing the traditional working royals they left behind? Could their return, if managed well, inject energy into the institution as King Charles III enters his twilight years?



‘Non-royal royals’ Charles has attempted to hold the line his mother drew. After Harry and Meghan’s return to Britain in late August, a letter was sent on the King’s behalf to government officials, stiffly reminding them that the Sussexes were “private citizens” who must not be addressed as “His and Her Royal Highness”. The difficulty for Buckingham Palace is that, while it could strip away their official status, it cannot strip away their star power. Harry and Meghan at an event at the European Parliament in Brussels, Belgium. Getty Images On the day the Sussexes swept through Nottingham, the King was in Cardiff opening the Senedd, the Welsh parliament. While the BBC covered both events, ITV’s evening bulletin only found room for Harry and Meghan.



The following day, Peter Hunt, a former BBC royal correspondent, highlighted the newspaper front pages smothered in Sussex coverage, writing on social media: “The palace spin is failing on contact with reality. Harry and Meghan are royals. End of.” The daily grind of the British crown is not, by design, thrilling. It’s built on unglamorous routine – bronze plaques unveiled at rain-swept civic centres and ribbon-cuttings at community clinics – the stoic pattern perfected by Princess Anne, Charles’ sister. Princess Anne during a recent visit to the Falkland Islands. Getty Images “One of the biggest risks of Harry and Meghan coming back is that they take attention away from the core work of the monarchy, which is slightly dull at times,” said Craig Prescott, a constitutional scholar and author. That dynamic is particularly delicate around major overseas excursions, when palace orthodoxy holds that royals should not compete with royals on big tours. When Charles toured the Caribbean this month, the Sussexes avoided rival public appearances.



Other overlaps are harder to prevent. Prince Harry’s GQ interview was published as Charles and Queen Camilla welcomed the Sultan of Oman on a state visit to Windsor Castle. Critics immediately claimed Harry was upstaging a diplomatic event, but supporters noted that the interview had been taped a month earlier in New York and that its publication had been scheduled by the magazine. Sultan Haitham bin Tarik of Oman with King Charles and Queen Camilla at a state banquet at Windsor Castle, in October. Aaron Chown/Pool PA via AP The couple’s carefully curated schedule of activities since returning to England certainly resembles, at times, the diplomatic and charitable engagements that define royal life. In September, Harry attended London’s WellChild Awards, honouring seriously ill children. The couple appeared at the European parliament in Brussels, where Harry spoke about digital safety and child protection.



This month, Harry made a surprise visit to Ukraine, meeting wounded veterans preparing for his Invictus Games, and last week he made an unannounced appearance on ITV’s This Morning, where he joked that he was “squeezing” the American accents out of his kids and helped make a Christmas cake. “You might describe them as non-royal royals,” Prescott said. Off camera, the couple has settled into a quieter routine. While they have not disclosed where they are living and have asked the media not to reveal their children’s schools, they have been spotted in pubs around the Cotswolds – an idyllic pocket of southern England beloved by wealthy Americans. Their commercial interests complicate the picture. Meghan continues to build her lifestyle label, As Ever, and recently signed on as a guest judge for Junior MasterChef Australia.



‘A quiet rehabilitation’ Related Article Royal family Harry and Meghan’s battle to be accepted into Cotswolds high society But their present arrangement is fundamentally different. They carry no official duties, hold no royal patronages. Whether that proves sustainable may depend on how the couple and the palace manage the attention. While Harry has reconciled with his father, his relationship with William, the heir to the throne, appears to be as frosty as ever, with no reported interactions since the Sussexes returned. Nor does a warm reception at a charity signal a broader recovery in public affection.



A recent YouGov poll put Harry’s domestic approval at 29 per cent and Meghan’s at 20 per cent, with deep scars lingering over their noisy 2020 exit. Ed Owens, a royal historian, noted that a “quiet rehabilitation” is never out of the question in Britain, pointing to Camilla’s decades-long journey from tabloid pariah to queen consort. King Charles, then the Prince of Wales, with Diana, Harry and William at the family’s country home, Highgrove, in picturesque Tetbury, in 1986. Tim Graham/Getty Images Charles, too, has lived a life of many chapters – deeply unpopular during the breakdown of his marriage to Diana, he has since seen both his public standing recover and his environmental views become mainstream. “As long as there isn’t deliberate, direct and obvious competition between the working royals and Harry and Meghan, both could stand to benefit from their association with each other,” Owens said.

World.title: Trump wants to work with Democrats on healthcare. Can they find a compromise?
World.content:
The Trump administration has signalled little interest – and, in some cases, opposition – to some of the main ideas Democrats are contemplating. But drug and medical service pricing is one area of potential compromise.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

US President Donald Trump says he wants to find common ground with Democrats on healthcare. But doing so will not be easy. “There’s a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done, especially on healthcare,” Trump told reporters last Friday during a news conference at the White House. “I’m open to great healthcare. Now, can it be what they want? No, but it can be a combination of what we all want.” Democrats, fresh off their sweeping electoral victories this month, are seeking to make healthcare a central part of their agenda for the next Congress. But the party is still building consensus around which ideas it will pursue, such as a progressive push for Medicare-for-all and more moderate proposals on adding hearing, vision and dental care to Medicare. Donald Trump has historically been open to Medicare drug price negotiation. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson The Trump administration has signalled little interest – and, in some cases, opposition – to some of the main ideas Democrats are contemplating. However, an area of potential compromise could be drug and medical service prices. Both Trump and congressional Democrats have, for years, blasted the cost of medicines, and the president has frequently touted his administration’s actions meant to lower drug pricing, including deals made with pharmaceutical companies during his second term. When discussing those deals recently with conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt, Trump suggested there was room to go further, saying, “Great things can be done between the Democrats and Republicans on healthcare”. The two parties have also been seeking to increase transparency into healthcare’s opaque pricing structures, with the Trump administration finalising a revamp last month of rules requiring health insurers to publish the prices they negotiate with doctors and hospitals.



A Centres for Medicare and Medicaid Services spokesperson said in a statement that the agency “welcomes opportunities to work with Congress on healthcare issues, including efforts to reduce the cost of prescription drugs, increase price transparency, and deliver better value for patients and taxpayers”. “President Trump has made lowering healthcare costs while protecting program integrity a priority,” the spokesperson said. Related Article Trade wars CSL signs deal with Trump administration to slash prices for its medicines Under president Joe Biden, Democrats tried reducing drug prices by passing legislation that empowered Medicare to begin negotiating the price of some medicines for the first time. Since then, top Democratic lawmakers have sought to build on those efforts, pitching plans to increase the number of drugs the program can negotiate costs on per year and to extend those lower prices to the commercial market. Unlike many Republican lawmakers, Trump has historically been open to Medicare drug price negotiation, alleging in 2017 that pharmaceutical companies were “getting away with murder”. But the Trump administration and Democrats have tried before, unsuccessfully, to negotiate on drug pricing. During Trump’s first term, discussions between his administration and then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi collapsed. Wendell Primus, who was serving as Pelosi’s senior health and budget adviser at the time, said he believed they had a real shot at hammering out a deal. But, he said, “the House Republicans were not on board”.



House Democrats wanted to allow the government to directly negotiate prices for Medicare, with an option for private insurers to take advantage of the deals, and impose excise taxes on non-compliant drugmakers, which Republicans opposed. A narrower, bipartisan Senate bill that would have targeted lower drug prices for Medicare, such as capping seniors’ out-of-pocket costs, stalled over Republican opposition to a provision that would have required pharmaceutical companies to pay the government if they raised a drug’s prices faster than the rate of inflation. “Legacies are important to presidents,” said Chris Jennings, a long-time Democratic health policy consultant. “That’s why I think the best advice I give to anyone who asks on Capitol Hill is: be prepared to be able to move, because there may be time and opportunities and vehicles that suddenly become available for progress.” Next year, House Democrats’ sizable majority should allow them to pass legislation without any GOP assistance, although Senate Democrats will need Republican help to pass bills unless they use a procedural move to bypass the filibuster. And Trump is almost certain to veto policy changes that he dislikes. Loading Democrats have ambitious proposals unlikely to receive White House support – chief among them is reversing Medicaid cuts that were imposed in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act and reviving generous Affordable Care Act subsidies that have lapsed. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (New York), who has been nominated to lead Democrats as House speaker in the next Congress, has framed those proposals as necessary to “fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that’s been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years”. Yet, Democrats broadly say that the party needs to do more than simply undo Republican actions.



Democrats have been attempting to build consensus around ideas to expand Medicare coverage, including lowering the eligibility age and adding hearing, vision and dental care to the program. They also want to ensure all children have health coverage. Meanwhile, some progressive Democrats want the party to go even further and establish a universal healthcare program that would cover all Americans – Medicare-for-all, which some Trump officials have lambasted. Related Article Pharmaceuticals Trump takes aim at ‘foreign freeloading nations’ over drug prices in new threat to PBS Independent senator Bernie Sanders, who is expected to lead the Senate health, education, labour and pensions committee in the next Congress, planned to use his position to press for a four-year plan to enact the policy, he told reporters this month. Roughly two-thirds of Americans support the idea of Medicare-for-all, according to a September poll from KFF, the highest share since the health policy research and news organisation began asking about the idea a decade ago. Yet, pollsters have found opinions shift as Americans hear competing claims from supporters and critics of the policy, suggesting views could be highly malleable amid a public debate. Mehmet Oz, Trump’s Medicare and Medicaid chief, has panned the idea of Medicare-for-all in recent days, arguing that such a massive change would create a major budget deficit that, in turn, would lead to the rationing of healthcare. “If you crush the system, which is what’s being proposed, then you will devastate the systems that we already have and leave nothing in their place,” Oz said in a November 20 Fox News interview.



A White House official pointed to an analysis conducted last month by the administration’s Council of Economic Advisers that asserted Medicare-for-all would raise the federal deficit by approximately $US47.4 trillion ($71 trillion) over 10 years. While there is no official analysis from the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office on how much Medicare-for-all would cost, the independent Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget estimates that the proposal would increase federal spending between $US25 trillion and $US35 trillion over 10 years, depending on policy details. Michigan Democratic senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has suggested naming a universal healthcare program “Trumpcare”. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson Even among Democratic lawmakers, the notion of single-payer healthcare is divisive, making the likelihood of Democratic leadership attempting to pass it in the next Congress an open question. But some progressives argue that appealing to Trump’s penchant for seeking to place his name or likeness on everything, including buildings, gold coins and passports, could help. Democratic senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed campaigned on passing a version of Medicare-for-all that maintains private insurance alongside a public option, which differs from the proposal that some other progressives have called for that would mostly phase out private insurance. In a post on X this month, El-Sayed suggested naming a universal healthcare program “Trumpcare”. Trump shared a screenshot of El-Sayed’s post over a week later on Truth Social without adding a caption. Trump told the New York Post this week that he planned to meet with El-Sayed. “Maybe there’s some place in the middle that we could go,” Trump told the news outlet.

World.title: Pilot found guilty of killing wife, staging death as mower accident
World.content:
Breaking NationalQueenslandQueensland courts Pilot found guilty of killing wife, staging death as mower accident Cloe Read and Zarisha Bradley Updated November 27, 2026 — 3:44pm ,first published 3:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Former Royal Australian Air Force pilot Robert Crawford has been found guilty of murdering his wife, whose death prosecutors said was staged to look like a lawn mower accident. The former squadron leader, who was described as a love rat, top gun, and master manipulator, was accused of killing his wife Frances in July 2024 at their sprawling property in Upper Lockyer, west of Brisbane. In the prosecution case, he killed her after years of infidelity, as he stood to lose out financially in a divorce settlement. Robert John Crawford arriving at the Supreme Court in Brisbane on Friday. AAPIMAGE Following a five-week trial, including three days of deliberation, the jury on Friday found Crawford guilty of murder.



As the verdict was read out in court, family members were visibly happy, breaking down in tears and embracing each other. Frances’ parents read out a victim impact statement, saying: “Never in our worst nightmares did we ever expect to lose our girl in such a terrible way.” Frances Crawford’s body was found near a ride-on mower at her home. One of Robert Crawford’s sons described his father as “an endless source of grief and sadness in my life from the moment I was born”. “Just as things started getting better for my mental health, you killed mum,” he said.



“Mum was the only parent I ever knew. Mum is gone. It wasn’t a car crash or accident, she was killed by my father. I miss my safe person. I miss mum.” His daughter also spoke in court, saying it was the first time in her life she was in a position to tell him what she really thought. “Not only did this man completely and utterly fail as a father, he went on to take the only parent I had,” she said. “Robert lied, claiming false innocence and dragging us through 2½ years of hell. “I have always hated you. For my entire life you have been cruel. You made me afraid to exist in my own home. The violence, the rage – the entire country can see you for the monster you are.



“I look at you now and I see a weak, pathetic, insecure bully. I’m no longer afraid of you. I hope you spend the rest of your life locked away in prison.” Crawford showed little emotion as the statements were read to the court. ‘He staged the scene’ In his closing address, Crown Prosecutor Chris Cook had told the jury Crawford was motivated by a desire to keep their home, valued at up to $2.6 million, and his $1.7 million superannuation. “He staged the scene, he created a false narrative, he led police on a wild goose chase,” Cook said.



The prosecution case was that Crawford strangled his wife, before causing her body to be at the bottom of a retaining wall in their yard, near a ride-on mower. The Crawford property in the Upper Lockyer Valley. The jury heard this took place between 6pm on July 29, and 3.37am the following morning, when Crawford called Triple Zero. Central to this case was a series of messages discussing the mower, sent between the two Crawford phones that night. Crawford had also unlocked his phone during periods between 1.09am and 1.51am, and 2.35am and 3.20am, the court heard. The jury heard Crawford told police he thought his wife moved the mower because she believed the sprinklers would come on.



Related Article Courts Inside the crumbling marriage of a ‘love rat’ pilot accused of murder Graphic images of Frances’ bloodied and bruised body were shown to the trial, with both prosecution and defence witnesses called to give expert evidence. Forensic pathologist Andrzej Kedziora told the court Frances suffered injuries consistent with being strangled. He said he could not reconcile the accident scenario with her injuries, but also could not rule it out. UK-based forensic physician Professor Jason Payne-James, a defence witness, said some of her injuries were consistent with the mower accident, and also that she was attacked. Crawford was represented by top barrister Saul Holt, KC, who told the jury that while his client’s infidelity and lies were awful and unforgivable, it did not mean he killed her.



“There is a world of difference between cheating on your wife, and being guilty of murder,” he said in his closing address. He said while Frances, whose death was an unspeakable tragedy, was entitled to feel furious at her husband, she imposed boundaries during their reconciliation period that would have left him feeling controlled or trapped. Holt questioned the police investigation, and asked how a fake mower accident could have been staged in the middle of the night. The defence case ultimately did not sway the jury. After three days of deliberation, they reached a unanimous verdict of guilty on Friday afternoon. Get alerts on significant breaking news as happens.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Labor’s gas reservation laws pass, parliament concludes for the year; Houthis strike Saudi oil refineries
World.content:
Telstra has switched on emergency roaming for the first time in Australia, opening its network to customers of rival telcos on bushfire-hit Flinders Island.

Telstra is the only mobile provider on the Bass Strait island, so visitors and emergency crews on other networks would normally have no coverage.

About 150 people are now using Temporary Disaster Roaming to make calls, send texts and access basic data at no extra cost.

The telco said the capability is available in only three other countries globally.

The phones need to support VoLTE roaming - so must be newer models - and medical alarms and Eftpos terminals are not covered.

World.title: Erin Patterson launches High Court appeal in last-ditch bid for freedom
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts Erin Patterson launches High Court appeal in last-ditch bid for freedom Erin Pearson Updated November 27, 2026 — 4:00pm ,first published 12:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Mushroom cook killer Erin Patterson has launched an eleventh-hour High Court bid for freedom over her convictions for murdering three family members and attempting to kill a third. Last month, the 52-year-old mother of two had her appeal thrown out by the Court of Appeal and her sentence was instead increased, with her prospects of parole scrapped. Three Court of Appeal judges – Stephen McLeish, Lesley Taylor and Peter Kidd – found Patterson’s crimes so cold, calculated and shocking that they ruled she should die in jail. Erin Patterson outside court in April 2025. AAP That ruling meant Patterson became the first Victorian woman, and only the second in the country’s history, to be sentenced to life without parole, after she served beef Wellington laced with death cap mushrooms to four lunch guests at her Leongatha home in July 2023.



On Friday afternoon, Patterson’s legal team filed paperwork with the High Court in the hope of securing a second appeal hearing in the county’s highest court. The appeal is against both conviction and Patterson’s life sentence, according to legal sources. In 2025, Patterson was found guilty by a jury of the poisoning murders of her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail’s sister, Heather Wilkinson. She was also convicted of attempting to murder Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, who survived the lunch. From left: Don Patterson, Gail Patterson, Heather Wilkinson and Ian Wilkinson were poisoned. The Court of Appeal found Patterson’s persistent murderous intent had protracted the suffering of her victims.



The appeal court judges found Patterson had coldly planned and carried out the murders over nearly three weeks. This, they said, included extending the invitation to lunch, false denials of having foraged for mushrooms, false assertions she had cancer, and hiding the truth for nearly a week as her victims lay dying. This, the judges found, represented a cruel breach of trust. Following their dismissal of Patterson’s appeal, the killer’s legal team had 28 days to file an appeal application with the High Court before the 5pm deadline on Friday. Defence barrister Richard Edney outside the Court of Appeal in August. Joe Armao In fighting for a fresh trial, Patterson’s appeal barrister, Richard Edney, earlier argued there were a number of potential irregularities in his client’s case, including during the jury’s seven-day sequestration at a Gippsland hotel while they were deciding Patterson’s fate. The jurors stayed in the same Traralgon hotel as the prosecution and police involved in the case. Edney claimed this amounted to a catastrophic and fundamental failure to comply with the trial rules.



Patterson was found guilty on all charges following an 11-week trial in Morwell, in Victoria’s east, in mid-2025. The trial heard from more than 50 witnesses. During Patterson’s recent appeal, Director of Public Prosecutions Brendan Kissane, KC, dismissed Edney’s concerns as baseless and not warranting the granting of an appeal. Heather Wilkinson and Gail Patterson died on August 4, 2023, from multiple organ failure, with a diagnosis of amanita mushroom poisoning. Don Patterson died the following night. Ian Wilkinson, a pastor in the area, survived after spending several weeks in an induced coma. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Manhattan scores $30M Canadian gold farm-in
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Manhattan scores $30M Canadian gold farm-in Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward November 27, 2026 — 3:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Manhattan Gold Corporation has struck a massive deal worth more than A$30 million to fast-track exploration at its Hook Lake gold and base metals project in Nunavut, Canada, signing on US-based USFM Corporation as its new farm-in partner. USM is a private US exploration company based in Colorado that has just agreed to agreed to reverse merge with Nasdaq listed Twin Vee Powercats Co. The agreement will see USFM pump A$28 million into exploration over three years to earn an 85 per cent stake in the project. In addition, USFM will pay the company US$1.5 million (A$2.27M) in cash within 90 days, US$1M (A$1.513M) on signing of the transfer agreement for a 7.5 per cent interest and a further US$500,000 (A$757,000), for a total of 12.5 per cent. Once the A$28M is spent, Manhattan will retain a 15 per cent interest that will be free-carried all the way through to a bankable feasibility study. Manhattan Gold’s Hook Lake project in Nunavut, Canada has attracted a significant farm-in partner on the back of impressive maiden drilling results. The deal is structured in stages, with USFM earning its interest as it meets cash payment and expenditure milestones. It can earn a 51 per cent majority stake by spending A$8 million on exploration within 12 months. Its interest can grow to 75 per cent with an additional A$10 million spend in the second year, and finally to 85 per cent with a further A$10 million in the third year. The agreement also includes a provision for USFM to sell a 1 per cent net smelter royalty, with Manhattan receiving 50 per cent of the proceeds from any sale. Importantly, the company has confirmed with the ASX that shareholder approval is not required for the transaction, removing a key hurdle for deal completion. The sale of the initial 12.5 per cent project interest and the earn-in is subject to any necessary regulatory or third-party approvals as well as signing of the formal agreements, which is expected to happen within the next 30 days.



‘USFM’s significant commitment of over $30m over 3 years enables development of Hook Lake at pace and scale.’ Manhattan Gold Corporation general manager Bayard Rezos The deal lands on the back of a stellar maiden 25-hole, 4592-metre reverse circulation drilling campaign, at Hook Lake by Manhattan in 2026, the first at the project since 1988 which delivered a suite of high-grade gold and polymetallic hits. Drilling at its Jaws prospect returned a cracking 41.15-metre intersection grading 4.66 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 83.82m which included a richer 7.62-metre core of 18.67g/t gold. Other significant intercepts at Jaws featured hits of 74.67m assaying 1.61g/t gold from a shallow 21.34m and 51.82m grading 1.88g/t gold from 47.24m. The drilling doubled the known mineralised strike at Jaws to more than 1.8 kilometres, with a tantalising 1km gap between two of the drill holes remaining untested. Additionally, maiden drilling at the nearby Spectre prospect confirmed a high-grade volcanogenic massive sulphide (VMS) system. One hole hit a stunning 19.81m at 1.77 per cent copper, 84.3g/t silver and 0.8g/t gold from just 42.67m. That hit included a sweet 6.1-metre section going 3.18 per cent copper, 147.9g/t silver and 1.37g/t gold. Adding to the intrigue, a separate near-surface zinc zone in the same hole yielded 19.82m running at 5.55 per cent zinc, with a remarkable 3.05-metre section landing an eye-watering 29.5 per cent zinc. Adding further flavour, assays are also pending for a further three drillholes and over 550 till samples from the company’s Omega prospect along with continuing metallurgical test work and the interpretation of final airborne magnetic data from both Jaws and Spectre.



Manhattan Gold Corporation general manager Bayard Rezos said: “Bringing USFM in as funder and operator at Hook Lake is a strong endorsement of the results of our 2026 maiden program. USFM’s significant commitment of over $30m over 3 years enables development of Hook Lake at pace and scale without Manhattan relying on capital markets. With Manhattan retaining 15% of Hook Lake, free-carried all the way to a Bankable Feasibility Study, our shareholders will be able to benefit from USFM’s efforts in defining both a gold resource and a polymetallic copper, zinc, gold and silver resource at Hook Lake across this district-scale project.” The new partnership will see an aggressive exploration program kick off early next year, with USFM planning an initial 10,000m diamond drilling campaign as part of its first A$8 million commitment. The program will target extensions to the Jaws gold system, follow up the high-grade VMS zones at Spectre and test new targets generated from recent geophysical and sampling work. The A$2.27M cash injection will allow Manhattan to turn its attention to its 100 per cent-owned Tibooburra South licences in New South Wales which cover an 80-kilometre strike of deep-seated faults that have not yet been tested by modern drilling. The cash will fund geophysics, mapping and a maiden drill campaign. The 2195-square-kilometre exploration package at the Tibooburra gold project in New South Wales covers a significant portion of the emerging Koonenberry gold district, which shares structural characteristics with the rich Stawell goldfields zone in Victoria. To keep costs down, the northern section of the project is managed under a strategic farm-in agreement with Novo Resources. Novo is actively funding and executing exploration on this ground, allowing the company to retain exposure to any discovery upside without incurring direct capital expenditure.



With a well-funded partner now set to unleash the drill rigs on its Canadian ground and cash in the bank to get the rods spinning in NSW, Manhattan has effectively added two fully-funded exploration plays. For a company with a market cap of just over A$30 million, securing a free ride on a A$28 million exploration spend while retaining a meaningful stake in a project with this much potential could be a game-changer. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: ‘Alarmed’ UN experts call out Vietnam over alleged kidnapping of Australian
World.content:
WorldAsiaAustralians abroad ‘Alarmed’ UN experts call out Vietnam over alleged kidnapping of Australian Zach Hope November 27, 2026 — 3:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Singapore: United Nations experts have called out Vietnam for the alleged transnational kidnapping of Australian pro-democracy campaigner Tran Hiep alongside two of his colleagues while they were travelling in neighbouring Cambodia. It is the first time the UN has weighed in publicly on the highly sensitive case since the men disappeared on September 18 and turned up in Vietnamese detention on alleged terrorism offences. Australian human rights activist Tran Hiep. “We are alarmed by these alleged transboundary abductions, which violate international human rights law, including the prohibitions on arbitrary detention, enforced disappearance and torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment,” the panel of 11 independent experts said in a statement published by the UN on Thursday (Geneva time). The panel also said Cambodia had an international obligation to investigate, including “whether Cambodian officials knew of, facilitated, or tolerated their alleged arbitrary detention and transfer”.



View post on X Hiep and Norwegian citizen Nguyen Duc Thuan, along with Vietnamese man Thai Cong Truong Son, are members of Viet Tan (VT), a diaspora political party championing human rights and a transition to democracy from one-party, communist rule. The Vietnamese government brands it a terrorist organisation. Related Article Cambodia Australian activist charged in Vietnam as pro-democracy group accuses Hanoi of kidnapping VT said the men were in Cambodia to meet with other members when they were snatched and driven across the border, labelling it a “brazen act of transnational repression”. The group said the Australian and Norwegian men were booked to fly to Bangkok on September 19, the day after they went missing, before flying home to their respective countries. The trio’s fate was a mystery for 10 days until Vietnamese authorities announced they were arrested while allegedly trying to enter Vietnam, which holds that VT is responsible for “recruiting, training and directing its members to infiltrate into Vietnam to provoke protests and riots, undermine security, conduct assassination [sic] and kidnapping”.



Hiep told Australian officials on an October 15 consular visit he “never entered or crossed the Vietnam border on his own” and that he “remained terrified and traumatised from being attacked and kidnapped in Cambodia”, according to VT. The UN panel agreed witness accounts were “inconsistent” with the Vietnamese government’s explanation of events. “We urge Vietnam to disclose the circumstances and legal basis of the arrests, investigate any involvement of its officials in the alleged abductions, transfers and enforced disappearances, and co-operate fully with Cambodia’s investigation,” the experts said. “We are concerned by the growth of transnational repression in the region and prevailing impunity surrounding it. We call on states to combat it, including through the Association of South-East Asian Nations (ASEAN).”

World.title: Backed by Helen Haines, this rural doctor is putting a safe Liberal seat in play
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Backed by Helen Haines, this rural doctor is putting a safe Liberal seat in play Annika Smethurst November 27, 2026 — 3:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A rural doctor who made the switch to politics at the urging of federal independent MP Helen Haines is turning one of the safest Liberal electorates in the state into a contest. Independent Lachie McKeeman is riding of wave of support in Benambra fuelled by anti-major party sentiment, the retirement of veteran Liberal MP Bill Tilley, and the community’s ongoing shock at the attack on Haines. Helen Haines with Lachie McKeeman. Instagram His feel-good strategy has even extended to his rivals – photographed arm-in-arm with the local One Nation candidate, saying it had been a pleasure to campaign alongside her. Three Liberal sources, speaking to The Age on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal party polling, said the party had become increasingly convinced it would lose the once-safe electorate despite the Coalition being on track to form government after Saturday’s poll.



“We are worried about Benambra and Prahran,” one senior Liberal source said. “But Benambra has always been ours.” Held by conservative parties at a state level since 1877, the electorate is based around Wodonga and takes in the towns of Beechworth and Chiltern. McKeeman’s campaign has sought to capitalise on longstanding frustrations with the major parties and underinvestment in regional healthcare, prompting the Liberal Party to pledge $100 million towards the Albury Hospital redevelopment if elected. “As a doctor, you’re inherently a very political person because you engage with people in a very close, caring way ... and you see the impacts of political neglect on their everyday life,” McKeeman told The Age.



The father of three’s candidacy is backed by Haines, who represents the overlapping federal seat of Indi. The 65-year-old MP lost both legs as a result of an allegedly targeted attack outside her Wangaratta office on October 19. Floral tributes fill the pavement outside Helen Haines’ electorate office. Jason South Four sources, linked to both Haines and the Liberal Party and speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss the campaign, said McKeeman was benefiting from an outpouring of community support for her. McKeeman, who worked alongside the Indi MP while advocating for better hospital infrastructure, said it was Haines who first encouraged him to run for politics. “Helen’s the one who probably lit the fire and asked would I ever entertain it,” he said.



“She’s an excellent role model for what community independent representation can deliver. “But if you live in an area with such a scale of political neglect ... eventually you can either get angry at the system from outside or you can try and contribute and affect meaningful change.” The contest comes just months after voters across the border in Sussan Ley’s former federal seat of Farrer abandoned the Liberals in favour of One Nation. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election ‘A shocker for working people’: Bracks pleads with Labor voters to reject One Nation While One Nation how-to-vote cards for the state election put McKeeman in last position, local candidate Kellie Sheappard told voters at a recent forum to put McKeeman or Libertarian candidate Tim Quilty second.



“I am sitting in this seat today because I am incredibly passionate about youth mental health and our hospital,” Sheappard said at the Better Border Health forum. “My how-to-vote card has obviously come out today ... I have to be honest it doesn’t necessarily reflect what I would have chosen. “I would personally have gone with the other candidates who most closely aligned with my values which would be Tim or Lachie.” Related Article Queensland votes Katter party considers running candidates in Brisbane amid One Nation’s rise The retirement of Liberal veteran Tilley, after two decades in parliament, has further opened up the race for Benambra where the margin, now sitting at less than 1 per cent, has repeatedly narrowed after strong challenges by community independents at the 2018 and 2022 state elections.

World.title: ‘Non-royal royals’: How Harry and Meghan are finding their feet back in Britain
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeRoyal family ‘Non-royal royals’: How Harry and Meghan are finding their feet back in Britain Karla Adam November 27, 2026 — 3:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

London: When Prince Harry and Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, visited a food bank last month in Nottingham, England, they had a request. No formal etiquette. No need for the bows or curtsies that are traditional for members of the royal family. They could be greeted simply as “Harry and Meghan”. Prince Harry and Meghan’s return to the UK has resurfaced questions about their status. AP The co-founder of the charity, Sajid Mohammed, obliged with an ordinary handshake. But around him, people curtsied, some volunteers wept with emotion, and six parents tried to bring their babies forward. Even royals who have stepped back from official duties still inspire reflexive ceremony in some parts of the British public, it turns out.



“It’s very much like Harry’s mother, the late Princess Diana,” Mohammed said in an interview afterwards. “There’s an aura around the couple. It’s beyond normal celebrity.” The rapturous response they received in Nottingham underlines the challenge, and potential benefit, that the newly repatriated Sussexes offer to Britain’s monarchy, six years after they left the country and their royal duties. Loading Queen Elizabeth II reluctantly blessed their self-imposed exile in 2020 but said they must give up state funding and could no longer be considered full working royals. Their return to Britain, which Harry said in a recent GQ interview was to pursue “opportunities for the family” and to school their children, has resurfaced questions about their status. They appear intent on carving out a specific profile, managing public appearances on their own terms and tightly controlling what they share, including where in England they have chosen to live, a fact that remains undisclosed.



Their careful image management partly reflects the couple’s fraught relationship with the British media and its often hostile coverage in the past, which they previously said had contributed to their departure from Britain. Related Article Analysis

Royal family Why King Charles felt he had to clarify Prince Harry’s status For now, their popularity in opinion polls remains low, particularly compared with Harry’s older brother, Prince William, and his wife Catherine, Princess of Wales. But can a pair armed with Hollywood glamour and global celebrity operate on their own terms without eclipsing the traditional working royals they left behind? Could their return, if managed well, inject energy into the institution as King Charles III enters his twilight years?



‘Non-royal royals’ Charles has attempted to hold the line his mother drew. After Harry and Meghan’s return to Britain in late August, a letter was sent on the King’s behalf to government officials, stiffly reminding them that the Sussexes were “private citizens” who must not be addressed as “His and Her Royal Highness”. The difficulty for Buckingham Palace is that, while it could strip away their official status, it cannot strip away their star power. Harry and Meghan at an event at the European Parliament in Brussels, Belgium. Getty Images On the day the Sussexes swept through Nottingham, the King was in Cardiff opening the Senedd, the Welsh parliament. While the BBC covered both events, ITV’s evening bulletin only found room for Harry and Meghan.



The following day, Peter Hunt, a former BBC royal correspondent, highlighted the newspaper front pages smothered in Sussex coverage, writing on social media: “The palace spin is failing on contact with reality. Harry and Meghan are royals. End of.” The daily grind of the British crown is not, by design, thrilling. It’s built on unglamorous routine – bronze plaques unveiled at rain-swept civic centres and ribbon-cuttings at community clinics – the stoic pattern perfected by Princess Anne, Charles’ sister. Princess Anne during a recent visit to the Falkland Islands. Getty Images “One of the biggest risks of Harry and Meghan coming back is that they take attention away from the core work of the monarchy, which is slightly dull at times,” said Craig Prescott, a constitutional scholar and author. That dynamic is particularly delicate around major overseas excursions, when palace orthodoxy holds that royals should not compete with royals on big tours. When Charles toured the Caribbean this month, the Sussexes avoided rival public appearances.



Other overlaps are harder to prevent. Prince Harry’s GQ interview was published as Charles and Queen Camilla welcomed the Sultan of Oman on a state visit to Windsor Castle. Critics immediately claimed Harry was upstaging a diplomatic event, but supporters noted that the interview had been taped a month earlier in New York and that its publication had been scheduled by the magazine. Sultan Haitham bin Tarik of Oman with King Charles and Queen Camilla at a state banquet at Windsor Castle, in October. Aaron Chown/Pool PA via AP The couple’s carefully curated schedule of activities since returning to England certainly resembles, at times, the diplomatic and charitable engagements that define royal life. In September, Harry attended London’s WellChild Awards, honouring seriously ill children. The couple appeared at the European parliament in Brussels, where Harry spoke about digital safety and child protection.



This month, Harry made a surprise visit to Ukraine, meeting wounded veterans preparing for his Invictus Games, and last week he made an unannounced appearance on ITV’s This Morning, where he joked that he was “squeezing” the American accents out of his kids and helped make a Christmas cake. “You might describe them as non-royal royals,” Prescott said. Off camera, the couple has settled into a quieter routine. While they have not disclosed where they are living and have asked the media not to reveal their children’s schools, they have been spotted in pubs around the Cotswolds – an idyllic pocket of southern England beloved by wealthy Americans. Their commercial interests complicate the picture. Meghan continues to build her lifestyle label, As Ever, and recently signed on as a guest judge for Junior MasterChef Australia.



‘A quiet rehabilitation’ Related Article Royal family Harry and Meghan’s battle to be accepted into Cotswolds high society But their present arrangement is fundamentally different. They carry no official duties, hold no royal patronages. Whether that proves sustainable may depend on how the couple and the palace manage the attention. While Harry has reconciled with his father, his relationship with William, the heir to the throne, appears to be as frosty as ever, with no reported interactions since the Sussexes returned. Nor does a warm reception at a charity signal a broader recovery in public affection.



A recent YouGov poll put Harry’s domestic approval at 29 per cent and Meghan’s at 20 per cent, with deep scars lingering over their noisy 2020 exit. Ed Owens, a royal historian, noted that a “quiet rehabilitation” is never out of the question in Britain, pointing to Camilla’s decades-long journey from tabloid pariah to queen consort. King Charles, then the Prince of Wales, with Diana, Harry and William at the family’s country home, Highgrove, in picturesque Tetbury, in 1986. Tim Graham/Getty Images Charles, too, has lived a life of many chapters – deeply unpopular during the breakdown of his marriage to Diana, he has since seen both his public standing recover and his environmental views become mainstream. “As long as there isn’t deliberate, direct and obvious competition between the working royals and Harry and Meghan, both could stand to benefit from their association with each other,” Owens said.

World.title: Trump wants to work with Democrats on healthcare. Can they find a compromise?
World.content:
The Trump administration has signalled little interest – and, in some cases, opposition – to some of the main ideas Democrats are contemplating. But drug and medical service pricing is one area of potential compromise.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

US President Donald Trump says he wants to find common ground with Democrats on healthcare. But doing so will not be easy. “There’s a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done, especially on healthcare,” Trump told reporters last Friday during a news conference at the White House. “I’m open to great healthcare. Now, can it be what they want? No, but it can be a combination of what we all want.” Democrats, fresh off their sweeping electoral victories this month, are seeking to make healthcare a central part of their agenda for the next Congress. But the party is still building consensus around which ideas it will pursue, such as a progressive push for Medicare-for-all and more moderate proposals on adding hearing, vision and dental care to Medicare. Donald Trump has historically been open to Medicare drug price negotiation. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson The Trump administration has signalled little interest – and, in some cases, opposition – to some of the main ideas Democrats are contemplating. However, an area of potential compromise could be drug and medical service prices. Both Trump and congressional Democrats have, for years, blasted the cost of medicines, and the president has frequently touted his administration’s actions meant to lower drug pricing, including deals made with pharmaceutical companies during his second term. When discussing those deals recently with conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt, Trump suggested there was room to go further, saying, “Great things can be done between the Democrats and Republicans on healthcare”. The two parties have also been seeking to increase transparency into healthcare’s opaque pricing structures, with the Trump administration finalising a revamp last month of rules requiring health insurers to publish the prices they negotiate with doctors and hospitals.



A Centres for Medicare and Medicaid Services spokesperson said in a statement that the agency “welcomes opportunities to work with Congress on healthcare issues, including efforts to reduce the cost of prescription drugs, increase price transparency, and deliver better value for patients and taxpayers”. “President Trump has made lowering healthcare costs while protecting program integrity a priority,” the spokesperson said. Related Article Trade wars CSL signs deal with Trump administration to slash prices for its medicines Under president Joe Biden, Democrats tried reducing drug prices by passing legislation that empowered Medicare to begin negotiating the price of some medicines for the first time. Since then, top Democratic lawmakers have sought to build on those efforts, pitching plans to increase the number of drugs the program can negotiate costs on per year and to extend those lower prices to the commercial market. Unlike many Republican lawmakers, Trump has historically been open to Medicare drug price negotiation, alleging in 2017 that pharmaceutical companies were “getting away with murder”. But the Trump administration and Democrats have tried before, unsuccessfully, to negotiate on drug pricing. During Trump’s first term, discussions between his administration and then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi collapsed. Wendell Primus, who was serving as Pelosi’s senior health and budget adviser at the time, said he believed they had a real shot at hammering out a deal. But, he said, “the House Republicans were not on board”.



House Democrats wanted to allow the government to directly negotiate prices for Medicare, with an option for private insurers to take advantage of the deals, and impose excise taxes on non-compliant drugmakers, which Republicans opposed. A narrower, bipartisan Senate bill that would have targeted lower drug prices for Medicare, such as capping seniors’ out-of-pocket costs, stalled over Republican opposition to a provision that would have required pharmaceutical companies to pay the government if they raised a drug’s prices faster than the rate of inflation. “Legacies are important to presidents,” said Chris Jennings, a long-time Democratic health policy consultant. “That’s why I think the best advice I give to anyone who asks on Capitol Hill is: be prepared to be able to move, because there may be time and opportunities and vehicles that suddenly become available for progress.” Next year, House Democrats’ sizable majority should allow them to pass legislation without any GOP assistance, although Senate Democrats will need Republican help to pass bills unless they use a procedural move to bypass the filibuster. And Trump is almost certain to veto policy changes that he dislikes. Loading Democrats have ambitious proposals unlikely to receive White House support – chief among them is reversing Medicaid cuts that were imposed in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act and reviving generous Affordable Care Act subsidies that have lapsed. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (New York), who has been nominated to lead Democrats as House speaker in the next Congress, has framed those proposals as necessary to “fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that’s been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years”. Yet, Democrats broadly say that the party needs to do more than simply undo Republican actions.



Democrats have been attempting to build consensus around ideas to expand Medicare coverage, including lowering the eligibility age and adding hearing, vision and dental care to the program. They also want to ensure all children have health coverage. Meanwhile, some progressive Democrats want the party to go even further and establish a universal healthcare program that would cover all Americans – Medicare-for-all, which some Trump officials have lambasted. Related Article Pharmaceuticals Trump takes aim at ‘foreign freeloading nations’ over drug prices in new threat to PBS Independent senator Bernie Sanders, who is expected to lead the Senate health, education, labour and pensions committee in the next Congress, planned to use his position to press for a four-year plan to enact the policy, he told reporters this month. Roughly two-thirds of Americans support the idea of Medicare-for-all, according to a September poll from KFF, the highest share since the health policy research and news organisation began asking about the idea a decade ago. Yet, pollsters have found opinions shift as Americans hear competing claims from supporters and critics of the policy, suggesting views could be highly malleable amid a public debate. Mehmet Oz, Trump’s Medicare and Medicaid chief, has panned the idea of Medicare-for-all in recent days, arguing that such a massive change would create a major budget deficit that, in turn, would lead to the rationing of healthcare. “If you crush the system, which is what’s being proposed, then you will devastate the systems that we already have and leave nothing in their place,” Oz said in a November 20 Fox News interview.



A White House official pointed to an analysis conducted last month by the administration’s Council of Economic Advisers that asserted Medicare-for-all would raise the federal deficit by approximately $US47.4 trillion ($71 trillion) over 10 years. While there is no official analysis from the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office on how much Medicare-for-all would cost, the independent Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget estimates that the proposal would increase federal spending between $US25 trillion and $US35 trillion over 10 years, depending on policy details. Michigan Democratic senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has suggested naming a universal healthcare program “Trumpcare”. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson Even among Democratic lawmakers, the notion of single-payer healthcare is divisive, making the likelihood of Democratic leadership attempting to pass it in the next Congress an open question. But some progressives argue that appealing to Trump’s penchant for seeking to place his name or likeness on everything, including buildings, gold coins and passports, could help. Democratic senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed campaigned on passing a version of Medicare-for-all that maintains private insurance alongside a public option, which differs from the proposal that some other progressives have called for that would mostly phase out private insurance. In a post on X this month, El-Sayed suggested naming a universal healthcare program “Trumpcare”. Trump shared a screenshot of El-Sayed’s post over a week later on Truth Social without adding a caption. Trump told the New York Post this week that he planned to meet with El-Sayed. “Maybe there’s some place in the middle that we could go,” Trump told the news outlet.

World.title: Pilot found guilty of killing wife, staging death as mower accident
World.content:
Breaking NationalQueenslandQueensland courts Pilot found guilty of killing wife, staging death as mower accident Cloe Read and Zarisha Bradley Updated November 27, 2026 — 3:44pm ,first published 3:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Former Royal Australian Air Force pilot Robert Crawford has been found guilty of murdering his wife, whose death prosecutors said was staged to look like a lawn mower accident. The former squadron leader, who was described as a love rat, top gun, and master manipulator, was accused of killing his wife Frances in July 2024 at their sprawling property in Upper Lockyer, west of Brisbane. In the prosecution case, he killed her after years of infidelity, as he stood to lose out financially in a divorce settlement. Robert John Crawford arriving at the Supreme Court in Brisbane on Friday. AAPIMAGE Following a five-week trial, including three days of deliberation, the jury on Friday found Crawford guilty of murder.



As the verdict was read out in court, family members were visibly happy, breaking down in tears and embracing each other. Frances’ parents read out a victim impact statement, saying: “Never in our worst nightmares did we ever expect to lose our girl in such a terrible way.” Frances Crawford’s body was found near a ride-on mower at her home. One of Robert Crawford’s sons described his father as “an endless source of grief and sadness in my life from the moment I was born”. “Just as things started getting better for my mental health, you killed mum,” he said.



“Mum was the only parent I ever knew. Mum is gone. It wasn’t a car crash or accident, she was killed by my father. I miss my safe person. I miss mum.” His daughter also spoke in court, saying it was the first time in her life she was in a position to tell him what she really thought. “Not only did this man completely and utterly fail as a father, he went on to take the only parent I had,” she said. “Robert lied, claiming false innocence and dragging us through 2½ years of hell. “I have always hated you. For my entire life you have been cruel. You made me afraid to exist in my own home. The violence, the rage – the entire country can see you for the monster you are.



“I look at you now and I see a weak, pathetic, insecure bully. I’m no longer afraid of you. I hope you spend the rest of your life locked away in prison.” Crawford showed little emotion as the statements were read to the court. ‘He staged the scene’ In his closing address, Crown Prosecutor Chris Cook had told the jury Crawford was motivated by a desire to keep their home, valued at up to $2.6 million, and his $1.7 million superannuation. “He staged the scene, he created a false narrative, he led police on a wild goose chase,” Cook said.



The prosecution case was that Crawford strangled his wife, before causing her body to be at the bottom of a retaining wall in their yard, near a ride-on mower. The Crawford property in the Upper Lockyer Valley. The jury heard this took place between 6pm on July 29, and 3.37am the following morning, when Crawford called Triple Zero. Central to this case was a series of messages discussing the mower, sent between the two Crawford phones that night. Crawford had also unlocked his phone during periods between 1.09am and 1.51am, and 2.35am and 3.20am, the court heard. The jury heard Crawford told police he thought his wife moved the mower because she believed the sprinklers would come on.



Related Article Courts Inside the crumbling marriage of a ‘love rat’ pilot accused of murder Graphic images of Frances’ bloodied and bruised body were shown to the trial, with both prosecution and defence witnesses called to give expert evidence. Forensic pathologist Andrzej Kedziora told the court Frances suffered injuries consistent with being strangled. He said he could not reconcile the accident scenario with her injuries, but also could not rule it out. UK-based forensic physician Professor Jason Payne-James, a defence witness, said some of her injuries were consistent with the mower accident, and also that she was attacked. Crawford was represented by top barrister Saul Holt, KC, who told the jury that while his client’s infidelity and lies were awful and unforgivable, it did not mean he killed her.



“There is a world of difference between cheating on your wife, and being guilty of murder,” he said in his closing address. He said while Frances, whose death was an unspeakable tragedy, was entitled to feel furious at her husband, she imposed boundaries during their reconciliation period that would have left him feeling controlled or trapped. Holt questioned the police investigation, and asked how a fake mower accident could have been staged in the middle of the night. The defence case ultimately did not sway the jury. After three days of deliberation, they reached a unanimous verdict of guilty on Friday afternoon. Get alerts on significant breaking news as happens.

World.title: National's Mike Butterick reacts after losing Wairarapa seat to Labour's Kieran McAnulty
World.content:
Labour's Kieran McAnulty is celebrating a narrow victory that's flipped the marginal Wairarapa seat.

National's Mike Butterick was ahead by 139 votes on election night, but a swing in the specials has given Labour a buffer of 81.

McAnulty said he's confident his lead will hold, with 40 votes the historical margin where a recount could make a difference.

"One thing this election has shown us is there's no certainties in politics, but they've declared me the winner and I'm going to have a beer tonight to celebrate."

He said he's "real stoked" to be returning as an electorate MP where he feels his voice carries more weight.

"It's the job that I wanted in politics, this is why I got into politics, I wanted to be the local MP to do good things for the region, and I've done it.

"I'm just real happy."

McAnulty acknowledged Butterick, saying politics is a brutal game.

"The bloke's lost his job and he's a good guy. You know, we're opponents, but we're not enemies, so whatever he chooses to do next, I wish him well."

'Very disapointing'

It was been a "long old day" for ousted Wairarapa MP, Mike Butterick, who while disappointed, says he has no regrets.

The National Party candidate was unseated by fewer than 100 votes, losing to Labour's Kieran McAnulty.

As it stands, it means the first time politician, Butterick, is out of Parliament.

National's Mike Butterick. VNP / Phil Smith

"It's obviously very disappointing, but the voters have spoken and as they say, the voters are always right and it's sort of like, close but no cigar."

Butterick - a Masterton-based sheep and beef farmer - says he needed something to keep his mind occupied until the results went live at 2pm on Friday.

"I went and jumped on the tractor, which I haven't been on for the best part of three years, and went and did some topping on some paddocks."

He says dodging concrete troughs kept his thoughts from wandering too much.

The National candidate had been in front on election night by a lead of 139 votes.

But after counting just over 5000 special votes for the electorate, the result swung to Labour's candidate for a margin of 81, although National extended its party vote lead with 30.2 percent, compared to Labour's 28.6 percent.

It's not the first time McAnulty and Butterick have gone head-to-head.

In 2023, it was another two-horse race between the National and Labour candidates. McAnulty, who had the seat was unable to keep it, losing to first time MP Butterick as a blue wave swept the country.

Butterick, who has been Land Information Minister as well as the Associate Minister for Agriculture says he was still taking in the result, and that it's too soon to talk about recounts.

"It's probably way too early to, you know, to say anything regarding that.

"It'll be taken into consideration and it'll be a bit more hurry up and wait, I guess - perhaps."

He says either way, it's been "one hell of privilege".

"And I can say that very genuinely, to have the opportunity to advocate not only just for your electorate, but also New Zealanders as a whole is a pretty extraordinary privilege that very few people get.

"Absolutely no regrets whatsoever and really proud to have been part of that team and done the best that we possibly could."

Butterick says the Wairapapa electorate, which extends from Dannevirke to South Wairarapa, was a wonderful part of the country to live and run a business in.

He thanked his supporters and the volunteers who put in an "extraordinary" number of hours and congratulated his Labour rival.

"They ran a hard campaign."

McAnulty won 19,688 votes compared to Butterick's 19,607, while New Zealand First candidate Ron Mark came in third on exactly 4000 votes.

As number 16 on the party list, Mark, the former Defence Minister would not return to Parliament.

World.title: Election 2026 final results: Wong won't rule out sending voters back to polls, Luxon says 'challenging' talks coming
World.content:
Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong is not ruling out forcing New Zealand back to the polls, as the final election results leave National's Christopher Luxon reliant on Opportunity to break the deadlock.

The right bloc needs Opportunity to govern, and if a deal cannot be reached, it will trigger another election.

Wong said on Friday nothing could be ruled out.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6408936265112

She reiterated that Opportunity's five bottom lines are minimum non-negotiables for coalition or confidence and supply deals - and that she would not agree to govern with the right bloc if Winston Peters is Foreign Minister.

Wong said there had been no formal discussions with any of the other parties, and she had not spoken with Peters.

She said she would sit down with National first "but how the rest of the negotiations plays out, I think, is a topic for discussion with everyone".

Wong is ready to begin negotiating immediately, adding that Opportunity's team is made up of herself, deputy Daniel Eb and chief of staff Iain Lees-Galloway, which its caucus decided on.

Wong could not comment on whether a government could be formed before the new year.

"All we can do is be as constructive and proactive as possible to make this happen. But it's not just us around the table."

Wong said she was feeling a lot of pressure.

"The last couple of weeks being in this induction has really weighed on us, the level of responsibility that all MPs have when they come into this place, and so we take that responsibility very seriously."

Opportunity's bottom lines

Here is a reminder of the five non-negotiable things the party wants in any governing arrangement:

Bring prices down by giving the Commerce Commission more teeth and greater independence to tackle excessive market power in supermarkets and other uncompetitive sectors.

Regulating lobbying and capping political donations at $30,000 to 'clean up politics'.

Develop a 10-year health plan alongside health professionals, with clear commitments on funding, workforce, and infrastructure.

Phase out bottom trawling.

Uphold New Zealand's international climate commitments and protect the Climate Change Commission's independence.

Luxon on negotiations: 'It'll take as long as it takes'

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6408936372112

Luxon says he is ready to negotiate with Opportunity - the party he ruled out repeatedly throughout the campaign.

For most of the year Luxon said he would not work with Opportunity but softened his stance after the preliminary election result.

But on Friday he said one of the strongest messages he heard throughout the campaign is that Kiwis want more cross-party collaboration.

"They want their leaders to find common ground and to get on with delivering for them.

"I've heard the message, and I'll be taking that into these negotiations. Over the past few weeks, I have spoken with Winston [Peters] and David [Seymour] and Qiulae [Wong], and with the final result now known, formal negotiations will begin."

Luxon warned coaliton negotiations would be challenging and would take some time.

"Kiwis won't thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart, or for sending them back to the polls."

There were a range of arrangements on the table under MMP, Luxon said, and he would leave that to the negotiating table.

"I'm entering this in a spirit of good faith, believing that I can work with all those three other leaders as well, and find that common ground and form a strong government."

He said they would work as quickly and urgently as possible.

"My wish is to do so in such a way that I actually have a government that lasts the full three years and is going to be enduring, it'll be strong and stable," he said.

"It'll take as long as it takes."

Luxon said he would not stand down as National's leader, despite a poor party vote result which saw the ousting of some senior MPs.

Seymour looking forward to negotiations

Meanwhile, ACT Party leader David Seymour says he looks forward to working with "all of our colleagues" as results point to the coalition needing Opportunity's support.

"There are people that bring different things to the table. I think that we can have a constructive relationship. Certainly, when I've sat down with Qiulae Wong, I can see that we're going to be able to work together. And now, thanks to the wonders of democracy, the voters have ensured that we must work together."

Seymour said both he and Wong would have different views on certain policies, but both had the same basic commitment to making New Zealand a better place.

However, one of Opportunity's bottom lines includes recommitting to Paris Agreement obligations, while ACT wants to pull New Zealand out unless major changes were made to allow lower emissions targets.

"They're thoughtful and evidence-based people, so you have to think: do you want to put New Zealanders out of work so that New Zealand consumers who will have less money can buy, say, cement from Asia or dairy products from overseas, where they actually emit more into the climate because our rules were too strict?" Seymour asked.

"I think that they are smart enough to see that being tougher is not always better when it comes to climate."

Swarbrick calls on Opportunity to 'hold those bottom lines'

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6408936459112

Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick would not entertain a question on if the Greens should have worked with Labour to ensure a Green candidate did not split the vote (as in Nelson), saying they decided not to play into cynicism.

"No electorate, no voters belong to political parties or to politicians. We have always run in different electorates in order to give New Zealanders a real option," she said.

"I dispute the very notion that if we did not have a Green candidate running in certain places then all of those votes would necessarily flow to one political party."

Swarbrick called on Opportunity to "hold those bottom lines" in negotiations.

"That is the very reason they are in this Parliament."

NZ First, Te Pāti Māori silent on final election result

Neither NZ First leader Winston Peters, nor Te Pāti Māori co-leaders Debbie Ngarewa-Packer and Rawiri Waititi, were expected to talk to media on Friday.

World.title: Māori electorate results confirmed, Aperahama Edwards extends Te Tai Tokerau lead
World.content:
The final election count has confirmed the results across Aotearoa's Māori electorates, with Te Pāti Māori's Aperahama Edwards extending his winning margin in Te Tai Tokerau to 583 votes.

The result means Te Pāti Māori will bring five MPs into Parliament, with four overhang seats.
