It also denies Green MP Hūhana Lyndon a historic first win for the Greens in the Māori seats.

Edwards led by 436 votes ahead of Lyndon, Labour's Willow-Jean Prime and incumbent Mariameno Kapa-Kingi.

In a statement posted online Aperahama Edwards said he was honoured to have been elected to represent Te Tai Tokerau.

He thanked the voters, his campaign team and the volunteers who supported him.

He acknowledged the other candidates, saying they are "connected by whakapapa and a shared commitment to serve our people and our rohe."

"I enter Parliament knowing where I come from and who I am there to serve. Te Tai Tokerau is the kaitiaki of He Whakaputanga and Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

"Our tūpuna left us with a responsibility to stand for the mana of our people, our whenua and our mokopuna. I will carry that responsibility with me."

Green Party candidate Hūhana Lyndon told RNZ she was grateful for the thousands of votes she received, and said the Greens' increased support across the Māori electorates was something the party did not take for granted.

Green Party candidate Hūhana Lyndon on election night. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

She said her campaign, alongside her mahi in Parliament, in communities and on marae, had helped demonstrate there was support for the Greens in the electorate.

"Those over 9,000, nearly 10,000 votes that tautoko me demonstrate that there is tautoko for a green voice in Tai Tokerau," she said.

The party vote in Te Tai Tokerau gave 36.9 percent of votes to the Green Party.

"So it's an absolute privilege to have that level of tautoko, and is something we do not take for granted."

Lyndon will remain in Parliament as a Green list MP, but said her next steps would need to be considered carefully.

She said campaigning on the basis of being an electorate MP meant she had planned to have offices open and kaimahi visible on the ground in Te Tai Tokerau. Being a list MP changed that, she said, and she had previously acknowledged her workload was not sustainable.

"We're going to go on to wānanga next week as the Greens. We will see what happens in terms of where we go on the forming of government. That will inform a lot," she said.

"But whether we're in government or in opposition as the Greens, we will be staunch in the way that we represent te taiao and protecting te taiao and also looking out for the wellbeing of our people and our places."

The official election results have left Parliament evenly split, with National, ACT and New Zealand First holding 65 seats, the same number as Labour, the Greens, Te Pāti Māori and Opportunity combined.

The final count has erased the coalition's majority, leaving the Government reliant on Opportunity to support it on key votes or negotiate an agreement to avoid a return to the polls.

As Aotearoa waits to see what the next government will look like, Lyndon said there was still plenty of work to do.

"All is not lost. We've developed this awesome momentum of positivity and mahi moving forward. Whatever the outcome is in the formation of government, there is much to do," she said.

Final voter turnout was 77.2 percent of enrolled voters, down from 78.2 percent at the 2023 election. Turnout across the Māori electorates increased to 72.9 percent, up from 68 percent in 2023.

A total of 604,188 Māori voters were enrolled on either the Māori or general roll, compared with 567,012 at the previous election.

But Lyndon said voter participation remained a concern, with more than 14,000 eligible voters in Te Tai Tokerau not casting a ballot.

She said a combination of legislative changes and disillusionment may be contributing to people not voting.

"The changes in legislation and the way that you could not enrol to vote and vote on the day is a significant barrier for young people, for iwi Māori, Pacific and other communities," she said.

"On top of that, it is the feeling of like, why? Why should we? Will my vote matter?"

Lyndon said there was also a need to reflect on how whānau were mobilised to enrol, but not necessarily to vote.

What about the other Māori seats?

Te Pāti Māori's Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke secured the largest margin in the Māori electorates, leading Labour's Kingi Kiriona by 13,425 votes in Hauraki-Waikato.

Labour's Cushla Tangaere-Manuel won Ikaroa-Rāwhiti by 3117 votes over Te Pāti Māori's Haley Maxwell, while Te Pāti Māori's Oriini Kaipara led Labour's Kerrin Leoni by 9,350 votes in Tāmaki Makaurau.

Te Pāti Māori co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer won Te Tai Hauāuru by 4,798 votes over Labour's Te Pūoho Kātene.

World.title: Ferris wheel approved for Auckland city waterfront, will open this summer
World.content:
Auckland Council has approved plans for a Ferris wheel to open on the downtown waterfront this summer, close to where cruise ships moor.

There's no opening date yet but the 32-metre-tall attraction will have 24 gondolas holding up to 144 people on the Quay Street promenade.

Nighttime light displays will illuminate the Ferris wheel with audio telling the story of Tāmaki Makaurau.

Auckland mayor Wayne Brown said it is part of our bigger plan to open up more of the waterfront to the public.

Auckland mayor Wayne Brown. (File photo) Jessica Hopkins / RNZ

"It's about making the most of one of our greatest assets; our stunning harbours," he said.

"The Ferris Wheel is part of a trial that will help us understand how people use this space and inform future waterfront planning and activation through the Central Wharves Masterplan and Long-term Plan, which the public will be consulted on."

Once up and running, the ferris wheel will be open from 10am till 10pm, extended till 11pm on public and school holidays and 12.30am on New Years Eve.

Skyline Attractions will operate the wheel on the Queens Wharf Breastworks, the waterfront promenade near the Downtown Ferry Terminal.

The proposal drew concern from local residents, concerned about their views and also what Ferris wheel riders might see from their goldolas.

The Auckland City Centre Residents' Group held a meeting to discuss their concerns about the plans earlier this month.

Maryanne and Alan Mummery have lived in an apartment building on Quay Street for more than 33 years and earlier said the wheel would be metres from their bedroom, and would affect the entire apartment building, as well as others around them.

The view from their apartment. Supplied / Maryanne Mummery

"What a 30-plus years it has been. We've watched a complete reshaping of our waterfront and our much-loved port. The Hilton Hotel was built, The Cloud was built, all the wharf sheds, apart from Shed 10, were pulled down. Covid arrived. And now, in 2026, the most bizarre suggestion of all: a giant Ferris wheel right opposite the living spaces of hundreds of people," Maryanne Mummery said.

"Not only did we not know about this outrageous absurdity, it simply is an untenable suggestion for a small piece of port-gifted recreational land."

She said that the Council had been encouraging people to move into the CBD, but the wheel would end any sense of privacy for them and their neighbours.

"You can't sit in your bed with hundreds of people, sitting, gawping at you."

Auckland Council's Manager Premium Unit, Planning and Resource Consents, Dean Wiliams, granted the resource consent.

"Although a relatively large structure, the Ferris wheel is also a predominantly open, lattice type structure allowing views through it such that will not be physically dominant in form," he said in the report.

"The applicant has positioned the structure so that it sits at the end of Commerce Street rather than directly in front of neighbouring buildings on the opposite side of Quay Street."

Williams said that adverse effects on the landscape will be minimised and the outlook to the north for neighbours will still largely be preserved.

"The placement of the Ferris wheel, coupled with the separation distance and elements of the operation will ensure that any privacy effects are minimised."

His report noted the benefits of having the attraction.

"In terms of positive effects, the proposal utilises vacant land and provides a high-quality temporary visitor attraction. The project will contribute to the city centres vibrancy and amenity, providing social, economic, environmental, and cultural benefits," he said.

"The applicant has commented that the proposal presents an efficient use of land that is largely vacant and will provide high-quality visitor experience which will contribute positively to the amenity and vitality of the city centre locality, and will enhance social, environmental, economic and cultural related outcomes. This assessment is agreed with."

The wheel will have a nearby shop and ice-cream cart and a cultural centre.

Tātaki Auckland Unlimited director of destination, Annie Dundas, said the attraction is part of a wider programme to reconnect Aucklanders with the waterfront.

"There's something special about seeing Auckland from a different perspective, and a Ferris wheel on our waterfront will offer exactly that.

"But this is about more than a new attraction. It's an opportunity to open part of our waterfront, bring people closer to the harbour and create a vibrant, welcoming space for Aucklanders and visitors to enjoy," says Annie Dundas.

Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei chief executive Lisa Davis said they want a city where their people prosper, their culture and stories are celebrated, and everyone feels welcome.

"We're proud to work alongside Tātaki Auckland Unlimited and the wider project team to bring this attraction to life. We want our waterfront full of life, our businesses thriving and our whānau and manuhiri enjoying everything our beautiful city has to offer."

World.title: How much would another election cost us?
World.content:
Audio player for " How do I tell a scam from a real bank call? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/politics_election-2026/2829558%2Fhow-much-would-another-election-cost-us

How do I tell a scam from a real bank call? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 15m

How much would it cost the country if we had to have another election?

The final election result on Friday revealed a hung parliament. National, ACT and New Zealand First are at 65 MPs, exactly the same number as Labour, the Greens, Te Pāti Māori and Opportunity combined.

Both groups are one MP short of a majority in what will be a 130-seat Parliament due to a 10-seat overhang, six from National and four from Te Pāti Māori.

The current coalition will need Opportunity if it is to form a government - and its leader Qiulae Wong is not ruling out sending the country back to the polls if it cannot come to an agreement.

This year's election cost $180 million, including staff costs, communications, property costs and printing and post.

That funding was decided after the Electoral Commission put in a request to the Justice Minister, who then submitted it for the Budget.

Chief electoral officer Karl Le Quesne said it was hard to say how much another election would cost.

"It would depend on the timeframe and service levels provided. Property leases for headquarters and voting places would need to be negotiated again, voting places chosen, voting supplies organised, and staff recruited. Funding for all this activity would need to be put in place."

Otago University law professor Andrew Geddis said it was possible that an emergency appropriation bill would have to be passed, in particular to fund the broadcasting allocation that has to be distributed before any election.

Parliamentary Services referred questions to the Electoral Commission.

Another election would be unusual but not unheard of.

Israel had to hold two new elections after an April 2019 vote repeatedly failed to result in a coalition.

Belgium went more than 500 days without a government in 2010 and 2011.

World.title: Labour leader Chris Hipkins will decide on leadership after government formed
World.content:
Labour leader Chris Hipkins says he'll decide on the future of his leadership once a government has been formed.

The Labour leader was tight-lipped on the matter when he addressed media following the official election result which left his party with no path to power.

That's despite it netting the biggest share of the party vote at 29.9 percent.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6408937555112

Hipkins opened his post-result press conference by emphasising Labour was once again "the most popular political party in New Zealand."

But he acknowledged Labour could not form a government, saying he was "very disappointed".

"As to my own future, that's something that I'll make further decisions on once it's clear a new government has been formed and we've had a chance to regroup as the Labour team," he said.

The Labour Party rules dictate a leadership vote within the three months after an election, Hipkins said.

"But we're not going to be making decisions on that until it's clear what the outcome of this election is, and at this point, that is still not clear."

Hiplines said there was a need for stability while there's a hung Parliament and negotiations are underway on the right.

"There is a need to allow this process to run its course, and that's what we will do."

Deputy leader Carmel Sepuloni said she had full confidence in Hipkins.

"I back Chris Hipkins," she said.

"We're really proud of the leadership that Chris has shown... the unity that we've seen in our caucus as a result of his leadership."

World.title: 'Status quo' would meet Opportunity's climate bottom line
World.content:
Maintaining the "status quo" on New Zealand's climate commitments would largely fulfil one of Opportunity's bottom lines, party leader Qiulae Wong says.

The final election count, released today, erased the incumbent coalition's majority and leaves Christopher Luxon reliant on Opportunity's support to break the deadlock.

Opportunity laid out five bottom lines for coalition negotiations ahead of the election, including one to recommit to New Zealand's Paris Agreement obligations and protect the Climate Change Commission's independence.

Following today's results, Wong was asked to clarify what that meant.

"Our bottom line on climate change is largely about preserving the status quo and we have to do that, because that is under threat at the moment," she said.

"We've got parties that are threatening to remove the Climate Change Commission and to withdraw from Paris altogether."

There was "a lot more" that the party would like to do on climate change beyond that, "but that is our minimum bottom line", she said.

Each of Opportunity's potential coalition partners on the right went into the election with a different stance on that bottom line.

Christopher Luxon said staying in the Paris Agreement was also a non-negotiable for National in coalition negotiations.

National Party leader Christopher Luxon applauds supporters at the National Party 2026 election night event at the Viaduct Events Centre. MICHAEL BRADLEY / AFP

"It's in New Zealand's interest to be in the Paris Agreement, because as soon as we would come out, we're in bad company, there's only four countries that have pulled out," he told Morning Report in August.

Doing so would make the country poorer, because New Zealand products would be "kicked off the shelves" overseas, Luxon said.

New Zealand has pledged to halve its emissions by 2030, as its first nationally determined contribution to the Paris Agreement goal of maintaining global temperatures below 2°C of warming, and 'pursue efforts' to limit warming to 1.5°C.

However, current trajectories show that New Zealand will miss its pledge by a full year of emissions, and Luxon and other incumbent ministers have previously ruled out paying billions of dollars for overseas carbon credits to make up the shortfall.

Opportunity has said that it supports meeting the NDC and the only realistic way to do so now is through purchasing offshore credits.

National also supports retaining the Climate Change Commission, though the government removed some of its consultation and advice requirements in the last term.

New Zealand First strongly opposes remaining in the Paris Agreement.

It wants the country to withdraw from it altogether, arguing meeting the target could cost the country up to $22 billion in offshore credits.

Treasury has placed the cost at up to $5 billion.

The party does not have a specific policy on the Climate Change Commission, although deputy leader Shane Jones, in particular, has been critical of its advice.

ACT, on the other hand, wants to abolish the commission, transferring its responsibility for assessing progress towards emissions targets to the Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport.

It also proposes repealing the Zero Carbon Act, and the 2050 net-zero target for long-lived gases that is enshrined in that law.

ACT's stance on the Paris Agreement is more nuanced, saying New Zealand should withdraw unless it submits a refreshed target.

Ahead of the election, ACT's agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard confirmed to RNZ that his party would support remaining in the agreement if New Zealand switched its international goal to a 'split-gas' target.

ACT's agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

At the moment, New Zealand reports its goal, known as a nationally-determined contribution (NDC), as a single target for all greenhouse gases, equivalising them to carbon dioxide.

The only country not to do this is Uruguay, which reports separate targets for each gas.

Hoggard told RNZ that the simplest way of reporting a split-gas target was to do as Uruguay did, and commit to a percentage reduction in the tonnage of each gas.

That would marry up with New Zealand's domestic targets, which are split into carbon dioxide and other long-lived gases, and methane, he said.

"It makes hell of a lot of sense to line that external up with the internal."

However, the maths underpinning New Zealand's domestic target for methane is itself based on a method known as 'no additional warming', where a steady level of methane emissions is allowed - contributing to a fixed level of warming but not adding more.

That domestic target is a 14 to 24 percent reduction from 2017 levels, after the incumbent government weakened it in 2025 to align with 'no additional warming'.

Climate advocates and some climate scientists have criticised the end result of a 'no additional warming' approach because they argue that deeper cuts to methane are needed to actively cool the planet in the short-term.

World.title: Waioweka Gorge traffic management in place after slip
World.content:
State Highway 2 through the Waioweka Gorge remains open under 24 hour stop/go traffic management following a slip near the Monument recovery site on Sunday afternoon.

A temporary 30 kilometre an hour speed limit is in place, with traffic crews managing vehicles through the affected areas.

NZTA said specialist crews have inspected the slope and identified loose boulders and cracking on the Opotiki side of the site.

Concrete barriers have been installed to provide additional protection between the slope and traffic lane.

The agency said the crews will remove loose material from above the slip to reduce the risk of further debris falling onto the highway.

Further investigations will be carried out into the cracking to determine whether additional work is needed.

The existing traffic management will remain in place while the work continues.

World.title: Lyon's career in limbo as he faces Test axe
World.content:
Nathan Lyon is set to be axed from Australia's squad for the first Test in a move that raises questions over the 39-year-old's future in the team.

Australia will on Saturday name their squad for the December 9 series opener against New Zealand in Perth, but it is understood Lyon will not be included.

Lyon has been Australia's first-choice spinner when fit for more than 13 years, but selectors have shown a willingness to go without a specialist tweaker more often recently.

Selections and strategy in the spotlight After a disastrous series loss to South Africa, Australian cricket faces some tough decisions.

He has three times been left out of Australia's team over the past 18 months, with selectors picking four quicks in Tests against West Indies, England and South Africa.

But the spinner's omission from the squad is even more notable, given previous such calls have been made on seeing the final wicket closer to the toss.

Lyon has made no secret of his desire to continue playing, with legacy-defining tours of India and England in the next nine months.

The sixth-leading wicket-taker of all time with 577 scalps, Lyon worked around the clock to recover from a hamstring injury last summer and return to the Test side.

His push has included giving up alcohol and spending more time in the gym, having previously described how he is trying to squeeze every last bit out of his career, with 145 Tests already to his name.

Nathan Lyon struggled to make a breakthrough in the latter stages of the third Test against South Africa. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Grant Pitcher)

Where that career goes from here is now in question.

Lyon took six wickets at 43.67 in Australia's most recent tour of South Africa, where he was overlooked for Scott Boland in a wet second Test in Gqeberha.

Included in that was Australia's inability to take wickets on the fourth day of the final Test in Cape Town, as South Africa recovered from a 100-run first-innings deficit.

South Africa spinner Simon Harmer then bagged 6-16 on the final day to bowl the Proteas to victory.

NSW draw against Queensland Thanks to a sporting declaration by Queensland and some exceptional bowling, the SCG was treated to one of the best Sheffield Shield finishes in years as New South Wales hung on for a draw.

Lyon has since taken seven Sheffield Shield wickets across two matches on return to Australia, but was out-bowled by Queensland leg spinner Mitchell Swepson in Sydney this week.

Australia coach Andrew McDonald had indicated after the loss in Cape Town that Lyon remained Australia's number one spinner, when asked if that would be reviewed.

"Review it?" McDonald responded at the time.

"I don't think it's something to review now. We'll sit back and we'll go through Shield cricket.

"Nathan will be preparing for the first Test match in Perth."

AAP

World.title: Results of independent Sandpapergate forum to be made public
World.content:
Cricket Australia's forum into the ball-tampering scandal of 2018 will not determine responsibility or make adverse findings against any individual, according to its terms of reference published today.

Justin Langer's spray An Australian player suggested tampering with the ball in the nation's first Test after Sandpapergate before the intervention of then-coach Justin Langer. The scandal was reignited this month after former Australia batter Usman Khawaja said the whole team had known about the ball-tampering plot during the tour of South Africa, not just the three players found culpable by CA's integrity unit.

Cricket Australia (CA) announced on November ‌18 it would open an independent forum for all the players and staff to give their accounts of what happened in 2018 without fear of sanction.

The six-week forum, to be overseen by Australian barrister Fiona ‌McLeod, will be an "information-gathering and listening process", rather than a disciplinary process, its terms of reference said.

It will not make "any adverse findings about, or determine the ‌responsibility of, any individual", nor revisit the sanctions previously imposed. There will ‌be no recommendations for retrospective punishment or legal action and participation will be entirely voluntary.

"Its purpose is to support the welfare of those impacted and to provide Participants with an opportunity to be heard and to have their experience acknowledged and understood without fear of retribution ‌or disadvantage," the terms said.

CA's investigation in 2018 found only three players culpable — former captain Steve Smith and opening batters David Warner and Cameron Bancroft.

Smith and Warner were banned for 12 months, with Bancroft suspended for nine.

Khawaja's ‌former teammates Warner, Bancroft and Chadd ‌Sayers have supported his claims that the wider playing group and staff were aware of the ball-tampering.

However, ‌captain Pat Cummins and bowlers Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood have flatly denied any prior knowledge.

CA backed Cummins to remain captain of the test and one-day ‌international sides last week and rejected any suggestion his integrity had been compromised amid the renewed furore.

The scope of CA's forum will include "ball-management practices" by the men's team during all four tests of the South Africa tour and not just the Newlands test where Australia's ball-tampering was exposed.

It will also include the conduct and scope of CA's investigation in 2018.

CA said a report into the forum would be published ‌in full and ‌it would respond within 30 days.

"This forum is the best opportunity for people to speak and be heard, and for CA to listen and learn," CA chairman David Boon said in a statement.

Reuters

World.title: Opinions split ahead of Supercars move to MotoGP track
World.content:
Every year Supercars teams count down the days to racing on the Adelaide Parklands Circuit, and some say this year's event is tinged with a touch of sadness.

Racing gets underway today with a 100-kilometre race, followed by 250-kilometre races on both Saturday and Sunday to crown this year's title winner.

Currently Matt Payne leads, with Brodie Kostecki, Broc Feeney and Chaz Mostert still in contention.

It is the last time the drivers will race around the street circuit, a shortened version of the track unveiled in 1985 to host the Formula 1 Australian Grand Prix, before the race was moved to Victoria in 1995.

This year's Adelaide Grand Final will be the last race on the current circuit before a major overhaul. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The track made a comeback in 1999 for the newly created Adelaide 500 event up until a brief COVID hiatus, and a 2022 revival brought on by the Malinauskas election win.

Spectators and drivers alike have said they love the current circuit, with its tight corners and compact walls which make for exciting racing.

But in 2027, the Supercars race, now known as the Adelaide Grand Final, will move to the soon-to-be-built and controversial MotoGP track in the eastern parklands — with both the events scheduled for November next year.

The new track has some teams worried, including Ryan Walkinshaw, director of Walkinshaw TWG Racing.

"Is it going to dilute the value that we currently have in this current event? That's entirely a possibility," he said.

"It is perfect for Supercars, so the fact that's going to change I do have some concerns about."

Drivers have been consulted about the design of the supercars track. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Tom Moore, team manager for Dick Johnson Racing said he also shared some of those concerns.

"This circuit in particular will lose some of its raw edge that makes Adelaide different to everyone, but there will be some advantages," he said.

Triple Eight Race Engineering Team Manager Mark Dutton had a more positive view.

"As much as we all love this track, change is awesome, we'll all come here next year and we'll all adapt," he said.

Drivers were consulted about the design of the Supercars track and Ryan Wood said he was ready to embrace it.

He said he could see the benefits of a track that would have greater flow with the race walls being further back.

"Probably a bit more flowing than what the track's like at the moment, but I tell you what, it's always exciting to have a new track on the calendar, hopefully the locals can get around it," he said.

The street circuit will look different next year to also accommodate for the MotoGP circuit. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

While racing over the next three days, the drivers will also spend some time reminiscing.

Current series leader Matt Payne said turn eight on the current track was not your average stretch of bitumen.

"I've lost the championship at turn eight and I've won one the next year in Supercar twos," he said.

Brodie Kostecki was more blunt when asked if he would miss the notorious spot.

"Not really," he said, with a chuckle.

World.title: The remarkable journey behind one of oldest Wallabies debutants
World.content:
James Ramm, the late-blooming, one-time gymnast who has finally made the international rugby grade at the age of 28, wants his long, battling journey to the top to inspire a new generation of wannabe Wallabies.

When winger Ramm takes the field at Twickenham against Ireland for his Australia debut on Friday night (Saturday AEDT), it will be the culmination of a road beset by injuries and false starts, one on which he switched sports and had to move to the other side of the world to reboot his career.

But now, when he thinks how the one-time gangly kid who couldn't even break into his first-team at Sydney's St Joseph's College is going to be one of the modern-day Wallabies' oldest wing debutants after years of perseverance, he declares: "I'm really proud of my journey."

James Ramm shot to stardom with Northampton Saints in England. (Getty Images: David Rogers)

"And all I hope from it is that other people who are in similar situations, playing seconds or thirds at school who want to pursue rugby, realise that school's not the be-all and end-all," he said.

"As soon as you leave school, you understand that, but when you're in it, it's quite hard to see. A couple of years ago, I went back to Joey's actually to talk to the second XV players at the school and explain my story and show that not everyone's journey is the same.

"If you really want it, you can get it from whatever position you're in at school."

So it was that Ramm's rugby adventure really only began after he'd given up on his promising gymnastics career, which had once dealt him dreams of being an Olympian.

Yet he couldn't crack the rugby hierarchy at "Joey's", unlike his schoolmate Tom Wright, with whom he'll now be working in the back three at Twickenham.

"Wrighty was sort of a superstar at school, and I'd love it if he ever talked to me," said Ramm, as he sat next to a chuckling Wright at the Wallabies' team hotel in London on Thursday.

Ramm did finally break through for Randwick and represented the Junior Wallabies.

He went on to a brief spell in Dave Rennie's Australia squad while with the Waratahs, but injury woes and lack of progress at home led him to head for England, his mother's home country.

There, he really blossomed with Northampton, scoring 32 tries and helping them win two English titles and reach the final of last year's Europe's Champions Cup Final, before also going on to impress while propelling Northland to the NPC final in New Zealand.

Now firmly back in the Australian fold having signed a two-year deal with Western Force, he's suddenly burst back into the picture under coach Les Kiss, admitting he was "overwhelmed" when he got the call to play this week after not even being in the 23 the previous weeks on the Nations Championship northern tour.

Beale back in Wallabies team The return of Kurtley Beale to the Wallabies team for cap number 96 after a five-year absence is a reward for his continuing excellence, coach Les Kiss insists.

He's going to make his debut at the home ground of the country that even sniffed around trying to sign him up as an England player.

Having not even settled back at his new home in Perth before being jetting back out to the UK with his Wallabies teammates, Ramm said: "I didn't think I'd sort of be touching down in Sydney and then a couple of days later be back over here in this beautiful weather as quickly as I have."

That "beautiful weather" will be a bone-chilling night at HQ, but it will all be worth it for Ramm, who calls Twickenham "a sick stadium", having got used to the ambience in big finals with Northampton. He reckons he's ready for anything.

"Age is definitely just a number. My rugby career started a bit later than probably what's usual, so I'm hoping that I can bank those years at the back end of my career," Ramm said.

"And for me, this validates every time you wanted to take an easy option, or thought 'I'm gonna have a day off or skip this' but didn't. It validates the fact that all that hard work pays off.

"It's tough sometimes, and you're in the dumps, but it really shows that if you persist with it and you keep on that line, it's all worth it."

AAP

World.title: Everything you need to know as Roos hunt historic AFLW three-peat
World.content:
The AFLW is on the cusp of history as an all-conquering North Melbourne side looks to claim its third consecutive premiership in this year's grand final.

Standing in the Kangaroos' way will be Melbourne, a team that has been one of the most consistent over the last couple of years.

Here is everything you need to know ahead of tonight's decider between the Roos and Dees.

What time is the AFLW grand final?

This year's AFLW grand final takes place on Friday, November 27. Here is the first bounce time according to which state or territory you are watching from:

7:45pm AEDT: Victoria, New South Wales, Tasmania

Victoria, New South Wales, Tasmania 7:15pm ACDT: South Australia

South Australia 6:45pm AEST: Queensland

Queensland 6:15pm ACST: Northern Territory

Northern Territory 4:45pm AWST: Western Australia

Where is the AFLW grand final being played?

This year's grand final venue — Princes Park — hosted the first ever AFLW contest in 2017. (Getty Images: AFL Media/Adam Trafford)

This year's AFLW grand final will once again be hosted by Princes Park in Melbourne.

Princes Park hosted the last three AFLW grand finals and also the 2018 decider between the Western Bulldogs and Brisbane.

Where can I watch the AFLW grand final?

Fans can watch the game on free-to-air TV on Channel 7 as well as its streaming services.

Kayo Sports will also broadcast the grand final.

ABC Sport will run a live blog where you can follow all the action and analysis, while you can also listen to the match live on ABC Sport via the website, local radio or the Listen app.

What are the AFLW grand final team line-ups?

North Melbourne

No change FB: Libby Birch, Jasmine Ferguson HB: Eliza Shannon, Erika O'Shea, Emma Kearney C: Taylah Gatt, Eilish Sheerin, Tess Craven HF: Alice O'Loughlin, Bella Eddey, Blaithin Bogue FF: Tahlia Randall, Vikki Wall FOLL: Kim Rennie, Ash Riddell, Jasmine Garner INT: Nicole Bresnahan, Amy Gavin Mangan, Ruby Tripodi, Jenna Bruton, Kate Shierlaw

Melbourne

IN: Lauren Pearce OUT: Laela Ebert (omitted) FB: Tahlia Gillard, Sarah Lampard HB: Sinead Goldrick, Molly O'Hehir, Paxy Paxman C: Maeve Chaplin, Shelley Heath-Barker, Eliza McNamara HF: Ryleigh Wotherspoon, Alyssa Bannan, Maggie Mahony FF: Kate Hore, Tayla Harris FOLL: Georgia Campbell, Olivia Purcell, Tyla Hanks INT: Jordyn S. Allen, Lauren Pearce, Megan Fitzsimon, Aoife Horisk, Mia Austin

Who are the key players for each team?

Ash Riddell has led all AFLW players with 33.8 disposals per game this season. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: James Wiltshire)

North Melbourne will once again rely on its star duo of captain Jasmine Garner and midfield maestro Ash Riddell.

Riddell led the league in disposals per game with 33.8, while Garner added 30.1 touches herself, with both players making 14 appearances this season.

Melbourne's back line will also have to be wary of Kangaroos forward Tahlia Randall, who has slammed home a team-high 27 goals this season, while Garner has also hit the scoreboard with 14 goals.

The Demons also have their own dynamic duo in the midfield, with Olivia Purcell's 30.8 touches per game good for fourth in the league, while Tyla Hanks has added 25.5 touches of her own.

Mia Austin is Melbourne's leading goalkicker this season with 17 goals in just eight appearances, while skipper Kate Hore has kicked 10 goals and averaged 19.1 touches per game.

Who are the coaches for the AFLW grand finalists

Darren Crocker (left) has led North Melbourne to its two premiership wins over the last two seasons. (Kelly Defina/AFL Photos/via Getty Images)

North Melbourne is still coached by Darren Crocker, who has led the team to the last two AFLW premierships.

Crocker, who played 165 games for North Melbourne's men's team, has coached the women's side since 2021.

Before his AFLW coaching career, Crocker led the Kangaroos men's side as caretaker coach in 15 matches during three separate seasons.

Tom Wilson has led Melbourne to the AFLW grand final in his first season in charge. (Getty Images: Kelly Defina)

Melbourne is coached by Tom Wilson, who is in his first season in charge of the Demons after taking over from the club's inaugural AFLW coach Mick Stinear.

Wilson joined the Demons after spending two seasons with Collingwood as the club's midfield coach and head of development.

He played 176 games for the Northern Blues/Bullants and Collingwood's reserves team between 2011 and 2025.

What is the recent history between North and Melbourne?

The Kangaroos have had the wood over the Demons in the last five meetings, winning four.

Here is a look at how exactly these two teams have fared against each other of late:

Round 7, 2026: North Melbourne 10.5 (65) def. Melbourne 5.4 (34) @ Princes Park Preliminary Final, 2025: North Melbourne 6.10 (46) def. Melbourne 5.6 (36) @ Princes Park Round 3, 2024: North Melbourne 11.5 (71) def. Melbourne 3.3 (21) @ Casey Fields Qualifying Final, 2023: North Melbourne 7.8 (50) def. Melbourne 1.3 (9) @ Princes Park Round 8, 2023: Melbourne 5.7 (37) def. North Melbourne 2.2 (14) @ Princes Park

How many AFLW premierships have these teams won?

North Melbourne has won the AFLW premiership over the last two seasons. (Getty Images)

North Melbourne has won two premierships over the last two years and hopes to be the first team in AFLW history to claim three straight wins.

This grand final appearance is North Melbourne's fourth, with the previous three coming over the last three seasons.

Melbourne has won one AFLW premiership during S7 (2022).

The Demons were runners-up during S6 (2021) and are making their third grand final appearance.

Who is doing the pre-match entertainment?

The Jungle Giants will provide the half-time entertainment this year. (ABC)

The Jungle Giants, an indie rock band from Brisbane, will headline this year's AFLW grand final entertainment.

The group's four members are Sam Hales, Cesira Aitken, Andrew Dooris and Keelan Bijker.

Their opening act will be Super Disco Club, who will also play music during breaks in play.

Kate Miller-Heidke will sing the national anthem.

World.title: Aussie rugby sevens star driven to 'tick off' goal of Olympic gold
World.content:
Tia Hinds may only be 24, but she's already experienced much in her young rugby career.

Representing Australia, claiming world titles, travelling to almost every continent and even playing alongside her mum, Janine, in a Randwick club match.

"She played on the wing for one game," Hinds told ABC Sport with the hint of a giggle.

"We were short of numbers."

There's one experience, though, Hinds hopes she can reflect upon when the time comes to hang up the boots.

The goal of winning an Olympic gold medal burns brightly for the unassuming Sydneysider, as it does for her Australian women's rugby sevens teammates.

Following the historic 2016 Rio Olympics triumph, Australia didn't reach the podium at the Tokyo and Paris Games, finishing fifth and fourth respectively.

Tia Hinds made her Olympic debut in Tokyo. (Getty Images: Dan Mullan)

The Paris result was a particularly bitter pill to swallow, given Australia was reigning world series champions.

"We're such a high-performing team on the world series circuit, it's been a bit hard to deal with that," said Hinds, who was a member of Australia's Tokyo and Paris squads.

"We've fallen short two times now."

The Australians, who won last season's World Championship, are chasing automatic qualification for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

To book their berth, they must finish inside the top four in the 2027 World Championship, which will be decided across three tournaments (Hong Kong, Valladolid and Bordeaux) in April and May.

The six-leg world series takes place before those events, beginning in Dubai on Saturday.

Tia Hinds is among Australia's major attacking threats. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Under the guidance of new coach Reg Tayler, Australia is expected to meet New Zealand in the final of the season-opening tournament on Monday morning, AEDT.

But ahead of any potential match-up with its trans-Tasman rival, Australia must advance from its round-robin pool, which includes the well-credentialed USA and France.

"It's definitely one match at a time, as the USA and France are two powerhouse teams," Hinds said.

"We would love to play in the final and of course it's usually against the Kiwis, so it would be naive not to have a look at how they're doing in their pool matches.

"But we definitely will focus on the pool stage first."

Hinds's pivotal role

A calf injury robbed Hinds of the chance to play in last season's World Championship-deciding tournament in Bordeaux.

But Australia wouldn't have been in a position to lift the silverware in France if it hadn't been for the talented playmaker.

At the preceding World Championship leg in Valladolid, she triggered Australia's comeback in its thrilling 28-26 semifinal win over New Zealand.

Tia Hinds played a key role in Australia's World Championship victory last season. (Getty Images: Caean Couto)

With Australia trailing 14-0 in the first half, Hinds's outstanding ability to read the game came to the fore when she took advantage of lazy defence to score a runaway try.

Hinds's goal kicking also proved crucial, perhaps the by-product of playing Australian rules as a junior with the Maroubra Saints, where Sydney Swans AFL star Errol Gulden was a teammate.

A loss to New Zealand in Valladolid would have effectively dashed Australia's hopes of clinching the World Championship.

Expressing modesty when speaking about her influence on the result, Hinds instead heaped praise on captain Bella Nasser for steering Australia home.

"We've got a really captain in Bella, who is really composed and got her head screwed on," said Hinds, who sustained her season-ending injury in the Valladolid semifinal victory.

Tia Hinds represented the Wallaroos this year. (Getty Images: Phil Walter)

Rugby sevens isn't the only international stage graced by Hinds, as she also represents Australia's national 15-a-side team, the Wallaroos.

Making the Wallaroos squad for the 2029 Women's Rugby World Cup is among her ambitions, especially as the tournament will be held on home soil.

But before the dream of playing in her second World Cup can be realised, climbing the podium at the LA Olympics remains a major priority for Hinds.

"There's some unfinished business, to tick off that goal of hopefully medalling at an Olympic Games," Hinds said.

World.title: Returning Matildas star Cooney-Cross wants to make late mum 'proud'
World.content:
When Kyra Cooney-Cross returned to the pitch for Arsenal in the Women's Super League in September, she shared a moving message from her mum.

Its essence is one that so many parents would have relayed to their kids in one manner or another in their sporting careers, whether they were as decorated as a Matildas' linchpin, or finding their feet for the first time in the under 5s.

"Kyra, try to remember what it felt like when you were little … when you just loved having the ball at your feet, playing with your mates, testing yourself against the boys or adults for the fun of it," the message read.

"Play because you love the ball at your feet, the rhythm of the game. Train because it feels good to move and challenge your body and feel strong.

"This is how you start doing it for you again — Mum."

Amongst the pain of losing her mother Jess to terminal bile duct cancer in July, Cooney-Cross has taken the message to heart, and three months after returning to club football, she's back for the Matildas.

Kyra Cooney-Cross returned for her club side Arsenal in August. (Alex Burstow/Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

The 24-year-old is in the squad for friendlies against Colombia in Canberra and Geelong, in a key test just seven months out from the Women's World Cup in Brazil.

"It's bittersweet. It's my first time back with the national team since everything that's happened with my mum and our family," she told ABC News Breakfast.

"But playing for your country, this is the highest level I can play at, and it's the highest level I can make my mum proud.

"So I'm really looking forward to it and being back at home in Geelong in front of my family and friends and just being back with the team."

Cooney-Cross last played for the Matildas at the Women's Asian Cup in March. (Getty Images: Corbis/Steve Christo)

Cooney-Cross's last international appearance was in March's Women's Asian Cup, and after her breakthrough tournament at the now fabled 2023 World Cup, she's eager to recreate those highs.

"It's definitely flown by. I don't think a lot of us players had even the time to process the World Cup and what we had done in this country and for women's football in Australia," she said.

"We're just going to work really hard. Stick together and focus on these next two games.

"The World Cup is obviously really important and we want to get really far."

McKenna making moves

Cooney-Cross will play a pivotal part in Brazil next year but others on the fringe, like midfielder Leticia McKenna, hope for their own breakout moment.

Leticia McKenna made her Matildas debut earlier this year. (Getty Images: Alex Grimm)

McKenna, 24, made her international debut in April, and starred for Melbourne City before securing a move to Nottingham Forest in the second tier of English women's football.

She was also recently named PFA Young Footballer of the Year.

"It's been very surreal. It's been a really big year, something I'm extremely proud of," she said.

McKenna's UK move made waves, setting an A-League Women's record with her transfer fee.

"It was a very, very hard decision to leave. It came up at quite short notice as well and I was very happy at the position I was in with Melbourne City and I was looking forward to the upcoming season in that regard," she said.

"But it was something I felt I was ready for. It was always in the back of my mind to make that step and move overseas."

Having made the most of her opportunities with the national side so far, and with only a handful of games left in the lead up, McKenna is eyeing off a berth in that final World Cup squad.

"You always gotta have a goal and aspirations and it's always been a dream," she said.

"Super grateful to be here and it's just making me even hungrier to keep dreaming."

World.title: NRL scraps All Stars game for 2027 preseason
World.content:
The NRL is looking at whether the All Stars clash could form part of an expanded grand-final week in 2027, after a cluttered preseason squeezed the annual fixture off the calendar.

The sheer number of players returning to training late from the World Cup, as well as early-season overseas travel, has left no room for the match next February.

The fixture has been part of every NRL preseason since 2010, except in 2014 and 2018, when it was skipped due to World Cups.

Earlier this year, NRL executive chair Peter V'landys floated permanently shifting the game to grand-final week, before the idea was talked down by Maori and Indigenous players.

The All Stars game has been a fixture on the NRL calender since 2010. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

Chief among their concerns was the unavailability of players from teams in grand-final sides, and that players would be carrying injuries that could stop them playing.

But the nature of next year's schedule means an end-of-season fixture may be the only way the match could be fit in.

"Ideally, and it's a matter of getting everybody on the same page, we should be holding the All Stars at the end of the year," V'landys said.

"We want to give the All Stars a much greater profile. It doesn't get that profile at the beginning of the year.

"It should be right at the end in the grand-final week.

"What was proven from this World Cup: if you've got clean air, look at the ratings you get."

V'landys still has his sights set on the All Stars match being one of several in grand-final week, as part of an expanded carnival.

Part of that could still include the NRLW grand final being played as a standalone event, with V'landys leaving the door open to that in 2027.

The NRLW grand final could become a standalone event in 2027. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"You could have it at Allianz Stadium on a Friday night," V'landys said.

"Because I'm proud of how good the women are going, we want to take them to the next level at some point.

"We've got the best women's sport in Australia. Cricket has always been pretty high up there, but I think we've caught them.

"Our ratings show it. They got over a million viewers [for the World Cup final]. What did the Bleeding Cup [Bledisloe Cup] get? It got 600,000. The women beat them."

NRL to tweak rules again for 2027 The NRL will come down harder on hip-drop tackles in 2027 but has ruled out the possibility of rolling back the controversial set restart rule.

An underage State of Origin match has also been proposed as an option to be played in grand-final week.

A third-place playoff between the two losing preliminary finalists was also floated in August, before it was largely laughed down by critics and players.

"I know that it got, everybody wanted to pot it. But it was the highest-rating FIFA [World Cup] match," V'landys said.

"If you're a Tigers' fan and you're up against the Eels, you'll watch it. It's third against fourth.

"It's like anything else. You've got to market it properly and have prize money or sponsors involved.

"If we listen to all the traditionalists all the time, we'd be playing for a couple of hundred dollars a game because you wouldn't get the revenue."

AAP

Tech.title: Netflix’s coziest show has made a very quiet return
Tech.content:
The bigger Netflix gets, the easier it is to miss stuff. This is true of all digital platforms, of course, but it’s especially true of Netflix of late, as the streaming service’s lineup now also includes a growing library of reality shows, live-programming, and even games. It makes it easy for some of the best shows to zoom right past you, unnoticed — which almost happened to me with Midnight Diner.

If you haven’t seen it, Midnight Diner is probably the most comforting thing available on Netflix. The show follows the patrons of a cozy little restaurant tucked away in the backstreets of Shinjuku, which is only open during the unusual hours of midnight to 7:00AM. This, in turn, attracts a unique blend of customers, who help each other out under the watchful eye of the shop’s owner (Kaoru Kobayashi), known only as “master.” The show aired for three seasons on Japanese TV, before being picked up by Netflix for a handful more under the subtitle Tokyo Stories.

What’s especially notable about the show’s return is the huge gap: season 2 of the Netflix iteration streamed in 2019, and it took seven years for it to come back. The break was so long that season 3’s first episode, which premiered in October, is about the restaurant’s struggles during the pandemic. There are a bunch of cute scenes of the diner’s regulars sneaking outside to check if the restaurant is open yet, and wondering if it will ever be able to. If nothing else, the break was a chance for the reliable master to finally take a vacation.

But once Midnight Diner’s new season gets going, it’s right back to everything that made it beloved. Each episode uses a different dish as a way of exploring a particular story. An overworked manga artist imagines the life he missed out on over plates of spicy konjac, while a pair of old friends reconnect while munching on pork cutlet sandwiches. What’s remarkable about the show is the way it balances being a charming, comforting watch with exploring truly difficult and heartbreaking topics. It’s the combination of sweetness and sadness that makes it work so well. It’s as likely to make you laugh as it is to make you cry.

And unlike most Netflix series, the whole season isn’t streaming all at once. Instead, new episodes come out every Tuesday; so far six of a planned 10 episodes are available. It’s a welcome way to spend an evening, as the show’s slow pace and warm sense of humanity can feel like all-too rare traits in the current streaming landscape.

But the main reason I’m even writing about Midnight Diner’s return is that it has been so easy to miss. There’s been next to no promotion for it — all I could find was a trailer on Netflix’s Japanese YouTube channel — and I only happened upon it accidentally after the initial premiere while browsing aimlessly through Netflix’s new releases. This, despite being someone who has watched and rewatched the previous seasons multiple times. You’d think I’d get a notification or something. Netflix has always been full of hidden gems, but now that it’s busier than ever, those gems are all the more hidden.

This particular watch is best suited for folks who want something a bit slimmer and smaller, enjoy a pop of color, and want a little extra fitness tracking prowess — but don’t need the whole kit and caboodle that sends the price up by hundreds.

Tech.title: Android app developers will soon have to share their address publicly
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Independent Android app developers are worried about their privacy after Google announced that from next year many of them will be required to share a phone number and address publicly. The policy change is intended to meet European Union regulations under the Digital Services Act, but Google says contact details will be made public worldwide.

Developers have until February 1st 2027 to declare whether or not they’re a “trader” under UK and European law. Broadly speaking, Google says the definition applies if you earn revenue from your apps, especially if that revenue is regular or at high volume. Developers are exempt if their apps are only a hobby or non-commercial, or if they simply don’t publish them in the UK or Europe.

If they self-declare as a trader, developers’ contact details will be shared publicly starting March 1st, including a phone number and address. Google doesn’t accept PO boxes for developer payment profile addresses, meaning many independent developers without an office will either have to share their home address online or pay for a registered agent or other service that provides a business address. One independent developer told The Elec they were considering renting a private office solely to comply with the new rules. We’ve asked Google to confirm why developers aren’t permitted to publish a PO box address, and why details are being shared globally, and will update this article when we hear back.

Apple is subject to the same regulations, but is handling them differently to Google. It will only display developer addresses within the relevant European countries, rather than publishing them worldwide. It’s also allowing developers to supply PO box addresses, so long as they provide Apple with a receipt or bill that links the PO box to their regular address.

Update, November 26th: Added mention of developers’ option to use a registered agent service for a business address.

Tech.title: Federal judge blocks the FCC from reviewing ABC’s licenses early
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

US District Judge Loren AliKhan has blocked the Federal Communications Commission from conducting an early review of ABC’s broadcast licenses in a preliminary injunction, and rejected its efforts to dismiss ABC’s First Amendment lawsuit. ABC has accused the FCC of violating its free speech rights and claims the agency “waged a retaliatory campaign” against the network over content it broadcast. In her ruling the judge noted that the network was “likely to succeed on their retaliation claim.”

Although Disney, ABC’s parent company, wasn’t set to renew its broadcast licenses until 2028, last April the FCC ordered the network to file for an early license renewal claiming it was part of an investigation into Disney’s policies on diversity, equity, and inclusivity. The FCC’s move came a day after President Donald Trump demanded ABC fire late-night talk show host Jimmy Kimmel following a skit about Melania Trump.

In response to the FCC’s order, Disney and ABC sued the agency in August and accused the FCC of “punishing ABC for its speech” by threatening its broadcast licenses. The preliminary injunction issued by the judge on Wednesday prohibits the FCC from taking any further action in the early review of ABC’s broadcast licenses and noted that the network had shown that the court’s intervention in the agency’s actions was in the public interest.

”No one doubts that the Commission may enforce the law in the manner it sees fit,” the judge wrote. “But in doing so, Defendants may not retaliate against or punish Plaintiffs and other broadcast license holders for disfavored speech.”

Tech.title: GTA VI developers vote against unionization
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Workers at Grand Theft Auto VI developer Rockstar Games won’t unionize, after the vote for a formal recognition agreement failed, with only 25 percent of votes in favor of unionization. The Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB) said that Rockstar workers in the union will continue organizing even without formal recognition.

Voting ran from November 12th through 26th, covering the launch of GTA VI. If successful, the vote would have established a formal framework for collective negotiation with the studio over pay, overtime, bonuses, leave, and pensions, along with a right to consultation over future changes including AI implementation and layoffs. Without it, Rockstar won’t have an obligation to meet union representatives, though workers and union members can still lobby for change informally.

“For anyone at Rockstar who believes in a fairer workplace, a fairer sector and a fairer society - this isn’t a sign to retreat, it’s a sign to double down on what we stand for,” IWGB said in a statement sent to The Verge. “Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favour of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognise we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues. We’re ready to put in the effort to make that happen.”

When Rockstar fired 31 IWGB members last year, the union accused it of “the most blatant and ruthless act of union busting in the history of the games industry.” That case has gone to a UK employment tribunal, with a judgment still pending.

“We are extraordinarily proud of our team, the culture we’ve built together and the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI,” Rockstar head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe told Bloomberg News. “This result reflects our team’s strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong. As we look ahead, we’re excited to build on all we’ve accomplished together.”

Tech.title: Nvidia hits pause on chip shipments to Southeast Asia
Tech.content:
In Brief
